item.title: [SCMP] Under higher scrutiny, will Singapore remain Chinese firms’ first overseas port of call?
item.description:
With domestic profits narrowing and production capacity expanding, China’s firms are continuing to widen their overseas footprints in search of new, more lucrative markets. In this series, we examine China Inc.’s next phase of “going global” and the complex, challenging international environment its companies have chosen to enter.

On a weekday afternoon, the basement food hall of a central shopping centre was packed. Office workers queued for Chongqing noodles, while a different noodle joint from a major Chinese hotpot chain drew its own crowd.

At opposite ends sat two restaurants specialising in fish: one founded in Shenzhen and the other serving the dish Sichuan-style. Across the aisle, a milk tea shop from Xiamen served iced drinks alongside a busy Luckin Coffee counter.
item.content:encoded:
With domestic profits narrowing and production capacity expanding, China’s firms are continuing to widen their overseas footprints in search of new, more lucrative markets. In this series, we examine China Inc.’s next phase of “going global” and the complex, challenging international environment its companies have chosen to enter.

On a weekday afternoon, the basement food hall of a central shopping centre was packed. Office workers queued for Chongqing noodles, while a different noodle joint from a major Chinese hotpot chain drew its own crowd.

At opposite ends sat two restaurants specialising in fish: one founded in Shenzhen and the other serving the dish Sichuan-style. Across the aisle, a milk tea shop from Xiamen served iced drinks alongside a busy Luckin Coffee counter.

In almost every way, the scene resembled a commercial district in a major Chinese city, except for its location: the heart of Singapore.

A wave of Chinese firms in a wide range of sectors, from food and drink to technology, has flooded the Southeast Asian nation over the past few years, amid sluggish domestic demand at home.

Singapore has emerged as a top destination for Chinese companies seeking new growth markets abroad, offering a springboard for wider global expansion. But competition is also heating up in the city state, alongside scrutiny over the companies’ mainland ties – with a renewed bout of attention almost certain to arrive in the wake of the Nvidia scandal.

“Singapore is a great place to test your business in overseas markets because it offers a mix of Western tastes and consumer habits,” said Chris Pereira, the Singapore-based founder of iMpact, a consultancy that helps Chinese companies expand abroad.

Regulatory predictability allows firms to undertake long-term capital planning, Pereira noted, providing brands with a lower-risk environment to adapt their businesses.

It’s a good place to verify that the market accepts your product

Chris Pereira, iMpact

With some of the world’s top-ranked universities alongside prominent executive MBA programmes, Singapore also boasts a robust talent pool. Many founders from mainland China have also studied in the city state themselves, Pereira said.

“It’s a good place to verify that the market accepts your product, and it’s relatively safe to do that in a smaller market closer to home,” Pereira said.

Singapore, home to just 6 million people, has long been a major recipient of Chinese outbound direct investment.

China’s outbound financial direct investment into the country stood at US$16.9 billion last year, mainly in retail trade, manufacturing and business services, according to official data published in September – exceeding its flows to the rest of Southeast Asia, or to the European Union and the United States combined.

With an English-speaking multiracial population anchored by an ethnic Chinese majority, alongside a high concentration of multinational corporations, Singapore offers Chinese entrepreneurs familiarity and international exposure.

That mix has established the city state as a primary testing site for Chinese consumer brands expanding overseas.

Xiao Noodles, a Chongqing noodle chain founded in Guangzhou in 2014, made its international debut in central Singapore in late December. The company has opened three more outlets since and plans to expand across Southeast Asia and globally.

Luckin Coffee, which began its overseas expansion in Singapore in 2023, has since ventured into Malaysia and the United States. It opened its 100th Singapore outlet in September.

Several Hunan and Sichuan dining chains have followed, filling shopping malls and neighbourhoods across the city. Many retain their Chinese language-heavy menu and draw a steady crowd despite broader belt-tightening among local consumers.

Ava Cheong, a 27-year-old marketing manager, orders from Yunnan-founded tea chain Chagee at least once a week and holds top-tier status in its loyalty programme.

“I like the flavours, which are quite distinct from what other brands in Singapore offer,” Cheong said, adding that she also sought out the chain’s outlets when travelling abroad.

Chagee operates 46 stores in Singapore, having used the city state as an operational test bed before entering other markets like South Korea and the United States.

Eugene Lee, chief marketing officer of Chagee (Asia-Pacific), noted that Singapore stood out for its status as a financial hub and its “highly-developed and internationally-minded consumer market”.

“Singapore has been an important learning market for us because it gives us the opportunity to understand how Chagee translates outside China,” Lee said.

Chagee has established its regional research and development lab in the city state, he said. Lee added the company had adjusted operations based on what it had learned there, including having bigger physical store spaces that allow for dining-in and introducing alternative milk options.

The international focus is generating clear financial returns. Chagee’s overseas gross merchandise value more than doubled in the second quarter of the year, even as sales in Greater China edged down, according to the company’s latest earnings report.

Expansion abroad offers much-needed relief to Chinese brands operating in a domestic market where fierce competition has eroded margins across several sectors.

“There is a saying among Chinese entrepreneurs: the domestic market is for scale, and the international market is for profit,” said Wang Yanbo, an associate professor at the University of Hong Kong Business School.

That trend extends well beyond dining, as Chinese firms in fashion, automotive, new energy, shipping and technology seek their own slice of the pie.

Fast-fashion retailer Shein and HoYoverse, the global publishing arm of hit video game Genshin Impact, have both shifted their global headquarters to Singapore in recent years.

Particularly for digital and technology companies, having Singapore’s oversight on corporate governance and data architecture helps assure international clients and investors who are wary of Chinese legal jurisdiction, Wang said.

“Singapore’s greatest strength lies in its institutional framework; it is one of the very few societies in Asia characterised by genuine rule of law,” he added. “When Singapore makes a commitment, that commitment carries credibility.”

These factors also made Singapore a more compelling launch pad than Hong Kong for some Chinese enterprises with global ambitions, he added, as many in the international community perceived Hong Kong to be too close to the mainland.

This dynamic has contributed to the rise of so-called Singapore-washing, in which mainland firms move their corporate bases to Singapore to distance themselves from geopolitical risks. While the practice itself is not new, Western scrutiny has intensified in recent years.

“This heightened particularly during the Covid period, when relations between Beijing and Washington were at their lowest point,” Wang said, noting that international sentiment towards China and Chinese businesses was also deteriorating then.

ByteDance, the Beijing-based owner of TikTok, accelerated an expansion drive in Singapore in 2020, amid rising global popularity of the short-video app and threats of a ban during the first term of US President Donald Trump. Singapore became one of TikTok’s global headquarters alongside Los Angeles, and Singaporean citizen Chew Shou Zi was named chief executive officer in 2021.

But the platform continued to face a years-long tussle with American politicians over data privacy concerns and potential mainland influences, before finally closing a deal to divest its US operations earlier this year.

More recently, Nvidia chief Jensen Huang’s admission of an extramarital affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang – who has been accused of spying for Beijing – has brought greater attention to Megaspeed, the Singapore-based company she led. A spokesman for Beijing’s foreign ministry rejected the espionage claims as “groundless fabrication designed to smear China” in a press conference on Monday.

The US has been investigating Megaspeed for allegedly playing a role in diverting advanced Nvidia AI chips into China. Singapore authorities also opened an investigation into the company late last year for suspected breaches of domestic law, without specifying the alleged offences.

Meanwhile, Beijing is also tightening oversight of home-grown firms attempting to relocate critical operations abroad. In April, Chinese authorities blocked and forced the unwinding of Meta’s US$2 billion acquisition of Manus, an agentic artificial intelligence start-up that was founded in China and had shifted its headquarters to Singapore the previous year.

Analysts noted that while these high-profile interventions were unlikely to tarnish Singapore’s broader commercial appeal, the profile of Chinese businesses seeking to establish a presence in the city might shift.

Amid an intensifying US-China technology race, sectors such as AI and advanced semiconductors have become politically sensitive.

“It is not going to be easy, especially for Chinese ventures in strategic sectors, to move overseas and set up a separate entity now without paying attention to compliance back home,” Wang said, adding that the era of mainland tech firms in these sectors using bases in Hong Kong and Singapore to secure exits through US capital had largely drawn to a close.

Johnson Ma, director of risk and compliance at Dow Jones, noted that Singapore would continue to attract Chinese businesses in industries less susceptible to geopolitical risks, such as retail and logistics.

“Singapore itself is keen to maintain its neutrality; it is neither aligned with the United States nor does it wish to become too closely aligned with China,” Ma said.

Pereira of iMpact observed that fewer Chinese firms were attempting to use Singapore to obscure their mainland roots, given how easily corporate records and ownership structures could be traced.

“It is impossible to hide nowadays,” Pereira said. “You cannot avoid compliance rules just by pretending that you are from Singapore.”

Operational and compliance costs within the city state itself are also climbing, Ma noted.

Regulatory scrutiny over inbound capital has intensified in the city state following a landmark US$2.3 billion money-laundering bust in 2023 – the largest in Singapore’s history and among the largest in the world.

The 10 arrested individuals – all from southeast China’s Fujian province, though several of them held foreign passports – had funnelled funds through bank accounts, real estate and shell companies.

The incident prompted Singapore authorities to tighten vetting across the financial sector, raising the compliance barrier of entry for Chinese companies, Ma said.

Operational costs were also rising as more players crowded out the local market, he added.

The key is to integrate more fully into the local community and establish a model of mutual benefit

Johnson Ma, Dow Jones

Equipped with vast economies of scale and stronger bargaining power over suppliers, many of these large Chinese chains hold a clear advantage over smaller local firms.

Their rapid expansion has raised concerns among local consumers and business owners that imported competition could squeeze out home-grown firms, triggering growing debate online.

In the e-commerce sector, for instance, Chinese giant Pinduoduo’s aggressive push into Singapore in recent months sparked a round of discount competition, with Alibaba Group’s Taobao running similar campaigns such as free shipping on single items. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.

The intensifying competition was set to increase pressure on the city’s bricks-and-mortar stores and local e-commerce operators, such as Sea’s Shopee.

The moves mirror the aggressive tactics that have drawn regulatory pushback at home. Beijing has cracked down on “involutionary” competition – a race to the bottom within some industries that has driven down quality and prices – in recent months, slapping e-commerce giants with fines and summons.

In July, the State Administration for Market Regulation and the Ministry of Commerce issued draft amendments to the country’s E-Commerce Law, adding penalties such as bigger fines, business suspension orders and encouraging industry self-regulation.

Unlike earlier waves of Chinese enterprises expanding abroad to seize new markets, companies today should prioritise regulatory compliance and domestic partnerships, Ma said, adding that this could take the form of joint ventures with local partners or knowledge transfers.

“The key is to integrate more fully into the local community and establish a model of mutual benefit,” Ma said.

item.title: [SCMP] Stella Ma’s mission to make Cantonese opera relevant to Hong Kong’s children
item.description:
I WAS BORN in Sham Shui Po. I have one older sister and three younger brothers in Hong Kong. My father had another family in Guangzhou before coming to Hong Kong, so I have three older siblings there. My father first came to Hong Kong in the 1940s and worked at his uncle’s preserved-fruit factory as a clerk, then moved to an aluminium-pots manufacturer and worked as an accountant – this is where he met my mother. She was born in Dali, Guangdong province, and came to Hong Kong in 1950 with one of her fellow villagers. My mother told me how my father took her to see The Sound of Music after they got married.

I WENT TO Ying Wa Girls’ School, in Mid-Levels. Then, I attended Polytechnic University to study institutional management and catering, but I realised working in hotels wasn’t what I wanted as a career. In 1982, I finished university and then spent two months travelling to Xinjiang and Xian. After that, my father sent me to stay with the Guangzhou family. I was 20, and I was the first representative of the Hong Kong family to go and see them. I remember walking along the railway to their house – they worked for the railway. We were strangers to one another, so when we met, we were very polite and cautious. I sent them greetings from my father. A few years later, my mother, father and siblings in Hong Kong went to Guangzhou to visit the other family. My father and his first wife had not seen each other for more than 40 years.

AT THE AGE of 21, I went to work as a deputy warden at the China Coast Community, in Kowloon Tong, taking care of elderly residents of different nationalities. There was a Russian lady, who loved to smoke. When the doctor advised her not to smoke any more, our social-worker warden said, “She’s 90! Let her do what she likes.” Learning that there are different angles to a discussion was new to me. In 1986, I joined the Hong Kong Tourist Association (HKTA) in its tour-development department. I learned event management from organising the International Dragon Boat Festival and developing tours focused on heritage and feng shui.

I WAS BORN in Sham Shui Po. I have one older sister and three younger brothers in Hong Kong. My father had another family in Guangzhou before coming to Hong Kong, so I have three older siblings there. My father first came to Hong Kong in the 1940s and worked at his uncle’s preserved-fruit factory as a clerk, then moved to an aluminium-pots manufacturer and worked as an accountant – this is where he met my mother. She was born in Dali, Guangdong province, and came to Hong Kong in 1950 with one of her fellow villagers. My mother told me how my father took her to see The Sound of Music after they got married.

I WENT TO Ying Wa Girls’ School, in Mid-Levels. Then, I attended Polytechnic University to study institutional management and catering, but I realised working in hotels wasn’t what I wanted as a career. In 1982, I finished university and then spent two months travelling to Xinjiang and Xian. After that, my father sent me to stay with the Guangzhou family. I was 20, and I was the first representative of the Hong Kong family to go and see them. I remember walking along the railway to their house – they worked for the railway. We were strangers to one another, so when we met, we were very polite and cautious. I sent them greetings from my father. A few years later, my mother, father and siblings in Hong Kong went to Guangzhou to visit the other family. My father and his first wife had not seen each other for more than 40 years.

AT THE AGE of 21, I went to work as a deputy warden at the China Coast Community, in Kowloon Tong, taking care of elderly residents of different nationalities. There was a Russian lady, who loved to smoke. When the doctor advised her not to smoke any more, our social-worker warden said, “She’s 90! Let her do what she likes.” Learning that there are different angles to a discussion was new to me. In 1986, I joined the Hong Kong Tourist Association (HKTA) in its tour-development department. I learned event management from organising the International Dragon Boat Festival and developing tours focused on heritage and feng shui.

IN THE EVENINGS, I studied Chinese and English on a part-time Chinese University degree course for six years. I have always loved Chinese music, so I also took up music lessons while working and studying. In 1989, I left the HKTA and joined a public-relations company run by Doreen Leung Dor-ling. She was the first woman to win the JCI (Junior Chamber International) Ten Outstanding Young Persons of the World award, in 1984. I enjoyed working for Doreen. One of our pet projects was the Hong Kong Outstanding Students Award. Soon after joining Doreen, I had the chance to accompany 10 awardees to Singapore, and I still stay in touch with some of them.

WORKING IN PR was very demanding and I was still studying in the evening. In 1992, I decided to set up my own company, Management Service Centre, the idea being that I would find more time for myself. I thought I could do several things at the same time, so why not? I was writing letters for people and doing Chinese-to-English translations.

MY SECOND COMPANY was called the Cultural Link Centre, which works with a high-school exchange programme supported by the American government – it’s a chance for kids who don’t always fit the Hong Kong education system. It’s unlike the British or the Hong Kong system and it helps many students who don’t thrive here. Kids go to study in the United States, often in a small community or town where they are the only Chinese student, and they come away speaking fluent English, with their confidence increased and often a much better relationship with their family in Hong Kong on their return. A high percentage of them even get into world-class universities. I loved the exchange programme so much that, in 2011, I started a scholarship programme, called the Yes I Can Scholarship. Over the years, it’s had more than 50 awardees. We are now in our 16th year.

I GOT MARRIED in 2011. My husband runs a family business and is a philosopher. He is a life bonus for me! I’m retired from the overseas-studies business. I now focus on children’s Cantonese opera. My early memories of Cantonese opera are vague – I remember going with my mother to a Cantonese opera and finding it boring. In my 20s, I saw on the news the funeral of Cantonese-opera star Yam Kim-fai, with throngs of people crowded outside the funeral parlour. I wondered at the power of Cantonese opera, that it would draw such a crowd. I started watching old Cantonese-opera films.

BY THEN, I was interested in Chinese music, so I studied for a master’s degree in ethnomusicology at Chinese University. I took a unit in Cantonese opera under my sifu, Tsang Kin-man. He was a very good violin and pipa player and advised me on my dissertation on Cantonese-opera percussion music. When I was growing up, there was no opportunity to learn Cantonese opera at school; our education did not include Chinese music culture. Tsang encouraged me to write my own Cantonese opera. I realised that Cantonese-opera audiences were beginning to dwindle, and that young people could not relate to it, because the stories were often rather highbrow: Romance of The Three Kingdoms, Dream of the Red Chamber and so on. My grandparents’ generation loved Cantonese opera – they would hear it on the radio and then rush to the theatre to watch the show. But now, kids don’t understand the storylines because they are too removed from our lives.

CANTONESE OPERA IS so much a part of our cultural treasure – we need to make it known to the younger generation. In 2002, I started the Cha Duk Chang Children’s Cantonese Opera Association and began writing a full-length Cantonese opera for children, focusing on their daily lives, rather than the usual characters and plots in Cantonese operas, such as emperors, generals, beautiful ladies and love affairs.

MY FIRST CANTONESE opera for children was called The Quest for the Moon Fairy. It was about five children who were forced to stay home and study during the Mid-Autumn Festival. But when they looked outside, they could see fireworks and other children with lanterns, so they decided to sneak out. The story is about the adventure they had. Another one, The Three-Eyed Little Immortal in Distress, follows a character in the heavenly world who fails an exam and is sent down to the human world to take classes, so he can retake the test. That’s another story about children’s daily lives in a singing-and-acting style that is strictly Cantonese opera.

I WANT TO bring the joy of Cantonese opera to Hong Kong kids. We go into kindergartens and primary schools to do classes and workshops. We also organise an annual Cantonese-opera singing contest. We had our annual performance in September at the Xiqu Centre, in West Kowloon Cultural District, and our next performance will be in late December, in Zhuhai, Guangdong province.

WITH THE KIDS, Cantonese opera and the scholarship, I have been lucky to live a life where I can work on the things that really interest me, things that I really love.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity

item.title: [SCMP] How traditional Chinese medicine found its way onto fine-dining and bar menus in Hong Kong
item.description:
The age-old Chinese habit of drinking hot water has gone viral. On TikTok and RedNote, influencers clutch steaming mugs and extol the benefits of drinking warm water for digestion, circulation – of both blood and qi – and balance. What they are describing is yang sheng – the practice of nourishing life that exists at the heart of traditional Chinese medicine. TCM, once the nagging voice of your grandmother, is now what the cool kids post on their feeds.

The Mandarin term for this is guochao, loosely meaning “national wave” and describing the rebranding of Chinese heritage as something desirable rather than dowdy. It began with Li-Ning starring on the runway at New York Fashion Week in 2018, followed a year later by Florasis’ engraved lipstick cases – the designs of which were inspired by ancient Chinese relief-engraving craftsmanship.

Now, the trend has migrated to restaurant and bar menus – guochao in digestible form – steeped in a promise of wellness and cultural pride. The challenge, however, is how to translate a tradition defined by bitter medicine into something people actually crave.
item.content:encoded:
The age-old Chinese habit of drinking hot water has gone viral. On TikTok and RedNote, influencers clutch steaming mugs and extol the benefits of drinking warm water for digestion, circulation – of both blood and qi – and balance. What they are describing is yang sheng – the practice of nourishing life that exists at the heart of traditional Chinese medicine. TCM, once the nagging voice of your grandmother, is now what the cool kids post on their feeds.

The Mandarin term for this is guochao, loosely meaning “national wave” and describing the rebranding of Chinese heritage as something desirable rather than dowdy. It began with Li-Ning starring on the runway at New York Fashion Week in 2018, followed a year later by Florasis’ engraved lipstick cases – the designs of which were inspired by ancient Chinese relief-engraving craftsmanship.

Now, the trend has migrated to restaurant and bar menus – guochao in digestible form – steeped in a promise of wellness and cultural pride. The challenge, however, is how to translate a tradition defined by bitter medicine into something people actually crave.

For many younger diners, the first barrier to TCM is its sheer intellectual density. It can feel like an arcane maze of unseen bodily energies and ancient texts that have accumulated over the centuries. Jayson Tang, executive Chinese chef of Man Ho Chinese Restaurant, solves this by translating TCM’s abstract philosophy into a highly visual, intuitive language.

It helps that Tang grew up with TCM as a practical reality. “When I was a child, I suffered from frequent skin irritation,” he says. “My uncle would take me to see an old TCM practitioner. The herbal remedies worked.” Elsewhere, his mother brewed soups according to the calendar: “This one to clear heat, that one to strengthen the lungs,” he recalls.

It was later though, when studying at the Chinese Culinary Institute, that Tang began to understand the natural systems underlying the soups and remedies from his childhood and noticed how ingredients shifted in harmony with the seasons.

At Man Ho, Tang dismantles the esoteric nature of TCM using his Five Elements Menu, which draws inspiration from the 2,000-year-old Huangdi Neijing, one of the foundational texts of TCM that gained a following among Taoist practitioners. The text maps colours onto organs and elements: white is for the lungs and metal; green for the liver and wood; black for the kidneys and water; red for the heart and fire; yellow for the spleen and earth.

Tang uses colours to help select ingredients for the restaurant’s medicinal properties before applying contemporary culinary techniques. In doing so, he makes a 2,000-year-old medical text instantly legible on the plate.

Take one example on the current menu: the deep-fried fish maw with shrimp mousse and banana in a pumpkin and rice stock is built around yellow. Both banana and pumpkin are understood in TCM to benefit the spleen and aid digestion. Bananas are rarely used in Chinese cooking, which lends the dish an avant-garde appeal – but Tang first cooked with them 20 years ago, winning a competition with a banana-based dish. He brought that memory back for this menu, grounding his theory in something personal.

The entire menu follows a deliberate sequence, with the early courses cleansing while the later ones build strength. “This respects the TCM principle of beginning with detoxification before moving towards nourishment,” he explains.

If Tang seeks to decode the vernacular of TCM for regular diners, Sandy Keung wants to overcome the palatability barrier and Hongkongers’ memories of having to choke down aggressively bitter, dark, medicinal brews. The chef-owner of Table by Sandy Keung sidesteps this through a brilliant strategy of culinary camouflage.

Her current summer menu is built around the element of fire. “In TCM, summer is when yang energy rises; the body consumes more, and the heart works hardest,” Keung explains. According to traditional TCM theory, the flavour that naturally balances fire and clears internal heat is bitterness. Therefore, a summer wellness menu demands ingredients like bitter gourd.

But bitter gourd (fu gua) is an obviously hard sell. “It would be difficult to convince a client to eat a plate of fu gua only,” Keung jokes.

Yet she does not hide the gourd. It is clearly presented on the menu, and the vegetable is deliberately chopped into larger cubes rather than diced into smaller pieces that might be less detectable. To sweeten the pill, Keung pairs the bitter gourd with threadfin fish and layers it with a Pommery mustard-garlic-herb creme, cutting the harshness of the gourd without completely erasing it. “I still want diners to taste it,” she says.

Ultimately, Keung views her TCM menus not as a trend to exploit, but as a desirable cultural renaissance. “I’m not here to convince the hardcore, diehard TCM fans” who are already converts, she says. “I’m here to remind people of their heritage, especially the ones who are not believers.”

Reclaiming that forgotten heritage, however, requires overcoming one final obstacle. It’s not just that TCM seems obscure or tastes bad. It’s that it feels outdated; a relic belonging to musty old neighbourhood shops smelling of dried roots and lined with countless jars containing who-knows-what. Dennis Mak, co-founder of Clan & Co by Magnolia Lab, solves this by moving TCM out of the apothecary store and into the high-energy, social space of contemporary nightlife.

Like his culinary peers, Mak’s relationship with TCM was forged in childhood: the bitter herbal medicine his parents made him drink, the herbal tea stalls on the street, the gui ling gao herbal jelly eaten as a summer treat, the soups his mother brewed with purpose.

“Those memories shaped me,” he says. “Not because of the health benefits, but because of the meaning embedded in every flavour. It is knowledge passed down through generations, and what we are doing is keeping that conversation alive.”

At Clan & Co, that conversation is revitalised through a liquid remix of Hong Kong’s collective childhood. To bridge the generational gap, Mak takes the traditional remedies Gen Z usually avoids and repackages them into sophisticated, trendy cocktails.

Five Flower Tea, the mild herbal brew drunk in summer to clear heat, is reimagined as a vibrant cocktail built on Two Moons Five Flowers Tea Gin, Magnolia Lab Roselle, and Cynar. Sour Plum Soup, the classic sweet-sour drink served at hotpot restaurants to aid digestion, is used in a thirst-quenching cocktail tailored for the city’s humid months.

Mak is careful to draw a line between what he does and what a TCM practitioner would prescribe though. “We do not treat our drinks as medicine, nor do we promote any medicinal benefits,” he explains. To that end, the team selects milder herbs from the TCM category of “dietary herbs” rather than any potent medicinals.

However, Mak points out that alcohol has actually been an integral part of TCM for centuries, traditionally used to preserve herbs, alter their effects and even serve as medicine itself. On colder days, Clan & Co serves warm cocktails, honouring the TCM emphasis on harmony with the seasons and the body’s own needs.

Mak sees his work as part of something larger than mixology. Younger Hongkongers, he says, are losing touch with their traditions: “A lot of Gen Z have never stepped into a traditional herbal tea shop, nor tasted 24 Herbs and Chinese medicinal wine. They know these things exist, but there has always been a gap between knowing and appreciating.”

Clan & Co seeks to bridge that gap. When a customer tastes Mak’s Five Flower Tea cocktail and says it reminds them of their grandmother, a frayed cultural connection is restored. “TCM is not a trend,” Mak insists. “It is simply the local expression of a universal truth: people gravitate towards flavours that feel like home.”

What these innovative dishes and drinks offer is not a cure-all, and they don’t pretend to. Instead, they offer a younger generation permission to believe – for the length of a tasting menu or a few sips – that they are taking care of themselves, all while their ancestors look on from somewhere, nodding in quiet approval.

Placebo or profound, this is guochao at its most intimate. And Hong Kong is ordering another round.

item.title: [SCMP] Southeast Asian live streamers hustle to fuel booming e-commerce sales
item.description:
In a makeshift studio inside his public housing flat in Singapore, Shane Soh stands before his smartphone, running his fingers through a towel as he extols its softness to viewers watching his live stream.

A ring light illuminates his face while more than a dozen other products sit on a shelf behind him, waiting for their moment on camera.

“Don’t just buy one towel today, but get bedsheets as well. It’s perfect for Hari Raya or Christmas, and the thread count is 1,800 … It’s the best kind of quality you can get,” he tells hundreds of viewers on the other side of the screen.
item.content:encoded:
In a makeshift studio inside his public housing flat in Singapore, Shane Soh stands before his smartphone, running his fingers through a towel as he extols its softness to viewers watching his live stream.

A ring light illuminates his face while more than a dozen other products sit on a shelf behind him, waiting for their moment on camera.

“Don’t just buy one towel today, but get bedsheets as well. It’s perfect for Hari Raya or Christmas, and the thread count is 1,800 … It’s the best kind of quality you can get,” he tells hundreds of viewers on the other side of the screen.

It was Tuesday, the eve of the 11.11 Single’s Day – the biggest e-commerce event in Southeast Asia – and Soh was among thousands of hosts flashing discounted products and promotional codes on Shopee.

Live stream shopping has become big business in Southeast Asia, and Soh is one of many riding on the boom to boost their incomes. Customers get drawn in by personable hosts who try on clothes, cook or simply chat to the camera while promoting products, leading to billions of dollars in sales each year.

But the competition is heating up as more aspiring hosts try to get in on the action, raising questions about how many can realistically turn the gig into a sustainable source of income.

Soh, who has a full-time job as a market research analyst, first delved into live-streaming when he was a university undergraduate. He spends about 10 hours a week hosting streams – longer when gigs skyrocket due to e-commerce festivals such as Single’s Day.

“I picked live-streaming for additional income and exposure. Also, it aligns with my passion for presenting and hosting, which was something I was already doing back in the day,” he said.

Southeast Asia’s e-commerce market is expected to reach US$226 billion this year, accounting for more than 60 per cent of the region’s digital economy, according to the e-Conomy SEA Report 2026 released in October by Google, Temasek and Bain & Company.

Content-driven shopping, which includes live streams, short videos and affiliate sales, is projected to generate US$77.9 billion in transactions in the region this year, up from US$49.7 billion in 2025, according to a September report by research firm Momentum Works.

On Shopee, orders from live streams and short-form videos grew by more than 45 per cent year on year in the third quarter, accounting for over a quarter of physical-goods orders in Southeast Asia, the platform’s parent company Sea said on Tuesday.

Personal touch

Stephy Sin, who previously worked in corporate roles for about a decade, quit her job as a TV producer and embarked on a live-streaming career last year. The Malaysian’s usual clients typically span beauty and household appliance brands, and in good months she takes home around 9,000 ringgit (US$2,200).

“If you really want to do well, it’s hard to do it on the side because you want to make connections with as many brands as possible to gain exposure,” said Sin, 32. “And I made it my full-time job because I’m definitely able to get more money from it.”

Sin recalls a deluge of questions flooding a TikTok live stream she had been hosting for a well-known sports brand last year.

“People were dropping so many comments in different languages – English, Malay and Mandarin – and it was impossible to answer them all. I just had to hold my breath and keep switching between three languages,” she said.

Such engagements are one of the main reasons viewers continue to tune in to these streams. Instead of spending time looking at photographs and item descriptions on their phones, they can receive answers to their queries in real time.

“This creates a stronger sense of social presence, making consumers feel that they are interacting with a real person rather than simply browsing an online shopping platform,” said Chong Sin Er, assistant professor at the school of economics and management at Xiamen University Malaysia. “Such interactions can reduce perceived uncertainty and help consumers feel more confident in their purchasing decisions.”

Tracy Loh, a senior lecturer of communication management at the Singapore Management University, said such sales methods might also simulate a physical shopping experience with a friend. “Oftentimes shopping is more of a social experience than merely a utilitarian affair,” she said.

Good deals offered during live streams could add excitement and lead to feelings of scarcity and urgency, said Loh. Consumers might fear missing out and feel pressured to make purchases when seeing other viewers placing orders, she added.

While some firms have used artificial intelligence-generated avatars to host their live streams, Loh is confident real human interactions would retain their edge.

AI “defeated the purpose” of live-streaming, she said. “The key is to engage first, sell later. With engagement, you come across as a friend, making a recommendation rather than as someone trying to make a sale. With AI, you have less of this authenticity and relationship.”

Carving sustainable career

As the e-commerce market expands and consumer preferences evolve, live-streaming is becoming an increasingly important marketing tool for companies.

Big names have embraced the trend, including cosmetics giant L’Oreal, which last year launched a live stream studio in Vietnam.

The mix of live streamers is also quickly expanding, with actors and internet personalities joining the fray to boost their incomes and profiles.

Soh, who has over 20,000 followers on his Shopee account, worries about stiffer competition. “The pool of live streamers is growing, and so it’s harder for you to stand out against different brands and creators … The pie is only so big,” he said.

Chong said that with more live streamers, repetitive and heavily promotional streams focusing on ramping up sales numbers could risk viewer fatigue. “The initial novelty of live stream shopping may gradually diminish, meaning that live streamers and companies will need to offer genuine value beyond discounts and promotional campaigns,” she said.

Career sustainability ultimately depended on one’s ability to establish trust and a loyal community, Chong added.

For Samantha Dela Pena, a 19-year-old undergraduate in Manila, a community is what she aims to build. In search of inspiration and a bigger pay cheque, she left her part-time job at a fast food joint and started hosting live streams for a local cosmetics company.

In front of a camera, she rattles off lipstick shades and foundation tone numbers without missing a beat. As she dabs the products on her face, she shares make-up tips and tricks with her viewers.

Dela Pena said she hoped to continue live-streaming after her graduation. “I’ve always been passionate about make-up, self-care and women empowerment, and I think this role boosts these beliefs.”

item.title: [SCMP] 11 drills in 60 days: is India’s navy stretched too thin?
item.description:
In the space of just two months, India’s navy has held joint exercises off the coasts of Britain, France, South Africa, Oman, the Philippines, South Korea, Japan and Russia’s far east.

Such a run of exercises signals a bid for a larger maritime role on the world stage, analysts say. Yet it also raises questions about whether a navy currently short on submarines and struggling to expand can support such global ambitions while also guarding India’s home waters.

Since mid-September, over a span of fewer than 60 days, Indian ships have taken part in:
item.content:encoded:
In the space of just two months, India’s navy has held joint exercises off the coasts of Britain, France, South Africa, Oman, the Philippines, South Korea, Japan and Russia’s far east.

Such a run of exercises signals a bid for a larger maritime role on the world stage, analysts say. Yet it also raises questions about whether a navy currently short on submarines and struggling to expand can support such global ambitions while also guarding India’s home waters.

Since mid-September, over a span of fewer than 60 days, Indian ships have taken part in:

Slinex with Sri Lanka off Visakhapatnam (September 17-21)

ADMM-Plus drills with multiple countries off Subic Bay (September 21-25)

Varuna with France at Toulon (September 22-28)

AIME with Asean member states at Subic Bay (September 28-October 2)

Konkan with the UK off Plymouth (October 8-15)

Ibsamar with Brazil and South Africa at Simon’s Town (October 12-20)

Indra with Russia at Vladivostok (October 13-18)

Simbex with Singapore in the Bay of Bengal (October 21-26)

IN-RoKN with South Korea at Busan (October 26-29)

Malabar with the US, Japan and Australia near Yokosuka (November 5-12)

Naseem Al Bahr with Oman off Muscat (November 8-12)

Why so many drills?

Indian officials cite the navy’s ability to operate concurrently across the Western Pacific, Mediterranean, North and South Atlantic and Indian Ocean as proof of its operational reach, logistics and endurance – and a reflection of both New Delhi’s policy of strategic autonomy and its global maritime vision and security doctrine, dubbed “Mahasagar”.

Analysts who spoke to This Week in Asia said the raft of recent drills helped India strengthen relationships and prove it could project maritime power beyond its immediate neighbourhood.

“Exercises and deployments are a tool of India’s multi-aligned foreign policy, for deepening relations with partners and adding nuance to its political-military signalling too,” said Antoine Levesques, a senior fellow for South and Central Asian defence at the International Institute for Strategic Studies.

India’s participation in so many exercises could also be understood “as a form of diplomatic manoeuvring”, said Dongkeun Lee, a policy fellow at the Asia-Pacific Leadership Network specialising in maritime security.

“The Indian Navy not only participates in extra-regional exercises but also invites partner navies to the Indian Ocean region, showing that India’s partner countries are interested in Indian Ocean security and thereby contribute to the region’s balance of power,” he said.

“Demonstrating the Indian Navy’s capabilities overseas implies that [it] … could be deployed to other regions, coordinating with extra-regional partners in the event of a contingency against China.”

Walter Ladwig, a senior lecturer in international relations at King’s College London whose research focus includes South Asian security, agreed that experience gained from joint military exercises “would all be relevant in a scenario where the Indian Navy had to respond to Chinese naval activity in the Indian Ocean” – even if the countries taking part in such drills might not necessarily envisage fighting alongside one another in a conflict.

Retired Indian Navy captain Kamlesh K. Agnihotri, who now works as a senior fellow at the National Maritime Foundation in Delhi, told This Week in Asia that multinational drills such as Malabar and the biennial US-led Rim of the Pacific Exercise also had a deterrent effect.

“[They] send a clear strategic communication … that a coalition of like-minded nations and their forces will stand up to the coercive measures that are intended to alter the status quo and create a new normal by undermining the freedom of navigation and overflight,” he said.

With that in mind, India’s navy deploying for exercises far beyond the Indian Ocean region was about “much more than only diplomatic visibility”, Agnihotri added.

A changed world

Speaking at this year’s Delhi Defence Dialogue on November 3, India’s navy chief Admiral Krishna Swaminathan stressed the need to develop a fighting force suited for “the 21st century operating environment”.

“The world has changed very vastly today from just a few years back,” he said. “Growing geopolitical tensions have inflamed a lot of old historical fault lines and today we find the use of force as an acceptable instrument of national policy. In fact, it’s not just an acceptable instrument, it is a preferred instrument.”

The world has changed very vastly today from just a few years back

Admiral Krishna Swaminathan, India’s navy chief

The number of wars being fought globally had increased, Swaminathan noted, citing “about 65 state-based armed conflicts” last year alone – “perhaps the highest since records began being kept in 1946”.

Against such a backdrop, he said India was “quite cognisant of the capabilities of our adversaries”, adding that the country’s navy was keeping “a very good watch” on critical chokepoints such as the Strait of Malacca, in particular.

India currently operates two aircraft carriers, 13 destroyers, around 20 active frigates and over 20 smaller corvettes – plus dozens more auxiliary and support ships – crewed by more than 67,000 active personnel.

By 2035 it aims to have a 200-ship navy, with around 50 vessels and submarines on order – the vast majority of which are being built in Indian shipyards.

Analysts say submarine availability, ageing vessels and shipbuilding delays are some of the main obstacles hindering progress.

“The navy is not acquiring new boats fast enough to offset the old ones, let alone expand,” Ladwig said, adding that the size of India’s submarine fleet “needs to grow”.

Indeed, naval chief Swaminathan stressed at the defence dialogue in Delhi this month that India needed to speed up turning technological innovation into usable military capability, so it can “fight, sustain and adapt by itself without being constrained”.

Spread too thin?

As a “blue-water” navy, meaning one able to operate far from home, around two-thirds of India’s fleet is always kept available for sustained operations, according to Agnihotri, the naval veteran.

No more than three or four ships were ever deployed outside the Indian Ocean at any one time, he said – and only after the navy had calculated “the force level required for operations” at home.

“So if some serious crisis erupts near Indian waters, the available force level should be enough to handle that effectively,” Agnihotri said.

Lee said the types of ships deployed also mattered. Aircraft carriers and large destroyers were best suited to distant military operations, he said, while frigates and conventional non-nuclear submarines were better kept in reserve for a “serious crisis close to home”.

None of the recent exercises India took part in involved the two aircraft carriers it has in service, with the lion’s share of the Pacific engagements being handled by the INS Sahyadri, a Shivalik-class stealth frigate, and the INS Trishul of the Talwar-class being deployed to Europe. Around 10 vessels were reportedly deployed in total.

Levesques said overseas deployments, including for joint exercises, did “exact a toll” on a navy’s ships and increased demand for maintenance and repairs, which is why most navies tended to group drills by region.

Many of India’s older ships and submarines are also of Russian origin, making the continued supply of Russian spares important – though the war in Ukraine does not appear to have disrupted deliveries, according to Levesques.

“Moreover, India’s steady induction of new naval platforms rests on ever greater proportions of indigenous content, increasing India’s overall ability to sustain its ambitions to exercise and deploy peacefully,” he said.

For Ladwig, “probably the most important constraint” on India’s ability to challenge Chinese naval operations in the Indian Ocean is its struggle to grow fast enough – “far more than a frigate spending a few weeks in Europe”.

“There are certainly capacity constraints in particular areas, most notably submarines, which have been a significant problem for some time,” he added.

item.title: [SCMP] Indonesian VP resignation drama raises stakes for Prabowo as alliances strain
item.description:
The prospect of Gibran Rakabuming Raka stepping down as Indonesia’s vice-president has raised the stakes for President Prabowo Subianto, with analysts warning that his departure could trigger a scramble for power within the governing coalition and reshape the country’s political alliances.

While they differ over whether Gibran, the eldest son of former president Joko Widodo, genuinely wants to relinquish his position, observers say his dilemma reflects shifting political loyalties and the weakening influence of his father.

At a press conference on Tuesday in Jakarta, Minister of State Secretary Prasetyo Hadi announced that Prabowo had been informed of Gibran’s intention to resign during a morning meeting, although no formal resignation letter had been submitted.
item.content:encoded:
The prospect of Gibran Rakabuming Raka stepping down as Indonesia’s vice-president has raised the stakes for President Prabowo Subianto, with analysts warning that his departure could trigger a scramble for power within the governing coalition and reshape the country’s political alliances.

While they differ over whether Gibran, the eldest son of former president Joko Widodo, genuinely wants to relinquish his position, observers say his dilemma reflects shifting political loyalties and the weakening influence of his father.

At a press conference on Tuesday in Jakarta, Minister of State Secretary Prasetyo Hadi announced that Prabowo had been informed of Gibran’s intention to resign during a morning meeting, although no formal resignation letter had been submitted.

Prasetyo later emphasised that Prabowo “had not rejected Gibran’s offer of resignation”.

The announcement followed rulings by Indonesia’s Constitutional Court and Supreme Court concerning Gibran’s secondary school qualifications. The Constitutional Court dismissed a challenge on procedural grounds despite finding insufficient evidence of his educational credentials, while the Supreme Court subsequently invalidated his diploma equivalency certificate.

On the same day, about 50 members of Indonesia’s 580-strong House of Representatives submitted a motion to exercise parliament’s right to express an opinion on Gibran’s qualifications, potentially paving the way for impeachment proceedings.

Gibran told the press gathered outside his official residence that Prabowo, “whom he regarded as his own father,” had urged him to “fight on” by appealing through the State Administrative Court.

However, Yusril Ihza Mahendra, the Coordinating Minister for Law, Human Rights, Immigration, and Correctional Institutions, pointed out that an appeal would be “futile.”

“The ruling by the Supreme Court is final and binding, against which there can be no appeal.”

In the same vein, Syahganda Nainggolan, head of the Government Communication Agency, dismissed Gibran’s recollection of events.

“It’s almost unthinkable that the president would have advised Gibran to appeal against the court verdicts.”

Rendy Pahrun Wadipalapa, a political scientist at the National Research and Innovation Agency, told This Week In Asia that Gibran’s reference to Prabowo as a paternal figure must be read within the Javanese cultural context.

“The line reads like a Javanese shadow play metaphor in which the language of kinship and deference says one thing in public, while the private defiance is the shrouded undertone.”

Political commentator Lukas Luwarso believes that Gibran’s declaration might all be “smoke and mirrors” to gauge public reactions to his possible resignation.

“He seemed to be testing the waters, which means he still wants to cling on to his vice-presidency and won’t give it up without a fight.”

Legal expert Herlambang Wiratraman stated that Gibran’s best course of action was to resign for the greater good of the nation.

“Otherwise, an impeachment process would further tax the administrative capacity of the state, at a trying time.”

Lukas also warned that Gibran was risking “total humiliation” and “political suicide” if he dared to go down the impeachment route.

“He may find unwanted things crawling out of the woodwork during the process.”

Marcus Mietzner, a political scientist at Canberra’s ANU and who has written a biography of Widodo, said Gibran faced a dilemma over his resignation.

“From Gibran’s standpoint, resigning would be an admission of guilt, while being impeached is also unpalatable.”

Under Indonesia’s constitution, a vacancy in the vice-presidency would trigger a process to choose a replacement through the People’s Consultative Assembly (MPR), which comprises members of the House of Representatives (DPR) and Regional Representative Council (DPD).

The assembly would then convene to choose a new vice-president from the two candidates nominated by the president within 60 days.

According to Rendy, Gibran’s political arsenal “is pretty much spent”, rendering him “in no position to fight”.

“He rose on Jokowi’s patronage and Prabowo’s coalition arithmetic without a party base of his own; once those calculations shift, nothing anchors him,” he said, referring to Widodo by his popular nickname.

Made Supriatma, a visiting fellow at Singapore’s ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, agreed with Rendy’s assessment.

“Gibran’s political demise ties in with his father’s diminished influence in the wake of the wiretapping scandal due to his political proximity with Listyo Sigit.”

Former police chief Listyo Sigit Prabowo, known to be an ally of Widodo’s, was arrested on November 3 on suspicion of illegally wiretapping Prabowo and dozens of other prominent figures.

Made said Widodo’s political stature had received two recent major blows.

“First, there’s the ongoing scandal concerning his own supposedly fake diploma.”

On November 5, Widodo testified at the East Jakarta Court in two court cases with two different defendants, Roy Suryo and Tifauzia Tyassuma, charged with defamation against the former president for claiming that he had forged his university diploma and used it to nominate himself for public office.

“And there was the resignation of three cabinet members from the PSI party.”

On November 9, Forestry Minister Raja Juli Antoni, Deputy Culture Minister Giring Ganesha and Deputy Minister of Population and Family Development Ratu Ayu Isyana Bagoes Oka resigned their respective positions from PSI, a political party headed by Widodo’s younger son, Kaesang Pangarep.

Since his retirement from office, Widodo has actively campaigned on behalf of PSI and publicly displayed his membership card on September 26.

Meanwhile, speculation is rife among analysts about whom Prabowo will nominate as candidates in the event of Gibran’s formal resignation from the race.

Rendy believes that there will be a “jostle” for the job among the elite of Prabowo’s seven-party coalition.

“Parties inside the governing coalition would have reason to bid for the post, and elites who accepted Gibran’s place on the old ticket might now press their own claims.”

Political scientist Made argued that Prabowo’s first choice would be to consolidate his power after Gibran’s exit.

“His first instinct would be to reach out to figures outside his own party Gerindra, such as Puan or AHY.”

Puan Maharani, a PDIP politician and Speaker of the House of Representatives, is the daughter of former President Megawati Sukarnoputri, chairperson of PDIP. AHY or Agus Harimurti Yudhoyono, currently coordinating minister of infrastructure and regional development and chairman of Partai Demokrat, is the elder son of former President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono.

When asked by reporters on Tuesday, Puan was cautiously guarded in her response.

“We will wait and see until there is an official announcement. Gibran is still the vice-president until then.”

“If [both Puan and AHY] turned down the offer, Prabowo would likely go inward by opting for junior figures from his party. Names such as Sugiono and Sudaryono have cropped up.”

Both Sugiono and Sudaryono are known to be Prabowo’s protégés. Sugiono, 47, formerly the foreign minister, is now the coordinating minister for human development and cultural affairs. Sudaryono, 41, formerly deputy minister of agriculture, is the current chief of the National Nutrition Board, which governs Prabowo’s flagship Free Nutritious Meals programme.

Rendy noted that Gibran’s declaration of intent came at a time when the government faced lethargic economic indicators, worries over a possible stock market downgrade, falling public approval, and sustained public protests over its flagship programmes.

“The temptation to spin Gibran’s resignation into a short-lived distraction, with Gibran as the scapegoat, might be too great to resist.”

However, Mietzner believes that removing Gibran as vice-president might not be advantageous to Prabowo.

“So why get rid of him and trigger a tense contest among his coalition parties about the vacancy?”

item.title: [SCMP] Why Philippines is muzzling anti-China rhetoric ahead of crucial Asean talks
item.description:
The Philippine foreign affairs department’s rare rebuke of officials and agencies over anti-China rhetoric could signal Manila’s bid to rein in tensions ahead of the Asean summit next week – but also internal disagreements over strategy, according to analysts.

The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) on Sunday said public criticism of China could undermine diplomatic efforts. “In high-stakes diplomacy, a disciplined and coherent national voice remains essential to advancing our national interests,” it said in a statement.

The Chinese embassy in Manila has recently been embroiled in a war of words with Philippine uniformed services and officials.
item.content:encoded:
The Philippine foreign affairs department’s rare rebuke of officials and agencies over anti-China rhetoric could signal Manila’s bid to rein in tensions ahead of the Asean summit next week – but also internal disagreements over strategy, according to analysts.

The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) on Sunday said public criticism of China could undermine diplomatic efforts. “In high-stakes diplomacy, a disciplined and coherent national voice remains essential to advancing our national interests,” it said in a statement.

The Chinese embassy in Manila has recently been embroiled in a war of words with Philippine uniformed services and officials.

Last month, several senators called for Chinese ambassador Jing Quan to be declared persona non grata after he suggested Beijing could “easily win” any confrontation with Manila. Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr later called Jing’s remarks a “threat” and “not very diplomatic”.

The heated exchanges are the latest in cycles of tension between the two countries over disputed waters in the South China Sea. China claims nearly the entire waterway, rejecting an arbitral decision in 2016 that ruled in favour of the Philippines as illegal.

The DFA statement added that “under the constitution, the president is the chief architect of Philippine foreign policy” and all government officials should align with this.

“Individual officials, agencies or sectors do not independently determine the direction of our international relations. Whatever personal convictions public officials may hold, their public platforms carry institutional responsibilities,” it said.

“They may not pursue preferred approaches towards China, or any other international partner, without regard for the consequences on the government’s overall policy.”

The DFA issued the statement after Foreign Affairs Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro and her Chinese counterpart, Wang Yi, had a “frank, pragmatic and constructive” call on November 3 in an effort to maintain bilateral relations ahead of major meetings.

Observers said the timing of the statement was deliberate and tied to the Philippines’ role as Association of Southeast Asian Nations chair and host of its November 16 summit.

“As chair, the Philippines wants to be seen as a steady, unifying host, not a battleground for bilateral friction,” said Dennis Coronacion, associate professor of political science at the University of Santo Tomas.

Containing the rhetoric ensured the summit stayed focused on shared priorities, such as economic integration and finalising a substantive South China Sea Code of Conduct, “rather than getting bogged down in a public spat between Manila and Beijing”, Coronacion said.

The statement was intended to assuage concerns by Asean member states of the tensions becoming a distraction at the summit, he added. “Asean relies on consensus, quiet diplomacy and stability, so when polemics turn into public threats and diplomatic snubs, member states worry it will hijack the entire regional agenda.”

‘Good cop, bad cop’

There has been precedent. During the Asean Defence Ministers Meeting on October 28 and 29 in Cebu, China sent a defence attache, the lowest rank it has dispatched to such meetings despite being a dialogue partner.

He was welcomed by Manila’s defence undersecretary rather than Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jnr, who shook hands with his counterparts from Asean countries and dialogue partners instead. Teodoro defended the arrangement, saying it was “more than courteous” for a defence undersecretary to welcome a defence attache.

Next week’s summit will see more illustrious guests. Chinese premier Li Qiang is reportedly expected to attend, although Beijing has yet to confirm this. US President Donald Trump will also be among the attendees.

“Ahead of high-stakes talks, including ongoing negotiations on the South China Sea Code of Conduct and the Apec summit in China, the DFA is ensuring Manila speaks with one disciplined, strategic voice so external parties cannot exploit internal friction,” Coronacion said.

While the Philippines has taken a more assertive stance against China in maritime disputes, analysts suggest Marcos’ statements towards China have become more measured. The president has said he was seeking a “reset” in ties in March following the economic fallout from the Iran war.

Teodoro’s hardened stance compared to Marcos’ diplomatic tone is not a divergence in policy but a “deliberate division of labour”, according to Coronacion.

“In any administration, the defence secretary and the president serve very different institutional roles,” he said.

“Secretary Teodoro’s job is deterrence, defence readiness and speaking plainly about operational threats to our sovereignty. President Marcos, as chief architect of foreign policy, must keep diplomatic channels open and manage the broader bilateral relationship, especially ahead of the Asean and Apec summits”.

This was the “classic ‘good cop, bad cop’ dynamic”, he said. “Teodoro draws the hard security red lines, while Marcos preserves the diplomatic space to negotiate.”

Manila’s negotiating stance, however, could be undermined if the “friction” among government bodies as to communication styles was left unchecked. “When executive agencies, uniformed services, and lawmakers appear to pull in different directions, Beijing can exploit those divisions to stall talks or question our diplomats’ authority.”

Other observers were not as optimistic about the efficacy of the DFA’s move.

Victor Andres Manhit, president of the Manila-based think tank Stratbase Institute, said the government “must not allow diplomatic considerations to weaken its defence of Philippine sovereignty”.

“Diplomacy remains essential, but it cannot replace transparency and public accountability. There must be room for responsible public discussion, especially when developments at sea directly affect our sovereign rights, national security and the livelihoods of Filipino communities,” he said in a statement on Tuesday.

Gary Ador Dionisio, dean of the De La Salle-College of Saint Benilde’s School of Diplomacy and Governance, called the rebuke “unnecessary”.

“Although DFA wants to reduce diplomatic uncertainty and prevent public exchanges from narrowing the president’s room for negotiation, it sends signals to China and the Asean community that the national government is not in control of these issues,” he said.

The foreign affairs department’s public intervention “suggests that at least some differences have become difficult to manage internally”, he added.

As Asean chair, the Philippines should defend its interests “while demonstrating its capacity to convene difficult conversations,” Dionisio said, adding that while other member-states had different relationships with Beijing, “we are certain they share an interest in preventing maritime incidents or diplomatic confrontations from escalating”.

item.title: [SCMP] Singapore Airlines backs new business class seats amid ‘dental chair’ criticism
item.description:
Singapore Airlines (SIA) said on Wednesday that the cabin colour palette for its newly unveiled business class seats was “carefully selected” after the reveal drew criticism from some content creators and travel writers, including those who likened them to “dental chairs”.

Much of the reaction has focused on the grey-and-yellow colour palette of the seats, which were developed by SIA in collaboration with seat manufacturer Recaro and creative design firm Designworks.

An SIA spokesperson said the new seats were “designed to enhance comfort, privacy and functionality, while supporting a more seamless travel experience”.
item.content:encoded:
Singapore Airlines (SIA) said on Wednesday that the cabin colour palette for its newly unveiled business class seats was “carefully selected” after the reveal drew criticism from some content creators and travel writers, including those who likened them to “dental chairs”.

Much of the reaction has focused on the grey-and-yellow colour palette of the seats, which were developed by SIA in collaboration with seat manufacturer Recaro and creative design firm Designworks.

An SIA spokesperson said the new seats were “designed to enhance comfort, privacy and functionality, while supporting a more seamless travel experience”.

“The colours, materials and finishes were carefully selected to create a fresh, contemporary and refined ambience, complemented by adjustable in-flight LED lighting throughout the journey,” SIA added.

The spokesperson pointed out that the seats feature full-grain premium leather upholstery, sliding privacy doors, an electronically-powered centre divider, enhanced ergonomics, a full-flat bed and a spacious footwell that gives customers greater freedom of movement while resting.

“Frequent fliers who attended the launch praised its privacy, spaciousness, comfort and thoughtful convenience features, including the larger display screen, enhanced charging options, intuitive physical seat controls and companion-bed configuration,” SIA said.

The airline said it appreciated the feedback on the cabin’s colour palette and is committed to offering a world-class end-to-end travel experience.

“As with all our products, we will continue to closely monitor feedback and draw on operational insights to refine and enhance elements of the customer experience,” SIA said.

Singapore’s national carrier unveiled last Friday its next-generation long-haul cabin products, which include new first class suites with double beds, redesigned business class seats with sliding doors and upgraded premium economy and economy class cabins.

The backlash over the new business class seats has largely focused on their aesthetics.

Content creator and former Singapore Airlines cabin crew member Darshen Kuna was among the critics.

“As a PPS (Priority Passenger Service) Club member, I’m very loyal to you guys, but after I see the new business class seats, it’s very hard for me to be loyal,” he said on social media.

“You all spent more than S$2 billion for the new business class seats to look like what? Dental chairs?”

While he welcomed the sliding doors for added privacy, he took issue with the colour scheme, particularly the “green line” on each seat.

“I sit on that new business class seat, instantly I will think I’m seeing my dentist, which is not usually a good experience,” he said.

“So please, can you change the business class colour palette or not? It’s not too late because you all haven’t revamped yet.”

SIA is investing more than S$2 billion (US$1.57 billion) in the new cabin products across all four cabin classes, which it has described as “a key part of SIA’s elevated end-to-end travel experience”.

Aaron Wong, founder of travel website The MileLion, wrote after the unveiling that he was “still shaking [his] head at the business class colour scheme and aesthetics” and that the seats’ use of plastic did not feel very premium.

Wong also highlighted criticism from The MileLion’s Telegram group, with one reader likening the seats to Secretlab chairs.

Ben Schlappig, founder of travel website One Mile at a Time, said SIA had “botched” its business class finishes.

“It looks like Scoot and Spirit Airlines had a baby,” he said, referring to the SIA subsidiary and the now-defunct US carrier. Both are known for prominently using yellow in their branding.

He also described the finishes of the first class and business class products as “completely mismatched”, saying the latter looked “cheap”.

“I guess the argument from executives is that they want the cabin to look more modern and high tech, and go after a younger crowd, but I just don’t follow the logic,” Schlappig said on his website.

“What in the world happened to this business class seat?” said Max Do of Max Miles Points on social media.

“This neon yellow colour is not really part of the Singapore Airlines colour palette, and the light grey colours kind of just make it feel cheap.”

He also compared the seats to furnishings one would be more likely to see in doctors’ or dentists’ offices.

Not all reactions were negative, however. Some who tried the new seats praised their comfort and practical features.

MileLion’s Wong said he had “no complaints” about the functionality.

“The seat is comfortable – at least as comfortable as a seat can be for a 10-minute on-ground tour – and fixes a lot of the long-standing issues customers have had with the current 2013 business class seat,” he said on his website.

Singaporean singer-songwriter Tay Kewei, 43, said that “the privacy doors are the best part of the upgrade”.

In an online post showing her trying the new seats, she said: “Just the best in the business showing everyone how it’s done!”

In captions accompanying the video, she described the experience as being “cocooned in luxury with lumbar and leg support”.

However, she said: “I’m not sure why the seats are now not as wide as before, even though the footwell has now more space.”

Content creator Edo Lio, who tried the new seats, said that he “can see why some people are upset about the colour palette, as SQ has definitely strayed from the warmer, more traditional colours they usually use”.

However, the 29-year-old said that there was more to the seats than just the colours. He said he also enjoyed the added privacy the new business class seat doors provide, as well as the seats’ “ergonomics and space design”.

“I love Singapore Airlines for many reasons beyond just the aesthetic of the brand – among others, I find them reliable, I believe in their safety standards and find the overall experience of flying with them a pleasant one.

“These are all factors we must take into consideration when assessing them as a brand.”

The new cabin products will be progressively introduced from the second half of 2027 on the airline’s 41 retrofitted Airbus A350-900 long-haul and ultra-long-range aircraft, as well as its new Boeing 777-9 fleet.

The new first class cabins were designed by PriestmanGoode, while premium economy class and economy class cabins were designed by Factorydesign. The three cabin classes were manufactured by Collins Aerospace in collaboration with SIA.

According to SIA, the new cabin designs were informed by research involving more than 5,000 frequent travellers, customers, staff and industry experts worldwide.

In a social media video posted by user Zappchrisone, Designworks CEO Julia de Bono said that Singapore Airlines “wanted to go with something more progressive and refreshing”.

When asked about public reactions to the new colour palette, she described the design as “modern and fresh”, with the yellow accents “adding to the freshness”.

She noted that yellow already features in some of SIA’s design details, but said its use in the new business class cabin was “something that is not seen so much”.

Writing for aviation news website Runway Girl Network, Mary Kirby said the seats’ grey tones would “act almost like a blank canvas, reflecting virtually any LED cabin lighting cast upon them”.

“Clad in full-grain premium leather, the 1-2-1-configured seats are primed to undergo a continual visual transformation during boarding, mealtimes, bedtime and landing – and during simulated sunrises and sunsets,” she said.

“Ambient lighting within each mini-suite and custom embroidery on both the seat bottom and seat back will add further depth.

Former radio DJ Rosalyn Lee, who now organises tours and attended the unveiling, voiced approval for the seats, describing the reactions to their colour scheme as “wild”.

“Look. Singapore Airlines is our national carrier, so I completely understand why expectations are sky high and where the disappointment stems from,” she said on social media.

“But to get so worked up by a colour scheme is just wild.”

She added: “It’s literally just a colour palette. If a splash of yellow or a shade of grey gives you an existential crisis about your luxury status, then it really sounds like a you problem.”

She also took issue with what she saw as “disrespect” towards Scoot in the criticism, calling it one of the world’s best low-cost carriers.

Lee said the business class seat she tried out was “really, really comfortable” and had a “generous footwell” and enough space for bags.

She added: “If you think millions of dollars in customised ergonomic engineering, next-gen privacy doors and premium finishes look ‘cheap’ just because of a colour accent, you’re missing the forest for the trees.”

This story was first published by CNA

item.title: [SCMP] China, Russia and US try to nail down AI nuclear agenda in time for Apec talks
item.description:
Talks between China, the US and Russia could yield a commitment to control AI in nuclear arsenals as part of a broader agenda on global governance, sources told the South China Morning Post.

The three nations have engaged in weeks of back-and-forth discussion to nail down the agenda and protocol for talks between the countries’ leaders on the sidelines of the Apec summit in Shenzhen next week.

The sources said that the war in Ukraine and denuclearisation of the Korean peninsula had largely fallen off the table as possible topics, with the focus shifting to areas of potential consensus, particularly the role of artificial intelligence in nuclear command and control.
item.content:encoded:
Talks between China, the US and Russia could yield a commitment to control AI in nuclear arsenals as part of a broader agenda on global governance, sources told the South China Morning Post.

The three nations have engaged in weeks of back-and-forth discussion to nail down the agenda and protocol for talks between the countries’ leaders on the sidelines of the Apec summit in Shenzhen next week.

The sources said that the war in Ukraine and denuclearisation of the Korean peninsula had largely fallen off the table as possible topics, with the focus shifting to areas of potential consensus, particularly the role of artificial intelligence in nuclear command and control.

They said working-level teams had discussed AI in critical weapons systems, as well as a possible joint statement against any future nuclear war.

The US has also insisted on raising nuclear arms controls between the three countries, a suggestion that China has long rejected.

One of the sources said China offered discussions on nuclear transparency, likely as a lighter alternative to full strategic-stability talks.

The source said Beijing appeared to see progress on nuclear and strategic issues as a way to stabilise the overall relationship with the United States.

They also said China would prefer that any talks on Ukraine be held directly between the United States and Russia, and discussions about the Korean peninsula to be between the US and North Korea.

As a result, AI governance on nuclear weapons remained a safe but “stale” choice, an “easy deliverable”, and consistent with past policies, one source said.

Heather Williams, a senior fellow at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies, said a joint statement among the three affirming that a nuclear war could not be won and must never be fought was possible.

Williams noted that the three countries had already agreed to this language as part of the five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council. “But within the nuclear community, this phrase means a lot and carries a lot of weight.”

Missile-launch notification could also come up for discussion. China came in for heavy criticism in July when it tested a missile from a nuclear submarine without following standard notification practice for other countries.

Williams described an agreement on the issue as the “lowest-hanging fruit” for any substantive trilateral outcome.

In recent years the three powers have occasionally co-sponsored one another’s broader UN General Assembly resolutions on AI governance, most notably in 2024 when the US and China co-sponsored one another’s texts on safe, secure and trustworthy AI, and again on capacity-building, with Russia supporting the Chinese resolution.

Russia has been more cautious than China about formal curbs on AI in nuclear command and control. While engaging in broader discussions on the technology’s risks, Moscow has resisted commitments that could limit its military freedom of action and has not publicly endorsed the US-China position that humans must retain control over nuclear-use decisions.

Williams also pointed to “some sort of agreement on human control of nuclear weapons, nuclear command and control” as a possible outcome.

She added that Trump remained committed to sealing some form of cooperation with the other two powers on “superintelligence” to distinguish his efforts from those of the Joe Biden administration.

Trump and Xi discussed superintelligence in September. Biden, Trump’s predecessor, also addressed human control of nuclear weapons in 2023, when sources indicated that an agreement was within reach but fell apart at the last moment.
