Biden and Xi returned to the issue in Peru in 2024, with both sides issuing separate statements.

Trump has said he wants the meeting to focus on nuclear issues. Last month he said “we would have it to talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearisation” and that “we would schedule a meeting based on the denuclearisation, and that’s a very positive thing for the world”.

On Sunday, he said one of his meetings in China would likely involve both Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping and cover “a lot of things, including denuclearisation”.

Beijing has repeatedly said that its arsenal is much smaller than those of the other two and that Washington and Moscow should first substantially reduce their own forces before Beijing joins any such negotiations. China continues to adhere to a no-first-use policy and a self-defence nuclear strategy based on minimum deterrence.

Other proposals, considered less likely but still possible, include an agreement to prohibit cyber or AI-enabled attacks on nuclear command, control and communications systems.

While not interested in nuclear arms control talks, China was keen to explore some form of limits on strategic competition or the deployment of nuclear weapons in space, Williams said. Iran could also feature, with Trump likely to seek a joint statement affirming that Tehran must never acquire nuclear weapons.

Still, one source described progress towards next week’s trilateral talks as slow.

With one week until the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, scheduling might be a “hurdle” given all three leaders’ “packed calendars” during the November 18-19 meetings.

The three-way talks, framed by some as a “G3” gathering of the world’s three biggest nuclear powers, is also closely watched by other countries. There is growing unease among some middle powers about being left out without a say in shaping a new world order.

One source said that Japan, in particular, had raised concerns, wary that the three leaders could frame their cooperation in language evoking their wartime alliance against Japan, as Trump and Xi did during the Chinese leader’s state visit to Washington in September.

But hosting both the US and Russian presidents at a multilateral event would help Beijing cement its role as a major player in global governance and an international diplomatic hub. Another source said the Chinese side wanted the trilateral talks to be a major part of Xi’s diplomatic legacy.

Meanwhile, Trump’s interest in meeting Putin in Shenzhen was less about Ukraine and more about positioning himself as the leader who delivered nuclear peace, one source said.

Citing Trump’s preference for leader-to-leader diplomacy and high-profile geopolitical theatre, another person said the chance to appear alongside Xi and Putin was very appealing to the US leader, despite concerns in the US security and diplomacy establishments that Xi and Putin stood to gain more from the meeting.

For Putin, stuck in the quagmire of the Ukraine war, it was the opportunity to reestablish himself and Russia as a major global actor despite Western isolation, a source said.

item.title: [SCMP] How Asian-American campaigners helped turn the US deep-red South blue
item.description:
On tote bags distributed by Asian-owned businesses in the US state of Georgia, three Asian-American women appeared in a design inspired by the Three Ladies rice brand. The bags were part of a campaign that put a voting twist on the online “Asian baby girl” meme.

“We had an ‘Asian Ballot Girls’ campaign,” said Chany Chea, programme director of the Asian-American Advocacy Fund. “We had merch which went viral.”

As Democrats won races in Republican strongholds across the southern United States in last week’s midterm elections, Asian-American organisers in Georgia, Texas and North Carolina drew on years of local outreach efforts.
item.content:encoded:
On tote bags distributed by Asian-owned businesses in the US state of Georgia, three Asian-American women appeared in a design inspired by the Three Ladies rice brand. The bags were part of a campaign that put a voting twist on the online “Asian baby girl” meme.

“We had an ‘Asian Ballot Girls’ campaign,” said Chany Chea, programme director of the Asian-American Advocacy Fund. “We had merch which went viral.”

As Democrats won races in Republican strongholds across the southern United States in last week’s midterm elections, Asian-American organisers in Georgia, Texas and North Carolina drew on years of local outreach efforts.

In Georgia, that meant working with artists and shop owners. In Texas, it was to build a multilingual guide to the ballot. In North Carolina, it meant helping young people get involved before they were old enough to vote.

Beyond the governor’s race, in which Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms defeated her Republican opponent, Chea pointed to state Senate district 48 as another sign of Asian-American political growth in Georgia.

Few expected the district, which covers parts of Forsyth, Fulton and Gwinnett counties, to be competitive, but Chea’s group saw an opportunity and made 72,000 voter contact attempts there this year. Democrat Laura Murvartian went on to defeat Republican incumbent Shawn Still by 53 per cent to 47 per cent.

Georgia has around 300,000 eligible Asian-American voters, concentrated in some battleground areas, Chea said.

“We’ve spent years intentionally developing trusted leaders across our diverse [Asian-American and Pacific islander] communities here in Georgia,” Chea said. “This year we really leaned into those relationships.”

The group distributed door literature in seven Asian languages: Hindi, Chinese, Korean, Urdu, Vietnamese, Bangla and Tagalog. It also ran in-language digital and ethnic media ads, while its canvassing and phone-banking teams collectively represented nine languages.

Among other high-profile victories, Democrats James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa won a Texas Senate seat and the governorship, respectively. Roy Cooper flipped a North Carolina Senate seat, and Annie Andrews defeated Senator Darline Graham in South Carolina.

Graham was appointed to the seat in July following the unexpected death of her brother, Lindsey Graham. She also had the backing of US President Donald Trump.

Polling data supports the trend. A survey of 10,141 voters conducted by BSP Research and the African-American Research Collaborative from October 20 through to Election Day found that Asian-American respondents – 2,130 of those polled – backed Democratic candidates over Republicans by 64 per cent to 33 per cent nationwide.

Taeku Lee, a Harvard professor of government who worked on the poll, said the results were similar among Asian-American voters in the South, who favoured Democrats by 62 per cent to 35 per cent. He did not specify how many Asian-American respondents were from the South.

Texas: a hard-fought battle

Talarico’s win was among the most high-profile Senate victories for the Democrats. It shattered a Republican stronghold in Texas, where no Democratic candidate has won a Senate race since 1988, and the party had been locked out of statewide office entirely since 1994.

Texas has about 19 million voters, including some 1.2 million eligible Asian-American voters, Stephanie Cho, executive director of the Asian-American Texas Action Fund, said. Many live in the Houston and Dallas areas, with smaller communities in Austin and San Antonio.

The Asians for Talarico group knocked on 70,000 doors, made 300,000 calls and sent 300,000 MMS messages, according to Asian Texans for Justice Action Fund. “Nearly seven out of every 10 Asian voters canvassed said yes to Talarico,” it wrote in a media release.

Alice Yi, co-founder of Asian Texans for Justice, began registering Asian voters in Texas more than a decade ago. In 2012, about 17 per cent of the Asian population was registered to vote in the state, but by 2024, that figure had climbed to over 68 per cent, according to Yi.

“This is not just this year,” she said. “This is over a decade of advocacy, and community in coalition building, and education.”

New York Times data show that Asian-American voters in the Texas Senate race backed Talarico over Republican Ken Paxton by 69 per cent to 30 per cent. The estimates draw on the Times/Siena poll, precinct-level election results and voter file data, among other sources.

In addition to door knocks, calls and MMS messages, Asian Texans for Justice also leaned into digital and YouTube advertising, as well as Google search, leading up to the election.

“I also found so many first-time young Asian voters, which is very rewarding,” Yi said.

Asian Texans for Justice also offered a “Ballot Builder” online tool on its website. It allowed voters to see who was running, learn what each race is about, and save their picks, all in their preferred language.

“That is a big help for the people who don’t understand the English language,” she added.

The Chinese community in Texas was split around 50/50 between Democrats and Republicans in 2016, Yi said, but this year it is expected to “swing about 65 per cent” with the economy the key issue for voters.

“Our Asian community really did have a swing vote, and had the margin of victory,” she said. “Almost 30 years involved in Texas politics, I feel like finally, my job is well done.”

Cho stressed the importance of year-round engagement, including cultural events rather than activities focused solely on work.

She said the anti-trans, anti-China and anti-Muslim rhetoric in many of the campaign ads running across the South had ultimately backfired.

“The extreme racism and the extreme anti-trans rhetoric really backfired,” she said. “It soured people because it was too extreme. What I was hearing a lot is that most people don’t want to hear that.”

North Carolina: playing the long game

Shruti Parikh, director of education and political engagement at North Carolina Asian-American Together in Action, credited the results to “playing the long game” by engaging young people.

This meant engaging this demographic before they were eligible to vote, training young leaders, registering first-time voters and helping people see democracy as a habit rather than something to participate in only every two to four years.

Asian-Americans are the state’s fastest-growing electorate, with about 150,000 registered voters, she said.

“We had wins from the top of the ticket down to the state and local races,” she said. “That was very exciting for us.”

Asian-American turnout more than doubled in 2022, she said, while early voting among younger Asian-American voters this year was 145 per cent higher than in 2022.

She cited a recent survey of 744 Asian-American voters statewide, in which 68 per cent said North Carolina officials listened to their needs “not much” or “not at all”. The group responded by expanding its in-language educational materials.

The organisation reached 100,000 voters during early voting and ran a multilingual hotline that received more than 150 calls over the 17 days of early voting and on election day.

“This kind of infrastructure matters, and it doesn’t come overnight,” Parikh said. “These community organisations were there before the campaign ads started, and we’re there after election day as well.”

item.title: [SCMP] Will Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair become another ‘spy balloon’ saga for US-China ties?
item.description:
China hawks in Washington could weaponise allegations that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by Chinese intelligence, despite denials from Beijing, Chinese experts warn.

They said controversy would give US hardliners fresh ammunition to push for tougher curbs on AI chip exports to China.

One of them compared the potential fallout to the 2023 “spy balloon” incident, when the US shot down in its airspace what Beijing said was an off-course weather balloon, putting relations on ice for months.
item.content:encoded:
China hawks in Washington could weaponise allegations that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by Chinese intelligence, despite denials from Beijing, Chinese experts warn.

They said controversy would give US hardliners fresh ammunition to push for tougher curbs on AI chip exports to China.

One of them compared the potential fallout to the 2023 “spy balloon” incident, when the US shot down in its airspace what Beijing said was an off-course weather balloon, putting relations on ice for months.

Huang admitted over the weekend to having an extramarital affair after the New York Times reported that a Chinese businesswoman with whom he had close ties might have been working for Beijing’s intelligence services. Beijing has rejected the espionage claims as “groundless fabrication designed to smear China”.

The report identified the woman as Alice Huang, or Huang Le, chief executive of a Singapore-based data centre company.

More restrictions on chip exports?

The revelations come amid an already aggressive US campaign to restrict China’s access to cutting-edge chips. Washington has already barred direct exports of the most advanced American AI chips to China, including Nvidia’s flagship Blackwell and Rubin graphics processing units or GPUs.

Analysts in China say the controversy will only intensify the US regulatory clampdown, even if no formal espionage charges are filed.

Zhu Feng, dean of Nanjing University’s school of international studies, expects heightened AI decoupling and an “increased crackdown” on China’s hi-tech sectors.

“What’s important now is that committees in both the Senate and the House [of Representatives] will have hearings and investigations on this. So my view on this matter is simple: it will become another balloon event in China-US relations,” he said.

“The key is not the investigation result; the process of the investigation itself will bring on another anti-China wave,” Zhu said, adding that congressional hawks would seize the moment to demand wider export controls and harsher restrictions against Chinese AI platforms.

Ties hinge on US response

Xin Qiang, a professor and deputy director of the Centre for American Studies at Fudan University, said regardless of whether the allegations led to formal charges, the controversy would still weigh on China-US ties, even though the impact might not be too severe.

“It won’t come to the degree of derailing China-US relations,” he said, pointing to the balloon incident as precedent for how tensions might ease once the media frenzy subsided.

However, he warned that the fallout could hit Nvidia’s chip exports to China directly. The US was likely to tighten oversight even for less advanced processors, he said, enforcing stricter end-user checks and tracking of chips routed through third countries.

“The two countries’ efforts to cooperate on AI governance, which was mentioned during the Xi–Trump summit, will also become more difficult,” Xin added, referring to the Chinese president’s state visit to Washington in September.

Sun Chenghao, a fellow with Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy, also said the controversy was unlikely to trigger a diplomatic crisis comparable to the 2023 balloon incident, as there was no public evidence establishing Chinese government involvement.

However, it could intensify scrutiny of semiconductor exports and disrupt trade talks, he warned. “If the relevant restrictions are written into law, Trump’s room to adjust chip licences in negotiations with China will narrow,” Sun said.

The greatest impact would be on industrial cooperation, he added, with tighter checks on chip purchases, cloud computing and joint research.

“This is a test of whether China and the United States can maintain strategic stability amid intensifying technological competition.”

The Huang scandal broke just days before US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping are expected to meet on the sidelines of next week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, southern China.

Huang was part of the US delegation during Trump’s May state visit to Beijing. Four months later, the tech billionaire and his wife, Lori, sat alongside Xi at the head table during a White House state dinner hosted by Trump.

On Monday, Trump defended the Nvidia chief as “an honourable guy” who had done an “amazing job for our country”.

Trump said he asked Huang directly whether he knew Alice Huang was a foreign spy. “He said ‘I had no idea that she was a spy’ and I really believe him,” Trump told reporters.

Trump has said he is open to bringing Huang with him to Shenzhen.

Huang has long lobbied against stricter controls on AI chip exports to China, arguing that blanket bans could force Beijing to fast-track domestic alternatives such as Huawei Technologies.

Zhu said: “What happens next will depend on how the Trump administration responds, what kind of scrutiny the relevant committees in the US House of Representatives and Senate undertake, and what legislation they might pass.”

Three House Republican committee chairs have asked Huang to attend a closed-door joint briefing on November 18 regarding Nvidia’s “security protocols against foreign adversary espionage”, though it remains unclear whether he will appear.

Is it racial bias?

Prominent neurobiologist and Peking University professor Rao Yi said the uproar exposed double standards rooted in racial bias against ethnic Chinese in the United States.

In a social media post on Tuesday, Rao said that while white tycoons rarely faced questions over national allegiance in similar scandals, Huang’s personal situation had quickly been elevated into a national security crisis.

“Is an affair with a Chinese person a national security issue? Why wasn’t [Australian-born US media mogul Rupert] Murdoch’s case treated the same way? Is it because the person involved was white, so no national security problem would arise, and his media would not be ‘coloured’ as Chinese media?” Rao posted, referring to Murdoch’s 1999 marriage to China-born Wendi Deng. The pair divorced in 2013.

“For an ethnic Chinese person, however, intelligence agencies monitor their private life, US government sources leak it to the press, and investigations immediately follow,” Rao wrote.

Silicon Valley precedents

American technology executives have previously faced public scrutiny over extramarital affairs and workplace relationships, with revelations involving Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates and Amazon founder Jeff Bezos attracting widespread media attention. But those scandals never amounted to much more than tabloid fodder.

Gates, whose 27-year marriage to Melinda French Gates ended in 2021, acknowledged three extramarital affairs during testimony before the US House Oversight Committee in June this year as part of its investigation into convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Bezos’ relationship with TV presenter Lauren Sanchez emerged during his 2019 divorce from MacKenzie Scott. He and Sanchez married in June last year.

Additional reporting by Caroline Lin

item.title: [SCMP] Lithuanian president confirms talks on renaming Taiwan office in diplomatic U-turn
item.description:
Lithuania is in talks with Taiwan over changing the name of a controversial representative office in Vilnius, with its president saying the government is “not obligated” to follow policies that predate it.

Gitanas Nauseda, speaking to the state broadcaster LRT on Monday night, confirmed that the Baltic state’s foreign ministry had sent a letter to Taiwan’s representatives asking to recalibrate the relationship.

“Without a doubt, we are coordinating and, without a doubt, the new ruling majority is not obligated to somehow continue the policy of the former ruling majority,” Nauseda said, adding that “changing the name of the Taiwan mission is … only part of the whole picture and far from the most significant”.
item.content:encoded:
Lithuania is in talks with Taiwan over changing the name of a controversial representative office in Vilnius, with its president saying the government is “not obligated” to follow policies that predate it.

Gitanas Nauseda, speaking to the state broadcaster LRT on Monday night, confirmed that the Baltic state’s foreign ministry had sent a letter to Taiwan’s representatives asking to recalibrate the relationship.

“Without a doubt, we are coordinating and, without a doubt, the new ruling majority is not obligated to somehow continue the policy of the former ruling majority,” Nauseda said, adding that “changing the name of the Taiwan mission is … only part of the whole picture and far from the most significant”.

The leader was talking following local media reports that the foreign ministry had asked Taipei to change the name before Beijing’s National Day last month.

The twist comes as Vilnius seeks to restore diplomatic ties with Beijing, which have been frozen since the opening of the office in 2021.

Reports in Delfi, a Lithuanian news portal, on Monday said a deputy foreign minister delivered a letter to Taipei’s representatives – including the head of the “Taiwanese Representative Office” – on September 24, asking them to change the office’s name by October 1.

According to the report, Lithuania offered to send a vice-ministerial delegation to Taipei in exchange and sign agreements on investment and taxation.

Nauseda downplayed the significance of the saga but insisted that it should have been done publicly rather than through backchannels.

“I honestly don’t understand why it needs to be made into a special secret, because all of this could have been publicly known from the very beginning,” the president said.

Beijing delegation heading to Lithuania in sign of thaw

Meanwhile, a delegation of diplomats from Beijing is due to land in Vilnius on Wednesday for two days of meetings, in a further sign of a thaw.

Meetings are expected with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, but not at ministerial level, the South China Morning Post understands.

Nauseda – who said nobody from his office would meet the visiting party – said the visit will help determine the trajectory of the normalisation process.

“We will probably have fairly clear conversations about what the expectations of both sides are, and I very much hope that we will be able to gradually restore normal diplomatic cooperation.”

Earlier on Monday, Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys confirmed talks with Taipei were ongoing even if he said the information had been “inaccurately presented”.

“I confirm that we have spoken with the Taiwanese side about various aspects of our relations, maintaining the foundation – which is constructive cooperation and utilising the full potential of our capabilities,” Budrys was quoted as saying in LNK Zinių, another Lithuanian media outlet.

“We talked about various aspects,” he added, when asked they had requested Taipei to change the name of the mission.

The Lithuanian foreign ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment, nor did China’s.

Representatives of Taipei did not respond to questions about whether the office name had been or would be changed, but told local news portal 15min that it did not intend to change the name.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China and has not ruled out the use of force to reunify it. Most countries, including Lithuania and the rest of the European Union, do not recognise the self-ruled island as an independent state.

However, the EU states that it wishes to expand business and cultural ties with Taipei, short of diplomatic recognition.

China-EU relations were hit by opening of Vilnius’ Taiwan office

While Taiwan retains a diplomatic presence in other European countries, Lithuania is the only place to feature “Taiwanese” in the name. In other capitals, it bears the name Taipei.

After the office was opened in 2021, China removed Lithuania from its customs system, meaning Lithuanian exporters could not ship goods to the country.

Beijing claimed Vilnius had violated the EU’s one-China policy and expelled its ambassador in 2021, while also withdrawing its own envoy from Lithuania.

It also deepened tensions between the EU and China, which worsened further because of Beijing’s close relationship with Russia.

The EU has said that Lithuania had not breached its one-China policy and launched a World Trade Organization case against the trade embargo, although that case was subsequently dropped.

Since the Social Democrat-led Lithuanian government took office in 2024, it has tried to smooth relations with China.

Successive centre-left prime ministers have also condemned the previous centre-right leadership’s decision to open the office, claiming that Vilnius got little in return.

EU sources said, however, that whenever delegations from Lithuania had gone to Beijing in an effort to normalise ties, they had been told they would have to accept all of China’s terms, including changing the name of the office.

In a post on its Facebook page last Friday, the “Taiwanese Representative Office” in Vilnius wrote: “We believe that public discussions concerning Taiwan-Lithuania relations should be grounded in verifiable facts rather than unsubstantiated assumptions or speculation.”

Speaking earlier on Monday, Nauseda again tried to play down the significance of the stories, even if he did not deny their substance.

“I repeat once again, we want to restore normal relations [with Beijing] and maintain normal relations with Taiwan,” Nauseda said, according to Lithuanian National Radio and Television (LRT).

“We’ll see, we’ll wait, we’ll see,” he replied when asked whether Vilnius wanted to see the name changed.

“Now we have a meeting with Chinese diplomats and then we will see, we will move forward,” he said, adding that he wished to restore relations with Beijing to the level of “diplomatic hygiene”.

“The issue of the Taiwanese mission, yes, is a linguistic issue; it was expected that it would provide large political dividends for Lithuania. There was talk of big things that would start in 2021,” LRT quoted Nauseda as saying.

“This did not happen, so one of our goals is not only to talk about the names of the mission, but also about the reasons why this did not happen”

item.title: [SCMP] Abby Choi’s ex-brother-in-law tells court he treated her like a ‘biological sibling’
item.description:
The former brother-in-law of slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung has said he treated her like a biological sibling and that she had maintained a “very close” relationship with her ex-husband after he absconded ahead of a trial for his alleged role in a HK$6.3 million theft case.

Testifying in the High Court for the first time on Monday, Anthony Kwong Kong-kit also claimed that Choi’s mother had provided his younger brother with a hideout in her native Hainan province after he illegally left Hong Kong on a speedboat in June 2015 to evade criminal proceedings.

The 35-year-old is contesting a joint count of murder for allegedly conspiring to kill the influencer alongside his father Kwong Kau, 68, and his younger brother Alex Kwong Kong-chi, 31, on February 21, 2023.
item.content:encoded:
The former brother-in-law of slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung has said he treated her like a biological sibling and that she had maintained a “very close” relationship with her ex-husband after he absconded ahead of a trial for his alleged role in a HK$6.3 million theft case.

Testifying in the High Court for the first time on Monday, Anthony Kwong Kong-kit also claimed that Choi’s mother had provided his younger brother with a hideout in her native Hainan province after he illegally left Hong Kong on a speedboat in June 2015 to evade criminal proceedings.

The 35-year-old is contesting a joint count of murder for allegedly conspiring to kill the influencer alongside his father Kwong Kau, 68, and his younger brother Alex Kwong Kong-chi, 31, on February 21, 2023.

The Kwong brothers admitted to preventing the burial of the 28-year-old model’s body before the trial began in late September. Kwong Kau, a retired police sergeant, also pleaded guilty to the charge midway through the trial.

Prosecutors contended that Anthony was behind the wheel on February 21, when his brother attacked Choi with a hammer in the back seat of their car. The brothers allegedly led Choi to believe they were on their way to pick up her eight-year-old daughter from her international school in Pak Shek Kok.

Parts of Choi’s dismembered remains, including her head and legs, were discovered in a 600 square foot rental flat in Tai Po’s Lung Mei village three days later.

Opening the defence’s case on Monday, Anthony’s legal counsel, Trevor Beel, highlighted his client’s close relationship with the deceased as he sought to counter accusations that he had clung onto his former in-law’s wealth before the alleged offences.

The court heard Anthony, who said he preferred to be addressed as Damon, had primarily relied on his father’s retirement savings and his mother’s earnings from her boutique business to pursue a degree in the United States between 2011 and 2015.

He said he had planned to stay in the country after completing a two-year economics degree at the University of California, Irvine.

But he was forced to return to Hong Kong in May 2015 after his mother told him his brother had become involved in a theft case, the court heard.

Anthony said he was asked to look after his nephew and niece, who were both infants at the time, in case Alex “went away” to mainland China.

According to Anthony, Choi’s mother, Cheung Yin-fa, made arrangements to pick up Alex and provided him with accommodation in Hainan after he illegally entered the mainland in June 2015.

Anthony said Choi had maintained regular contact with the father of her first two children while being aware that he had been wanted by police. She would talk to him daily through video calls and meet him in person during leisure trips on the mainland, the defendant added.

Anthony said his brother started investing in real estate projects across the border after he became acquainted with people whom he described as “capable and rather wealthy”.

Alex regularly sent part of his investment profits to a Hong Kong money exchange shop, and Anthony would collect it and give it to Choi, the court heard.

The defendant also told the court that Alex and Choi had been supporting their two children financially until 2023 through earnings from investments on the mainland and from reselling luxury watches.

Anthony said he was not close to Choi at first and did not realise she had broken up with his brother in 2015. When she became pregnant the following year, he initially thought the baby belonged to Alex instead of her new partner, Chris Tam Fong-chun.

The defendant said his relationship with Choi became closer after his brother’s departure.

“I did not want the children [between Alex and Choi] to grow without paternal love, so I spent most of my time with them unless I had other engagements with friends,” he said.

“I saw Abby every day and as time went by, month after month and year after year, naturally the family bond developed … The bond between us became like one shared by biological siblings.”

Anthony said his relationship with Choi and Tam became so close that they would go out for meals five days a week, and that he would regularly join gatherings with the couple and their friends, who included company owners and investment bankers.

But he said neither Tam nor the couple’s friends knew his humble background or that he was living at a subsidised flat in Tsuen Wan’s Sheung Man Court.

“Abby cared more about her face. She liked people around her to look relatively wealthy in order not to damage her reputation,” he said.

The influencer also allegedly asked Anthony to lie about his residential address by claiming he was living at the Ocean Pride development near Tsuen Wan West station.

Cheung previously told the court that Anthony coaxed her daughter into funding an egg waffle shop he operated in 2021 and 2022.

Anthony on Monday maintained that the shop in Sham Shui Po was opened at the model’s suggestion to kill time because they both had nothing to do during the Covid-19 pandemic. He said Choi had invested HK$600,000 in the shop, which constantly ran at a loss before he sold it in April 2022.

Questioned why the influencer did not ask her partner Tam to run the business, Anthony said he “did not really work at all”.

He also alleged that Choi’s former chauffeur, Chin Kei-shun, had stolen the store’s profits twice when he was asked to deposit the cash into the shop’s bank account.

In a family meeting with Anthony and his mother, Choi decided against dismissing Chin or reporting the matter to police. The model found Chin was “doing quite well” and that he was always punctual to collect her children from school, Anthony said.

Chin, who gave evidence in an earlier court session, said Choi appeared to run into cash-flow difficulties after she and Tam incurred a HK$5 million (US$637,090) debt during a leisure trip to Macau in August 2021.

Anthony corroborated the driver’s account, saying Choi had borrowed money from him personally while seeking a HK$600,000 loan from his uncle.

Beel pointed out that Choi could have borrowed money from her mother, but the defendant said: “Her mother would borrow money from her, but she would not lend any money to her.”

The trial continues before Deputy Judge Brian Keith and a nine-member jury.

item.title: [SCMP] China’s tech funding divide faces test as fears of an AI bubble rattle markets
item.description:
For Jason Wang, a media operator based in Zhengzhou in central China’s Henan province, switching his long-held investment strategy of buying gold to tech-themed funds was a bittersweet decision.

The 28-year-old retail investor, who has no idea about tech company fundamentals, started buying tech funds – focused on China’s semiconductors, robotics and similar sectors – at the end of last year amid a bull run that lasted until the middle of this year.

Watching returns on his semiconductor funds surge to a peak of 170 per cent before plunging to just over 10 per cent recently has been an emotional roller coaster.
item.content:encoded:
For Jason Wang, a media operator based in Zhengzhou in central China’s Henan province, switching his long-held investment strategy of buying gold to tech-themed funds was a bittersweet decision.

The 28-year-old retail investor, who has no idea about tech company fundamentals, started buying tech funds – focused on China’s semiconductors, robotics and similar sectors – at the end of last year amid a bull run that lasted until the middle of this year.

Watching returns on his semiconductor funds surge to a peak of 170 per cent before plunging to just over 10 per cent recently has been an emotional roller coaster.

“It’s easy to imagine how painful it must be for people who bought near the peak,” he said, adding that he only stopped buying the dip recently when some stocks kept falling with no sign of rebounding. “I was naive and had never been tested by market swings.”

Meanwhile, industry insiders and professional investors, who had been flocking to artificial intelligence, semiconductors and robotics companies over the past few years – a trend that added to those firms’ ever-growing valuations – are sharing the same concern over market turbulence with retail investors like Wang.

A founder at a Shanghai-based tech company focusing on AI-powered video gaming, who declined to be named, said that it was “absolutely terrifying to wake up and see all stock markets plunge”.

Amid a global bloodbath in tech stocks exacerbated by concerns over the future of the US AI infrastructure buildout following a “blue wave” of Democratic Party victories in the midterm elections, listed tech firms in Shanghai and Hong Kong have also been battered by a wave of selling in recent months.

Shanghai’s Star 50 Index, which tracks 50 leading companies on China’s Nasdaq-style technology board, had plunged nearly 50 per cent from its late-June peak by November 3. And Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Tech Index fell 11.7 per cent in October alone, bringing its losses for the year to nearly 32 per cent as of October 30.

The Shanghai start-up founder said that he worried the volatility would deal a blow to public companies and deter others from going public in the next few years.

The technology industries in the US and China – the two leading powers of the AI era – had both enjoyed the recent frenzy of high valuations and, in the downturn, are facing the same fears of an AI bubble.

However, the US tech sector had withstood boom-bust cycles before, including the dotcom bubble in the late 1990s and 2000s, and the 2008 global financial crisis, while the Chinese tech industry is too young to have experienced those.

The question at present is how the current storm will play out to reshape funding dynamics across the Chinese landscape.

Analysts said China’s technology industry faced a growing test of its ability to sustain investment amid intensifying competition with the US, as recent developments threatened to widen the funding gap between its national champions and smaller players.

Chelsey Tam, senior equity analyst at Morningstar, said current market conditions would make it more difficult for local tech firms to raise capital, either through initial public offerings (IPOs) or private investments. Nevertheless, she said it still made sense for companies to tap channels such as equity or debt markets as long as they were “fairly or still overvalued after the share price decline”.

The ability to raise capital has become increasingly uneven, with investors favouring established technology giants over smaller, cash-strapped start-ups.

“We do see a crowding-out effect … as capital providers prefer backing AI initiatives housed inside cash-generative incumbents over stand-alone, loss-making start-ups,” said Ivan Su, Morningstar’s director of equity research.

A Beijing-based investor at a state-backed venture capital company said his firm had already stopped backing consumer-facing AI agent start-ups, focusing instead on business applications that could deliver measurable productivity benefits with a clear revenue path.

The investor, who requested anonymity due to the sensitivity of the topic, said the current sell-off was exacerbated by heavy institutional holdings in previously surging computing and semiconductor stocks, with losses now spreading across the technology supply chain.

The rout was weighing on some start-ups’ funding, according to Lin Jie, managing partner at Fuzhou-based Pioteer Investment.

Early-stage, highly valuable and cash-burning hard-tech companies would also be under apparent pressure, with some companies’ funding cycles extended from three months to up to a year.

Our assessment of the companies remains unchanged, but we will adjust the pace of our investments

Lin Jie, managing partner at Pioteer Investment

Furthermore, investors should get used to “value discounting” as the venture market would now benchmark against the stock market, according to Lin.

Still, Lin argued, the current market sell-off was not a replay of the last dotcom bubble but more likely a “healthy correction” following a sharp rally in technology stocks, particularly in computing infrastructure, optical components, semiconductors and memory chips.

“Our assessment of the companies remains unchanged, but we will adjust the pace of our investments,” he said, adding that long-term trends such as AI infrastructure expansion and semiconductor self-sufficiency remained intact.

For the US market, anxiety over returns came against the backdrop of an unprecedented infrastructure build-out worldwide, exacerbated by fears that the sweeping midterm election victory by the Democrats could derail its AI data centre construction campaign, which some estimated to be as high as US$10 trillion over the next five years.

By comparison, capital expenditure on AI infrastructure among 13 major Chinese companies is projected to surge 103 per cent this year to 932 billion yuan (US$139.6 billion), before exceeding 1.2 trillion yuan in 2027, according to a September study by research firm Rhodium Group.

The firm noted that China’s AI industry faces different financial risks from those in the US, reflecting its greater reliance on equity financing and bank loans to fund AI infrastructure, compared with American technology companies’ increasing use of bond markets.

In the Chinese public equity market, among the hardest hit were optical component suppliers Eoptolink Technology, Suzhou TFC Communication and Zhongji Innolight, whose shares fell around 55 per cent, 53 per cent and 44 per cent, respectively, between October 8 and November 9. Fears of slower AI growth overshadowed the upbeat earnings.

Another example was Chinese AI chip developer Biren Technology’s October fundraising. It raised about HK$4 billion (US$510 million) through a share placement priced nearly one-third below that of a similar placement in July.

In China’s embodied AI sector, financing fell to 33.3 billion yuan across 185 deals in the third quarter, from a quarterly average of 46.8 billion yuan in the first half, according to data compiled by start-up database platform ITJuzi.com and cited by local outlet Yicai.

“Financing channels for smaller projects that lack the ability to generate sustainable cash flow are narrowing, making it increasingly hard for them to survive independently,” Miao Tianyi, managing partner at Puzhuo Capital, was quoted as saying in the Yicai report this week.

Miao expected mergers and acquisitions to become increasingly important as smaller players struggled to secure fresh capital.

Start-ups face another obstacle to securing capital: a slowdown in IPOs, a crucial exit route for venture capital and private equity investors.

China’s three mainland stock exchanges in Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing accepted 242 IPO applications in the first half of 2026, compared with just six from July to early November, according to a report by Yicai on Wednesday.

In Hong Kong, about one-in-four planned IPOs failed to reach completion so far this year, the highest proportion since the 2008 global financial crisis, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. The unfinished offerings included deals that were postponed, withdrawn or allowed to lapse.

The funding squeeze came as Beijing sought to steer more capital towards strategically important technologies, while cracking down on indiscriminate investment, highlighting the challenge of supporting smaller innovators without encouraging wasteful spending.

At a November 3 press conference, Ren Zhongbao, deputy director of the National Development and Reform Commission’s Department of Innovation and High-Tech Development, warned that some local governments were crowding into the same emerging industries, calling for stronger national coordination and investment based on regional strengths.

Yet policymakers remain committed to expanding financing support for emerging industries and, by comparison, the rout has done little to deter investment in China’s leading AI players.

DeepSeek, a leading Chinese rival to US frontier AI labs, has raised about 100 billion yuan in its most recent funding round from investors including chipmaker GigaDevice, according to a Reuters report on October 22, citing unidentified people. Local media reports suggested state-backed investors contributed a significant share.

DeepSeek has not publicly confirmed the transaction. The Hangzhou-based company did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Amid the market turmoil, some of China’s national champions have sought to reassure investors about their prospects, pointing to robust earnings and sustained demand for AI-related products. They also pledged to buy back shares to shore up confidence.

Chinese AI chipmaker Cambricon Technologies said strong demand for computing power would support its long-term growth despite short-term share-price volatility.

ChangXin Technology, the nation’s No 1 memory chipmaker, forecast continued revenue growth in the fourth quarter, while semiconductor equipment supplier Advanced Micro-Fabrication Equipment proposed a share buy-back worth up to 500 million yuan.

According to a tally by Chinese media outlet Financial News, companies listed on Shanghai’s Star Market had disclosed 183 new share buy-back and shareholding-increase plans as of November 2, with a combined maximum value of 24.27 billion yuan.

On Friday, after a US tech sell-off that sent the Nasdaq 100 index down 6.4 per cent – the biggest drop in six years – Beijing called for more efforts to stabilise the stock market in a State Council executive meeting chaired by Premier Li Qiang.

“The different financing channels imply the two sides are constrained by different factors – China by government excess and the US by market pushback,” said Charles Chang, Greater China country lead for corporates at S&P Global Ratings.

Lu Ting, chief China economist at Nomura, said in a note on Friday that unlike the fragmented and politically contentious power grid landscape in the US, China’s domestic data centre expansion was guided by centralised state coordination.

“China is advancing a massive, state-orchestrated push to build a nationwide network of AI data centres, spearheaded by the 15th five-year blueprint,” he said, adding that the “blue wave” in the US election could overall benefit China’s AI economy.

Michael Zhang, a Shanghai-based investor who has traded mainland Chinese stocks for more than two decades, said his portfolio had swung from a 50 per cent gain earlier this year to a 20 per cent loss.

“I lost 5 per cent today alone,” he said. “With 1.2 million yuan in capital, that’s 60,000 yuan gone in a single day.”

But as a seasoned retail investor, Zhang said he remained cautiously optimistic, because he had confidence that government intervention would come.

Additional reporting by Mia Nurmamat, Ann Cao and Sherry Wang

item.title: [SCMP] Indonesians furious as Batam data centres drain taps: ‘we cannot cook without water’
item.description:
Cooking and bathing became difficult when taps ran dry in Batam, an Indonesian island where residents are protesting against data centres springing up to power the global artificial intelligence boom.

The area had suffered a “long drought” caused by low rainfall, the local water utility operator said, as a strong El Nino cycle exacerbates dry weather.

But, as in other countries, anger has been directed at the data centres, warehouse-like facilities that keep apps and AI tools running, with water often used to cool their humming servers.
item.content:encoded:
Cooking and bathing became difficult when taps ran dry in Batam, an Indonesian island where residents are protesting against data centres springing up to power the global artificial intelligence boom.

The area had suffered a “long drought” caused by low rainfall, the local water utility operator said, as a strong El Nino cycle exacerbates dry weather.

But, as in other countries, anger has been directed at the data centres, warehouse-like facilities that keep apps and AI tools running, with water often used to cool their humming servers.

Frustration is bubbling over in Indonesia and Malaysia, especially in regions bordering Singapore that are seen as a prime location for new tech facilities.

At first the main reaction was, “thank God industry is coming” to Batam, 54-year-old tradesman Juniardi Adinda Sembiring Gurukinayan said.

But severe recent outages hitting the municipal water service in some Batam communities meant “sometimes I skipped my shower”.

“We cannot eat rice without water. We cannot cook vegetables without water,” he said.

At the worst point, dozens of angry residents staged spontaneous protests outside Nongsa Digital Park, a new cluster of data centres and other amenities, designated a special economic zone.

People in the district believe “that the water shortages are related to the construction of data centres”, Juniardi said.

The drought caused the nearby Nongsa Reservoir to run very low and supply systems were further disrupted by an electrical fault, said Ginda Alamsyah, a spokesman for water utility operator Air Batam Hilir (ABH).

The tech park receives water from a different source, Duriangkang Reservoir, an industry source said.

Authorities in late September told developers they must build plants to desalinate seawater for cooling, to avoid straining local resources.

Companies behind operational or planned data centres at Nongsa Digital Park include the Singapore-headquartered BW Digital, DayOne and Princeton Digital Group.

Another owner, Hong Kong-based Gaw Capital Partners, said it was “aware of the distress and frustration expressed by local residents in Nongsa and surrounding Batam communities” over water shortages.

To ensure sustainable operations, “our data centre facilities must deploy a combination of advanced engineering, efficient architectural designs and renewable energy sourcing”, it said.

That includes using so-called closed-loop water systems that reuse resources and so require less fresh liquid.

As residents demanded a return to normal water supply at one protest last month, a police officer filled up buckets they had brought to Nongsa Digital Park.

In nearby coastal village Mata Ikan, people had to use seawater to wash after defecating, said demonstrator Rahmat, 52, who like many Indonesians goes by one name.

“The water crisis has been going on for the past year, but it got worse in the last six months,” 38-year-old Sulastri said at her home, where supply was out, so she poured water from a plastic bottle to wash dishes.

“Many of us here run small stalls. We used to make ice cubes, but we can’t any more.”

The government has been distributing water from tanks driven around, but Sulastri said it was “smelly” and “yellowish”.

Local government BP Batam and Indonesia’s Ministry for Economic Affairs, which regulates Nongsa Digital Park, declined to comment.

Recent disruption to water distribution “was not caused by data centres or AI or investors entering that sector”, Amsakar Achmad, Batam mayor and head of BP Batam, said in October, according to local media.

The decline in water supply was instead “due to weather and climate factors”, he said.

Data centre capacity in Southeast Asia is projected to triple from 2025 levels by 2030, driven by a tenfold surge in AI use, according to a KPMG report.

This can put pressure on water supplies, but also electricity grids still heavily reliant on planet-warming fossil fuels.

The data centre construction boom in Indonesia and Malaysia began when resource constraints led hyper-connected Singapore to halt new developments between 2019 and 2022.

It has since ramped up, boosting both countries’ economies as governments and tech giants pour hundreds of billions of dollars into training and running AI.

Ginda said water provider ABH supports policies to encourage investment and development in Batam, south of Singapore and connected to it by undersea cables.

But he added that water demand must be managed properly, adding that ABH is trying to boost the capacity of Batam’s six reservoirs by dredging them, with cloud seeding another option in dry periods.

North of Singapore, Malaysia’s Johor region has become “one of the largest emerging AI infrastructure clusters in the world”, according to researcher James Chai of the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute.

Just half a decade ago, Johor hosted 10 megawatts of data centre capacity. That has ballooned by a factor of 200 to 2.1 gigawatts today, Chai said.

The environmental cost could be high.

By 2035, data centres are forecast to swallow up one-third of Malaysia’s total energy consumption, the deputy prime minister told parliament in July.

The government said at that time it would only approve data centre projects after ensuring sufficient energy and water supply capacity.

Johor residents have protested against dust pollution and flash floods linked to data centre construction, as operators build closer to residential areas.

“Johor is at a critical inflection point,” Mohd Fadhil Md Din of Malaysia’s University of Technology said.

He said “it has the potential to become Southeast Asia’s leading sustainable data centre hub”, but only if it manages resources and spatial planning carefully.

Pushback sometimes works.

In Kota Damansara on the outskirts of Kuala Lumpur, a plot of land intended for a data centre remains empty after local opposition.

The developer withdrew its planning permission application in August after its neighbours spoke out online, lobbied their MP and gathered more than 9,000 petition signatures.

Jahaidi Harun, 72, had been concerned that the proposed data centre could be noisy and pressure existing infrastructure.

Data centres “use a lot of water”, the retiree said, adding that, as in Batam, “if the rain doesn’t come for one month, we all feel it”.

Following the withdrawal, Malaysia’s Human Resources Minister Ramanan Ramakrishnan told local media he was not against “development or investment”.

But “for large-scale projects that could affect the residents’ lives, the people must have a say”.

item.title: [SCMP] How Hong Kong’s humble plastic stool became a design-world darling
item.description:
Whether you are eating at the Queen Street Cooked Food Market in Sheung Wan, weaving through a back alley in Tsim Sha Tsui to avoid the crowds on Nathan Road, or waiting for the bus at a covered stop in a rural village in the New Territories, there is one object that has come to symbolise a moment of respite in non-stop Hong Kong. It invites anyone, regardless of age or background, to sit and pause: the plastic stool.

Few objects have transcended time and space quite like this modest piece of plastic. First locally manufactured in the 1960s by Star Industrial under its Red A plasticware brand, the plastic stool was designed as an economical choice to make the most of limited spending power and limited space in the small flats of post-war Hong Kong.

Lightweight and inexpensive, the stools in the Red A collection came in many shapes and sizes, but the most iconic of all might be the taller, rounded, four-legged iteration – usually red, with a small hole in the centre of its fluted seat to drain water or chain a stack together.
item.content:encoded:
Whether you are eating at the Queen Street Cooked Food Market in Sheung Wan, weaving through a back alley in Tsim Sha Tsui to avoid the crowds on Nathan Road, or waiting for the bus at a covered stop in a rural village in the New Territories, there is one object that has come to symbolise a moment of respite in non-stop Hong Kong. It invites anyone, regardless of age or background, to sit and pause: the plastic stool.

Few objects have transcended time and space quite like this modest piece of plastic. First locally manufactured in the 1960s by Star Industrial under its Red A plasticware brand, the plastic stool was designed as an economical choice to make the most of limited spending power and limited space in the small flats of post-war Hong Kong.

Lightweight and inexpensive, the stools in the Red A collection came in many shapes and sizes, but the most iconic of all might be the taller, rounded, four-legged iteration – usually red, with a small hole in the centre of its fluted seat to drain water or chain a stack together.

By the 70s, plastic stools had become fixtures in restaurants, wet markets, shops and homes, their popularity driven by sheer practicality and resilience, whether made by Star Industrial or not.

In the decades since, however, the unassuming stool has found its way into art galleries, exhibitions and collections, transforming from a merely utilitarian item of furniture into a piece of Hong Kong heritage.

Plastic stools join a long line of everyday objects that have transcended their humble origins to become cultural symbols, alongside the Coca-Cola bottles and Campbell’s canned soups of Andy Warhol fame, and Marcel Duchamp’s bicycle wheel, one of his “readymades”.

As architect Roger Wu Tsan-sum, who also serves as the director of business development and projects at the Hong Kong Design Centre and the president of the Hong Kong Institute of Architectural Conservationists, puts it, “the plastic stool is just part of our DNA”.

“Every Hongkonger has a personal relationship with the red stool,” he says. “When I see that stool, I have memories of myself sitting on it doing my homework, with my grandmother by me.”

Post-World War II, a drive for reconstruction and innovation shaped a generation of creatives who went on to challenge conventions in the arts, in music, painting, film and design. In Hong Kong, Wu explains, that generation found a blank canvas, as the city’s colonial history had left it without a single dominant aesthetic.

Meanwhile, the local manufacturing industry took off as the city restructured its economy from entrepôt to producer. Hong Kong became the third-largest textile exporter in the world, and the leading fabricator of plastic flowers. Decades of mass production informed the city’s identity.

Among those on the up-and-up in Hong Kong’s plastic industry was Star Industrial, founded in 1949. It quickly found success as the city’s main plasticware manufacturer for household staples, producing more than 1,700 items under its Red A brand, from buckets and water canteens to lampshades, trays, children’s briefcases and, of course, plastic stools.

Wu says the latter is “built on our culture of efficiency. It survives typhoons, heavy rain and heat. It stays unchanged even in the dustiest closet”. Its sturdiness and versatility – as a chair, table or step, stored indoors or exposed to the elements – ensured its place in our everyday lives.

Over the years, as Hong Kong evolved and old neighbourhoods were redeveloped, authorities tightened regulations on street-level commerce to ease pedestrian congestion and improve public hygiene. In the early 70s, the government stopped issuing new hawker licences; as a result, the number of casual, street-side eateries – such as dai pai dongs – started to decline. And as the economy and living conditions improved, demand for the plastic stool diminished. But as it faded into the background, it began to accumulate a different kind of currency: character.

According to Wu, advancements in technology, especially artificial intelligence, are contributing to rapid global shifts, “and the concept of reality, of originality, is being challenged. So, art is coming back to something concrete, something we can touch, something thought by a human”.

From a revival of traditional crafts to a resurgence of point-and-shoot cameras and a renaissance in printmaking and handmade zines, nostalgia for the old, tangible and tactile is taking many forms, and the plastic stool that has served Hongkongers for more than half a century is finding a new home in the world of art and design, as creatives introduce the household item to a new generation.

Contemporary ink painter Angel Hui Hoi-kiu used them as makeshift plinths and props in her Angel Hui Pop Up Store (2024) multimedia installation, to support the display of her ceramic handbags, inspired by the craftsmanship of the Yuan and Ming dynasties.

In 2025, the international interior-design showcase Maison&Objet Intérieurs, held at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre, welcomed an installation by local practice Lim + Lu and CL3 Architects’ William Lim Ooi-lee, featuring thousands of stools. Rethinking its form for a modern environment, their goal was to transform the plastic pieces into striking ceiling and floor lamps, shelves and other structures.

“We wanted to reinterpret a humble yet iconic object found throughout the city,” says Elaine Manzi Lu, co-founder and managing director of Lim + Lu. By removing the stools from their original context and setting them against “luxurious marbles, rich fabrics and silk carpets”, the installation sought to evoke comfort and familiarity while presenting the soul of Hong Kong to a global audience. Staged in “Le Club”, a gathering space at Maison&Objet Intérieurs, it reflected Lu’s belief that the plastic stool is universal.

“Everywhere around the world, different cultures have their [own] different plastic seats,” says industrial designer and artist Law Chi-hin, who creates under the moniker OrangeTerry. “In Europe, it’s the white Monobloc chair. In Hong Kong, we have the Red A plastic stool.”

“In Hong Kong, the Red A plastic stool never belongs to you – it belongs to every Hongkonger”

Law Chi-hin, aka OrangeTerry

Law argues that these plastic seats have become a common language understood by all, even if they are made from different plastics and to different designs. What connects them all is their affordability and utility. Leveraging this universality, he uses them in his art “to send a message” about cultural kinship. As he explains, the stool embodies a shared Hong Kong identity: “In Hong Kong, the Red A plastic stool never belongs to you – it belongs to every Hongkonger.”

His series, Singular Stack (2025), fuses seven Red A plastic stools into one pedestal-like piece, with the deliberately profligate act serving as a critique of overconsumption: “It’s ridiculous, if you think about it. I’m using a very wasteful method to make one stool for one person. But that’s exactly the point: for people to look at it and think it wasteful.”

He also likes playing around with the stackable properties of the plastic stool. “We don’t have much space in Hong Kong – that’s why we like the stools so much and why they became such an important element in our daily lives, in our home as furniture.”

Painter Joannah “Jobey” Hon Pui-yan agrees. Growing up between Hong Kong and Australia, with parents from contrasting socio-economic backgrounds and tensions that could arise around the dinner table, she feels the Hong Kong plastic stool was an equaliser, one that required everyone to eventually sit down at the same level, on an even playing field.

Once sat on them, around the same table, “we were all [just] Hongkongers eating delicious beef brisket for HK$40 [US$5]”, she says, the parity afforded by the stool settling the differences between her family members.

It is one of the reasons she includes the piece of furniture in her art. Another, she says, is to archive local culture.

Hon made a name for herself with large-scale paintings of everyday scenes of Hong Kong. “I’m interested in iconic Hong Kong characters who represent the heart of the city, and the plastic stools are inherently part of them,” she says.

Plastic stools are prominent in Slipper Hitters (2026), her portrait of the villain-hitting practitioners who set up their stalls underneath the Canal Road Flyover, between Causeway Bay and Wan Chai.

“As artists, we ought to take our time and paint, with our own hands, what we believe is worth remembering,” says Hon. “Our world is changing so fast, and I’m worried the next generation won’t have these villain-hitters under the bridge any more, or these red plastic stools.”

As the plastic stool migrates from wet markets to white cubes, Wu wonders what tomorrow holds for the object if it is no longer in daily use. If the piece of furniture still exists in the years to come, he asks, “will future generations have the same emotional connection to it”.

At the end of the day, the plastic stool may not reclaim its place in every Hong Kong home, but it is unlikely to vanish entirely from the city and our collective consciousness. As Wu sees it, its future is less about style and more about persistence. “Fifty years later, or 1,000 years later, there’s still gravity, and we’ll still [need somewhere to] sit,” he says.

Whether the plastic stool survives on Hong Kong’s pavements or inside artworks and in galleries, it will keep doing the same job: holding the weight of people’s bodies, and the weight of their memories.

item.title: [SCMP] By all memes: why Asia’s Gen Z are revolting
item.description:
All across Asia, anti-establishment protests have been flaring up, led by a generation that came of age in the digital era.

Memes are mobilising a young, permanently online cohort against specific government policies, insults and injustices – its many members determined to seize their own destinies before the future they fear takes root.

Asia is home to 60 per cent of the world’s adolescents and young people, or some 1 billion in total, according to UN estimates.
item.content:encoded:
All across Asia, anti-establishment protests have been flaring up, led by a generation that came of age in the digital era.

Memes are mobilising a young, permanently online cohort against specific government policies, insults and injustices – its many members determined to seize their own destinies before the future they fear takes root.

Asia is home to 60 per cent of the world’s adolescents and young people, or some 1 billion in total, according to UN estimates.

Gen Z, roughly defined as those born between 1997 and 2012, are among the most vocal, their grievances and values often first coalescing on social media before shape-shifting into street protests at a speed that can catch authorities cold.

In India, the viral youth movement of the moment took a cockroach as its emblem. This year’s student-led protests against the government, which began in May, have since merged into a wider pro-democracy challenge to the country’s perennial prime minister of 12 years and counting, Narendra Modi.

In Indonesia, student protesters last year adopted the Straw Hats’ Jolly Roger, a skull and crossbones flag ripped from the pages of Japanese anime One Piece, to rail against economic pressures and perceived mismanagement. It made a return last month as youth anger at toxic air from the worst wildfire season in over a decade boiled over.

Each protest has its own unique triggers, but they share a common wellspring of discontent – the rising cost of living, anger at corruption and nepotism, and education systems that no longer prepare them for a job market whose only real guarantee appears to be menial, low-paid gig work.

Humour, desperation and a loss of fear of authority have combined to form movements that have shattered “the stereotype of apathy” attached to Gen Z, according to Indonesian sociologist Oki Rahadianto Sutopo of Gadjah Mada University in Yogyakarta, displaying a previously unappreciated “capacity for collaborative efforts and engagement on issues they care about”.

The phenomenon is not confined to Asia, either. Buildings in Paris, Milan and Lisbon also bear the scorch marks of unrest as the youth of Europe, similarly anxious about their uncertain futures, have taken to the streets in protest.

Virality makes today’s protests far faster to spread than many governments can react. Officials all too often blame agitators, fifth columnists or the temper tantrums of political rookies for the upheaval, before sending in police armed with batons and tear gas.

Yet underestimating the power of Gen Z protest is a mistake, as Asia’s recently ousted autocrats can attest.

Sheikh Hasina, who ruled over Bangladesh for more than two decades all told, was one of the first to fall. In August 2024, she was driven from power by a mass uprising against her kleptocratic government that police tried, and failed, to quell with violence.

A year later in Nepal, student-led protests took aim at a governing elite derided for its cronyism, corruption and nepotistic tendencies, ultimately toppling the government after a violent struggle and a bungled social media shutdown that aimed to hush the baying crowds.

In Myanmar, Gen Z protesters were some of the first to resist the 2021 coup that ousted the civilian government of erstwhile democracy icon Aung San Suu Kyi – and they have been fighting the generals ever since.

Connecting these disparate, far-flung protest movements is one quintessentially 21st century thread: social media.

It was “instrumental” in organising Bangladesh’s protests, according to student organiser Rezwan Ahmed, pointing to a blockade of Dhaka in July 2024 that brought the capital to a standstill. Ahmed, now 25, ran a viral Facebook group that had amassed over a million followers by the time Hasina’s regime crumbled and she fled the country.

In the Philippines, where nearly 96 million people are on social media, memes have become a vehicle for political messaging that helped spawn last year’s anti-government protests over a multibillion-dollar flood control corruption scandal.

Mark Anicas, the 29-year-old founder and media director of satirical Facebook page Filipino Trends That Matter (FTTM) – curated by a Gen Z team and boasting around 4.6 million followers engaging with its daily sideswipes at government policies – says such platforms are now where the real power lies.

“Our goal isn’t necessarily to tell people what to think, but to encourage them to think,” he told This Week in Asia.

A movement with legs?

Nowhere has dominated this year’s narrative of Gen Z discontent more than India, where a dismissive remark by a chief justice, who called jobless young people “parasites” and “cockroaches”, lit the fires of defiance that gave rise to the eponymous movement.

Its founder, political strategist Abhijeet Dipke – himself a younger millennial, aged 31 – unwittingly launched the viral online movement for Gen Z Indians with what began as a simple, satirical question on the X platform aimed squarely at Chief Justice Surya Kant: “What if all cockroaches come together?”

The remark landed like a bombshell in a country where the UN estimates around 400 million people, or around one in four of the population, are Gen Z.

Millions liked Dipke’s post and with it the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), an online movement whose name lampoons Modi’s own long-governing Bharatiya Janata Party, was born.

Within weeks, its members had taken to the streets wielding memes of cockroaches wearing sunglasses with the Indian tiranga (tricolour) flag draped over their shoulders.

Ayush Bhattacharya, 24, was typical of those who joined the rallies that began on June 6 at Jantar Mantar – a historical observatory in the heart of the Indian capital, a short walk away from parliament, that doubled as a designated protest site until its official removal last month.

“There was a lot of frustration among the youth,” said the college graduate from Mumbai, citing both the country’s politics and its lack of job opportunities for young people.

“Our parents’ generation always made us feel that we did not know well enough about what was happening when they talked about politics. When the chief justice made the remark and Dipke tweeted about it, the post simply got amplified.”

A series of loud, colourful protests followed, attracting a crackdown that spurred allegations of police brutality and ultimately forced the resignation of an education minister in July after demonstrators took aim at a scandal involving exam papers being leaked to wealthy students.

In late September, the movement launched another campaign, organised through WhatsApp and Instagram, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, who oversaw the removal of some 130 million names from electoral rolls nationwide on the grounds that they were supposedly duplicates or belonged to dead people.

Critics, including the main opposition Congress party that has joined the protests, said it was an attempt to disenfranchise millions by stealth, in another flagrant assault on democratic rights by Modi, a Hindu nationalist leader who has repeatedly been accused of fomenting animosity against religious minorities in the world’s largest democracy.

CJP spokeswoman Mehr Pasricha linked the movement’s protests to a rebuttal of “the shift towards right-wing governments [that] has been happening over the past decade” across the globe.

“Young people have just seen the short end of the stick,” she said. “They have gone through a bad schooling system, entering into an economy where there are no jobs, so what does one do?”

Rohit Sharma, 21, spoke to This Week in Asia from a CJP rally in central Delhi on October 16 calling for Kumar to go. It was his third protest.

“The aim of coming here is to save democracy,” said Sharma, a student at the Maharaja Agrasen Institute of Technology in Delhi. “Manipulation of voter lists is not acceptable in a country like ours … This is our democratic right to hold the government accountable.”

Though India’s protests have been growing, they do not appear to pose an existential threat to Modi’s government, at least for now.

Ahmed, the Bangladeshi student leader, said that toppling an entrenched power required a confluence of preconditions to be in place. Bangladesh was already a tinderbox for revolution when Hasina fell, with years of state repression building resentment among the country’s youth and opposition parties’ boycott of an election months earlier stripping her government of its legitimacy.

“It was in the back of our minds that this kind of dictatorial authoritarian regime will not be able to be toppled by mainstream parties of protest alone,” he said. “The people have to be prepared, society has to be prepared … In India I don’t see that at all.”

Burning anger

Back in Southeast Asia, Indonesia has seen multiple rounds of angry protests in recent years over economic conditions and the treatment of gig workers.

The death of delivery driver Affan Kurniawan, who was run over by an armoured police vehicle in August 2025, added fuel to the fire of that year’s anti-government protests against a pay rise MPs had given themselves. The rallies prominently featured the flag from One Piece, the hugely popular anime whose story follows a pirate crew fighting for freedom against a tyrannical regime.

Last month, Indonesia’s protesters returned to the streets, this time with a new cause: choking pollution from the wildfires raging in Kalimantan and elsewhere across the Indonesian archipelago.

On October 28, simultaneous student protests swept across Jakarta, Yogyakarta, Solo, Malang, Bandung and Surabaya on Java island, Makassar on Sulawesi, Palangka Raya in the heart of Kalimantan and even Banda Aceh, thousands of kilometres away at the far northwestern tip of Sumatra.

The mostly Gen Z protesters demanded that the government acknowledge the full scale of the disaster, but their anger also spilled over to other issues, including allegations of widespread corruption, the militarisation of civilian life and costly, wasteful state policies. Demonstrators clashed with police, who used tear gas to disperse the crowds.

“There’s a definite lack of urgency in how they [officials] have treated what is essentially an ecological disaster,” said Naomi Artika Simamora, the 21-year-old head of the student council at the University of Palangka Raya’s law faculty who travelled some 1,000km (620 miles) from Kalimantan to join a rally in Jakarta.

She was joined by Yosafat Menteng, 23, who said they both wanted to pressure the government to declare the ongoing fires a “national disaster” – a status that would allow logistical aid and funding to reach affected areas more efficiently.

Nearly 2 million hectares (4.9 million acres) of forest and peatland in Sumatra, Kalimantan and Papua have burned this year, producing a toxic haze that has blanketed much of Indonesia and neighbouring countries.

Government spokesman Kurnia Ramadhana has said President Prabowo Subianto’s administration “appreciates and understands the students’ concerns” and is working to address them.

But as yet, there has been no declaration of a national disaster. “Our fight continues,” Naomi said.

Delimiting dissent

Across much of the rests of Southeast Asia, protest is neither uniform nor sometimes even possible. Governments wield powerful tools, including defamation, treason and subversion laws, to curb opposition and silence dissent.

In Malaysia, online anger has brought young protesters out onto the streets, but racial and religious divisions impede a broader generational revolt against the political establishment.

“We are not organised by class, but still by race, religion,” said Syaza Farhana Mohamad Shukri, an associate professor of political science at the International Islamic University Malaysia.

Shared concerns about jobs and living costs had yet to overcome these loyalties, she said, further pointing to a “political culture where we are encouraged to be respectful, parochial basically” and to show deference to leaders “even if they make mistakes”.

Dobby Chew, co-founder of Mandiri, a civil society organisation founded in 2024 to strengthen democratic participation, social justice and civic engagement among young people, said politicians’ “hypocrisy and double dealing” did motivate young Malaysians to become politically active, but that their frustrations had been largely “channelled through social media” with only the slightest “potential of crossing into physical protest”.

Earlier this year, young activists joined the hundreds who rallied in the capital demanding the tangkap (arrest) of former anti-corruption chief Azam Baki, who denies any wrongdoing, over his suspiciously large shareholdings.

Yet rights groups have repeatedly flagged limitations on freedom of assembly in Malaysia and a “systemic disregard for student activism”. Efforts to give young voters a political home have also struggled. The youth-focused Malaysian United Democratic Alliance, also known as Muda, lost all four seats it contested in Johor’s election this July, including the one it already held.

Efforts to give young voters a political home have also struggled. The youth-focused Malaysian United Democratic Alliance, also known as Muda, lost all four seats it contested in Johor’s election this July, including the one it already held.

In neighbouring Thailand, protest is routinely repressed and defused. Mass youth-led demonstrations against military-aligned rule in 2020-21 did open up previously untouchable assumptions of power – including the role of the monarchy – to public debate.

But the establishment pegged them back, arresting and prosecuting scores of young protest leaders and reshuffling the political deck behind the scenes to ensure its interests came out on top.

That included dissolving the radical reformist Future Forward party and banning its leaders from politics, as well as banning the leadership of its wildly popular successor, the Move Forward Party, in 2024. With momentum for change stalled, Thailand’s conservatives reasserted their dominance. Current Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul anchors the elite settlement in power.

But observers say social media still provides the region’s youth with an outlet and a way to organise, often with unpredictable results.

In the Philippines, memes do much of the leg work. “Political memes speak to concrete frustrations towards institutions and politicians,” said Petronilo Figueroa, a media and communications lecturer at the University of the Philippines Diliman.

Satirical Facebook page FTTM often used humour “to make complicated or sometimes uncomfortable issues more accessible” to its millions of followers, founder Anicas said.

Among its biggest draws, he said, were posts about last year’s flood control corruption scandal that sparked mass street protests amid allegations that officials and contractors had siphoned off billions in state funds by using substandard materials or inventing non-existent projects.
