The page has also faced legal backlash, including libel charges brought by a Caloocan city official over a viral post about a traffic violation and a subpoena from a provincial governor over a separate post he claimed was malicious and factually incorrect.

Yet Anicas said the public stuck by them. “People actually look up to [us], especially the Gen Zs … they say, ‘I’ve started involving myself because of you’,” he said.

That support could help shape the country’s next presidential election in 2028, when the Commission on Elections projects nearly one in three Filipino voters will be members of Gen Z.

That said, “Gen Z is far from a homogeneous bloc”, Figueroa cautioned. “So winning their support will take more than a single message.”

item.title: [SCMP] Lithuania builds world’s biggest ultra-fast laser factory amid China tensions
item.description:
Amid tensions with China, a small European country is anchoring itself at the centre of the global semiconductor and artificial intelligence (AI) hardware supply chain as a laser powerhouse.

The latest sign of Lithuania’s growing footprint in the sector came last month, when laser maker Litilit launched a new factory in the capital, Vilnius. The company’s expansion unfolds as the Baltic nation of fewer than 3 million people navigates fraught ties with Beijing, which has targeted Lithuania with a slew of informal trade restrictions over its Taiwan stance.

In 2021, Lithuania emerged as a symbol of Taiwan’s expanding diplomatic ties in Europe by allowing the opening of a Taiwanese representative office in Vilnius, breaking the long-standing convention of using “Taipei” in the names of such offices.
item.content:encoded:
Amid tensions with China, a small European country is anchoring itself at the centre of the global semiconductor and artificial intelligence (AI) hardware supply chain as a laser powerhouse.

The latest sign of Lithuania’s growing footprint in the sector came last month, when laser maker Litilit launched a new factory in the capital, Vilnius. The company’s expansion unfolds as the Baltic nation of fewer than 3 million people navigates fraught ties with Beijing, which has targeted Lithuania with a slew of informal trade restrictions over its Taiwan stance.

In 2021, Lithuania emerged as a symbol of Taiwan’s expanding diplomatic ties in Europe by allowing the opening of a Taiwanese representative office in Vilnius, breaking the long-standing convention of using “Taipei” in the names of such offices.

Beijing responded sharply to the move, downgrading its diplomatic ties with Lithuania and imposing trade measures, including banning certain food and alcohol products from the country and blocking many Lithuanian exporters from the Chinese market.

Lithuania’s new government, which took office earlier this year, has pledged to normalise ties with Beijing, but frictions persist.

In June, Beijing said it hoped Lithuania would “take early and decisive action to correct its mistakes, return to the right track of adhering to the one-China principle and create conditions for the normalisation of China-Lithuania relations”.

One month later, the Chinese commerce ministry put Lithuanian laser manufacturer Ekspla on its European dual-use exports control list, alongside 13 other European Union entities.

Despite this setback, the Lithuanian laser industry continues to thrive. The new Litilit facility will be able to produce 3,000 femtosecond lasers per year at full capacity.

These advanced lasers can emit pulses of light so short that they can process materials, including glass, with high precision and minimal heat damage to surrounding structures. This ability has become crucial for chipmakers as they explore glass as a substrate for the next generation of AI infrastructure.

According to Litilit, the new factory boasts the world’s largest potential production capacity for this class of advanced laser. By comparison, global output stood at an estimated 9,600 units last year.

Litilit plans to produce an initial 1,000 units in its first year before scaling to full capacity, exporting most of its output to Europe, North America and Asia, according to the company.

Nikolajus Gavrilinas, Litilit’s co-founder and CEO, said the commercial reality of the supply chain often overrode political posturing.

“We are absolutely in line with Lithuanian official policies about US, Chinese, European and [other] political alignments,” Gavrilinas said.

“We are looking for strong partnerships with all three [regions]: Europe, the US and Asia. Together with our partners, we are ready to expand our capacity to tens of thousands of lasers per year.”

He said that while he had observed some tensions between European countries and China, if one side needed a technology and another needed a different technology, and they were part of each other’s global supply chain, they would not be easily stopped from doing business.

“Until it becomes a real resistance for each other, everything is very smooth,” he said.

While public discussion of AI often focuses on software and algorithms, Gavrilinas said the growth of AI data centres was driving demand for the advanced manufacturing tools – including femtosecond lasers – needed to build their hardware.

As AI models require more processing power, data centres are changing how their chips are assembled. One emerging approach, known as advanced packaging, stacks multiple chips on a single board.

A glass interposer is a thin piece of glass connecting chiplets and memory to the package substrate. The thermal expansion properties of glass can be tuned to closely match that of silicon, making it a promising material for advanced semiconductor packaging.

However, light from conventional lasers passes through transparent materials, making processing difficult. Femtosecond lasers overcome this by focusing energy directly within the glass to form precise pathways and internal structures.

Gavrilinas noted that femtosecond lasers could be used to carve electrical paths inside glass in a method similar to 3D printing, adding that this application “opens a lot of possibilities”. He said this process could also be used on other transparent materials, such as polycrystalline diamond, an ultra-hard material for cutting tools and metalworking dies.

“Imagine … glass coming back to the main domain of everything, like as a base plate for electronics, chips and so on. This is a fabulous transformation,” he said.

“Our goal is to move the femtosecond laser from niche applications to the commodity market,” Gavrilinas said, comparing its present growth phase to earlier lasers that moved from labs to everyday tasks such as engraving names on cups.

While legacy laser manufacturers rely heavily on manual assembly, typically producing around one laser per worker each year on average, the Litilit facility has achieved around 85 per cent automation with a workforce of around 100 to 200 people.

“When we have this level of automation … we can scale it up in any country, in any region,” Gavrilinas said, adding that this helped limit the effects of “turbulence” in labour costs or politics.

The company is evaluating further expansion with potential production hubs in Singapore, Japan, the United States and Europe to meet surging demand, according to Gavrilinas.

When asked about the potential for even faster attosecond lasers, Gavrilinas said femtosecond technology would be the industry standard for the next 20 years.

“For the next two decades, we believe that it will be femtosecond. Maybe later [when] we broaden our experience and everything around it, it may be attosecond,” he said.

The Baltic nation’s laser industry traces back to 1962, when Lithuania was still part of the Soviet Union and three students were sent to Moscow to study laser physics and quantum electronics. By 1966, the country’s first laser was fired at Vilnius University.

Today, Lithuania has more than 60 laser and photonics companies and over 2,000 specialists across its research centres, and the country exports more than 90 per cent of its laser output, according to Vilnius University.

Undeterred by the threat of blacklists, the Lithuanian laser sector has sought to work with experts from Taiwan, a global semiconductor powerhouse.

According to the Research Council of Lithuania, which provides research and development funding, 60 researchers from Lithuania and Taiwan explored new partnership opportunities and exchanged knowledge last month at a three-day laser technology workshop in the European nation.

The event was organised as part of a 2023 agreement between the research council and Taiwan’s National Science and Technology Council to fund joint research projects in biotechnology, laser and materials science, engineering and computer information technology.

item.title: [SCMP] From clay to cuisine: the ceramicists reshaping fine dining in Hong Kong
item.description:
“I was thinking about something crazy like a pumpkin orange. Mustard … kind of like a terracotta orange. You’ve been to Morocco, Marrakech?”

Ricardo Chaneton, chef-owner of Michelin-star restaurant Mono, in Central, is bent over a table laden with samples of glazed ceramic tiles. Across from him is Queenie Chan Kwan-wai, a ceramicist and the founder of Ephelis, who has collaborated with him for the past five years.

“What about this kind of orange?” Chan suggests.
item.content:encoded:
“I was thinking about something crazy like a pumpkin orange. Mustard … kind of like a terracotta orange. You’ve been to Morocco, Marrakech?”

Ricardo Chaneton, chef-owner of Michelin-star restaurant Mono, in Central, is bent over a table laden with samples of glazed ceramic tiles. Across from him is Queenie Chan Kwan-wai, a ceramicist and the founder of Ephelis, who has collaborated with him for the past five years.

“What about this kind of orange?” Chan suggests.

“No … it’s too brown,” says Chaneton. “You see the orange there. Something like that, but not that ‘screaming’.”

Chaneton and Chan go back and forth like this for a while, in Mono’s private dining room, between lunch and dinner service. In anticipation of his progressive Latin American restaurant turning seven next month, the chef has begun preparing for the anniversary with a “refresh” of the interiors, completed in early September, to make the space feel “less industrial and more like home”. He has commissioned Chan to make new tableware to match the updated look – hence the debating of colours.

It’s a scene that would have been unrecognisable to Auguste Escoffier, the French chef who served in the Franco-Prussian War (1870-71) and returned with a vision of the kitchen as a brigade. His hierarchical system, based on military structure, made haute cuisine possible at scale and standardised the fine-dining experience, allowing restaurants to expand their offerings and serve more diners with greater consistency.

But back in the 19th century, the porcelain diners ate from was not designed for beauty – it simply emerged from industrial convenience. In 1813, British potter Charles James Mason patented ironstone – a white, chip-resistant earthenware that could survive rough, repeated hotel use. It was a standardised, mass-manufactured product, cheaper to make than porcelain and easy to replace in bulk. By the 1920s, the white plate was being praised for another reason: it didn’t distract from the food, the front-and-centre priority.

Identical plates as the default changed in 2006, when René Redzepi, of Noma, commissioned custom, hand-thrown plates from KH Würtz, a father-and-son studio in rural Denmark. Described as “rough-hewn crockery in speckled earth tones” with “cracked glazes”, early buyers even thought the plates “looked like a disease”.

But when Noma was named the Best Restaurant in the World, in 2010, attitudes quickly shifted. Suddenly, the plate wasn’t supposed to be just a blank surface. Its rustic aesthetic is now a part of the restaurant’s story and a sign of locality, craftsmanship and luxury.

It is in this context that Chaneton began looking for pieces that would form part of his restaurant’s personality. On a trip to Spain for the Best Chef Awards in 2019, he noticed many of his peers buying knives, chinaware and pottery. He followed them to an atelier in Barcelona, where Chicago-born ceramicist Cara Janelle was based. He fell in love with a large oval plate she had made and asked her to make it in green for Mono, instead of brown. He still uses them today, as show plates on the restaurant counter.

But shipping tableware such a long distance was never going to be sustainable. So, in 2021, he turned to someone local – Chan.

Chan came to ceramics through fashion. She trained at Central Saint Martins in London, Britain, and worked as a fashion designer at Dior’s maison de couture in Paris, France, where she learned to think in silhouettes – how a form reads from a distance, how it feels up close, how much weight it can carry without collapsing. She returned to Hong Kong in 2017, and launched her studio, Ephelis, the following year, going full-time with it in 2020.

Chan’s first restaurant client was Mono. She was still new to producing ceramics at that scale, still figuring out how a piece that looks right on a shelf behaves under the weight of hot food. But she found her way in through the room and the environment. “When I am given complete freedom on a piece,” she says, “I create something inspired by the interior of the restaurant itself, like the stone flooring at Mono, for example.”

It’s an instinct that informs how she works with Chaneton. He tells her the purpose – a plate for the amuse-bouche, a bowl for birthday cake, a show plate to welcome guests – and she decides the rest. Size first, then the clay colour and the glaze, which is where most of the work happens. She experiments, shows Chaneton prototypes and he chooses.

“Working with clay is a bit like the process of fermentation,” she says. “We still do a lot of tests, but each stage simply takes a great deal of time. Sometimes, you have to put a piece aside and come back to it much later.”

Watching the activity of Chaneton’s kitchen – fast, high-pressure, non-stop action, with constant tasting and adjusting – makes her appreciate how different their rhythms are. His is measured in seconds; hers in weeks.

“Morocco orange” was one of those long conversations. Chan understood the direction, but not the exact tone. Over three weeks, she made more than 40 miniature samples, each a small clay base with a different colour applied. She tested them twice: first on white clay, to see the precise colour reaction, and then on terracotta, the clay Chaneton prefers. Each sample blended different pigments – “Mono blue” and Morocco orange, for example – until they landed on the one he envisioned.

For all the dissimilarities in their pace, Chan sees her craft and Chaneton’s as the same kind of work. “Whether it’s clay or food, you’re taking something from a formless, raw state and transforming it into a finished piece entirely through your own hands and creative energy,” she says.

Some of her plates are already in service at Mono, including those holding the amuse-bouche: an arepa ground-maize flatbread with Kaluga caviar and a Scottish razor-clam tart. “When I see them being used at Mono – holding a dish Ricardo has created, being lifted by a diner – I feel a quiet sense of completion,” says Chan, “because the plate becomes part of his creation and his food gives the piece a new life.”

Her Morocco-orange set is still a work in progress, but the relationship between restaurant and tableware goes even deeper than merely collaboration between chef and ceramicist.

Chan collected leftover oyster shells from Mono, incorporating what would have been tossed as food waste into her creation process, forming what she calls “a special link” between them. Oyster shells are calcified, burnt into powder and used in the glaze for the plates, “so I always feel a particular connection between my work and the restaurant”, she says.

Chaneton is already thinking about the possibilities: “Once I receive them, I’ll be inspired to create something new. I’m looking forward to seeing [the plate] for a special dessert I’ve been working on, probably something monochromatic and cold. I’m planning to use chocolate made from scratch.”

Not too far from Mono, chef-owner Vicky Lau Wan-ki, of Tate – formerly Tate Dining Room, before its recent relocation – has been having similar conversations with local ceramicists.

Lau started in the art world, working in ceramics, before she became a chef, in 2011. When she began looking for vessels for the third and latest iteration of Tate, which opened this August, on Lok Ku Road, in Sheung Wan, she was already familiar with both sides of the exchange.

“You can feel the hand of the artist, the raw earth and that magic moment when it transforms in the kiln,” she says. For the table, Lau commissioned more than 20 ceramicists, including Jess Kong and Hin Wan of Mui Wo-based Lantau Shanto Studio, who make ceramics from wild clay dug out of the island’s soil.

Kong recalls taking samples to the restaurant’s previous location, on Hollywood Road. Lau had held the plate and the ceramic leaf, and smiled. She told Kong she wanted guests to run their fingers across the tableware, to feel the texture of Hong Kong’s soil.

Her ceramic leaf is a small piece, its glaze made from wood ash collected at the HKYWCA Sydney Leong Holiday Lodge – on Lantau, near San Shek Wan village – where the camp had built a wild-clay pizza oven using earth from the site. Fired at 400 degrees Celsius, the wood leaves an ash that reacts with the wild clay in the kiln to produce a finish that resembles a dried autumn leaf, in rich orange and brown tones.

For Kong and Wan, sourcing local materials is central to their practice: “Commercial clay is chemically balanced, predictable and convenient. Wild clay requires time, patience, flexibility and physical work. We can’t just open a bag.”

She tells the story of an organic farmer who goes by the name Keung Gor, whose Grassland Farm sits five minutes from their Mui Wo studio. He let them dig two metres (6.6 feet) down into his fields, and they found what Kong calls “the ideal wild clay”, the material they had been searching for. Ever since, she says, they “have felt a deep connection between the Hong Kong clay we use for our ceramics and the local vegetables and crops that grow out of the very same soil”.

But the very soil that gives the clay its character also makes it erratic. Kong had warned Lau she couldn’t guarantee that every plate would have identical dimensions or finishes. Working with wild clay has been a lesson in unpredictability, she says. “It taught me to let go of rigid perfectionism and to stop seeing cracks in early pieces as failures.”

For Tate, Lantau Shanto Studio made a set of two plates – one slightly larger than the other, set at two heights, with the smaller of the pair bearing a ceramic magnolia-leaf adornment – to hold the amuse-bouche that opens the meal. On the larger plate sits a crispy cone of razor clam and zucchini with mussel and black bean; on the smaller, a jellyfish tartlet with steamed daikon and Yunnan ham. Each vessel is hand-thrown in raw clay with a touch of uneven white glaze – unique, impossible to replicate.

A lack of uniformity is precisely what Lau wanted. “No two hand-thrown pieces are identical,” she says. “Every mark on the clay tells a story, which gives the dining experience a soul you can’t get from a factory line.”

She brings that same philosophy to her cuisine. Ode to Pigeon, which she has served for years, used to arrive in a single bowl. Working with the new vessels, she separated the dish’s components – the protein on its own, the soup and rice together in a small bowl. Food and ceramics, working together, have transformed how guests interact with the meal.

Kong sees the same idea from the other side. “A piece should never compete with or overwhelm the dish,” she says. “Wild clay’s subtle, raw tones serve as a natural canvas, symbolising the soil, with the food placed upon it representing a fresh harvest directly from the same soil.”

Clay, for Lau, is the physical anchor of the whole project. In her restaurant’s Chinese name, Tai Di, the first character is found in both the terms for “artistic form” and “natural ecosystems” – and clay is where those two concepts meet. Clay starts in the soil, is shaped by hand, fired by flame and ends up holding the bounties of land and sea. “It is the tangible bridge connecting the earth to the guest’s hands and palate,” she says.

Tate 3.0 revolves around this instinct. Lau brought on China-born, New York-based designer Chris Shao, and they agreed that fine china and ceramics were the ultimate expression of what she calls “feminine strength, elegance and tactile precision”. He built the interiors to match: floor motifs that resemble a puzzle of fractured shards, ceramic lighting and curved lines that echo hand-thrown pottery.

If the room sets the tone, then the plates are where design becomes palpable. Lau knows exactly what she wants a diner to feel when they pick one up. “I want them to notice the weight, the subtle irregularities of the surface and the tactile imprint of the artisan’s fingers,” she says. “In an era dominated by AI, mass production and cookie-cutter dining rooms, taking a moment to feel a vessel made from local earth grounds you in the present.”

Kong carries the same hope in the vessels she and Wan make. “As [diners] enjoy every bite of each dish,” she says, “I hope they feel a connection to Hong Kong and realise that even amid the hustle of this city, nature and stillness still flourish right beneath our feet.”

item.title: [SCMP] Is Lula’s upset win also a victory for Chinese firms in Brazil?
item.description:
With domestic profits narrowing and production capacity expanding, China’s firms are continuing to widen their overseas footprints in search of new, more lucrative markets. In this series, we examine China Inc.’s next phase of “going global” and the complex, challenging international environment its companies have chosen to enter.

A presidential election in Brazil, a country thousands of miles away, might seem like just another headline to many in China. But for Chinese companies doing business in South America, the stakes are considerably higher.

When right-wing candidate Flavio Bolsonaro took the lead in the first round of voting in early October, Ken Liu, a Chinese exporter of digital textile printing equipment operating in Brazil, grew concerned about the implications for his business.
item.content:encoded:
With domestic profits narrowing and production capacity expanding, China’s firms are continuing to widen their overseas footprints in search of new, more lucrative markets. In this series, we examine China Inc.’s next phase of “going global” and the complex, challenging international environment its companies have chosen to enter.

A presidential election in Brazil, a country thousands of miles away, might seem like just another headline to many in China. But for Chinese companies doing business in South America, the stakes are considerably higher.

When right-wing candidate Flavio Bolsonaro took the lead in the first round of voting in early October, Ken Liu, a Chinese exporter of digital textile printing equipment operating in Brazil, grew concerned about the implications for his business.

Brazil introduced a visa exemption for Chinese passport holders in May, allowing stays of up to 30 days for purposes including tourism and business.

With Bolsonaro seen as less aligned with China than incumbent president Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, Liu took a cautious approach, arranging for some employees to apply for work visas in case the policy changed. He was planning to send more staff to expand the company’s sales in the Brazilian market.

Lula’s upset victory in the run-off in late October was therefore welcome news for Liu.

“Lula will generally be more friendly towards Chinese companies than Bolsonaro,” he said. Bolsonaro has advocated closer ties with Washington.

As economic ties between Beijing and Brasilia deepen, Brazil has become an increasingly important destination for Chinese investors. Lula’s re-election offers the prospect of policy continuity and closer bilateral ties, but it is not an unqualified win for Chinese companies.

Lula is, above all, a pragmatic politician who understands well Brazil’s limitations when it comes to expanding its footprint in key industries ... in which China is a leader

Victor Gonzalez, PC Woo & Zhonglun Wende

His push for foreign investors to manufacture locally and help develop Brazilian industries could raise costs. Bolsonaro’s narrow loss in the run-off also showed that Brazil remains politically divided, adding another layer of uncertainty for Chinese companies operating in Latin America’s largest economy, businesses and analysts said.

“Lula is, above all, a pragmatic politician who understands well Brazil’s limitations when it comes to expanding its footprint in key industries such as electric batteries, chips and mobile phones, in which China is a leader,” said Victor Gonzalez, a senior adviser for China-Latin America legal affairs at Shenzhen-based law firm PC Woo & Zhonglun Wende.

Given the commercial sensitivities surrounding the sharing of Chinese companies’ valuable know-how – even among close partners – Lula has pursued a strategy of reciprocity, Gonzalez said.

“Lula’s most valuable attribute has been that of having offered quid pro quos as a way to potentially receive concessions, too.”

Since returning to office in 2023, Lula has made two state visits to China, seeking to attract investment and gain access to Chinese expertise in advanced technology, infrastructure and manufacturing.

He is also focused on rebuilding ties strained under his predecessor, Jair Bolsonaro, 71, the father of his presidential rival in this year’s election who was sentenced to prison in 2025 for plotting a coup to remain in power.

During his April 2023 visit, Lula secured 32 business agreements covering areas such as the digital economy and renewable energy, according to the Brazilian government. His May 2025 visit yielded a further 27 billion reais (US$4.96 billion) in investment pledges from Chinese companies.

As bilateral ties have strengthened, China has maintained its position as Brazil’s largest trading partner while increasing its investment in Latin America’s largest economy.

Chinese investment in Brazil rose 45 per cent year on year to US$6.1 billion in 2025, making Brazil the world’s largest destination for Chinese investment, according to the Brazil-China Business Council. The increase far outpaced the 1.3 per cent growth in China’s global outbound investment.

But the surge in investment also comes with expectations from Brasilia, as Lula wants Chinese capital to help Brazil develop its own industrial capabilities, rather than simply deepen its reliance on imported technology and manufactured goods.

In an October podcast interview, Lula said Brazil should develop its own battery industry rather than “depend on the Chinese”. He also called for the country to produce its own chips and mobile phones. At the same time, he described Chinese investors as “bold” and said Brazil was “taking advantage” of the opportunity.

The dual message reflects Lula’s approach to Chinese investment: welcoming the capital and expertise that Chinese companies can bring, while seeking to use them to strengthen Brazil’s domestic industries.

Launched in 2024, the Brazilian government’s New Industry Brazil plan aims to revive domestic manufacturing and upgrade the country’s industrial base by 2033. Its targets include digitalising 90 per cent of domestic industries and tripling the share of national production in selected new-technology segments.

“Brasilia will keep an open door for Chinese trading and investment, as long as Chinese leaders and executives also understand that Lula’s main demand will be that of supporting the development of local industries or at least preventing them from declining,” Gonzalez said.

For Chinese companies, such a shift would entail higher costs and could require companies to accelerate their investment plans.

But the opportunities in South America’s biggest economy make the trade-off worthwhile, particularly as Chinese electric vehicle (EV) makers face hurdles in other overseas markets and slowing sales growth at home, Gonzalez said.

Chinese carmakers are among the companies most actively expanding local production in Brazil.

BYD is seeking permits to double annual production capacity at its Brazilian plant to 600,000 vehicles, as it nears completion of its stamping, welding and paint facilities, Reuters reported in late October.

Great Wall Motor also launched local production in Brazil last year, while Geely completed production of its first locally manufactured model in cooperation with Renault in September.

The expansion of leading Chinese carmakers in Brazil could also bring more of their suppliers to the country, according to an overseas sales executive at a Chinese EV maker, who asked not to be named because he was not authorised to speak on behalf of the company.

“BYD has invested in battery factories and related supporting industries in Brazil,” he said. “Such deep commitment of major companies like BYD would help pave the way for a broader range of Chinese suppliers and businesses across the supply chain to invest into the Brazilian market.”

Beyond the costs of localising production, Brazil’s divided political landscape presents another challenge for Chinese companies.

Although Lula won re-election, right-wing parties strengthened their position in Congress. They are set to hold a majority of seats in the Chamber of Deputies, while the right will also command nearly two-thirds of the seats in the Senate, potentially complicating Lula’s efforts to advance his legislative agenda.

Lula’s narrow victory also underscores the country’s political divisions. He won 51.79 per cent of valid votes in the October 25 run-off, defeating Flavio Bolsonaro, who received 48.21 per cent, according to Brazil’s electoral authorities.

The result reversed Bolsonaro’s lead in the first round, when he won 47.03 per cent of valid votes against Lula’s 45.16 per cent.

For Chinese companies, the challenge will be navigating not only policy uncertainty but also a political system in which Lula may find it tricky to secure congressional support for his agenda, Gonzalez said.

“Something that could be a challenge for Chinese companies during Lula’s fourth mandate … will be to understand and navigate a still very divided country and fractured political system where the majority in both chambers of Congress will be partially dominated by conservatives,” Gonzalez said.

Despite these political uncertainties, some Chinese businesses remain optimistic about Brazil’s commercial prospects.

Chen Le, an overseas sales manager at Chinese kitchenware exporter Wujo Group, said many of his Brazilian customers had hoped Flavio Bolsonaro would win the election. Chen, however, welcomed Lula’s re-election.

“Our overall outlook for the Brazilian market over the next year remains optimistic, because our exports of kitchenware to Brazil grew throughout Lula’s previous term,” Chen said.

Meanwhile, Liu, the digital textile executive, expressed long-term confidence in the market, citing Brazil’s consumer spending and the potential to modernise its textile industry.

“While Brazil has a stark wealth gap and a large lower-income population, I only realised after arriving … that much of the money consumers earn goes straight back into the economy,” he said.

Liu said Brazil’s traditional textile sector was undergoing modernisation, creating opportunities for suppliers of Chinese equipment. He also saw scope for further growth as more Chinese companies entered the market.

“I feel that certain parts of Brazil still resemble the China of a decade ago. However, with the arrival of Chinese enterprises, better logistics and the widespread adoption of automated equipment, the local market will gradually transform,” he added.

item.title: [SCMP] Joshua Wong jailed for 10 years over bid to instigate sanctions on Beijing, Hong Kong
item.description:
Jailed Hong Kong opposition activist Joshua Wong Chi-fung has been sentenced to 10 years behind bars for his role in a global campaign to instigate sanctions against mainland China and the city in the aftermath of the 2019 anti-government protests.

The High Court ruled on Thursday that Wong and fugitive ex-lawmaker Nathan Law Kwun-chung had partly contributed to the imposition of sanctions and adverse measures against mainland and Hong Kong officials which significantly undermined national security.

The 30-year-old, who earlier pleaded guilty to conspiracy to collude with foreign forces, had been scheduled to complete a sentence of four years and eight months for conspiracy to commit subversion on January 7 next year.
item.content:encoded:
Jailed Hong Kong opposition activist Joshua Wong Chi-fung has been sentenced to 10 years behind bars for his role in a global campaign to instigate sanctions against mainland China and the city in the aftermath of the 2019 anti-government protests.

The High Court ruled on Thursday that Wong and fugitive ex-lawmaker Nathan Law Kwun-chung had partly contributed to the imposition of sanctions and adverse measures against mainland and Hong Kong officials which significantly undermined national security.

The 30-year-old, who earlier pleaded guilty to conspiracy to collude with foreign forces, had been scheduled to complete a sentence of four years and eight months for conspiracy to commit subversion on January 7 next year.

The court ordered two months and two days, representing the remaining time Wong is to serve his sentence in the previous national security case, to run concurrently with his latest jail term, meaning the activist’s expected release date is pushed back to November 2036.

Mr Justice William Tam Yiu-ho ruled that the present offence was serious enough to warrant at least 10 years’ imprisonment under a two-tier sentencing regime provided for the crime under the national security law.

He described Wong and Law as “advocates at the forefront colluding with foreign forces”. They and their associates had exploited their connections with top overseas officials and institutions to promote foreign interference at a time when Hong Kong was facing “very high risks to national security and the rule of law” following the 2019 unrest.

“At such a critical time, the joint enterprise by the defendant [and Law] and their affiliates to collude with foreign forces or elements and make blatant calls for sanctions and hostile measures certainly aggravated the serious predicament and difficulties that [Beijing and the Hong Kong government] had then to deal with,” the judge said.

Tam, who was handpicked by the chief executive to oversee national security proceedings, said Wong had persisted in his pursuit of an “international battlefront” after collusion with foreign forces became a crime, as the activist had provided “underground assistance” to his accomplices overseas by bolstering their calls for sanctions in the media.

The judge cut three years from a starting point of 13 years’ imprisonment, noting that the usual one-third discount for a defendant who pleaded guilty at the earliest opportunity was not available to Wong due to the national security law’s minimum sentence requirement.

Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu described Wong as one of the “primary culprits responsible for undermining Hong Kong’s prosperity and stability”.

“Wong Chi-fung, Law Kwun-chung and others persistently colluded with foreign countries or external elements, actively lobbied the United States to pass so-called legislation concerning Hong Kong, and openly solicited foreign countries to impose sanctions against China and Hong Kong,” Lee said in a statement.

“Such acts constituted extremely serious offences, which not only severely undermined national sovereignty, security and development interests, but also directly prejudiced the well-being of the public and the stability of society.”

A government spokesman also rejected Western criticism, saying Wong’s guilty plea reflected the strength of the evidence, and the detailed reasons for his sentence showed he had received a fair and open trial under the rule of law.

Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun described Wong’s offences as serious and stressed that Hong Kong upheld the principle that anyone who broke the law should be prosecuted.

He reiterated Beijing’s support for the city’s efforts to safeguard national security and urged foreign countries to stop interfering in China’s internal affairs and Hong Kong’s judiciary, and to respect the city’s rule of law.

Chief Superintendent Steve Li Kwai-wah of the police’s National Security Department described the sentence as appropriate, but said the force would nevertheless discuss with the Department of Justice whether to appeal for a heavier sentence.

Li criticised Wong for committing a raft of offences over his years of political activism.

“I sincerely hope that for the rest of his time in prison, apart from reflecting on the wrongdoings he has done to the country and to Hong Kong, he must seize the opportunity to learn to respect the law and properly understand his own country,” he said.

The chief superintendent also urged Law to return to Hong Kong and surrender himself.

Asked about the 2017 documentary Joshua: Teenager vs. Superpower, which remains available on Netflix, Li said police were concerned about whether it contained seditious content but declined to comment further.

The Security Bureau previously said it was following up on the matter and would handle it in accordance with the law.

The European Union deplored what it called the “politically motivated sentencing” of Wong to “an exceptionally long prison term” and called for his immediate release. It said the case demonstrated a “deterioration of the state of the rule of law” in the city and further weighed on Hong Kong’s international reputation.

The United States’ Congressional-Executive Commission on China called for Wong’s unconditional release in a social media post, saying he had been sentenced for “peacefully defending freedoms” and that the case showed Hong Kong’s courts were being weaponised as a tool of repression.

The US consulate in Hong Kong also condemned the sentence and called for his immediate release.

“Wong has been unjustly imprisoned since December 2020, demonstrating that Beijing will go to extraordinary lengths to silence those who advocate for fundamental freedoms in Hong Kong,” it said.

Wong pleaded guilty in early September to conspiring with the 33-year-old Law and others to garner international support for a resistance campaign aimed at forcing Beijing to repeal the national security law and grant Hongkongers greater political freedom.

A vocal critic of Beijing, Wong rose to prominence in 2014 as a student leader during that year’s Occupy protests, a civil disobedience movement calling for democratic reform in Hong Kong.

He co-founded the political group Demosisto two years later, which initially called for a referendum to determine Hong Kong’s sovereignty, before abandoning that stance in early 2020. The party was disbanded hours before the implementation of the national security law at the end of June that year.

The court heard Wong visited the United States in November 2016 and September 2019 to drum up support for a bill that would allow the country’s president to punish Hong Kong and mainland officials for suppressing basic freedoms in the city. The bill, called the Hong Kong Human Rights and Democracy Act, was signed into law in November 2019.

Wong and Law – who served as Demosisto’s secretary general and founding chairman, respectively – also urged Western governments to stop exporting weapons and crowd control equipment to Hong Kong during the 2019 unrest.

They further called on the West to include Hong Kong human rights provisions in trade deals with Beijing and to end the special status previously accorded to the city as a separate customs territory.

Wong continued to advocate for sanctions against China in the media even after the national security law came into effect, the court heard.

The activist urged private enterprises to avoid investing in the mainland and petitioned Israel-based forensic company Cellebrite to stop providing phone-hacking technology to Hong Kong’s police and related security agencies.

In a “presentencing work report” published on November 22, 2020, Wong revealed that he had also written to electronics giants Sony and Apple to warn them against business ties with Beijing.

item.title: [SCMP] How Dong Mingzhu, China’s manufacturing ‘iron lady’, is maintaining her cool in the AI era
item.description:
Dong Mingzhu chairs Gree Electric Appliances, a home-appliance giant based in southern China’s Guangdong province. Having worked her way up from a frontline sales job, she is one of China’s best-known figures in manufacturing. As a deputy to the National People’s Congress, she has long advocated for manufacturing innovation, higher incomes and greener consumption.

In this interview, conducted when she was named an inaugural “Cool Leader” at an assembly of the UN Environment Programme’s Cool Coalition in Singapore, Dong discusses Chinese companies’ overseas expansion, how automation transforms manufacturing and her management philosophy.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.
item.content:encoded:
Dong Mingzhu chairs Gree Electric Appliances, a home-appliance giant based in southern China’s Guangdong province. Having worked her way up from a frontline sales job, she is one of China’s best-known figures in manufacturing. As a deputy to the National People’s Congress, she has long advocated for manufacturing innovation, higher incomes and greener consumption.

In this interview, conducted when she was named an inaugural “Cool Leader” at an assembly of the UN Environment Programme’s Cool Coalition in Singapore, Dong discusses Chinese companies’ overseas expansion, how automation transforms manufacturing and her management philosophy.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

This summer, Chinese-made air conditioners helped Europeans cope with unprecedented heat. As the world faces growing climate risks, how is Gree expanding access to cooling while reducing its environmental impact?

In a quick response to the European market, we shipped air conditioners using R290, a propane refrigerant with low global warming potential, as well as portable units that require no installation. Both were developed with European Union regulations and local installation constraints in mind. When demand surged, retail sales of our air conditioners in certain markets, including France, rose 50 per cent year on year.

Of course, some of that growth may have been temporary, driven by the immediate need.

But fundamentally, climate change has become a more urgent problem. It threatens human survival and we have to address it. Even if someone can afford to run an air conditioner around the clock, there is a wider cost: we cool the room indoors while releasing heat outdoors. As populations grow, that pressure increases.

Ideally, cooling would use no energy at all. That is why we need technological breakthroughs.

We are working to cut energy use and reduce reliance on conventional power. For example, our solar-powered air conditioning can draw on clean electricity when the sun shines, while storage lets us save surplus power generated during the day for use at night.

We’ve established an internal framework for carbon neutrality, with targets for each year. We’re also working on energy-efficiency standards and making every stage of our products’ life cycle greener, from design and manufacturing to recycling. We have a national-level key laboratory focused on energy-efficient air-conditioning equipment and systems, as well as a dedicated research division for new-energy technologies.

There is more to explore. Can we harness heat in the air as a useful energy source? Can we cool a room to the temperature people want without adding heat to the air outside?

Gree has pursued greener cooling for more than a decade. We first proposed a design for powering air conditioners directly with solar electricity in 2012 and developed a working system in 2013.

Our solar-plus-storage range now spans more than 10 product categories, from centrifugal chillers integrating solar generation, storage and flexible use of direct-current power to screw chillers and refrigeration units.

These products can be used in different venues such as factories, shopping centres, offices and cold-storage facilities, and have reached more than 35 countries and regions.

If making money is not your only purpose, you keep asking harder questions and working to solve them. I want Gree to use its capabilities to make the world a better place.

Everyday consumer products should not be dragged into political conflicts. Whatever their skin tone or language, people pursue a better life and should have access to good products

Gree was among the first Chinese companies to expand overseas. In 2015, you came up with the slogan “Let the World Fall in Love with Made in China”. Now, more than a decade later, what has changed in the relationship between Chinese manufacturers and global markets?

The biggest change is that consumers increasingly recognise the quality of Chinese-made products. Chinese travellers may often spot Gree’s name on a building overseas, and local consumers will say they like our air conditioners.

At the core is that Chinese companies are moving from exporting products to building brands overseas.

For years, Chinese home-appliance makers competed globally mainly as original design manufacturers [known as white labelling]. Their share of global manufacturing grew, but their own brands had a limited presence in overseas retail markets.

That is changing. The global market share held by Chinese home-appliance brands rose from 2.9 per cent in 2015 to 10.9 per cent in 2025. Gree now sells to more than 190 countries and regions, with its own brands accounting for over 70 per cent of export sales.

Geopolitics and trade relations are growing more complex, with armed conflicts in some regions. What new challenges does this pose for Chinese companies expanding overseas?

Everyday consumer products should not be dragged into political conflicts. Whatever their skin tone or language, people pursue a better life and should have access to good products.

For Gree, the answer is to keep making the world’s best air conditioners, whatever happens around us. I do not have a separate playbook for overseas markets. I have never drawn a sharp line between domestic and international markets; China is part of the global market too.

What matters more is what consumers need. Europeans need heating in winter, for example. How can we make it more environmentally friendly? Oil-filled radiators and gas heating can come with high equipment and maintenance costs. If we can offer efficient, stand-alone heating, we can reduce the environmental impact and lower consumers’ bills. Whether it sells well, the numbers will tell.

That does not mean the challenges are not real. Tariff barriers are becoming more entrenched and complex. Building a brand overseas requires a deeper understanding of local needs, while swings in distributors’ inventories and regional conflicts can directly affect demand. We are still finding our way through these issues.

Gree carefully selects local business partners. If the market demand is massive, it is possible to establish local manufacturing plants.

Many companies are making acquisitions overseas, but a business cannot grow by just buying up assets. It is like a building: you need a solid foundation first. For us, that means making reliable products consumers want. Once the foundation is sound, you can build on it. I am not interested in playing a numbers game.

Gree’s 2026 interim report showed a decline in overseas revenue and cited the impact of setbacks in the Middle East. How do you view the drop?

The war has indeed affected the market. It would be unrealistic to say that “we go in regardless and avoid any decline.” We have to face the situation as it is, but it will not change our commitment to developing better technology and products for consumers.

Can anyone go through life without catching a cold? Sometimes you may even end up in hospital. What matters is whether you recover. Companies, communities, countries and societies all face difficulties as they develop. The important thing is to confront them.

Gree has been diversifying its revenue sources beyond air conditioners. Which sector do you see as the next growth engine?

We would all love to become a trillion-yuan company overnight, but you have to build a business step by step.

Gree has grown from an air-conditioning maker into a global technology company serving both consumer and industrial markets. Industrial products, intelligent equipment and green energy are emerging as new growth drivers.

In the first half of this year, revenue from our intelligent equipment business rose 19 per cent [to about 374 million yuan (US$56.05 million)], sales from computer-controlled machine tools and industrial robots rose 20 per cent. Our self-developed high-speed dual five-axis gantry machining centres are now being supplied in volume to several new-energy vehicle makers.

In the green energy sector, our silicon carbide business was up 200 per cent year on year. Our silicon carbide power devices are already in mass production for home appliances, and expanding into solar-plus-storage systems and charging stations.

Whether we’re improving our core products or entering new markets, we develop the key technologies ourselves. Over time, that builds capabilities that are hard to replicate. We’re focused on technical depth and a more independent supply chain, not scale for its own sake.

China’s consumer demand is under pressure, and Gree cannot be immune to that. How do you find the consumer market now? How have shopping patterns changed in recent years?

I think the market is just taking an afternoon nap. That’s all.

China’s real estate downturn has indeed had an impact, but our sector does not rely solely on property development.

Consumers are moving beyond asking whether they have an appliance to asking how good it is. They care more about quality, higher-end products and how those products make them feel. They also want appliances that work together across the home, and artificial intelligence that responds to their needs rather than simply adding features to a spec sheet. Old-for-new trade-in policies have become an important source of support for domestic demand.

That means future growth will come from improving our products’ market fit, not chasing volume for its own sake. Technology must solve real problems – whether that means avoiding cold air blowing directly on people, removing formaldehyde or keeping temperature and humidity steady. We are also expanding beyond air conditioning: sales in the home appliances segment grew more than 20 per cent in the first half of this year.

There is also more we can do in the existing market through equipment upgrades and trade-ins, while pursuing new opportunities in data-centre cooling, high-temperature heat pumps and zero-carbon parks.

In a market increasingly driven by replacement purchases, people will pay more for a better experience, higher energy efficiency and greener products. That is the market foundation for our long-term investment in research and development.

How far has Gree’s push into automation and smart manufacturing gone, what obstacles have you encountered, and what lessons does the journey offer to other Chinese manufacturers?

Intelligent manufacturing has two sides: smarter products and smarter production.

Opening the curtains or turning on the television with a voice command is a sort of progress. But real intelligence means devices can sense what is happening and interact with people. I’m in Singapore now, and I can check my air conditioner, refrigerator and washing machine at home from my phone. If food has been in the fridge too long, it tells me what I need to use soon. Technology like this should make life healthier, easier and more comfortable.

We are now making much more than air conditioners. We also make refrigerators, washing machines, dishwashers and other kitchen appliances. Because we design these products as part of one connected home system from the start, they can work together rather than being pieced together later.

Meanwhile, on the production side, automation can relieve workers of physically demanding, repetitive tasks and help them move from routine operations into skilled technical roles.

We have our own intelligent equipment business – manufacturing equipment that includes industrial robots and computer-controlled machine tools. We handle everything in-house, from design and components to system integration.

Our Jinwan plant in Zhuhai, selected last year as a “pioneer-level” smart factory [the highest tier of China’s national smart-factory programme], shows what this takes. We had to develop core equipment, connect data across R&D, procurement, manufacturing and sales, and move beyond automating individual tasks to coordinating the whole operation. That last step required changes to workflows and management, not just technology.

We made it through a coordination model, which connects design, suppliers, production, quality control, logistics and warehousing on a shared platform.

Twenty years ago, some labelled Chinese manufacturing as cheap and poor quality. That has changed. For China’s move towards smart manufacturing, the lesson is to combine the ability to build core equipment, connect operations digitally and use data across the entire process – and then turn that into a system others can adopt.

There’s no unique challenge. The question is whether you are willing to do the work and risk failure.

Automation frequently sparks public concerns regarding job losses. From a corporate leadership perspective, how do you address these concerns, and what specific programmes or initiatives have been implemented by Gree to upskill, reskill and help its workforce adapt to a technology-driven manufacturing environment?

We have never laid people off because of automation.

People do leave each year, for many reasons. Some return to their hometowns or move to be with a partner. Others want more freedom at work and find manufacturing’s rules and standards are not for them. Some learn a little and decide they are ready to strike out on their own.

Other home-appliance companies regularly poach our people. One company hired 600 to 700 Gree employees in a year, including frontline workers. I came to see that as proof that we train good people. Rather than recruit from companies I consider less capable, I would rather invest in developing young talent.

This year, we opened a Gree technical school. Its teaching team brings together experienced Gree engineers, senior technicians and specialist teachers. The school offers programmes geared towards fields including smart manufacturing, electrical technology and information technology.

In the past, we replaced people as they left; now we do not necessarily fill every opening.

Automation is about training the skilled workers that smart manufacturing needs. The more automated a factory becomes, the more it needs people who can operate and manage its equipment. By combining classroom learning with hands-on training, we want the skills that students acquire to match the technology our factories actually use.

Technology replaces repetitive tasks while creating demand for higher-level skills. Workers need to keep learning as jobs change

Automation does create a tension, but working through it can make a company stronger. A smart factory that once needed 14,000 people may now need only 2,000. That does not mean I would dismiss 12,000 workers.

Automation has changed the mix of jobs, so workers need to keep learning and upgrading their skills. Employees can move into more skilled roles. Someone who once drove a forklift might manage an automated logistics system instead.

A production line at our Jinwan plant needs just 20 skilled employees, but they must be able to monitor equipment, analyse data and diagnose faults.

Technology replaces repetitive tasks while creating demand for higher-level skills. Workers need to keep learning as jobs change.

We also recruited 5,000 university graduates this year. Many of Gree’s senior and middle managers joined after graduation and grew with the company. That is why they have such a strong connection to the group.

We have always aimed to become a diversified, technology-driven global industrial group. That means more than expanding into new businesses. We want to move beyond selling products to providing technology and helping build an industrial ecosystem. Our technical school is one way we’re developing the people needed to make that happen.

Historically, every major wave of technological innovation has forced companies to transform. How is Gree navigating the current rise of AI?

Before phones could store numbers, I was able to remember 200 or 300 of them. Now I sometimes struggle to recall my own. In that sense, technology can weaken an ability when we stop using it.

Of course technology should advance. But we need to think about where it takes us and how we use it. That is a question for society, not just Gree. Journalists worry that AI will write their articles. If we eventually lose the habit of thinking for ourselves, what is left of us beyond eating and drinking?

Problems are born with solutions. AI may create opportunities in services – for example, if people have more time and money, they may travel more, right?

Every era brings opportunities and setbacks. What matters is how we respond. Gree is changing every day, regardless of what happens outside. Our goal remains simple: make the world’s best products. There is no need to make a grand speech about it.

Listed on the Shenzhen Stock Exchange, Gree is one of the biggest home appliance makers in China, with a market capitalisation of more than 200 billion yuan. But there is a significant disparity in how Gree and some rivals are valued in the capital markets, with price-to-earnings ratios differing. How would you respond?

Someone once told me, “Our company is doing very well – our price-to-earnings ratio is 100.” I was startled. If a valuation is out of line with the business’s underlying assets, shareholders may be the ones who lose out.

Gree should be an honest, steady company. Over the years, we have raised only 5 billion yuan from the stock market and paid shareholders more than 160 billion yuan in dividends. Tell me, is that good or bad?

To build a business that lasts, systems matter, but choosing the right people matters more. A new leader can change the rules. You need someone who will preserve what works and keep improving it. People are crucial.

You started from Haili, Gree’s predecessor, and helped build a small Zhuhai factory into a company that made it to the Fortune Global 500. How do you view your relationship with Gree? Has your own mindset changed over the years? And how do you feel about being called the “Iron Lady” for your decisive, no-nonsense leadership style?

Gree is the soil. But even fertile soil cannot make a weak seed sprout and bear fruit; even the best seed will struggle in poor soil. The individual and the company need each other to grow.

I’m the same as I’ve always been. It’s that simple. Gree is my life.

As for “Iron Lady”, I do not care what people call me. What matters is whether I have done my job well.

You often speak about hard work, responsibility and helping others. Succession is a question facing Gree and many other Chinese companies that grew during the reform era. How do you think about it, and what values do you hope to pass on?

Every company has its own culture, so there is no single answer. Gree’s culture is straightforward: we must keep innovating, and everyone must be loyal to the company. Integrity comes first. The ideal is to have both integrity and ability; ability without integrity can be dangerous. Those values must endure. You cannot set integrity aside when a new generation takes over.

Hard work, responsibility and helping others are not uniquely Chinese values. They matter everywhere. People will see things differently, but we can work through those differences.

Your experience has inspired many young women along the way. What would you say to them?

People come from all walks of life and will have all kinds of different things to say. Just stay true to yourself.

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong helps mainland Chinese firms go global – but can they really win now?
item.description:
When Shenzhen-listed digital infrastructure provider Runjian Corporation expanded into the Middle East and Southeast Asia through Hong Kong, adapting meant more than translating software interfaces or navigating local data privacy laws.

It also meant changing the company’s working practices and abandoning the expectation, carried over from its domestic operations, that one mainland Chinese employee could match the output of three local hires.

“When expanding overseas, companies must do more than just take their products and technology abroad. We also need to respect local culture and truly integrate into the local market,” said Athena Zhao Hua, Runjian’s vice-president and president of its overseas business group. “When in Rome, you have to align with the local rhythm.”
item.content:encoded:
When Shenzhen-listed digital infrastructure provider Runjian Corporation expanded into the Middle East and Southeast Asia through Hong Kong, adapting meant more than translating software interfaces or navigating local data privacy laws.

It also meant changing the company’s working practices and abandoning the expectation, carried over from its domestic operations, that one mainland Chinese employee could match the output of three local hires.

“When expanding overseas, companies must do more than just take their products and technology abroad. We also need to respect local culture and truly integrate into the local market,” said Athena Zhao Hua, Runjian’s vice-president and president of its overseas business group. “When in Rome, you have to align with the local rhythm.”

The adjustments ranged from installing prayer rooms and arranging halal catering for team-building activities to an unwritten rule for Chinese staff: avoid eating or drinking in front of local colleagues fasting during Ramadan.

While Runjian relied on the Hong Kong government to establish local connections when it entered a new territory, such cultural adaptation was learned through its own hard-won experience. Zhao said she hoped Hong Kong could offer more targeted cultural training, market intelligence and links to local business networks to help expanding firms acclimatise more quickly.

Runjian was one of 340 mainland Chinese enterprises spearheading their global expansion with the help of Hong Kong’s GoGlobal Task Force over the past year. Its experience reflected how mainland enterprises venturing into Southeast and Central Asia were evolving, navigating steep cultural learning curves to survive.

While Hong Kong has positioned itself as an indispensable springboard – offering the cultural insights, regulatory advice and commercial networks these firms lacked – their rapid maturation poses a critical test for the city.

According to a local think tank, the real challenge is whether the city’s role as a “superconnector” can offer enough strategic depth and durability to remain relevant once these firms learn to stand on their own feet.

Ryan Ip Man-ki, vice-president of the think tank Our Hong Kong Foundation and executive director of its Public Policy Institute, said the task force had a positive start.

“The next test, however, should be the depth and durability of this engagement, rather than just the number of enterprises assisted,” he said.

“We should look at whether enterprises establish international functions, deploy talent and capital, and continue to use Hong Kong as they expand into overseas markets.”

East meets West

In an exclusive interview with the South China Morning Post, Secretary for Commerce and Economic Development Algernon Yau Ying-wah said the 340 mainland firms the task force had helped operated across sectors including logistics, construction, finance and technology. About 30 per cent sought to establish corporate treasury centres in Hong Kong to raise capital or handle offshore trading.

“Hong Kong is a place where East meets West. We had a good connection with the Western world for so many years in the past,” said Yau, who overseas the task force.

“We understand the way business is being done, and we understand their culture and language.”

He added that mainland enterprises did not have sufficient information regarding the situation in other countries, including legal systems, business practices, culture, communication, languages and professional services.

To bridge that gap, the government’s Economic and Trade Offices, together with offices operated by the Hong Kong Trade Development Council and InvestHK, provided information on countries’ legal requirements and business environments. The combined network spans 68 cities and covers 129 economies.

InvestHK, the government’s investment promotion arm, helped these enterprises plan and coordinate their visits to Hong Kong. It arranged meetings with potential partners and accompanied firms on key site visits to map out their internationalisation strategies, prioritise localisation and understand local culture.

It also organised industry-specific forums and media round tables where companies could share their expertise, connect with global industry stakeholders and strengthen their brand positioning.

The Trade Development Council also launched the GoGlobal Cross-sectoral Professional Services Platform, with a database of 200 qualified Hong Kong service providers in fields including law, accounting, testing and certification, to support companies expanding abroad.

“We work closely with companies to understand their needs, explore application scenarios in Hong Kong, and match them with suitable partners,” Yau said, adding that the government actively helped companies identify land suitable for AI data centres and other R&D operations.

With more than 60 million small and medium-sized enterprises on the mainland, Yau acknowledged that carefully matching companies with suitable markets was essential to avoid wasted effort.

“How can we take all of them going overseas? I think until the end of my life, I will not be able to take all of them going overseas. So, the most important thing is to do the matching correctly” he said.

“In all different places on the mainland, enterprises are willing to go overseas, but we have to be selective to pick the right enterprise to the right place at the right time, to the right country, with the right focus … Otherwise, that will be a waste of effort and time.

“Let’s say mining companies going to Uzbekistan or Kazakhstan will work, but if they are going to other places, it does not work.”

Yau added that Hong Kong’s overseas offices were identifying local market needs and matching them with suitable mainland enterprises. Those companies were then invited to establish a base in Hong Kong, raise capital and recruit local staff before expanding abroad.

He said officials and agencies supporting the effort included the chief executive, Yau himself, the Belt and Road Office, the Trade Development Council and InvestHK.

That matching process is increasingly being handled through a cross-border pipeline with Shenzhen.

Earlier this year, Shenzhen’s Qianhai Authority repositioned itself as an onshore scout to identify suitable companies and refer them to Hong Kong as a springboard for international expansion. The approach complemented Hong Kong’s efforts to attract overseas businesses into the Greater Bay Area.

“So, the point is how we are going to complement each other and use the strength of each other to make the Go Global effort even stronger and more eventful and fruitful,” Yau said.

Gary Wong Chi-him, chief Hong Kong and Macau liaison expert at the Qianhai Authority, said the Shenzhen Qianhai international business e-station had recorded 1.5 million visits and attracted 55,000 registered users since its launch in July 2024. The platform connects government services with market resources to help Chinese enterprises expand globally.

“By seamlessly combining Hong Kong’s world-class financial infrastructure with Qianhai’s status as the Chinese mainland’s institutional innovation pilot zone, the two regions are actively helping domestic firms scale internationally while simultaneously bringing global enterprises into the GBA,” he said.

Wong cited Nailoong, a chubby yellow cartoon dinosaur developed by a Qianhai-based company, as an example of how businesses were working with Hong Kong’s creative industries to take their intellectual property worldwide.

In the first half of 2026, Qianhai’s modern services sector recorded 25.01 billion yuan in foreign capital actually utilised, accounting for 76.5 per cent of Shenzhen’s total. It also attracted 1,335 new foreign-invested firms.

Actual utilised capital from Hong Kong reached 24 billion yuan, while 1,092 new Hong Kong-funded enterprises were established in Qianhai.

According to Wong, Qianhai was home to 11,333 Hong Kong-funded enterprises in total.

“The integration of Qianhai and Hong Kong establishes a powerful ‘dual headquarters’ infrastructure designed to eliminate operational friction and mitigate geopolitical risks for modern enterprises,” he said.

‘If you do not go out, you get out’

Behind Runjian’s willingness to absorb those cultural challenges in the workplace is fierce domestic competition.

“As the saying now goes in China, ‘If you do not go out, you get out’,” Zhao said, explaining that companies risked being pushed out of the market if they failed to expand overseas.

Since beginning its international expansion through Hong Kong in 2019, Runjian has entered Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia, the Philippines and Singapore, achieving a compound annual growth rate of 33 per cent in its overseas business.

Earlier this year, the company expanded into Saudi Arabia after identifying opportunities in new energy to support AI development in the Middle East, amid geopolitical tensions and surging oil prices.

Zhao said Runjian had sought advice from the Hong Kong government on local policy incentives, compliance requirements, tax efficiency and whether to invest directly through its mainland parent company or its Hong Kong subsidiary for its expansion into Saudi Arabia.

With demand for new energy and data centres rising, the company also planned to expand into Central Asia, including Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan.

Despite Runjian’s extensive international footprint, it continued to rely on the Hong Kong government’s backing across various expansion phases.

Zhao said Runjian was part of a delegation Yau led to Malaysia in August, where the company was connected to senior local officials, business chambers, legal bodies and potential business partners, even though it first entered the country in 2023.

She noted that the Hong Kong government could connect the company to high-level contacts that it normally would not have access to, adding that this official endorsement also bolstered local clients’ trust in the firm.

Zhao also said that as the company gained a foothold locally, it faced another challenge.

“How do we better adapt to local markets or we risk operational friction?” she said.

In Indonesia, its first overseas market, Runjian recruited local executives to gradually replace Chinese staff in senior leadership roles. Zhao said those executives had a better understanding of the local business environment, sharpening the company’s competitive edge.

While Runjian focused on adapting its operations to local cultures, other Chinese businesses sought to take centuries-old cultural traditions to international markets.

State-owned Guangzhou Pharmaceutical Corporation (GPC), the parent company of herbal tea brand Walovi, recently drew global attention with viral advertising campaigns featuring Norwegian football star Erling Haaland during the World Cup.

Tracing its roots to the Chen Li Ji pharmacy, founded in 1600, GPC established a presence in Hong Kong in 1988 to pursue international markets. Last year, it based its global research and development and treasury operations in the city.

In a statement, the company cited Hong Kong’s strengths in scientific research, talent, capital, access to global resources and international communications.

According to GPC, Walovi’s international footprint has expanded 6.5-fold over the past decade to cover more than 100 countries. Recent launches included Riyadh, Kuala Lumpur and Sydney, while a new international headquarters opened in Singapore in August.

The company also planned to establish an overseas production line for its flagship drink.

But taking a traditional Chinese medicine business global presented a different set of challenges. GPC said it had encountered fragmented overseas regulatory frameworks, complex drug registration systems and strict cold-chain distribution requirements for medical products.

Despite those hurdles, the Fortune 500 company was pressing ahead with plans to establish a subsidiary in Vietnam and explore emerging markets in Central Asia.

With some of its medicines already registered and available overseas, GPC aimed to expand the international reach of its products and brand while promoting the industry and the culture of traditional Chinese medicine.

“We are committed to preserving and promoting traditional Chinese medicine culture, allowing consumers worldwide to experience its unique charm,” the company said.

Evolving role

Lawmaker Rock Chen Chung-nin said Hong Kong’s role had evolved from providing basic business referrals to serving as a high-value regional operating base, a problem-solving centre and a “resource allocation centre” for more mature enterprises.

He said the city could attract mainland enterprises to establish regional headquarters and treasury centres in Hong Kong for cross-border settlement, remittances and financing. He also suggested Hong Kong further refine listing mechanisms and lower listing thresholds for technology and innovation enterprises and small and medium-sized enterprises.

Chen said the government could establish “market-corridor teams” for priority markets such as Asean, Central Asia and the Middle East to combine the practical experience of mature enterprises with the objective insights of Hong Kong professionals to build highly resilient, compliance-ready international business operations.

“In my view, the challenge is not a lack of willingness among Hong Kong service providers; rather, it is the increasing complexity of the overseas expansion environment,” he said.

He added that the government should remind professional service providers to proactively assist enterprises in assessing geopolitical risks, data governance and legal and regulatory compliance in target markets.

It should also address the talent gap in emerging markets such as the Middle East and Central Asia, and expand outreach on the mainland and strengthen interdepartmental coordination.

Ip of Our Hong Kong Foundation said that although some mainland companies could share their experiences in overseas expansion and operations, such knowledge was often highly market-specific. Moreover, they could not provide the tailored professional services other companies needed.

He said companies that had already expanded globally still needed high-quality professional services and a hub to cluster their international functions.

Hong Kong could provide highly customised support with its comprehensive professional services. “Hong Kong can offer these unique, irreplaceable values,” he said.

Looking ahead, Ip said Hong Kong could continue to play a key role in facilitating the overseas expansion of mainland enterprises.

He said the city should move from one-stop services to end-to-end support, from setting up in Hong Kong to operating overseas. It should also strengthen its role as a place where enterprises could test, certify and showcase products and services for global markets.

Ip also urged the government to deepen market-specific support, focus on creating lasting economic value for Hong Kong and strengthen the city’s role as a two-way gateway for both companies expanding overseas and those entering the mainland.

“The objective should gradually move from helping companies ‘go through’ Hong Kong to ‘grow through and expand in’ Hong Kong,” he said.

“It means that enterprises do not simply use Hong Kong for a one-off service to access overseas markets, but continue to use Hong Kong’s professional and financial services, retain substantive business functions here, and generate sustained economic value for the city.”

item.title: [SCMP] Pump pressure: how rising fuel costs leave Hong Kong drivers running on fumes
item.description:
Van driver Wong Siu-po, 48, feels life is becoming more difficult than ever as rising fuel prices cost him an additional HK$5,000 (US$640) a month, about a third of his monthly income.

With an 11-year-old daughter and an unemployed wife to support, he feels the pressure mounting.

“I need to work three hours longer per day to make up for the loss of income,” he said. “I will cut down on air conditioning to save costs.”
item.content:encoded:
Van driver Wong Siu-po, 48, feels life is becoming more difficult than ever as rising fuel prices cost him an additional HK$5,000 (US$640) a month, about a third of his monthly income.

With an 11-year-old daughter and an unemployed wife to support, he feels the pressure mounting.

“I need to work three hours longer per day to make up for the loss of income,” he said. “I will cut down on air conditioning to save costs.”

Wong’s plight echoes survey findings showing that nearly 98 per cent of commercial drivers deem the government’s support “inadequate” or “very inadequate” as rising fuel prices, driven by the Middle East war and a global energy crisis, take a toll on their livelihoods.

Drivers have called for further government support after a two-month subsidy ended in June.

The poll of 770 respondents, conducted earlier this month by the Talk To You Now People Livelihood Progress Group – a concern group active in the Tuen Mun, Yuen Long and Tin Shui Wai areas – found that 98.7 per cent reported higher monthly fuel costs after a government subsidy ended.

More than a quarter said they paid at least HK$5,000 extra a month, while many said they worked longer hours, dipped into savings or cut maintenance to stay on the road.
