Ganewati Wuryandari, a professor of international relations and energy security at Indonesia’s National Research and Innovation Agency, said China-linked projects had always received adequate priority and regulatory coherence at the national level.

Some were designated national strategic projects from the start, “bypassing a lot of red tape and otherwise cumbersome processes”, she said.

Ganewati gave the example of Indonesia Morowali Industrial Park, a joint venture between China’s Tsingshan Group and Indonesia’s Bintang Delapan Group that Widodo inaugurated in 2015 and is now one of the world’s largest nickel processing centres.

Syahdiva Moezbar, an industry analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air in Jakarta, said long-term success would depend on “turning industrial momentum into real technology transfer and building local manufacturing capabilities beyond model assembly”.

Community discontent

Local opposition has also caused issues in the recent past. On October 28, hundreds of residents of Subang, West Java, protested outside a factory Chinese EV maker BYD opened the month before, demanding more jobs for local people.

Industry Minister Muhammad Sarmuji acknowledged the dispute, telling local media there were “sometimes different perspectives between industry and the community” when it came to employment opportunities.

West Java authorities said BYD had advertised about 3,000 positions and hired more than 800 workers through a provincial recruitment platform, and had met local officials and representatives of the protesters.

Ganewati said the dispute showed how deals struck at the national level could encounter difficulties with local implementation.

“While our central government is generally good at negotiating with its Chinese counterpart, it often overlooks mitigating local aspirations and conditions,” she said.

Muhammad Zulfikar Rakhmat, director of Celios’ China-Indonesia desk, identified a lack of coordinated communication as another issue.

He said the two governments typically communicated via separate forums with no shared agenda, leaving disputes to be handled on a case-by-case basis.

“Indonesia needs one forum, one project list and one ministry in charge of all the projects involved,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Nvidia scandal may test fragile US-China truce, experts say
item.description:
The fallout from the Nvidia scandal may test the fragile truce between the US and China, analysts say, as calls in Washington grow to tighten semiconductor export controls just days before US President Donald Trump is due to meet Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China.

“I think that [scandal] could have a bigger impact down the line during the meeting in Miami or even further down the line,” said Ilaria Mazzocco, a senior fellow at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies. Mazzocco was referring to another Trump-Xi meeting expected in December on the sidelines of the Group of 20 (G20) summit in Miami.

Mazzocco added that the bilateral arrangement was underpinned by the leverage each country held over the other, particularly China’s dominance in rare earths, which could limit Washington’s room to tighten restrictions.
item.content:encoded:
The fallout from the Nvidia scandal may test the fragile truce between the US and China, analysts say, as calls in Washington grow to tighten semiconductor export controls just days before US President Donald Trump is due to meet Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China.

“I think that [scandal] could have a bigger impact down the line during the meeting in Miami or even further down the line,” said Ilaria Mazzocco, a senior fellow at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies. Mazzocco was referring to another Trump-Xi meeting expected in December on the sidelines of the Group of 20 (G20) summit in Miami.

Mazzocco added that the bilateral arrangement was underpinned by the leverage each country held over the other, particularly China’s dominance in rare earths, which could limit Washington’s room to tighten restrictions.

“It has the potential to deepen mistrust between the US and China at a sensitive moment in bilateral relations,” wrote George Chen, a Partner and Chair of Digital Practice at The Asia Group, in a Substack post.

However, some experts argue that the controversy is unlikely to have an immediate impact on the coming meeting during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen, given Trump’s public backing of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and his continued efforts to build a closer relationship with Xi.

“I really don’t see this as having a huge impact on the summit,” said Sam Bresnick, a research fellow at Georgetown University’s Centre for Security and Emerging Technology.

Nvidia’s board launched a probe on Sunday after a New York Times report linked Huang to a Chinese businesswoman suspected by US intelligence officials of passing information to Beijing.

In a statement, Huang admitted he had been unfaithful to his wife and would fully cooperate with the inquiry.

Beijing calls allegations ‘nothing but smears against China’

Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun called the allegations “unsubstantiated” and said they amounted to “nothing but smears against China”.

Huang became a regular presence in Washington as Nvidia sought to sell its advanced chips to China, forging a close working relationship with Trump.

Several lawmakers and defence analysts have spent months opposing the Trump administration’s decision last year to permit sales of Nvidia’s H200 chips to China, the company’s second-best AI chips, warning the move compromises the push to contain Beijing’s AI ambitions.

The White House largely resisted calls for tougher oversight, as the administration sought to shield frequent Xi-Trump engagements and sustain the fragile trade truce negotiated in Busan, South Korea.

But with Huang – who aggressively lobbied to loosen those restrictions – now embroiled in an alleged espionage scandal, the fallout has refocused Congressional pressure on the administration to reverse course and impose tighter controls.

Lawmakers on Monday demanded an investigation and summoned Huang for a closed-door briefing on November 18.

“I’m pushing to investigate Jensen Huang and Nvidia to determine whether our national security was compromised,” Democratic Senator Chris Coons, who is also part of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, wrote on social media.

However, analysts say Trump could still ignore the pressure to preserve his personal ties with Xi.

“Congress can only do so much to force his hand,” said Ali Wyne, senior research and advocacy adviser at the International Crisis Group.

“Trump has largely ignored its counsel to date, and he has given every indication that he intends to continue focusing on burnishing his rapport with Xi,” Wyne said.

Bresnick believed the scandal would give Democrats further impetus to tighten export control restrictions again, with Trump’s response closely watched.

“It’ll be interesting to see how that works and if Trump is going to veto any sort of harsher export control measures and whether there will be enough bipartisan pushback to overwhelm that veto,” he added.

Hilton Root, a professor of public policy at George Mason University, argued that while Congress has “substantial power,” it operates through “investigation and legislation.”

“In the immediate term, Congress’s strongest leverage may be to establish a public record of failures that makes continued approvals politically difficult,” he added.

As pressure mounts, Trump has publicly defended Huang, calling him an “honourable guy” who has “done such an incredible job”.

Trump said: “I asked him that question: Did you have any idea that she was a spy? He said I had no idea that she was a spy, and I really believe him.”

Huang remains influential figure in US-China technology race

Huang has emerged as a key figure in the US-China technology engagement. In May, he was invited at the last minute to join Trump for his trip to Beijing to visit Xi.

He travelled with the president on Air Force One to China as part of the US’ high-profile tech delegation. The summit marked the first visit by a US president in nearly a decade.

Additionally, when Xi visited the US in September, Huang and his wife Lori were invited to the White House state dinner and given a prime seat at the table with both Xi and Trump.

Trump said on Sunday he would still invite the Nvidia CEO on his coming trip to Asia, adding: “I’d certainly take him.”

Trump is scheduled to travel to the Philippines from November 16 to 18 to attend the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit.

He will then visit Shenzhen for the Apec meetings, where he is due to hold his third bilateral meeting of the year with Xi.

“It doesn’t seem like this [scandal] is affecting president Trump’s confidence in Jensen Huang,” Mazzocco said.

Bresnick predicts that Trump’s view on Huang could change over time, depending on what comes next.

“I assume people on his staff will be trying to pry him away from Huang. The way that I see Trump making decisions is that when things get too toxic, he will finally distance himself,” said Bresnick.

“That could happen as we go forward here, and as investigations reveal other things, we could see Trump say, OK, maybe it’s politically too costly to align myself with this guy.”

item.title: [SCMP] Southeast Asian horror games unleash local nightmares on the world
item.description:
While some tropes like zombies are universally scary, others sources of terror require specific cultural knowledge to inspire dread – something Wyn Panichpakdee realised while watching both Thai and international players test his studio’s latest video game.

In Kumarn: The Wandering Spirit, players encounter phi nang rum, menacing dancing spirit dolls from Thai folklore. Wyn said Thai players instantly recognised the dolls and braced themselves for something horrifying, while foreign players required more visceral scares before they reacted.

“They were just surprised when there was a jump scare. They weren’t scared at the beginning,” said Wyn, who is managing director at Thai game maker Werebuff Studio.
item.content:encoded:
While some tropes like zombies are universally scary, others sources of terror require specific cultural knowledge to inspire dread – something Wyn Panichpakdee realised while watching both Thai and international players test his studio’s latest video game.

In Kumarn: The Wandering Spirit, players encounter phi nang rum, menacing dancing spirit dolls from Thai folklore. Wyn said Thai players instantly recognised the dolls and braced themselves for something horrifying, while foreign players required more visceral scares before they reacted.

“They were just surprised when there was a jump scare. They weren’t scared at the beginning,” said Wyn, who is managing director at Thai game maker Werebuff Studio.

Werebuff is among several Southeast Asian video game developers seizing on the growing popularity of horror-themed titles by tapping into local folklore and horror tropes. But as its playtesting showed, making culturally familiar sources of dread unsettling to international gamers can be a challenge.

Indonesia’s Separuh Interactive is another studio developing horror games by drawing on local culture for international audiences. It, along with Werebuff, has partnered with British publisher Wired Productions to bring its games to the world.

But translating local stories into games with international appeal is only part of the challenge, with funding and talent issues among other barriers that studios must overcome to succeed.

Regional spending

Southeast Asian gamers already represent a substantial market. A joint report by research firm Niko Partners and games-commerce company Xsolla put the region’s mobile and PC games spending at more than US$5.6 billion in 2025, projecting it to exceed US$7 billion by 2030.

Indonesia, Thailand and Vietnam together accounted for about two-thirds of that spending by consumers, rather than the earnings by local studios. This Week In Asia has reached out to Niko Partners for comment.

Southeast Asia’s game developers are also building on their established role producing content for overseas clients.

A 2024 report led by Malaysia’s Digital Economy Corporation (MDEC) described the region as an outsourcing hub and noted that independent studios were becoming more active in developing their own intellectual property.

The report’s findings drew on responses from 48 studios and 295 individuals across six countries, but the authors cautioned that the sample size was small and the results could not be widely generalised.

Governments are also trying to strengthen the production side of the industry.

In 2025, MDEC announced 3.5 million ringgit (US$862,325) in support for at least five game-development firms to help expand their intellectual-property portfolios and encourage global partnerships. This was followed by the 2026 Digital Content Grant, which offered up to 2 million ringgit per project for original animation or games intended for global markets.

In May this year, Le Quang Tu Do, director of Vietnam’s Authority of Broadcasting and Electronic Information under the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism, designated video games as one of six main strategic cultural industries.

Speaking at the Gameverse event in Ho Chi Minh City, Do said companies producing games centred on history and culture would receive tax incentives and reductions, Vietnamese media reported.

In the Philippines, the Department of Trade reported US$4.87 million in confirmed and potential sales from a government-backed Gamescom delegation in 2025. This extended beyond completed sales, including prospective publishing agreements, outsourcing contracts and co-production projects.

Financing a project

For individual studios, securing the resources to finish a game can be precarious, as Separuh’s chief operating officer and lead producer, Ardhan Fadhlurrahman, discovered.

AGNI: Village of Calamity began with the ambition to create an Indonesian take on the survival horror game Alan Wake 2. Its protagonist investigates supernatural events in a fictional village inspired by Central Java, with everyday details, from pickup trucks carrying vegetables to the market to the way she wears her hijab, setting the horror in contemporary Indonesia.

“Our purpose is to make a playable film,” Ardhan said. Players can inspect objects for additional context but do not need to understand every cultural reference to progress.

Ardhan said the studio emerged from developers and artists affected by lost outsourcing work, cancelled projects and lay-offs during the 2024 video games industry upheaval, which saw several big-budget games cancelled.

Initially a chat group of friends comparing their setbacks, the collective pooled about US$10,000 in savings and produced an early motion-capture teaser to test interest.

More funds came through a grant from an Xbox developer programme and angel investment, but Ardhan said that the team expanded too quickly before the project had sufficient direction, which pressured its finances.

Recounting his experience meeting prospective publishers, Ardhan said he was told Separuh’s targets were “excessive”. The studio then narrowed its focus to atmosphere, storytelling and visual detail, limiting gameplay to a maximum of eight hours.

An encounter with Wired Productions at Gamescom in Cologne in 2025 led to publishing discussions. Even then, finalising the agreement took about half a year.

“By the time Separuh signed, we only had three people remaining,” Ardhan said. “We had to ask them [the other staff] to stop working and recommended them to other studios, rather than promise wages we could not afford.”

Former staff returned after the deal was signed.

Ardhan praised Wired for helping connect the team with Nvidia specialists and other developers to improve performance on less powerful hardware. This Week In Asia has reached out to Wired Productions for comment.

Reversing horror tropes

Werebuff, meanwhile, aims to reverse the usual relationship between people and ghosts.

Kumarn follows a spirit taken away from its shrine and searching for somewhere to belong. Its protagonist draws on the kuman thong, which Wyn described as a spirit doll kept for good luck. The protagonist is accompanied by a zebra doll, also inspired by offerings found at Thai shrines.

“You imagine Annabelle, but like a friendlier version of Annabelle,” Wyn said, referring to the haunted doll from The Conjuring film franchise.

Wyn co-founded Werebuff with partners at Thai film and television company Kantana. The studio drew gameplay inspiration from hits like Little Nightmares, combining a vulnerable protagonist with exploration and puzzles. Rather than dialogue, the story relies on environments, animation and sound for gamer immersion.

Initial funds for Werebuff came from Wyn and Kantana, and marketing and production outsourcing work helped sustain operations.

“Initially, recruiting programmers experienced with the Unreal game engine was difficult, but we’ve grown to about 15 people, from the four or five we started with,” Wyn recounted.

Both AGNI and Kumarn are aiming for late 2027 releases, and Wyn and Ardhan are keen to ensure their titles are polished and ready by then.

For Werebuff, this includes returning to the problem revealed during its overseas testing: how to make the phi nang rum frightening even to players unfamiliar with the dancing spirits in Thai folklore.

Wyn said the team was refining the spirits’ designs and animations to make them as unsettling as possible while incorporating their backstories into the game.

“It doesn’t matter [if] they don’t understand that dancing spirit doll,” he said. “But if they can feel from the sight that it’s scary, I think … that’s OK.”

item.title: [SCMP] Escaping Russia’s web: Central Asia is caught between Chinese networks and US tech curbs
item.description:
Days after three Russian data centres were hit by Ukrainian drone attacks last month – paralysing taxi, delivery and payment apps across Central Asia – Tajikistan launched an internet link between its capital Dushanbe and Beijing.

The optical fibre, which runs through the Pamir Mountains, offers a direct link to Hong Kong – one of the largest internet traffic exchange points in the Asia-Pacific – and marks Tajikistan’s fifth international communication access point.

To the west, Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan have also forged an alternative route. Backed by the European Union’s Global Gateway Initiative on Digital Connectivity, the two nations inaugurated a 380km (236 miles) undersea cable across the Caspian Sea in October.
item.content:encoded:
Days after three Russian data centres were hit by Ukrainian drone attacks last month – paralysing taxi, delivery and payment apps across Central Asia – Tajikistan launched an internet link between its capital Dushanbe and Beijing.

The optical fibre, which runs through the Pamir Mountains, offers a direct link to Hong Kong – one of the largest internet traffic exchange points in the Asia-Pacific – and marks Tajikistan’s fifth international communication access point.

To the west, Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan have also forged an alternative route. Backed by the European Union’s Global Gateway Initiative on Digital Connectivity, the two nations inaugurated a 380km (236 miles) undersea cable across the Caspian Sea in October.

Connecting the port city of Aktau in southwest Kazakhstan to Azerbaijan’s Sumgait near the Caspian Sea, the subsea link bypasses Russian territory entirely. Central Asian data is instead channelled through Azerbaijan, Georgia and Turkey into Europe.

But observers said the ambitious effort to avoid Russian vulnerabilities might not deliver true digital autonomy for Central Asia – and it could turn the region into a frontier for geopolitical rivalry between China and the US.

Central Asia’s digital sovereignty has been constrained by geography. Kazakhstan, for example, has 17 fibre-optic lines with Russia but only two with China and five with its Central Asian neighbours, according to an April report by the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Centre.

More than 90 per cent of its internet traffic transits through Russia’s networks, while its internet service providers source around 80 per cent of their international bandwidth from Russian operators, the report said.

Russia’s top internet firm, Yandex, is a dominant presence in digital life across Central Asia – it is the company behind everything from ride-hailing and food delivery to search engines, cloud storage and fintech.

So when Ukrainian drones hit Yandex’s key data facilities in western Russia between October 8 and 11 it sent immediate shock waves across Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan.

Artem Khan, an analyst with Beijing-based think tank the Grandview Institution, said the recent Yandex disruptions were a “wake-up call that the region desperately needs to independently diversify its data transit and computing capacities”.

Since the start of the Ukraine war in 2022, Moscow has steadily tightened control over the internet in Russia, curbing independent services and ramping up digital censorship amid concerns over battlefield security.

Khan said that had made digital transit through Russia a “toxic asset”.

“Distancing the region from Russian platforms is no longer driven by geopolitics, but by elementary requirements for cybersecurity and business continuity,” said Khan, an expert on Central Asia’s ties with China.

But as governments across Central Asia look for other options, observers said they could end up with more dependencies.

“True diversification means redundancy: an outage in one direction can be compensated by another,” said Shairbek Juraev, the president of Crossroads Central Asia, an independent research institute in Bishkek.

“What is emerging instead is a division by layer. Russian influence in the region’s digital life sits mainly in platforms and consumer services. China’s role is growing in physical infrastructure and data,” he said.

“Each major power is becoming hard to replace in its own layer, so the region might be accumulating several dependencies rather than reducing any one of them.”

While the EU grapples with bureaucratic delays and limited funds and sanctions-hit Russia struggles with semiconductor shortages, China has a few advantages on the ground. They include ready-to-use equipment, accessible loans and the ability to rapidly build the sort of projects in remote regions that Western investors are reluctant to finance.

The Tajikistan-China internet route is one example. The cost of the project has not been announced but more than 90 per cent of Tajikistan is mountainous, meaning that laying fibre-optic infrastructure will be exceptionally difficult, costly and vulnerable to seismic activity.

China is also working with Central Asian nations on a remote-sensing and monitoring network in space.

Under the agreement, five satellites are to be launched by the end of the year in a constellation dubbed Tianwu. The project aims to provide Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan with artificial intelligence-driven monitoring of climate patterns and natural hazards.

Juraev said there was a real need for disaster monitoring in the region, and the project could also give China the ability to consistently observe the mountains and borders to the west of its Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region and the area near Afghanistan.

According to the Chinese Academy of Sciences, satellite data collected over the region will be processed by a computing centre in Xinjiang, where AI models will be developed for geological disaster prediction, agricultural pest detection, and glacial melt monitoring.

That has raised concerns among some observers that Beijing could secure crucial information regarding regional glacier dynamics and transboundary river basins – some of the most sensitive issues in Central Asian water-sharing diplomacy.

Khan said concerns over data leverage were overstated.

“From a purely pragmatic standpoint, China already controls the headwaters of key transboundary rivers in the region, such as the Irtysh and Ili,” he said.

“For our region, water is a matter of survival. The main threat is not data leakage, but climate change and inefficient resource management.”

According to Juraev, the digital landscape in Central Asia is complicated by internal disparities.

While indebted countries like Tajikistan have limited bargaining power when presented with infrastructure proposals from China, resource-rich states like Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan appear to have more leverage.

Kazakhstan – which has positioned itself as a neutral Eurasian digital bridge – has sought to benefit from both sides of the global tech divide.

It has joined both the US-led Pax Silica initiative and China’s World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation. It has also looked to America for the chips needed to develop its AI industry – a move highlighted by last month’s visit to Astana by Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang.

In June, Astana also announced a US$10 billion partnership with American AI cloud firm Firebird to build an advanced computing cluster powered by up to 100,000 GPUs.

But Kazakhstan could find itself caught between Chinese-built physical networks and Western-controlled computing architecture.

Under tightening US export controls, an export licence from the Department of Commerce is required for American AI chip exports, and projects involving Nvidia and Firebird in Kazakhstan would come with rigorous US auditing standards.

Khan said that to secure top-tier American processors, Kazakhstan must accept rigorous oversight.

“Astana is essentially forced to open its data centres to American auditors to prove that these computing powers are not being rented out to sanctioned Chinese or Russian companies,” he said.

Compliance could create friction with the Chinese hardware that underpins the region’s telecoms networks.

“Networks built heavily on Chinese equipment may face security concerns when they try to connect to Western-backed systems,” according to Juraev. “That could narrow the very diversification these governments are seeking.”

He said the stakes were particularly high for Kazakhstan.

“Kazakhstan faces a sharper version of this, as the top-end American chips come with US conditions on end use and access, while Chinese equipment and data services spread across the region,” he said.

“Keeping these layers separate enough to satisfy preferences of all partners will become a real policy task for Astana.”

Beyond geopolitics, there is another obstacle in the way of Central Asia’s digital ambitions: power shortages.

AI centres need a massive and uninterrupted supply of electricity to run – and that remains a headache for countries in the region.

In August there were large-scale blackouts in cities across Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. Kazakhstan’s energy ministry said at the time they had been caused by a “sudden change in the power flow” from the Central Asian grid.

Khan said the energy crunch could add a new dimension to the superpower rivalry in the region.

Powers including China, the US and Russia as well as the EU have been competing to supply energy infrastructure in Central Asia, from renewable megaprojects to nuclear power plants.

“Both the US and China understand that whoever ultimately builds new power plants for the country will gain actual control over these digital hubs,” Khan said.

item.title: [SCMP] Is the PLA rehearsing operations to keep US forces out of a Taiwan conflict?
item.description:
Recent mainland Chinese naval deployments in the western Pacific and South China Sea have raised questions over whether Beijing is rehearsing operations to stop US and allied forces from intervening in a Taiwan conflict, according to analysts.

Beijing has not announced any large-scale drill in relation to recent People’s Liberation Army (PLA) naval activities.

But a November 6 assessment by US-based think tank the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said the PLA could be conducting a major exercise simulating the isolation of Taiwan, with warships positioned to deter or prevent outside intervention.
item.content:encoded:
Recent mainland Chinese naval deployments in the western Pacific and South China Sea have raised questions over whether Beijing is rehearsing operations to stop US and allied forces from intervening in a Taiwan conflict, according to analysts.

Beijing has not announced any large-scale drill in relation to recent People’s Liberation Army (PLA) naval activities.

But a November 6 assessment by US-based think tank the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said the PLA could be conducting a major exercise simulating the isolation of Taiwan, with warships positioned to deter or prevent outside intervention.

The scale of the deployments – with more than 100 vessels reported – and the presence of naval formations farther into the Pacific rather than just around Taiwan suggest the aim is to stop US and allied forces from reaching the island during a conflict.

Activities include the Liaoning aircraft carrier sailing around the southern Philippines in late October and other PLA warships entering the Pacific through straits near Japan in late October and early November.

The ISW’s assessment drew in part on a November 3 report by Taiwan’s National Security Council secretary general Joseph Wu that said more than 100 PLA Navy and China Coast Guard vessels were operating across the region.

The ISW identified four naval task forces between Taiwan and Guam – alongside vessels near Taiwan – that were reportedly drawn from the PLA’s eastern, northern and southern theatre commands.

It said coordination of surface forces from three theatre commands was “rare”, with major Taiwan-focused drills usually carried out by the eastern military command. The ISW said the recent formations beyond the first island chain “could represent an effort to coordinate” their principal surface combatants.

The naval movements also coincided with increased PLA air activity around Taiwan. The island’s defence ministry said it had detected 49 PLA aircraft sorties in the 24 hours to 6am on November 3, including 36 to the south.

While those numbers were high compared to the year-long average, they were still significantly lower than during previous large-scale drills staged by the PLA near Taiwan, when there have been more than 100 sorties per day.

Southern flights could have been conducted to support warships farther into the Pacific, according to the ISW.

The Pacific is home to the strategically important first island chain that stretches from Japan through Taiwan to the Philippines. It separates the near seas from the Philippine Sea – a potential approach for US and allied forces responding to a Taiwan conflict.

In June last year, the Liaoning and Shandong aircraft carriers operated simultaneously beyond the island chain.

Jim Fanell, a retired US Navy captain and former US Pacific Fleet intelligence official, said the latest deployments suggested preparations for a “no-go zone” using naval, air and land-based missile forces.

“It is the presence of naval task forces from multiple theatre commands that makes me think this is about counter-intervention,” he said.

In a conflict over Taiwan, he said, PLA warships east of the island would seek out and attack US submarines, surface ships and aircraft to stop them from disrupting PLA operations.

Beyond attacking approaching forces, they would also need to disrupt resupply to forces already operating in contested areas, according to Bradley Martin, a senior policy researcher at the Rand Corporation and retired US Navy captain.

The movements could improve coordination among naval formations, increase pressure on Taipei and demonstrate readiness for conflict, said Lyle Goldstein, director of the Asia programme at Washington think tank Defence Priorities.

“My guess is that the concentric or layered defence of some kind of Taiwan operation is the best interpretation at this stage,” said Goldstein, who also heads the China Initiative at Brown University’s Watson School.

He said possible tasks included coordinating naval groups under limited communications, monitoring adversaries and establishing air, missile, drone and anti-submarine defence zones. Northern and southern formations could also screen against foreign intervention.

The Japanese defence ministry has also reported Chinese navy and coastguard vessels passing through straits near Japan in late October. Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said it was the first time the ministry had confirmed and publicly reported such a passage involving both services, though that did not establish their degree of coordination.

Farther south, the Liaoning sailed around the southern Philippines into the Philippine Sea in late October. USNI News subsequently reported the warship being spotted northeast of Luzon, citing Taiwan’s National Security Council.

The ISW suggested that route could help the PLA reach the Pacific without using the Luzon Strait and potentially practise isolating the Philippines. Goldstein highlighted its political signalling and relevance to a wider battlespace.

Fanell said the Liaoning’s passage around the Philippines suggested counter-intervention preparations could extend south towards US bases in the country.

But deployment does not demonstrate sustained combat capability. Michael Bosack, director of the Parley Policy Institute, identified the principal challenges as “reach, survivability and sustainability”.

East of Taiwan, PLA surface groups could face Japanese submarines, allied aircraft and counterstrike weapons beyond the densest protection of mainland China-based forces. Goldstein noted, however, that mainland China’s relatively nearby regional bases offered a logistical advantage.

For its part, Beijing has described the Liaoning’s deployment as routine annual training that complied with international law and was not directed at any particular country or target.

The ISW noted that the absence of an announced region-wide exercise differed from previous major Taiwan-focused drills, but there was no confirmation that the movements were part of a unified operation.

Bosack cautioned that the formations might be operating independently while giving the impression of a coordinated exercise.

“If they were truly integrated and well-orchestrated, that would indicate a level of readiness that would be disconcerting for those concerned of a near-term Chinese operation against Taiwan,” he said.

But while the extent of coordination remains uncertain, Fanell said the deployments pointed to Beijing’s longer-term ambition of developing a more integrated military force.

“The use of PLA naval forces from different theatre commands demonstrates the PLA is working to achieve an integrated joint force that has the command and control capability across theatre commands,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] AI pulls up the civil service ladder to Southeast Asia’s middle class
item.description:
Artificial intelligence promises to make government bureaucracies leaner across Asia, but its biggest effect on public-sector employment may not come from the widely feared wave of lay-offs.

Instead, analysts say the technology is more likely to reshape existing jobs and narrow opportunities for young graduates hoping to enter the civil service, even as governments seek to improve efficiency without sacrificing job security.

Unlike the Netherlands, which aims to cut an estimated 25,000 full-time equivalent civil service posts over the next decade in an efficiency drive that includes plans to harness AI, Southeast Asian governments face competing pressures to improve public services while protecting employment.
item.content:encoded:
Artificial intelligence promises to make government bureaucracies leaner across Asia, but its biggest effect on public-sector employment may not come from the widely feared wave of lay-offs.

Instead, analysts say the technology is more likely to reshape existing jobs and narrow opportunities for young graduates hoping to enter the civil service, even as governments seek to improve efficiency without sacrificing job security.

Unlike the Netherlands, which aims to cut an estimated 25,000 full-time equivalent civil service posts over the next decade in an efficiency drive that includes plans to harness AI, Southeast Asian governments face competing pressures to improve public services while protecting employment.

Analysts say those pressures, together with political considerations and employment protections, will determine whether productivity gains translate into better services, staff redeployment or fewer jobs.

Singapore offers a glimpse of the sensitivities surrounding public-sector restructuring, even when AI is not the cause of job cuts. GovTech, the public-sector technology agency, has announced two rounds of retrenchments affecting 131 officers, including 38 on October 22, but it insists the exercise is neither AI-driven nor a cost-cutting measure.

The first round, in July, came as a surprise to a public used to a secure public service. A commentary in the Business Times noted that some might interpret the cuts through the lens of wider fears about AI and jobs, but cautioned against drawing such a conclusion from GovTech’s case.

Augment vs displace

GovTech said the restructuring was aimed at changing its mix of skills so it could take greater ownership of government digital products and services, not to shrink its workforce to save money.

“Our overall demand for digital talent continues to grow,” the agency said in a written response to This Week in Asia’s questions. “We will continue to focus on retaining, retraining and redeploying officers, while providing support to those who will leave the organisation.”

In a written parliamentary answer on November 3, the Ministry of Digital Development and Information said 36 of the first 93 affected officers had left GovTech in August, while the remaining 57 were continuing on projects until their last day of service.

By October 30, 11 of those who left had found public- or private-sector jobs and 14 were receiving career coaching or applying and interviewing through support partners, it said. Another 11 had not used those services because they were pursuing personal plans, taking career breaks or exploring other options.

AI adoption must be undertaken in a way that augments, rather than displaces workers

Caryn Lim, Singaporean labour leader

Caryn Lim, assistant secretary general of the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC), said AI’s impact in Singapore had so far been more evident in job redesign and changing work processes than in job displacement.

Citing a Ministry of Manpower report issued in April, she said 18.9 per cent of firms adopting AI had redesigned job functions, while 6.2 per cent reported AI-related reductions in headcount or hiring.

“AI adoption must be undertaken in a way that augments, rather than displaces workers,” Lim said, adding that NTUC’s Company Training Committees involved workers and unions in identifying changes to jobs and the training needed for new roles.

Redundancies should remain a last resort, Lim said, with employers and unions first exploring job redesign, retraining and redeployment. Where cuts were unavoidable, early engagement with NTUC could help affected workers access job matching, career coaching and training advice, she added.

Lawrence Loh, director of the Centre for Governance and Sustainability at the National University of Singapore Business School, said businesses did not necessarily regard government AI adoption as a model to follow. Rather, they looked for “directions in the regulation or any necessity for compliance”.

But government job cuts could make similar corporate decisions easier to justify, he said. “If the government cut workforce, whether explicitly through AI or not AI … the act itself might legitimise private sector imitation.”

Reskilling was no quick fix, Loh said. Employees need time to develop AI skills and organisations face a mismatch between the skills available and those required to integrate the technology, which he called a “structural bottleneck”.

Employers must also weigh demand for new technical skills against the experience and institutional knowledge of existing staff, Loh said. “You cannot just let go of them because they don’t know AI, because actually they know a lot about business.”

Malaysia’s speed trap

In early 2024, Malaysia’s civil service union umbrella body, the Congress of Unions of Employees in the Public and Civil Services (CUEPACS), urged public officers to master AI.

Its president Adnan Mat said the technology could improve data processing, policy implementation and public-service delivery, calling on staff to complete the government’s introductory “AI Untuk Rakyat” (AI for Citizens) programme.

Last year, Adnan reiterated that workers needed to upgrade their skills to stay relevant as employers’ requirements changed. CUEPACS subsequently organised AI training.

Malaysian researcher Chan Xin Ying said the employment implications depended partly on where officers were needed, not just on which tasks could be automated. Her research focuses on civil servants and she previously drafted and implemented policies on care for the elderly, domestic violence and childcare for the Penang state government.

Drawing on that experience, Chan said AI-assisted case sorting and administrative processing could free up welfare officers for frontline work. Some services had too few caseworkers, she said, so faster processing could help meet unmet needs rather than justify “a mere reduction” in staff.

Still, Chan said she had mainly observed basic applications of AI such as data entry and online complaint filtering, rather than large-scale redeployment accompanying the technology’s adoption.

She also warned against equating faster processing with better outcomes. Automated categorisation could miss important details in cases involving children, elderly people and other vulnerable groups, she said.

Politics also influences staffing. Chan cautioned against assuming that preserving public-sector jobs would guarantee electoral loyalty. Malaysia’s many changes of government since 2018 had altered civil servants’ relationship with political parties, she said, making it less accurate to regard them as a single voting bloc than it was before that election.

Indonesia’s crowded ladder

For Indonesia, politics can determine whether AI-driven efficiency translates into fewer government jobs, according to Nicholas Kuipers, an assistant professor of politics at Princeton University who studies bureaucratic recruitment.

He said governments must weigh improvements in service delivery against the political importance of providing jobs. AI could improve services, Kuipers said, but handing out government jobs was also a way for politicians to build support.

“The motive of the government when it comes to … AI adoption is not necessarily only about efficiency,” he said.

Government jobs that offered stable incomes and a route into the middle class were “extremely sought after”, Kuipers said, noting that alternatives for graduates could be especially scarce outside Jakarta.

His published research recorded about 3.64 million applicants competing for 180,623 civil-service vacancies in the 2018-19 recruitment cycle, or about 20 applicants per post.

Given that level of demand, reducing recruitment would have an inevitable knock-on effect on young, college-educated applicants, Kuipers said.

“They’re going to see their opportunities for accessing a middle-class life … narrowing,” he said of would-be recruits, adding that he saw the job security of existing officers as a substantial constraint on dismissals.

“It is very hard for me to imagine current tenured civil servants being fired in Indonesia,” he said.

Indonesia is also assessing how ready its workforce is for digital government. A pilot assessment conducted in May covered civil servants’ digital literacy, proficiency, leadership and culture, with the aim of building a national picture of workforce capabilities.

Across the region, the main disruption from public-sector AI may not be immediate lay-offs but a restructuring of the civil service ladder, observers say.

The challenge for governments, according to Chan, is clearly communicating what technological adoption means for contract renewals, lateral transfers and day-to-day duties.

For existing tenured officers, employment remains relatively secure, but for the young graduates competing for a foothold in the bureaucracy, as in Indonesia, slower recruitment could close off one of the region’s main routes to the middle class.

item.title: [SCMP] Southeast Asia’s green push brings solar power, but who pays to keep it on?
item.description:
For most of his life, Osman Uki lived in a world dictated by the sun, relying on kerosene and leftover cooking oil to light his home in a remote indigenous village in Malaysia.

That changed in April when solar power finally reached Kampung Bertang in the state of Pahang, allowing families to power electric lights, refrigerators and rice cookers.

For Osman, one of the biggest changes is what happens after sunset.
item.content:encoded:
For most of his life, Osman Uki lived in a world dictated by the sun, relying on kerosene and leftover cooking oil to light his home in a remote indigenous village in Malaysia.

That changed in April when solar power finally reached Kampung Bertang in the state of Pahang, allowing families to power electric lights, refrigerators and rice cookers.

For Osman, one of the biggest changes is what happens after sunset.

“We are happy with the light we have at night. The kids can read at night now. We only use one light and that is enough for them,” he said.

But bringing electricity to the village, located roughly 170km (106 miles) from Kuala Lumpur, proved to be only half the battle. Keeping the power on carries recurring costs that residents must bear themselves, even after outside donors funded the installation.

The village’s experience highlights a dilemma confronting Southeast Asia as governments seek billions to shift towards cleaner power: how to ensure impoverished communities benefit from the green transition without shouldering an unfair share of the bill.

With the Cop31 UN climate summit opening in Antalya, Turkey, on Monday, the question of who pays and who benefits has become increasingly urgent.

For communities such as Kampung Bertang, home to more than 500 members of Malaysia’s Orang Asli population, the stakes are high. Many have yet to secure reliable electricity at all, even as the wider region grapples with making clean power affordable.

Costly transformation

At Cop29 in 2024, developed nations agreed to lead efforts to mobilise US$300 billion annually in climate finance for developing countries by 2035.

Southeast Asia, however, faces a widening investment shortfall. Clean-energy investments in the region reached just US$47 billion in 2025 – far short of the US$100 billion needed annually between 2026 and 2030 to meet regional climate commitments, according to the International Energy Agency’s World Energy Investment 2025 report.

In Kampung Bertang, deploying off-grid solar power cost about US$4,930 per household, according to Yeap Mei Yi, co-founder and chief operating officer at Bright Spots Energy. The social enterprise carried out the project alongside SHER Engineering, with financial backing from Yayasan Hasanah.

Yeap, who has worked on rural electrification since 2020, estimates that nearly 200 Orang Asli villages across Peninsular Malaysia still lack grid access.

Having seen previous off-grid installations fail in other remote settlements, she said the project was designed to ensure villagers could operate and maintain the system independently.

“It’s very, very common to see a solar project that is built, installed and then within a year or two, it’s not working and abandoned because nobody knows how to do maintenance and operations,” Yeap said.

To avoid that fate, each household contributes US$7 a month to a community fund that covers repairs, maintenance and modest payments to the village energy committee.

Battery replacements alone are estimated to cost more than US$980 per system, an expense shared across households. Bright Spots expects the committee’s pooled savings will be sufficient to cover the replacement when units come due within five years.

Hasil Gentiah, 51, a member of the village committee, said residents pooled their earnings from tapping rubber and harvesting fruits and other produce to meet the monthly contributions.

“Electricity from the main grid still hasn’t reached our village, so for now, we rely on solar power,” Hasil said, noting that daily life had nonetheless improved dramatically.

The financial burden of securing reliable, clean electricity extends across Southeast Asia, where continued dependence on fossil fuels leaves households vulnerable to price shocks.

In the Philippines, coal and natural gas accounted for 74 per cent of electricity generation in 2025, according to the Centre for Energy, Ecology and Development (CEED), a Manila-based think tank.

“For ordinary Filipino families, the burden of expensive energy goes beyond electricity bills. It translates into higher transportation fares, food prices and living expenses, hitting low-income households the hardest,” said Gerry Arances, executive director of CEED.

According to CEED, low-income Filipino households consume about 60 kilowatt-hours of electricity a month, compared with 210kWh among middle-income families, leaving poorer households with little margin to absorb rising energy costs.

Yet switching to domestic renewables presents its own challenge: CEED estimates a basic 500-watt rooftop solar system costs about US$437, yielding modest savings of up to US$5 a month.

Experts warn that without adequate financial support, the clean energy transition could widen domestic inequality.

“There is a real risk that the transition creates a two-tier energy system: those who can afford to decarbonise and those who continue paying the price of not being able to,” said Renard Siew, a sustainability and climate change specialist at Malaysian infrastructure conglomerate Yinson.

Beyond the high upfront cost of renewable technologies, Siew said households might face higher electricity tariffs as grid operators seek to recover the cost of upgrading transmission lines and energy storage infrastructure.

Fluctuating fuel subsidies could also increase transport, food and logistics costs.

“It is not enough to announce how much capital will be mobilised,” Siew said. “We need to ask who benefits, who pays and who carries the risk.”

Policy vs public buy-in

Governments across the region are trying to reconcile the push for low-carbon economies with the need to protect vulnerable households.

Malaysia launched its National Energy Transition Road map in 2023, aiming for net-zero emissions by 2050 by scaling up renewables and encouraging private green investment.

In September, the government expanded electricity bill protections by raising the domestic exemption threshold from 600kWh to 800kWh through the end of 2026. Under the relief measure, eligible households are exempt from automatic fuel adjustments, retail charges and service tax. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim framed the enhanced relief as an immediate measure to ease cost-of-living pressures.

Anjali Viswamohanan, director of policy at the Asia Investor Group on Climate Change, warned that the large investments needed to decarbonise regional power systems could erode public support if passed directly onto consumers.

“Unmanaged costs can deepen inequality and erode public support for the transition,” Anjali said, pointing out that rural and indigenous communities often bear the brunt of early disruptions.

Investors could address inequalities by assessing whether communities can benefit from projects, including access to affordable clean electricity.

“In due diligence, they can go beyond ‘do no significant harm’ and assess whether an investment makes a positive contribution,” she said.

Back in Kampung Bertang, Yeap said that grand regional targets must not lose sight of off-grid communities still waiting to secure reliable electricity.

“I hope that there will be funds committed towards ensuring that communities that have no access to electricity finally receive access to it,” she said.

For Osman, the arrival of electricity has transformed what he hopes the village’s children can achieve.

“I hope the new generations can be ambitious at school,” he said. “Because they can now have classes at night too.”

item.title: [SCMP] After US$474m gamble flops, what happens now to Elon Musk’s Tesla, SpaceX and China ties?
item.description:
Elon Musk bet nearly half a billion dollars that political spending could keep Washington friendly to his sprawling business empire. On Tuesday, that bet came up short.

As Democrats recaptured control of the US Congress in the midterm elections, the world’s richest man found himself facing an abruptly altered political landscape.

After pouring a record-breaking US$474 million into political groups – overwhelmingly backing Republicans – Musk now faces a divided Washington keen to examine his sprawling web of domestic government contracts and deep commercial links to China.
item.content:encoded:
Elon Musk bet nearly half a billion dollars that political spending could keep Washington friendly to his sprawling business empire. On Tuesday, that bet came up short.

As Democrats recaptured control of the US Congress in the midterm elections, the world’s richest man found himself facing an abruptly altered political landscape.

After pouring a record-breaking US$474 million into political groups – overwhelmingly backing Republicans – Musk now faces a divided Washington keen to examine his sprawling web of domestic government contracts and deep commercial links to China.

The political shift threatens to complicate operations across Musk’s corporate universe just as his enterprises, from Tesla and SpaceX to xAI, have become deeply intertwined with both Washington and Beijing.

Markets reacted swiftly on Wednesday morning. SpaceX shares fell 4 per cent and Tesla tumbled 5 per cent shortly after the opening bell.

Musk attempted to laugh off the setback on social media, writing: “Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time.”

He said in another post: “Data centres in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

Behind the bravado, billions of dollars are on the line. Under US President Donald Trump’s second administration, Musk’s ventures flourished on the back of major federal contracts and swift regulatory approvals.

Since stepping down from his controversial post heading the Department of Government Efficiency (Doge) in May 2025, his companies had secured at least US$10 billion in new federal deals, according to an October report by the Democracy Defenders Fund, a non-profit watchdog.

Nowhere is the scrutiny expected to bite harder than at SpaceX, whose role as a major defence contractor makes it a particularly obvious target for congressional oversight.

Democrats … want to examine Musk’s government contracts and potential conflicts of interest involving SpaceX and Tesla

Christopher Tang, University of California, Los Angeles

In May alone, SpaceX won two US Space Force contracts worth a combined US$6.45 billion, including a US$4.16 billion agreement to develop satellites capable of tracking airborne threats.

Meanwhile, his AI venture, xAI, landed a nearly US$200 million Department of Defence contract in July 2025.

“The new Democrat-controlled Congress will likely diminish Musk’s influence in Washington to some extent, although he still seems to have Trump’s ear,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution.

Chan noted that lawmakers could investigate SpaceX’s military deals as well as Musk’s conduct during his tenure at Doge, including allegations concerning the misuse of government data.

The Shanghai question

A key flashpoint on Capitol Hill is the intersection of Musk’s defence portfolio and Tesla’s extensive reliance on China.

Tesla’s Shanghai Gigafactory accounted for more than half of the company’s global vehicle deliveries last year, while production elsewhere depends on a network of Chinese suppliers.

The company also produces energy-storage batteries in Shanghai and has been in talks to buy nearly US$3 billion of Chinese solar manufacturing equipment to support its US expansion.

Musk’s recent hints at merging Tesla and SpaceX – announcing in October that the firms had formed special committees to explore a merger – could hand lawmakers an immediate opening.

“Democrats have already said they want to examine Musk’s government contracts and potential conflicts of interest involving SpaceX and Tesla, so expect Shanghai to be framed as a security question rather than a cost advantage,” said Christopher Tang, a professor specialising in global supply chains at the Anderson School of Management at the University of California, Los Angeles.

Any merger review is expected to examine whether sensitive aerospace and defence technology could remain effectively insulated from Tesla’s Chinese supply chain.

“Washington controls contracts and clearances, while Beijing controls inputs, cost and speed,” Tang said. “The election tightened the Washington side of that vice without loosening the Beijing side.”

Trouble on the home turf

Musk’s electoral setback was felt just as keenly in Texas, the de facto operational nerve centre of his empire.

He funnelled US$224 million into Texas races – nearly half of his overall midterm war chest – according to a CNBC analysis of campaign finance records. That did not stop Democrat Gina Hinojosa from ousting Republican incumbent Greg Abbott in the gubernatorial contest.

“The backlash over data centres has spread across the country, and some candidates made it a big part of their campaigns,” said Daniel Kollar, deputy managing director for Greater China at consultancy Intralink.

Hinojosa campaigned on freezing approvals for new data centres until environmental and energy safeguards were established, tapping into grassroots frustration over surging electricity bills and water usage.

While such restrictions would not halt existing operations at Tesla’s Austin Gigafactory, SpaceX’s Starbase in Boca Chica, or a planned joint semiconductor facility, they could complicate Musk’s ambitions to build out AI infrastructure in the region.

Ahead of its initial public offering in June, SpaceX pitched AI computing as a cornerstone of its future growth, citing an estimated US$28.5 trillion addressable market.

Congress can make Shanghai politically more expensive. It cannot make it less productive

Christopher Tang, University of California, Los Angeles

Resilience in China

Despite the political headwinds, analysts said Tesla’s Chinese production was unlikely to buckle under US congressional pressure.

Beyond vehicle assembly, Chinese suppliers play a critical role in Musk’s long-term robotics vision.

Tesla engineers audited Chinese component makers including Zhejiang Sanhua Intelligent Controls, Ningbo Joyson Electronic and Tuopu Group ahead of planned mass production of its Optimus humanoid robot, the South China Morning Post reported in September.

“Congress can make Shanghai politically more expensive. It cannot make it less productive,” Tang said.

“Given how many US companies still do business in China and rely heavily on Chinese suppliers, I think Congress would have a hard time explaining why it was singling out Tesla,” Kollar said.

Bai Wenxi, chief economist at China Enterprise Capital Union, expressed a similar view. “Tesla’s China operations won’t grind to a halt just because Musk faces investigations,” Bai said.

Sidelined in diplomacy

Where Musk may lose influence, however, was in his role as an informal intermediary between Beijing and Washington, analysts said.

Over the past year, some observers viewed Musk as a potential backchannel between the two governments. He joined Trump’s delegation to Beijing in May and secured a seat at the head table during the White House state dinner for President Xi Jinping in September.

That role had become increasingly irrelevant following the US-China trade truce reached in South Korea last year, according to Brookings Institution’s Chan.

“At the start of Trump’s second term, many wondered whether Elon Musk would play a moderating role in the White House’s approach to China,” Chan said. “After the Busan agreement, there seems to be less of a role for someone like Musk to play in US-China relations.”

Bai said Musk’s value as a diplomatic conduit had diminished.

“Musk himself has gone from being a ‘strategic bridge’ to just one of the American businessmen Beijing can engage with,” he said.

Ultimately, however, Trump remains in the Oval Office for the next two years, holding executive veto power and agency leadership that could shield Musk from major regulatory challenges. But the days of unfettered access may be over.

“My guess is Musk will keep a lower political profile for a while to draw less attention to his businesses,” Kollar said.

“There will likely be increased congressional scrutiny, but without executive action, I’d be surprised if he changed his merger plans or how Tesla operates in China.”

item.title: [SCMP] Australia jails Singaporean tourist for fatally driving over man who stole backpack
item.description:
A 29-year-old Singaporean man was sentenced to five years and nine months’ jail in Australia on Monday after he killed a man who stole a backpack from his rental car.

Lincoln Ng Jing Kai chased the man in a car and knocked him off his e-bike before driving over him.

He was originally charged with murder, but pleaded guilty to manslaughter in August after prosecutors agreed to accept the lesser charge.
item.content:encoded:
A 29-year-old Singaporean man was sentenced to five years and nine months’ jail in Australia on Monday after he killed a man who stole a backpack from his rental car.

Lincoln Ng Jing Kai chased the man in a car and knocked him off his e-bike before driving over him.

He was originally charged with murder, but pleaded guilty to manslaughter in August after prosecutors agreed to accept the lesser charge.

Sentencing him, Judge Terence Palmer said Ng’s actions “involved an element of taking the law into your own hands and a degree of vigilantism”, even if Ng did not intend to seriously injure the man and he was expecting the police to arrive.

The Supreme Court of Western Australia heard that Ng was on an eight-day holiday in Perth with his girlfriend and her family, and that he had planned to propose to her. They rented a car during their holiday.

On May 23, 2024, the group drove to East Victoria Park for dinner and parked the car nearby. The backpack was left in the boot of the car, and it contained a passport, iPad, some cash and an AirTag tracker.

The man, Mark John Burnes, had seen the family and Ng leave the backpack in the car and decided to break into the car to steal it. He had called his partner to tell her of his intentions.

After smashing the back window of the car, Burnes left with the stolen backpack and returned to the room he shared with his partner. They discovered the AirTag, which she attempted to dispose of by throwing it onto a vehicle parked outside.

When Ng and his girlfriend’s family returned to the car, they found that it had been broken into and they reported it to the police.

Later that evening, Ng’s girlfriend’s brother activated the AirTag to track it and noticed its location moving. He contacted police and was advised to call back once the location had stabilised.

The following day, Ng and his girlfriend’s family reported the theft and replaced their damaged car with the rental company.

At about 8am, they activated the AirTag again and saw it near a construction site. They called the police with the location.

The construction site was a short distance away from where Burnes and his partner were staying.

Sometime after 12.30pm, the group decided to drive past the location where the AirTag was. About an hour later, Ng’s girlfriend’s brother called the police.

While the group was at the construction site looking for the AirTag, Burnes rode past on an e-bike carrying what appeared to be the stolen backpack.

Ng’s girlfriend’s brother and his father saw Burnes go past and they got into the car. The older man told Ng to follow Burnes so they would not lose sight of him.

Ng pursued Burnes for about 10 minutes around the streets of Carlisle, Perth. His girlfriend’s brother remained on the phone with the police, updating them on their location.

As Burnes left the road onto a grass verge, someone from the back of the car told Ng to give the bike “a tap”, the court heard.

Ng hit the rear wheel of Burnes’ e-bike, causing him to fall. He made a U-turn to face Burnes and had to reverse a little to avoid an obstacle.

Burnes yelled threats at the group and Ng was scared he might attack. He thought Burnes was coming towards the car and he wanted to reverse away from him.

Ng stepped down hard on the accelerator, thinking that the car transmission was in reverse, but it was in drive.

The car moved forward and struck the man, who fell to the ground and went under the car. Ng then drove off the verge and onto the street, while the man was trapped under the front driver’s wheel.

Ng continued to drive about 25 metre (82 feet) up the street, dragging the man under the car.

The prosecution said it should have been evident to Ng that Burnes was trapped under the car, but Ng argued that he did not know that. The judge accepted that there was a risk he might have been under the car, but he was not persuaded that the risk was obvious to Ng.

Bystanders ran up to the car and attempted to stop Ng by yelling or banging on the window.

Ng reversed the car and Burnes was released from underneath it. Ng then waited by the side of the road for the police to arrive.

Burnes was declared dead in hospital at 2.42pm after sustaining multiple injuries. Ng was arrested at the scene.

He admitted to police that night that he had pursued Burnes and hit him so he would fall off his bike. Ng said it was a very light tap to cause him to fall to buy time for the police to arrive, after which Burnes shouted aggressively at him.

The judge said he accepted that Ng thought Burnes posed an imminent threat to the car and its occupants, and that the decision was a “split second decision made under pressure”.

However, he said if Burnes posed a threat to those in the car, it was because Ng was using a car to chase and confront him.

Justice Palmer also noted that Burnes was in a vulnerable position, as he was on an e-bike while Ng was in a car.

He said Ng should have stopped immediately after realising that the vehicle was moving forward instead of reversing.

“Your counsel suggested that you have not appreciated what you were doing because you were addled. While I accept that you may have panicked at the time, I am not satisfied that you were so addled to not appreciate the obvious risk associated with driving towards Mr Burnes,” the judge said.

In mitigation, the judge considered Ng’s guilty plea, lack of criminal history and genuine remorse.

Justice Palmer accepted that Ng’s actions were out of character and that he had excellent prospects of rehabilitation.

The judge also considered the influence of Ng’s prospective father-in-law, who had directed him to pursue Burnes, but he noted that Ng was driving the car and therefore had “ultimate control over the situation”.

Ng’s jail sentence was backdated to when he was first taken into custody on May 24, 2024, and he will be eligible for parole after three years and nine months’ imprisonment.

This story was first published by CNA

item.title: [SCMP] JW Marriott Hotel Hong Kong redefines luxury dining with zero-waste culinary innovation
item.description:
For Tony Wong Chi-chuen, the executive chef of JW Marriott Hotel Hong Kong, waste is never the conclusion of an ingredient’s story. Lemon ends can be used to perfume seafood, shrimp shells to deepen the nuance of a broth and fishbones to build a base for pasta dough. In Wong’s kitchen, food waste is simply ingredients waiting for a second life.

“Discarding something is easy,” says Wong. “[Reusing] is not about saving cost; saving is about reinvesting in more quality ingredients.”

In person, he doesn’t mince his words. As the conversation turns to his craft, Wong – who has 38 years of experience in the industry – becomes animated, revealing a passion honed over decades, rooted in a lesson learned long before he entered a professional kitchen.
item.content:encoded:
For Tony Wong Chi-chuen, the executive chef of JW Marriott Hotel Hong Kong, waste is never the conclusion of an ingredient’s story. Lemon ends can be used to perfume seafood, shrimp shells to deepen the nuance of a broth and fishbones to build a base for pasta dough. In Wong’s kitchen, food waste is simply ingredients waiting for a second life.

“Discarding something is easy,” says Wong. “[Reusing] is not about saving cost; saving is about reinvesting in more quality ingredients.”

In person, he doesn’t mince his words. As the conversation turns to his craft, Wong – who has 38 years of experience in the industry – becomes animated, revealing a passion honed over decades, rooted in a lesson learned long before he entered a professional kitchen.

His parents used to run a dai pai dong-style stall behind the Yau Ma Tei Police Station, peddling steaming bowls of fish-ball noodles, before it closed more than 40 years ago. From the age of 12, Wong would help out after school. He watched his parents work hard, stretch ingredients and make full use of what they had.

He recalls that “they didn’t throw anything away”: fishbones were simmered into broth for the noodles – an ingrained reflex that later inspired his fishbone fettuccine at JW Marriott Hotel Hong Kong, showing how every ingredient could be made to work harder. Wong came to understand that saving on food waste only mattered if it was turned into something better eventually.

“When I was 18, I realised being thrifty is not enough,” he says. “You have to use what you save and make it into something good for customers.” His philosophy – waste not, but elevate – became the bedrock of his kitchen. It is an exercise not in austerity, but in wringing maximum quality and flavour out of scraps.

Wong joined JW Marriott Hotel Hong Kong in 1990, a year after its opening. He started as a senior cook at the former Marriott Cafe, now JW Cafe, and steadily moved up the ranks: sous chef in 2003, executive sous chef in 2009 and, finally, executive chef in 2018.

As a young cook, he noticed how quickly bins filled up. Celery ends, carrot peels, onion trimmings and other offcuts were tossed aside because only the neatest parts were used. When he became sous chef, he began making changes: a bucket near a chopping board was added to hold bones, end cuts and trimmings to be reused.

Now, the system has become part of kitchen culture. Watermelon rind is blended into a light breakfast drink, valued in traditional Chinese medicine for its refreshing sweetness and cooling effects; leftover pieces from Peking ducks are shredded into a braised rice-vermicelli dish.

What it has done for food-waste numbers is significant – the hotel repurposes around 8.2 tonnes of watermelon rind a year, along with 900kg of lemon peel, more than 3.6 tonnes of fishbones and 3.65 tonnes of shrimp heads and shells, says Wong. At its core, however, his philosophy remains simple: an ingredient should have as many “lives” as possible before it leaves the kitchen.

“I see an ingredient and think, ‘How can it be used again?’”

Tony Wong

“I see an ingredient and think, ‘How can it be used again?’”

Across JW Marriott Hotel Hong Kong’s eight dining venues and multiple event spaces, Wong’s strategy goes beyond creating isolated “green” dishes – it is about building a circular kitchen system. His approach aligns with Marriott’s Serve 360 sustainability and social-impact platform, which is guided by the belief of “doing good in every direction”.

Furthermore, the culinary initiatives sit within the property’s broader push towards responsible luxury – a commitment that has won prestigious recognition, recently from the US Green Building Council for sustainable building operations and maintenance, and the International WELL Building Institute for health and wellness, ensuring that guest well-being and environmental stewardship are both fully considered.

In a five-star hotel, sustainability has to meet the expectations of luxury dining. Wong does not see a contradiction. He believes that responsible cooking should make food better, not lesser, and the clearest expression of this thinking is Fish Bar’s lobster fishbone fettuccine, one of the restaurant’s signature dishes. Instead of treating grouper bones as waste, Wong’s team dries and pulverises them into a fine powder, then blends the meal with gluten-free flour to make pasta. No mere sustainability gimmick, the bones add calcium and deepen the pasta’s umami, turning scrap into part of the dish’s flavour structure.

If anything, Wong says, zero-waste practices allow him to be more generous. Financial savings from careful portioning and cross-kitchen reuse are channelled back into premium buffet offerings, such as abalone, fish maw, sea cucumber, lobster and crab.

High-quality offcuts receive similar care: Australian Wagyu trimmings are crafted into burger patties, while at the hotel’s Michelin-star Man Ho Chinese Restaurant, prime cuts of Iberico pork are reserved for char siu and flavourful remnants are minced for xiaolongbao fillings at The Lounge.

For banquets and functions, Wong’s team makes enough food for no more than 10 per cent above the expected number of guests. At the buffet, dishes are prepared in smaller, more frequently replenished batches, ensuring that food does not sit for long periods. It is a more labour-intensive practice, but one that benefits the environment and creates a better experience for diners. “Other places refill food maybe twice; we do it 20 times,” says Wong.

Luxury diners used to fixate on origin – lobsters from France, tomatoes from Italy, sea urchin from Japan – but these priorities have shifted. “I think guests mainly care about the taste, quality and freshness of the ingredients – these are the three things they focus on now and they care less about where they come from,” says Wong.

For him, this change has widened the meaning of luxury. Premium dining is no longer defined only by provenance or price, but by how thoughtfully an ingredient is sourced, handled and cooked. If a dish tastes good and aligns with sustainable values, guests will often see it as something better.

JW Marriott Hotel Hong Kong prioritises local sourcing where possible, which helps reduce transport time, spoilage and carbon emissions. Suppliers are screened for certifications – including from organisations such as the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) and Aquaculture Stewardship Council (ASC) – and traceability. Purchasing decisions made by the procurement team are guided in part by monthly WWF recommendations of vetted seafood suppliers and sources, says Wong. Endangered species, such as bluefin tuna and shark, are off the menu, replaced by alternatives like yellowtail and vegetarian shark’s fin – a plant-based ingredient that replicates the texture of the original.

At Fish Bar, renovated in 2024, sustainability is built into the space as well as the dining programme. An open design allows for natural ventilation, reducing reliance on air conditioning. Uniforms were designed in partnership with the Caritas Bianchi College of Careers and incorporate coffee-ground materials. Bottled water has been replaced with a filtered system.

Meanwhile, JW Garden grows herbs such as rosemary, basil and perilla, which are used in drinks, dishes, amenities and even canned beverages that extend the farm-to-table idea into a “farm-to-home” experience. Edible surplus, such as croissants and muffins, is donated to organisations serving people in need, while food waste that cannot be reused is sent to recycling partners for renewable energy or composting. JW Marriott Hotel Hong Kong also works with The Nature Conservancy, turning discarded oyster shells into reef substrate for local marine restoration.

From Wong’s point of view, these hotel-wide initiatives connect back to the same principle: resources should circulate, not dissipate. His message for the next generation is clear: cooking well is no longer enough, because a chef must also think about impact.

His 180-strong team, many of whom have worked with him for decades, now closely follow his doctrine.

It has created a virtuous cycle: the kitchen grows increasingly efficient as reuse practices are streamlined; diners enjoy fresher, higher-quality food; staff develop discipline and pride – all while protecting the environment. Wong shares of his team that “they feel this is a good habit; they feel like they can be good people”.

Some might label the rethinking of food waste as accumulating good karma, but in hospitality terms, it’s simply good business.

item.title: [SCMP] History repeats in Shenzhen? China hosts another lame-duck US president
item.description:
A decade after hosting a politically hobbled Barack Obama at a Group of 20 (G20) summit in Hangzhou, China is preparing to welcome another “lame-duck” US president for a multilateral gathering: Donald Trump.

Following the Republicans’ loss of both chambers of the US Congress in the midterm elections on Tuesday – a drubbing that reached deep into historically red states – Trump is expected to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping in two weeks on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) leaders’ meeting in Shenzhen. It will be their third face-to-face meeting this year.

Obama’s five-hour talks with Xi in 2016 did not prevent ties from later unravelling into a trade war after Trump took office – raising questions over whether Trump’s post-midterm vulnerability will limit his room for lasting diplomacy, even if he clinches quick deals in Shenzhen.
item.content:encoded:
A decade after hosting a politically hobbled Barack Obama at a Group of 20 (G20) summit in Hangzhou, China is preparing to welcome another “lame-duck” US president for a multilateral gathering: Donald Trump.

Following the Republicans’ loss of both chambers of the US Congress in the midterm elections on Tuesday – a drubbing that reached deep into historically red states – Trump is expected to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping in two weeks on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) leaders’ meeting in Shenzhen. It will be their third face-to-face meeting this year.
