Obama’s five-hour talks with Xi in 2016 did not prevent ties from later unravelling into a trade war after Trump took office – raising questions over whether Trump’s post-midterm vulnerability will limit his room for lasting diplomacy, even if he clinches quick deals in Shenzhen.

The midterm “Waterloo” could prompt Trump to avoid new frictions in ties with China and make him keener to strike deals on trade and international flashpoints to burnish his political standing, according to one Chinese scholar.

However, the US leader is unlikely to yield ground on technology or Taiwan to avoid political attacks from within his own party, the expert warned.

“That contradiction would run through his Shenzhen trip,” said Mei Yang, assistant director of the Shenzhen-based Institute for International Affairs, Qianhai (IIA).

Writing in a note published on Thursday, Mei argued that Trump was “clearly reluctant” to accept the political narrative that he had become a lame duck, with the next Congress not convening until January.

A meeting with Xi could offer Trump a chance to show domestically that the midterm setback “did not diminish” his political clout and to show globally that he was capable of representing the US on major international issues.

If the Shenzhen talks produce progress, Trump could extend the momentum to the G20 summit in Miami in December, Mei added.

“For a Trump eager to prove he still has governing capacity, such an arrangement has real appeal,” Mei wrote.

The meeting between Xi and Obama 10 years ago made little headway on bilateral ties, especially over trade, cybersecurity, the South China Sea and Washington’s deployment of the Terminal High Altitude Area Defence (THAAD) anti-missile system in South Korea.

The two leaders jointly announced they would ratify the Paris climate agreement, though many saw the move as papering over deep-rooted differences. Trump later withdrew the US from the accord during his first term as president.

Still, Obama and Xi both stressed a commitment to managing differences constructively and expanding cooperation across a range of fields.

Like his predecessor, Trump is now working to keep relations with Beijing stable, though the concept of “constructive strategic stability” agreed on earlier this year by the US and Chinese leaders is expected to be tested following the midterms.

In Shenzhen, Trump might be willing to discuss extending the trade truce that expires in January, adjusting tariffs on some goods and expanding market access for China in exchange for more Chinese purchases of US agricultural and energy products or improved access to the Chinese market for American firms, according to Mei.

The US leader could also seek to keep China’s supply of critical minerals, such as rare earths, stable and to strengthen law enforcement cooperation to combat narcotics and telecoms fraud, he added.

“Trump can frame these outcomes as tangible gains he negotiated for the United States,” he wrote.

The US-Israel war on Iran is widely seen as the main cause of the Republicans’ midterm rout. US Vice-President J.D. Vance publicly voiced that view on Wednesday, though Trump has stood by his decision to launch the operation.

Mei said Trump might seek to tap Beijing’s channels of communication with Tehran to reduce the diplomatic cost of resolving the conflict, push for the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and create conditions for talks on Iran’s nuclear programme.

Trump might also hope to channel China’s ties with Russia to make progress towards a ceasefire and post-war arrangements in Ukraine, though he would not necessarily want China to act as a formal mediator, he added.

“Trump wants China to use its international influence to help the US solve problems, yet remains wary of China playing a greater leadership role in international affairs,” Mei said.

He said he did not expect Trump to significantly ease restrictions on China for high-end chips, artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure or other key technologies.

“There is even less room for compromise on Taiwan and military security,” he added.

Mei said Trump was likely to take a “rather cautious” dealmaking approach, avoiding commitments that could be perceived as weak on Beijing on those issues.

Faced with a Congress controlled by Democrats, Trump could become more reliant on his political base, while trying to prevent Republicans from blaming his foreign policy for the party’s midterm defeat, Mei noted.

Beijing regards Taiwan as part of China, to be reunified by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington opposes any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and remains committed to supplying it with weapons.

“China and the US can look for areas of cooperation on trade, energy, counter-narcotics, anti-fraud efforts and some international hotspots, but Trump’s short-term need for deals does not mean that America’s strategic position toward China has changed,” Mei wrote.

He added that a single meeting between leaders could not “automatically erase long-accumulated differences”.

“Trump hopes to use diplomatic deals to strengthen his hand for the second half of his term, while China needs an external environment that can manage differences, expand cooperation and avoid repeated swings in the relationship,” Mei noted. “The two sides’ interests overlap, but each has its limits.”

While the 2016 Hangzhou visit was Obama’s final trip to China as president, taking place during his final months in office, Trump still has two years remaining in his second term.

Whether an Apec encounter between the US and Chinese presidents leaves an enduring legacy depends on how well the consensus reached in Shenzhen is carried out, according to Mei.

item.title: [SCMP] In China’s fierce race for success, mental health struggles are starting earlier
item.description:
Moon Chen stared down at her textbook, struggling to make sense of the words on the page.

The 15-year-old felt a suffocating weight press into her chest, while her heart fluttered erratically.

Chen’s mother rushed her to a cardiologist – only to be told that she should see a psychiatrist instead.
item.content:encoded:
Moon Chen stared down at her textbook, struggling to make sense of the words on the page.

The 15-year-old felt a suffocating weight press into her chest, while her heart fluttered erratically.

Chen’s mother rushed her to a cardiologist – only to be told that she should see a psychiatrist instead.

Chen, now in higher secondary school in the southwestern Chinese city of Chongqing, vividly recalls the period before she was diagnosed with depression and anxiety. At the time, she did not know that chest tightness and palpitations are classic signs of psychological distress.

Her diagnosis came as a shock. “My mum broke down in tears,” said Chen, now 17.

However, it perhaps should not have been so surprising, as a growing number of young Chinese people of her generation are wrestling with mental health struggles. Experts say that as academic pressure is growing on younger students, so is the mental strain. It reflects the mounting pressure within Chinese society, where people are locked in cutthroat competition for opportunities, with serious implications for their lives ahead.

A nationwide survey led by Beijing Anding Hospital that was published in 2021 found that 17.5 per cent of children and adolescents in China suffer from mental disorders, with anxiety and depressive disorders among the most prevalent conditions.

The lead researchers told Chinese media that the 17.5 per cent figure may well be an underestimate for minors overall, as the survey only examined school-going children aged six to 16.

According to a 2022 report by the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS), 14.8 per cent of surveyed adolescents showed varying degrees of depression risk, a rate higher than that of adults.

According to an earlier report by CAS, roughly 30 per cent of surveyed junior high – or lower secondary – students reported depressive symptoms — a sharp jump from about 10 per cent among primary school pupils. The figure climbed to nearly 40 per cent for the senior high - or higher secondary – classes.

Psychologists noted that the surge in mental health issues among Chinese youth could not be reduced to any single cause.

“Rather, it reflects the convergence of multiple structural forces: the intensification of educational competition, the pervasive penetration of digital media, the transformation of family structures and a broader uncertainty about meaning accompanying rapid social transition,” said Shimin Zhu, an associate professor at Hong Kong Polytechnic University whose research focuses on adolescent well-being.

When her issues first surfaced, Chen said she was facing tough expectations and lacked emotional support.

During her time in the lower grades, Chen’s academic schedule stretched from 7.20am to 10.30pm, with weekends swallowed up by classes at cram schools.

“Almost everyone here takes extra classes. There are tutoring centres everywhere,” Chen said.

All her efforts were aimed at securing a place in secondary school, an increasingly challenging task.

Under China’s nine-year compulsory education system, schooling is guaranteed only through junior high.

Facing shortages of technical labour, policymakers are now relying on the senior high school entrance examination to sort students into academic and vocational tracks. Depending on the region, only around 50 to 70 per cent of test-takers can follow the academic track and get into senior high school.

But given the deep cultural preference for academic success, many families treat going to vocational school as a life-ruining failure.

Against this backdrop, Zhu said, the panic once reserved for the gruelling college entrance examination now gripped teenagers years earlier, right as they underwent dramatic physical and hormonal shifts.

While Beijing has pushed in recent years to elevate society’s view of vocational education, Zhu noted that winning widespread public acceptance was bound to be a long process.

“People are more likely to embrace vocational pathways when they see clear career prospects and better pay for skilled workers,” she said. “Academic competition can also intensify during this transition.”

Even entering university offers little relief. Zhu said the rapid growth in the number of college students and challenging graduate job market meant a degree no longer guaranteed stable employment, and this uncertainty has pushed youth stress to record highs.

China’s surveyed unemployment rate for urban youth aged 16 to 24 has hovered around 18 per cent in recent months, with August reaching 18.9 per cent – the worst reading in a year.

Outside the classroom, Chen found little refuge. Consumed by work, her parents had little time to offer companionship.

“They didn’t understand that I was in agony, nor did they realise how severe my physical reactions were,” Chen said. “They just thought I was too fragile.”

During her darkest moments, she began to self-harm, scratching her hands with staples.

While adolescents naturally yearn for autonomy, their sense of security still hinged on emotional support from home when a crisis hit, Zhu noted.

Citing her previous research, she added that when children enjoyed quality interactions and warm relationships at home, they showed greater confidence in facing challenges and a lower likelihood of self-harm.

Digital media penetration further complicates the landscape.

Video games, social media and emerging AI-generated microdramas increasingly crowd out physical exercise and face-to-face interactions – activities that are indispensable for adolescents’ development.

For depressed teenagers starved of real-life connection, screens offer an immediate escape. “Such readily available dopamine provides temporary emotional relief – a refuge some young people turn to when they feel overwhelmed,” Zhu said.

Yet the retreat into virtual worlds often worsens their social isolation.

This [AI] transition is like a subterranean tsunami. No one knows when it will fully strike or what dramatic upheavals it will bring

Shimin Zhu, associate professor, Hong Kong Polytechnic University

Beneath the depressive and anxious emotions lies a deeper existential disorientation: adolescents are struggling to find purpose in a society transforming at breakneck speed – with the rapid ascent of artificial intelligence (AI) serving as the latest disrupter.

“This transition is like a subterranean tsunami. No one knows when it will fully strike or what dramatic upheavals it will bring, stirring widespread anxiety among many people,” Zhu said.

Beijing has recognised the need to tackle the youth mental health crisis. The government has pledged to ease students’ academic burden while establishing a nationwide system of mental health screening and crisis intervention.

It has also said that by 2030 all primary and secondary schools should be staffed with a counsellor and host at least one psychological lecture or dedicated activity each school year.

Progress towards these goals is under way. According to the State Council, 92 per cent of primary schools and 95 per cent of junior high schools now have a counsellor.

But despite these promising numbers, major hurdles stand in the way of effective support.

For many sufferers, the social stigma surrounding mental illness is more suffocating than the condition itself, which stops them from seeking professional help.

“Many parents we encounter are terrified when their children need psychological counselling or psychiatric intervention,” Zhu said.

“Alongside concerns about getting appropriate care, some parents worry that a diagnosis recorded in their child’s medical history could affect future opportunities.”

This reluctance to arrange support means that minor emotional setbacks often turn into chronic, severe crises.

Lily Li, 17, took the initiative to ask for medical help after suffering recurring bouts of full-body numbness and shortness of breath. Her pleas were initially dismissed by her parents.

“I paid the hospital registration fee myself and took a 2½ hour subway ride to the hospital alone,” Li said. “Only when the intake desk refused to see me without a guardian present did my mother finally agree to come.”

Li was later diagnosed with moderate depression and severe anxiety.

Her experience mirrors national trends. According to a CAS study on adolescent depression and rehabilitation dilemmas in China, only 27.4 per cent of parents take their children to a clinic the first time a child asks for help, while nearly 30 per cent of parents act only after their child has made pleas four or more times.

Meanwhile, qualified medical professionals remain in short supply.

A 2019 paper published in the medical journal The Lancet said that China had only around 500 qualified child and adolescent psychiatrists nationwide, with the vast majority concentrated in metropolises such as Beijing and Shanghai.

“Whether we talk about certified psychotherapists or child psychiatrists, their numbers remain minuscule relative to China’s massive population base, and resources are unevenly distributed,” Zhu said.

The prohibitive cost of private therapy creates an equally daunting barrier.

Hourly rates for psychological counselling commonly range from 100 yuan (US$15) to upwards of 1,000 yuan, which would be a major expense for many Chinese households, and meaningful clinical progress generally requires at least three to five sessions.

For adolescents who do manage to get clinical care, ensuring treatment works is another challenge.

Mental health conditions are predominantly treated through medication and psychotherapy, but maintaining consistency is notoriously difficult.

According to the World Health Organization, medications for depression and anxiety take weeks to show initial benefits in sleep, mood and energy. They should also be continued for at least six months after remission to prevent relapse, with discontinuation carried out gradually under medical guidance.

Chen stopped taking her medication because she felt the drugs offered little relief, while Li also abandoned hers after suffering dizziness and nausea.

Beyond medical and financial access, another challenge lies in how society views distress itself.

While welcoming government initiatives to ease student burdens, Zhu noted that top-down measures should avoid treating all stress as something to be eliminated, as frustration was an inevitable part of life.

“Learning to cope with the ups and downs of life as we grow up is the core of educating the next generation and of educating ourselves,” Zhu said.

She added that policies should not merely focus on reducing academic pressure or on whether the children are happy. The goal, she emphasised, should be nurturing “psychological resilience and inner strength”, equipping adolescents to face adversity.

“Growing up is an incremental accumulation,” Zhu said.

“We must not let children feel that a single poor exam score means the sky is falling.”

item.title: [SCMP] In Malaysia, a shadow trade in DIY weight-loss jabs takes hold
item.description:
When her prescription for Mounjaro became too expensive, Bey* did what a growing number of Malaysians are doing: she found a cheaper vial online.

The 34-year-old from Kuala Lumpur started on the weight-loss drug about a year ago and hasn’t looked back since.

“I didn’t feel like eating, I didn’t feel hungry,” she said, recalling flying to Jakarta for a “food trip” recently during which she barely ate.
item.content:encoded:
When her prescription for Mounjaro became too expensive, Bey* did what a growing number of Malaysians are doing: she found a cheaper vial online.

The 34-year-old from Kuala Lumpur started on the weight-loss drug about a year ago and hasn’t looked back since.

“I didn’t feel like eating, I didn’t feel hungry,” she said, recalling flying to Jakarta for a “food trip” recently during which she barely ate.

Reviews on Threads and TikTok led her to online sellers offering “tirzepatide”, Mounjaro’s active ingredient, for a fraction of the price of her doctor’s prescription – so she bought it and started administering the drug herself.

A search by This Week in Asia across several platforms found “weight-loss injections” advertised for as little as 60 ringgit (US$15) per jab in Malaysia.

Over five months, with exercise and calorie control, Bey shed 30kg (66lbs) and was so pleased with her progress that she even began recommending the unregulated injections to a friend.

When one seller raised prices she simply switched to another; when a shop was banned from the e-commerce platform she used, she began looking for a different brand.

Mounjaro and Ozempic, which were originally developed to treat diabetes, belong to a class of drugs that mimic gut hormones to curb appetite and regulate blood sugar.

Demand is high in Malaysia, where the most recent National Health and Morbidity Survey, released in 2023, found that 54.4 per cent of the adult population were overweight or obese.

The price of thin

A month of prescribed Mounjaro used to cost Arun* 1,500 ringgit. The 37-year-old began treatment after being told he was prediabetic, meaning his blood sugar was raised but below the threshold for diabetes, and had a fatty liver.

He then moved to grey-market products, sold outside regulated channels and advertised as tirzepatide and retatrutide for about 400 ringgit a month. Retatrutide is an experimental drug. Its developer, the US pharmaceutical company Eli Lilly, said in October that no regulator in the world had approved it.

Arun said he sourced from sellers who used Chinese manufacturers he considered reputable. He checked laboratory reports, batch numbers and other buyers’ reviews before injecting.

“Peptides have changed my life, for the better,” he said, using the umbrella term popular in online fitness communities for these synthetic hormone-mimicking compounds. “Energy levels are great.”

However, Arun conceded that he had also experienced anhedonia – a reduced or complete inability to derive pleasure from activities you would normally enjoy – which he believed was linked to the injections.

“Who do you become when you are no longer hungry?” he asked.

This Week in Asia spoke to one seller in Johor Bahru, the Malaysian city closest to the Singapore border, who advertises a 10mg vial of retatrutide for 100 ringgit, with mixing liquid, syringes, alcohol pads and instructions. Also for sale in the seller’s online shop are products marketed for performance, skin health and longevity.

The seller, who requested anonymity, said the stock came from China and buyers chose to use “Reta”, a slang term for the drug, because it was affordable.

“I explain that Reta hasn’t received FDA approval. I don’t do my own lab tests, I only use the lab tests the supplier provides,” the seller said, referring to the US Food and Drug Administration.

Repeat customers were happy with the product and reported no unusual side effects, the seller added, putting this down to their guidance on starting with low doses.

Similar offers circulate through social media posts and private messages across Malaysia. In March, local outlet Sinar Daily reported that buyers could easily obtain prescription injections online without medical screening or follow-up care.

The risks, if not already self-evident, were illustrated by a recent case in Australia. In September, the country’s Therapeutic Goods Administration reported that a person who used a product sold as retatrutide suffered uncontrollable vomiting and a torn oesophagus, requiring hospital treatment.

Testing found no retatrutide in the vial. Instead, it contained semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic, at about eight times the concentration in legitimate prescription brands the regulator had assessed.

You may develop side effects … [that] present as a life-threatening risk

Dr Sharifa Ezat Wan Puteh, public health specialist

Dr Sharifa Ezat Wan Puteh, a public health specialist at the National University of Malaysia, warned that laboratory reports and batch numbers could be forged or copied from genuine products.

“The dose can be inaccurate and you may develop side effects,” she said, citing allergic reactions, diarrhoea and other complications such as pancreatitis from unsupervised use. “They may present as a life-threatening risk.”

Sharifa called for wider access to clinically appropriate treatments through public facilities and insurance arrangements, alongside medical advice on exercise, diet and existing conditions.

Malaysian Health Minister Dzulkefly Ahmad told parliament on Monday that officers had seized 341,000 ringgit (US$83,800) worth of unapproved retatrutide products in 12 raids between January 2025 and September this year. Seven additional raids on illegal Ozempic sales yielded products worth 64,170 ringgit.

Dzulkefly said Malaysia’s latest national budget contained no specific allocation for medicines such as Ozempic and Mounjaro, although he noted that patients could apply for treatment through a special approval mechanism.

Between January and September, 240 applications for treatment were approved at a cost of 2.56 million ringgit (US$629,000).

Following the money

The weight-loss trade extends across Southeast Asia. In September, Thai authorities announced the seizure of unregistered peptide products and equipment worth more than 52 million baht (US$1.5 million) after investigating a social media seller in Nonthaburi, north of Bangkok.

TRM Labs, a San Francisco-based firm that analyses blockchain transactions, has identified more than 150 Chinese chemical manufacturers accepting cryptocurrency, roughly three-quarters of which advertised both peptides and fentanyl precursors – the chemicals used to make the potent synthetic opioid.

Payments to vendors selling both product lines rose from US$28.2 million in 2023 to US$37.3 million last year, according to an October report from TRM. The figures cover multiple products and cannot show how much was spent on peptides alone.

“We have not traced Malaysian buyers to these suppliers, so we can’t say this applies to any specific purchase,” said Xue Peh, a senior analyst at TRM. “On-chain data shows how much was transacted, not what was bought.”

While cryptocurrency allowed suppliers to easily accept cross-border payments, public blockchains still left a digital trail, Peh said.

“Authorities can follow the flow of funds to connect transactions to suppliers, not just seller accounts,” she said, adding that issuers of stablecoins – cryptocurrencies pegged to conventional fiat currencies – could freeze assets and crypto exchanges could screen payments to known supplier wallets.

For Bey, the loss of her latest supplier has changed little. She credits the slimming injections with suppressing her appetite and helping her lose weight, alongside exercise and eating less.

Her latest dose was a week before she spoke to This Week in Asia and she was already weighing up the pros and cons of switching to another brand. “I have to buy it again,” she said.

*Full names withheld at interviewees’ request

item.title: [SCMP] In Malaysia’s largest state, ‘Sarawak First’ faces a Dayak election test
item.description:
Ethnicity plays out differently across Malaysia. On the peninsula, identity politics is comparatively rigid: Malay vs non-Malay, with Islam and Malay identity fused not just culturally but constitutionally. In the Borneo states of Sabah and Sarawak, however, the picture is less binary. Religion plays a smaller role in daily life, cultural identities are more diffuse, and ethnic lines are less clear-cut.

The Dayaks, a collective term for Sarawak’s non-Muslim indigenous peoples, are the state’s largest ethnic group at 42 per cent of the population. They comprise the Iban (28 per cent), Bidayuh (8 per cent), Orang Ulu (“people of the interior”) and other indigenous groups (6 per cent). Malays (24 per cent) and Melanau (5 per cent), most of them Muslim, make up much of the rest of the population, alongside Chinese (24 per cent).

Power struggles within the Dayak community – and between the Dayak, Malay-Melanau and Chinese blocs – are layered with personality politics and, increasingly, “Sarawak First” nationalism. The ruling Gabungan Parti Sarawak (GPS) coalition formally broke away from Barisan Nasional in 2018 and champions Sarawakian identity over ethnicity. Its dominant component party, Parti Pesaka Bumiputera Bersatu (PBB), has anchored the state government since the 1970s.
item.content:encoded:
Ethnicity plays out differently across Malaysia. On the peninsula, identity politics is comparatively rigid: Malay vs non-Malay, with Islam and Malay identity fused not just culturally but constitutionally. In the Borneo states of Sabah and Sarawak, however, the picture is less binary. Religion plays a smaller role in daily life, cultural identities are more diffuse, and ethnic lines are less clear-cut.

The Dayaks, a collective term for Sarawak’s non-Muslim indigenous peoples, are the state’s largest ethnic group at 42 per cent of the population. They comprise the Iban (28 per cent), Bidayuh (8 per cent), Orang Ulu (“people of the interior”) and other indigenous groups (6 per cent). Malays (24 per cent) and Melanau (5 per cent), most of them Muslim, make up much of the rest of the population, alongside Chinese (24 per cent).

Power struggles within the Dayak community – and between the Dayak, Malay-Melanau and Chinese blocs – are layered with personality politics and, increasingly, “Sarawak First” nationalism. The ruling Gabungan Parti Sarawak (GPS) coalition formally broke away from Barisan Nasional in 2018 and champions Sarawakian identity over ethnicity. Its dominant component party, Parti Pesaka Bumiputera Bersatu (PBB), has anchored the state government since the 1970s.

Over the ensuing decades, every Sarawak chief minister has come from the Muslim bumiputra – a Malay word meaning “sons of the land” – in an unbroken 56-year run: Melanau (Abdul Rahman Ya’kub, 1970–81; Taib Mahmud, 1981–2014) or Malay (Adenan Satem, 2014–17; Abang Johari, 2017 to present). That dominance traces back to 1966, when Kuala Lumpur used emergency powers to remove Iban chief minister Stephen Kalong Ningkan for resisting federal control. It has endured because Muslim bumiputra voters consolidated behind one party while the Dayak vote split across several.

The coming state election could be Abang Johari’s last as chief minister. With GPS’ return to power virtually assured, the more consequential question is succession: will a Dayak finally lead Sarawak? A Dayak successor would show that GPS’ “Sarawak First” slogan is inclusive. Another Malay-Melanau-Muslim successor would only keep alive the grievance on which ethnonationalist appeals, or “Dayakism”, thrive.

As Sarawak heads to the polls, the contest for the Dayak vote is once again under way. In a state where no ethnic group commands a majority on its own, no party can govern without the Dayak, the largest bloc.

Yet Dayak representation remains fragmented and uneven. Of the 82 seats in the state legislative assembly, 34 are Dayak-majority, meaning Dayaks make up more than 50 per cent of voters. GPS won all but two of them in 2021, spread across its component parties: PBB, Parti Rakyat Sarawak (PRS), the Progressive Democratic Party (PDP) and the Sarawak United Peoples’ Party (SUPP). PRS, the coalition’s main Dayak-based party, held 11 seats. No opposition party currently represents Dayaks in the assembly.

Social media has been awash with Dayak grievances, from calls to reclaim ancestral land to complaints of underrepresentation in government. One widely circulated table purported to show Dayaks far behind their Malay-Melanau-Muslim counterparts in key management positions. GPS’ response was pointed. At the PBB Special Convention in August, Abang Johari rejected the marginalisation narrative, declaring “siapa nya pandai, nya lah naik” (whoever is capable will rise), and framing leadership as a matter of merit, not ethnicity.

Past election results suggest Dayak bids for top leadership roles face steep odds. Even a clean sweep of all 34 Dayak-majority seats would leave a Dayak party short of the 42 needed to govern, forcing it into partnership with Malay-Melanau or Chinese parties already locked into GPS. In 2021, opposition parties, chief among them Parti Bansa Dayak Sarawak Baru (PBDS), dangled the prospect of a Dayak chief minister, but failed to shift loyalties in any meaningful way.

That appeal has a long history. Founded in 1983, PBDS mobilised Dayak sentiment more consistently than any other party and coined the rallying cry “Dayakism” during its failed 1991 bid to install a Dayak chief minister. Deregistered in 2004, it was revived in 2013 as PBDS Baru before reclaiming the PBDS name in 2022. Another opposition party, the now-defunct Parti Sarawak Bersatu (PSB), was formed in 2014 after a SUPP breakaway and dissolved in March 2024, with its members absorbed into GPS coalition party PDP. That leaves PBDS as the only visible Dayak-based challenger to GPS, though a far less formidable one than the online noise around it suggests.

GPS’ edge also lies in its track record of delivering development to rural, Dayak-majority areas. That record, paired with its skilful use of Sarawak nationalism, helped it comfortably win most of those 34 seats in 2021 – a measure of how little electoral purchase Dayakism holds.

The more significant contest is within GPS itself. Since PRS president James Jemut Masing died in October 2021, Dayak politics has lacked a leader of comparable stature. Many are asking whether PBB secretary general and Kapit MP Alexander Nanta Linggi might fill that void. He has said he will not defend his parliamentary seat at the next general election and has signalled his intention to contest a proposed new state seat in Melekun, within Kapit, pending gazettement.

In the coming election, the odds look unfavourable for anyone tempted to weaponise ethnicity to mobilise support

But Nanta would need the backing of Abang Johari and his deputy Douglas Uggah Embas, PBB’s most senior Dayak figure. The Dayak challenge facing GPS, then, is less external than internal: a quiet contest among its own Dayak leaders to become the community’s next standard-bearer.

Adenan, the former chief minister, brought Sarawak First into the political mainstream in 2014, framing demands under the Malaysia Agreement 1963 that Abang Johari has since carried forward. But Sarawak First sentiment is more than GPS’ state-level winning formula; it underwrites the coalition’s pivotal role in federal politics, where its 23 MPs are a pillar of Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s unity government. More uncomfortably, it also entrenches PBB, and with it Malay-Melanau-Muslim predominance within GPS, unless the coalition proves genuinely willing to hand power to a Dayak leader.

In the coming election, the odds look unfavourable for anyone tempted to weaponise ethnicity to mobilise support. Those stoking Dayak sentiment for electoral gain will have to convince not only the Dayaks but all Sarawakians of what matters more: Dayak First or Sarawak First.

Dr Arnold Puyok is a Visiting Senior Fellow at ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute. He is a Senior Lecturer in Politics and Government Studies at the Faculty of Social Sciences and Humanities, Universiti Malaysia Sarawak (UNIMAS). This article was first published on the institute’s commentary website fulcrum.sg.

item.title: [SCMP] From Hong Kong to the Olympics and beyond: swimmer Yvette Kong’s journey of resilience
item.description:
I WAS BORN in Toronto, Canada, in 1993, and moved to Hong Kong at six months old. My mother’s side of the family fled to Hong Kong from Shanghai in the 1940s; my father’s side is Hakka. My father grew up in a family that had long been in the shoe business and ran a shoe shop in Mong Kok. My parents met while studying at the University of Minnesota, in the United States. When I was little, they both worked in the shoe trade; that business went into decline after the 1997 Asian financial crisis and gradually disintegrated.

IN 1996, AT the age of three, I had a serious case of Kawasaki disease (which can cause damage to the heart and blood vessels and mostly affects children). I remember relatives arriving with lots of Sailor Moon gifts, my grandmother crying and my mother curling up on a plastic stool beside my hospital bed to sleep. A needle was stuck into my back while I screamed. Only years later did I realise it was a bone-marrow test to rule out cancer.

ALSO IN 1996, my mother enrolled me in swimming lessons, to learn a survival skill. I loved it but wasn’t really any good at first. As a child, I was very slow on land. I daydreamed at school and struggled with simple tasks such as connecting the dots on Kumon worksheets. My mother asked a doctor whether the illness had damaged my brain. Nicknames followed: “a lump of rice”, “a cloud” – I couldn’t sit still.
item.content:encoded:
I WAS BORN in Toronto, Canada, in 1993, and moved to Hong Kong at six months old. My mother’s side of the family fled to Hong Kong from Shanghai in the 1940s; my father’s side is Hakka. My father grew up in a family that had long been in the shoe business and ran a shoe shop in Mong Kok. My parents met while studying at the University of Minnesota, in the United States. When I was little, they both worked in the shoe trade; that business went into decline after the 1997 Asian financial crisis and gradually disintegrated.

IN 1996, AT the age of three, I had a serious case of Kawasaki disease (which can cause damage to the heart and blood vessels and mostly affects children). I remember relatives arriving with lots of Sailor Moon gifts, my grandmother crying and my mother curling up on a plastic stool beside my hospital bed to sleep. A needle was stuck into my back while I screamed. Only years later did I realise it was a bone-marrow test to rule out cancer.

ALSO IN 1996, my mother enrolled me in swimming lessons, to learn a survival skill. I loved it but wasn’t really any good at first. As a child, I was very slow on land. I daydreamed at school and struggled with simple tasks such as connecting the dots on Kumon worksheets. My mother asked a doctor whether the illness had damaged my brain. Nicknames followed: “a lump of rice”, “a cloud” – I couldn’t sit still.

DURING THE 2000 Summer Olympics, I sat in front of the television, hypnotised by the underwater footage and swimmers like (Ian) Thorpe, (Alexander) Popov – I announced that, one day, I would be one of them. Children don’t calculate winning odds.

WHEN I WAS seven, I joined the Good Hope School swim team as one of only two female Primary One pupils on the squad. For a girl who couldn’t organise herself on land, water became where I could be myself and feel my worth. I thought I should have been a fish.

BY THE TIME I was 10, my mother had started designing her own swimwear, based on what she had observed swimmers actually needed. She initially sold the swimsuits at my training sessions. Years later, that small poolside business grew into a shop for swimwear, in Tsim Sha Tsui, which she still operates today.

I FIRST REPRESENTED Hong Kong at age 11, at an interschool competition in Macau. At 13, I broke my first Hong Kong record – the 100-metre breaststroke, in 2006 – and everything changed. I was an up-and-coming prodigy. I set another Hong Kong record in the 200-metre breaststroke the next year. Swimming stopped being just something I loved, and turned into something everyone was invested in.

I MISSED QUALIFYING for the 2008 Olympics, in the 200-metre breaststroke, by about a second, even though a year later, I was ranked in the top 25 globally. Inexplicably, after hitting my peak, I plateaued. For the next six years, despite training harder and entering increasingly elite environments, I barely got faster.

THE NEXT OLYMPICS, in 2012, were worse: the qualifying rules changed and I landed on a wait-list. I flew to the Hong Kong team’s holding camp in Cardiff, Wales, anyway, to watch the athletes. My ego was too big at the time to let me walk away.

I WAS AT the University of California, Berkeley, in the US, from 2012 to 2015, on a sports scholarship to study cognitive science. Despite being in this elite environment, it felt like the harder I trained, the further backwards I went. By my second year at Berkeley, around 2013, I couldn’t even qualify for the NCAA (National Collegiate Athletic Association) Championships. I felt like a rock at the bottom of the pool. My body had stopped listening. I told my coaches I was quitting. I thought that would be the end of it, but memories and emotions from swimming that I had pushed down began resurfacing. I remember sitting in class and suddenly crying. I realised that emotions don’t simply disappear because you bury them.

I HAD ASSUMED that, if you did exactly what the Olympians did and had the best training, you’d go faster. What I eventually realised was that the body doesn’t respond to training in isolation. Performance is shaped by the whole person – psychology, stress, recovery, relationships, coaching and environment – and the human body isn’t a machine you can simply programme and expect an output from.

BECAUSE I WAS studying the brain anyway, I treated myself like a problem to solve. I found a book on EMDR (eye-movement desensitisation and reprocessing) therapy and thought, “Maybe I have trauma.” I found a therapist whose services I could afford and worked with her for months. Part of what I found was something simple: I’d started as a kid in la-la land who loved the water, and in the pursuit of excellence and competitions, I was lost.

AFTER I GRADUATED, I gave myself a year to swim on completely different terms. I read that the University of Edinburgh, in Scotland, turned swimmers who’d started nowhere near elite into internationally ranked breaststrokers. I cold-called and asked them to take me in. They were baffled: “You’re coming from Berkeley, where all the superhuman athletes are.” I arrived in Scotland in the summer of 2015, in flip-flops and shorts, and nearly froze. It became one of the best years of my life, mostly because my coach, Chris Jones, cared about me as a person. What I’ve carried into every workplace and classroom since is that humans are humans.

WHEN I QUALIFIED for the Rio 2016 Summer Olympics, I had already decided it would be my final try. I didn’t win a medal, but being there was more important, and the first place I went, in the Olympic Village, was the canteen. I sat watching athletes from every sport and country come and go. Every one of us had climbed a mountain to get there, I thought.

WEEKS BEFORE RIO started, I was hospitalised with a stomach bug. I thought performing at my best would take a miracle. I was anxious enough that I skipped the opening ceremony, which I now regret. When I walked out to the blocks at the start of my race, my senses seemed magnified. For a moment, it was only me and the race; the next, I was blended into the whole crowd and noise of it. I swam in that heat and went no further.

DEEP DOWN, I knew it would be my last proper race. Not to sound morbid, but it felt like the vision people describe at the end of their life – the child who wanted to be a fish, the 13-year-old breaking her first record, the girl who lost her way, the woman who found it again and even my future self, all converging at once, surrounded by everyone who had witnessed the journey.

POST-RIO, I was kind of at peace. I’d seen extraordinary athletes and how anxious and depressed they were, and I understood that achievement and well-being were not the same. It changed what success meant to me: results matter, but they are not the sole measure of life.

I JOINED MIND Hong Kong in 2017, as a founding board member. It started with just the three of us; now, there are more than 100 staff. I also gave myself a year of seriously practising martial arts and wushu, which I’d been interested in since watching Bruce Lee as a child – I’ve always been drawn to warrior-girl types such as Sailor Moon and Mulan.

THEN THE PART I never planned: I went corporate. I’d never even done an internship before, so it was a shock. I worked for half a year at Goldman Sachs, two years at McKinsey & Company and another two at Estée Lauder. I then went back to school remotely to study performance psychology at the University of Edinburgh during Covid-19. Later, I did an MBA at Tsinghua University, in Beijing, and an MSc at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, in the US, where professors asked me to stay on to teach. I went from student to lecturer and built my own course on transversal design for social impact.

ALL OF THIS led to my Hong Kong-based start-up, Arelyx, founded last year. We build what I call “human-capacity intelligence” for an artificial-intelligence-shaped world, starting with education. We help schools understand and develop capacities such as resilience, ethical judgment and agency. Our first deployment began in Hong Kong this September, at Catholic Mission School.

I SPOKE ABOUT my new book, The Unmeasured Human, in August at the International Olympic Committee, in Lausanne, Switzerland, and noticed it was exactly 10 years since I had represented Hong Kong at Rio 2016. When I retired from swimming, people asked if I’d write my story. I said I was too young and there was more I needed to find out. It took a decade.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity

item.title: [SCMP] Trump’s war secretary Hegseth and Pacific Command chief Paparo may ‘soon visit China’
item.description:
Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth and US Pacific Command head Admiral Samuel Paparo may visit China “soon”, according to a veteran China hand.

Stephen Orlins, president of the non-profit organisation National Committee on United States-China Relations (NCUSCR), disclosed the potential visit during a video address at a conference on Friday in Sanya, in southern China’s Hainan province. More than 400 Chinese officials, foreign diplomats and legal experts have gathered in the South China Sea resort city for the Global Maritime Cooperation and Ocean Governance event closing on Sunday.

Orlins said the prospective visit by Hegseth and Paparo would be critical to regularising military-to-military communication between Beijing and Washington.
item.content:encoded:
Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth and US Pacific Command head Admiral Samuel Paparo may visit China “soon”, according to a veteran China hand.

Stephen Orlins, president of the non-profit organisation National Committee on United States-China Relations (NCUSCR), disclosed the potential visit during a video address at a conference on Friday in Sanya, in southern China’s Hainan province. More than 400 Chinese officials, foreign diplomats and legal experts have gathered in the South China Sea resort city for the Global Maritime Cooperation and Ocean Governance event closing on Sunday.

Orlins said the prospective visit by Hegseth and Paparo would be critical to regularising military-to-military communication between Beijing and Washington.

The former US diplomat also warned that the South China Sea – rather than Taiwan – had become the flashpoint most likely to trigger an accidental military clash between the two powers.

“So here’s what I would ask of both governments: first, regularise military-to-military contact at every level, so mistakes don’t happen, and when they do, we are able to have immediate discussions on how to de-escalate,” Orlins, who has led NCUSCR since 2005, said.

“I understand that Secretary of War Hegseth and Admiral Paparo may soon visit China. This is very useful to establish that contact.”

The two sides have been in talks in recent months for a potential China visit by the US defence secretary, possibly before year’s end, the South China Morning Post has learned.

Sources earlier told the SCMP that military-to-military communication was increasing, and that Washington had for months been preparing for separate visits to China by Hegseth and Elbridge Colby, the undersecretary of defence.

Reciprocal visits by Hegseth and Chinese Defence Minister Dong Jun had also been discussed since Xi Jinping and Donald Trump met in Washington in September, the sources said.

It is unclear whether those plans have changed after this week’s midterm elections that saw major Republican losses.

If confirmed, Paparo’s visit will also be the first trip to China by a US Pacific command chief since 2015.

Headquartered in Hawaii, the US Pacific Command, reverting to its original name from Indo-Pacific Command in June, oversees American military operations across the Asia-Pacific. This places its commander on the front lines of potential confrontations with the People’s Liberation Army in flashpoints like the Taiwan Strait and the South China Sea.

Paparo, who assumed the post in May 2024, has advocated a sharp deterrence posture towards Beijing. He previously outlined a so-called hellscape strategy, proposing to deploy thousands of autonomous aerial, surface and underwater drones to deter the PLA and to buy time for the US and its allies to respond in the event of a cross-strait war.

In response to queries from the SCMP, the Pentagon and US Pacific Command said they had no announcements to make at this time.

Meanwhile, the prospect of a visit by Hegseth has been thrown into doubt as he faces mounting calls to resign or risk impeachment proceedings. Those demands have intensified following the Republican Party’s midterm drubbing – driven largely by public outrage over the ongoing war in Iran and the resulting spike in fuel prices.

Thomas Massie, an outgoing Republican House representative, has called for a vote to impeach Hegseth next week when the chamber reconvenes.

“There is one contingency in which I won’t reintroduce the articles of impeachment: Hegseth resigns,” Massie wrote on social media on Tuesday.

Hegseth has remained defiant, saying that he would “not back down” against a “lame duck” Congress and the calls for his impeachment “will not work.”

“Didn’t work against President Trump, and it won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that,” Hegseth said in a video post on Thursday.

Zhu Feng, dean of Nanjing University’s School of International Studies, said the potential visit could be a “positive step” towards constructive strategic stability, a new framework in ties agreed upon by Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing in May.

He noted that a visit by Paparo could also be part of the efforts to strengthen “working-level communications” between the two militaries.

High on the agenda, Zhu said, could be “urgent talks on the South China Sea, the Yellow Sea, and the East China Sea to prevent accidental friction”.

“The third area could be artificial intelligence, which is shaping new forms of military warfare, and the two sides must step up communication here as well to avert unpredictable crises.”

Sourabh Gupta, resident senior fellow at the Institute for China-America Studies, said the possibility of the visit was an “unmistakable plus” for the US-China political relationship.

“That a defence secretary would visit Beijing twice in a calendar year is remarkable in itself,” he said, in a reference to Hegseth being part of the US delegation during Trump’s state visit to Beijing in May.

“Such meetings do establish an important floor of stability for ties.”

According to Gupta, the two sides are making only “marginal and grinding progress on the trade and investment front”, which means that “the foreign-defence-national security side of things must pick up the slack”.

“It is my impression that the Chinese side has determinedly stepped up the level of engagement and problem-solving on military-to-military challenges,” he noted.

While economic ties remain strained by reciprocal tariffs, export controls and sanctions, military engagement has shown signs of a thaw, with both sides keeping communication lines open and pledging to preserve peace and deepen mutual understanding.

Gupta said although progress in restoring military ties and communication channels had been slow, the frequent military talks at multiple levels in the past few months were an “unambiguously positive sign”.

“Slow but steady is good enough, given the depth of geostrategic competition between the two sides in the Asia-Pacific theatre.”

US and Chinese defence officials held a two-day meeting of the newly created Crisis Communications and Prevention Working Group in Washington on Monday, the first such exchange in six years.

A Pentagon readout released on Tuesday said the two sides agreed on the importance of “advancing practical communication measures” to reduce risks in the US-China relationship.

The officials also discussed “additional channels” for “effective” crisis management and ways to communicate “expediently and effectively”.

The Pentagon said the November 2-3 meeting was attended by Cynthia “Xanthi” Carras, principal director for China, Taiwan and Mongolia at the Office of the US Undersecretary of War for Policy, and Senior Colonel Wang Wei, deputy director of the Americas and Oceania Affairs Bureau at the PLA Office of International Military Cooperation.

Command-level talks also resumed in August after a two-year hiatus, with Chinese General Yang Zhibin, commander of the Eastern Theatre Command overseeing the Taiwan Strait and the East China Sea, meeting Paparo in Canada.

“The two leaders discussed the importance of maintaining open lines of communication between senior US and Chinese military leaders to reduce the risk of miscalculation and promote safe and professional conduct between forces,” the US Pacific Command said in a statement.

In July, a senior Pentagon official attended a reception at the Chinese embassy in Washington to mark the 99th anniversary of the PLA, becoming the first senior US defence official in more than five years to attend such an event and deliver remarks.

“Under the leadership of Secretary [Pete] Hegseth, we are actively repairing a once broken military-to-military channel and making clear, steady progress,” Alvaro Smith, deputy assistant defence secretary for China, Taiwan and Mongolia, said in his address.

“This is how two powerful militaries should engage, and over the last year and a half, we [have] made this a reality.”

item.title: [SCMP] How North Korea turns child prodigies into crypto thieves
item.description:
North Korea rewards ⁠its top hackers, tasked with heists like the Binance crypto hack that netted a cool US$6.3 ⁠billion, with perks such as spacious apartments in the capital and huge hard currency awards in return for ⁠gruelling hours of work.

Leader Kim Jong-un has assembled an army of world-class hackers using such incentives in a programme more than a decade old that picks 200 of the smartest middle school students each year to study computer engineering, defectors and analysts say.

A fraction eventually become hackers in an investment that has paid off dramatically, as the group has evolved from the early days when it ran illegal gambling websites to pulling off the world’s biggest cyber heist last month.
item.content:encoded:
North Korea rewards ⁠its top hackers, tasked with heists like the Binance crypto hack that netted a cool US$6.3 ⁠billion, with perks such as spacious apartments in the capital and huge hard currency awards in return for ⁠gruelling hours of work.

Leader Kim Jong-un has assembled an army of world-class hackers using such incentives in a programme more than a decade old that picks 200 of the smartest middle school students each year to study computer engineering, defectors and analysts say.

A fraction eventually become hackers in an investment that has paid off dramatically, as the group has evolved from the early days when it ran illegal gambling websites to pulling off the world’s biggest cyber heist last month.

“They are actually one of Kim Jong-un’s secret weapons,” said Kim Heung-kwang, a North Korean defector who trained hackers on behalf of the state before fleeing to South Korea in 2004.

“There is no other country grooming hackers like this, systematically searching for the smartest children, solely to turn them into operatives,” ‌he added. “Whether they want to be a hacker or not does not matter.”

There is no other country grooming hackers like this

Kim Heung-kwang, North Korean defector

The FBI and Binance have blamed North Korea for the Binance hack, though Pyongyang has denied it. Blockchain investigation firms have attributed it to a North Korean group known as “TraderTraitor”.

The denial is part of a pattern in which the North dismisses such blame over the years as fabricated political provocations.

North Korea set up a cyber unit in 1998 but elevated its status after Kim came to power and declared in 2013 that cyber warfare was, along with nuclear weapons and missiles, an “all purpose sword” crucial to the country’s strike capability.

Candidate selection begins in middle school as early as 11 or 12 years of age, with authorities picking about 150 to 200 children a year to study computer science, said Kim Heung-kwang, the former trainer, and two defectors who worked in IT.

At 17, the top performers are sent to North Korea’s best universities and undergo further screening before a chosen few finally enter the military’s cyber unit as hackers, they added.

They are trained in areas such as cryptocurrency protocols and reverse-engineering foreign hardware devices in addition to more conventional topics ⁠such as advanced mathematics and foreign languages, one of the defectors said.

Those who do not become hackers are reportedly trained to turn out software or apps for Western firms via remote jobs.

“While South Korea’s best students may pursue medicine or other prestigious careers, North Korea channels top talent into nuclear and cyber programmes and ‌essentially guarantees their future,” said Lim Jong-in, professor emeritus at the school of cybersecurity at Korea University.

Other privileges on tap for the hackers are travel abroad to allied countries, such as China, where they can more freely access the internet.

Successful exploits can earn as much as 30 per cent of the heist’s profits in US dollars for the hackers’ military unit, and they can even receive a flat in the capital where their parents can also stay, Kim said.

“There are accounts that successful cyber ‌personnel are given apartments in Pyongyang,” Lim said, adding that the flats could range to as much as 132 square metres (1,420 sq ft).

High performers were also eligible for membership of the ruling party and high-status marriages into elite families, said one of the ⁠defectors.

But it is a small group. The North’s cyberwarfare operations employ about 8,400 ⁠people, South Korea’s National Intelligence Service estimated in 2024.

North Korean state media does not publicly celebrate such hackers’ achievements, but they regularly highlight students who show talent for programming.

In 2015, North Korea opened the Mirae Scientists Street in the capital, with Kim Jong-un closely involved in its construction, state media said.

Hackers’ formal designation in the North was “scientist” or “researcher”, said one of ‌the defectors.

Other hacking groups associated with North Korea include the Lazarus Group, also known as APT38, which the US accused in 2022 of having stolen hundreds of millions of dollars worth of cryptocurrency from the Ronin blockchain network. The FBI has said TraderTraitor is affiliated with Lazarus.

State backing made the North’s hackers more dangerous and harder to repulse, as they faced no consequences for hack after hack, enabling ‌them to ‌perfect their strategies, analysts said.

“In the world of cybercrime, often, if you make a mistake … that is all law enforcement needs to get you,” said Alec Zebrick, senior manager for Asia-Pacific global services at Chainalysis.

But North Korea’s hackers “are doing this for the regime, so they’re going to continue, even after ‌successes,” he added.

“Even after failures, they’ll continue, because it’s very hard for the international community to take action against them.”

Other groups that have engaged with North Korea IT workers who earn funds for the Kim regime by landing remote technology jobs at Western companies describe them as highly organised, polite in their interactions and avid ⁠users of AI.

“There clearly was a structure you would see in military. Strict times, cleaning boots, very orderly,” said YouTuber Deeveeaar, who claims to have hacked into cameras watching North Korean IT workers at their jobs.

“To say they ‘use a lot of AI’ is an understatement. AI is the very backbone ⁠of their operation,” he said, citing use of paid ChatGPT accounts, Claude Code and Cursor, among many other AI tools.

“They write code with it, alter their resumes and help make new ones. And even forge documents and identities.”

Binance said the hackers used a bogus job interview and software hidden in an advertisement to compromise employees’ computers before using an internal AI tool to seize control of systems.

In 2025, a sanctions monitoring team drawn from 11 United Nations member states said TraderTraitor had obtained both ChatGPT and DeepSeek accounts.

Yet the lifestyle of a hacker ‌or elite technology worker for North Korea is gruelling, particularly when given a ‌mission or sent abroad, say former IT workers and human rights groups.

Among the downsides were constant surveillance, strict targets and often having to work for longer than 10 hours a day, said former IT workers interviewed for a report last year by advocacy group PSCORE.

“There is always pressure to keep earning money,” said the group’s executive director, Nam Bada. “The stress is extreme, and because of the psychological strain people develop health problems they didn’t have before.”

IT workers must meet a monthly target in dollars, or face humiliation and other punishments, he said.

Still, the hackers’ success is likely to embolden the North Korean leader as they get better and grow more ambitious, analysts say.

“We see more and more them leaning towards what we call ‘big game hunting’,” Zebrick said.

“So they’re targeting some of these larger organisations, potentially have larger vaults of funds, that they could potentially get. These are harder targets … However, as we can see with the Binance case, the payout certainly can make it worth their time.”

item.title: [SCMP] What’s next after airlines? Asia data breach raises wider cyber fears
item.description:
A massive data breach that affected several airlines across Asia has underscored the need for industries in the region to revisit their reliance on third-party suppliers, analysts have said, warning that more critical infrastructure may soon be affected.

Last week, a wave of airlines reported that customer information was accessed in a data security breach involving Spanish software provider Amadeus.

Several of these breaches involved information found in booking details, including flight data, passenger names, booking reference numbers and travel itineraries.
item.content:encoded:
A massive data breach that affected several airlines across Asia has underscored the need for industries in the region to revisit their reliance on third-party suppliers, analysts have said, warning that more critical infrastructure may soon be affected.

Last week, a wave of airlines reported that customer information was accessed in a data security breach involving Spanish software provider Amadeus.

Several of these breaches involved information found in booking details, including flight data, passenger names, booking reference numbers and travel itineraries.

Cathay Pacific said on October 30 that the breach affected about 53,000 bookings, with additional personal information exposed in a subset of cases, but its systems and operations were fine. There was also “no evidence that financial or payment information was accessed”.

Singapore Airlines, the city state’s flagship carrier, made similar claims, noting in a statement on Tuesday that the breach affected a total of 46,000 booking records made between August 2023 and September.

Other affected airlines that reported recent customer data breaches include Malaysia Airlines, Japan Airlines, ANA, Qantas and South Korea’s Asiana Airlines.

In a statement to This Week in Asia, Amadeus said it “became aware of a vulnerability affecting a travel booking display environment”, where certain booking-display data was accessible.

“Although our investigations continue, we can confirm that there is no evidence that payment or financial data was accessed,” it said, adding that there were no indications the vulnerability “has been exploited for ransomware purposes”.

The company said it implemented measures to fix the vulnerability, enhanced monitoring and detection capabilities, and was in “direct dialogue with our customers and authorities”.

Tony Ridley, chief security and risk adviser at EMA Global, said the duration and concentration of the breach were concerning.

“One provider’s weakness reached many airlines at once, and the airlines learned of it from the vendor weeks after the vendor knew,” Ridley told This Week in Asia.

Ridley warned that the near-term risk to passengers could involve targeted phishing that would be more convincing because it used information from an actual trip. A name and a valid booking reference “[are] often enough to open a booking online” and could risk further compromise, he said.

Other details also open up further risk.

“Passport information means you could face identity theft,” said David Gee, a non-executive director, risk adviser, and former chief information security officer of organisations such as HSBC.

Gee said the Amadeus breach was reminiscent of a February 2021 cyberattack on aviation IT and data services provider SITA – which targeted its Passenger Service System servers – and indicated “poor risk management” on Amadeus’ end, such as lapses in its multi-factor authentication (MFA) system.

“The concern is that someone came in with compromised credentials, a login and a password, and was never kicked out. Normally accounts have to be renewed or have some sort of credential that expires, and it looks like this one hasn’t … based on the evidence, I’d say there have been gaps in [their] MFA policy,” Gee said.

Ridley pointed out that the Amadeus breach reflected “different failures and different fixes”, as several airlines had reported an unauthorised party using credentials assigned to an Amadeus system account.

“The window the airlines report, August 2023 to September 2026, matters more than the motive: access that long without detection is the central question,” Ridley said.

Analysts warn that the scheme likely targeted specific individuals for a sophisticated level of fraud.

“They’re probably after very specific individuals – ‘who’s moving around, who could we potentially defraud?’ It’s a very advanced fraud opportunity because they know where you’re going and come across as very credible,” Gee said.

“For most people, the realistic harm is convincing fraud: an email or call that knows your name, flight and booking reference, asking you to pay a fee or confirm details. Where passport numbers were exposed, add identity misuse,” Ridley said.

However, the breach also poses additional risks, as travel history and itineraries reveal certain patterns of movement.

“[This] matters for executives, officials, journalists, and anyone with a reason to be targeted,” Ridley said.

Analysts have warned consumers who have booked with affected airlines in the past three years to be more vigilant about unexpected messages.

“If you’re a high-profile person or an official, take extra caution, because you’re the one being targeted,” Gee said. Consumers in general should also “be on extra lookout for messages from airlines that don’t come from the app, or emails that look right but offer a travel upgrade for some payment. They know a lot about you, and that’s what makes those messages convincing”.

Gee advised consumers to take extra steps such as changing passwords and securing accounts with MFA. “And be aware, for the next 10 to 15 years, of anything that looks too good to be true.”

Consumers should also treat unexpected messages about a booking with suspicion, “even if it quotes correct details”, Ridley said, and visit an airline’s app or website directly instead of clicking links or calling numbers that were sent.

Third-party risk

The incident has highlighted the region’s dependence on shared platforms, and analysts warn that the breach could soon extend to other critical sectors.

“I wouldn’t single out Asia-Pacific as more vulnerable. What this case shows is where the region’s dependence on shared platforms is greatest, and where its arrangements for dealing with a vendor breach are weakest,” Ridley said.

Any sector where competitors ran on the same shared platforms, such as hospitality, financial services and payments, healthcare, logistics, retail, ports, telecommunications, and government and educational institutions, risked similar attacks, he said.

Gee warned that critical infrastructure, such as banks and water and power systems, was at risk of being targeted.

“We have to think about the top of the pyramid, the most critical industries for the country. How do those players organise to work well together to defend, and how do they make sure their supply chain is protected? Right now, it’s not,” Gee said.

“Any third party without mature cyber practices is a target.”

Gee also warned that AI integrated into enterprise tools could potentially compound these risks, and that AI security across organisations was “generally immature”.

“It’s a brand new area and they don’t have controls in place,” he said.

“[What could be] next is the AI these third parties are using, which the company sometimes doesn’t even know about. Most organisations aren’t there yet, so we need to start working on our maturity for AI security.”

item.title: [SCMP] Signs of Prabowo-Widodo rift grow as Indonesian lawmakers target VP Gibran’s credentials
item.description:
A growing push among Indonesian lawmakers to investigate Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka’s academic credentials is raising questions about the influence of his father, former leader Joko Widodo, as signs of a rift within the country’s ruling elite grow.

The challenge comes from within President Prabowo Subianto’s own coalition, underscoring how the political alliance that helped propel him to power in 2024 may be unravelling, analysts have said.

It also follows the arrest of a prominent Widodo ally in a widening wiretapping scandal and an unusually large military mobilisation in Jakarta, developments that have fuelled speculation about the former president’s waning influence.
item.content:encoded:
A growing push among Indonesian lawmakers to investigate Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka’s academic credentials is raising questions about the influence of his father, former leader Joko Widodo, as signs of a rift within the country’s ruling elite grow.

The challenge comes from within President Prabowo Subianto’s own coalition, underscoring how the political alliance that helped propel him to power in 2024 may be unravelling, analysts have said.

It also follows the arrest of a prominent Widodo ally in a widening wiretapping scandal and an unusually large military mobilisation in Jakarta, developments that have fuelled speculation about the former president’s waning influence.

Political factions in the House of Representatives (DPR) have begun discussing the use of parliamentary oversight powers following an October 30 Supreme Court ruling that Gibran’s high school equivalency certificate was “invalid”.

Gibran, Widodo’s eldest son, became Prabowo’s running mate in the 2024 presidential election after Widodo backed the former general’s successful bid for power.

Indonesia requires vice-presidential candidates to have completed at least senior high school education.

According to data from the General Elections Commission, Gibran attended Orchid Park Secondary School in Singapore from 2002 to 2004, followed by three years at the University of Technology Sydney (UTS) Insearch from 2004 to 2007.

The Constitutional Court ruled last month that it had not found “convincing evidence” that Gibran “possesses a diploma … from abroad that could serve as the basis for determining that he had completed at least senior high school”.

The court nevertheless dismissed the petition challenging his qualifications, while the Supreme Court ruling on his equivalency certificate did not automatically remove him from office.

The two rulings have prompted lawmakers to consider invoking the right of inquiry, the right of interpellation or the right to express an opinion – parliamentary mechanisms that allow legislators to investigate government actions, question officials or formally state their position on a matter.

“The Prosperous Justice Party [PKS] has received public input from civil society several times at the Central Executive Board office. PKS is committed to pursuing these aspirations democratically and constitutionally, using the rights afforded by the DPR,” Muhammad Kholid, a lawmaker and senior PKS official, told This Week in Asia.

PKS is one of seven parliamentary parties in Prabowo’s broad ruling coalition, which controls 81 per cent of the seats in the legislature.

“We are currently reviewing the options. We are also communicating with other parties. Clearly, DPR must follow up [on these] rulings, especially the Supreme Court’s, within its authority,” Muhammad said.

Habiburokhman, deputy chairman of Prabowo’s Gerindra party, said it would discuss the Supreme Court’s ruling after the parliamentary recess ended on November 10.

Another coalition member, the National Awakening Party, said in a statement on Monday that it was “seriously reviewing” the use of the right of inquiry in Gibran’s case.

While such an inquiry could intensify political pressure on Gibran, removing a vice-president would require a separate constitutional process involving the Constitutional Court and the People’s Consultative Assembly.

Gibran’s lawyer, Muhammad Rullyandi, stressed that the Supreme Court decision did not affect his client’s position as vice-president.

Widodo said on Thursday he would “respect all existing legal processes and also respect the constitutional rights” of parliament.

The former president is himself embroiled in a lengthy legal dispute over his degree from Gadjah Mada University, which opponents claim was fabricated. Widodo has denied the allegation.

Troop deployment

The proposed investigation into Gibran has emerged against a backdrop of political and security tensions following the arrest of three senior police generals – including Widodo loyalist and former presidential chief of staff Listyo Sigit Prabowo – over allegations of wiretapping the president, cabinet officials, journalists and civic leaders.

The presidential palace has said the alleged surveillance could amount to treason.

Soon after the arrest, Indonesia’s armed forces (TNI) deployed troops and personnel to Jakarta, including nearly 21,000 Navy members.

First Admiral Tunggul, a Navy spokesman, said in a statement on Wednesday that the move was to “maintain the security and stability” of Indonesia.

Muhammad Nas, a TNI spokesman, called the deployment “common practice because TNI is required to always be ready to protect the entire nation”. Both spokesmen did not elaborate on what threats Indonesia is facing.

‘Fatal strategic decision’

The latest controversies have raised questions about whether a deeper rift is emerging between Prabowo and Widodo as the latter’s political influence wanes.

Made Supriatma, a visiting fellow at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore, said Widodo made a “fatal strategic decision” when he aligned himself and his family with Prabowo ahead of the 2024 presidential election.

“The commitment at the time was that Prabowo would provide protection for Jokowi and his family,” Made said, referring to Widodo’s nickname. “Whether that commitment is still being upheld is unknown, but we can judge from the [fact] that Prabowo is allowing the [Gibran high school diploma] case to continue.”

According to Cecep Hidayat, a political science lecturer at the University of Indonesia, Widodo retains “non-institutional electoral capital”, including his supporter networks and his association with the non-parliamentary Indonesian Solidarity Party – headed by Kaesang Pangarep, his youngest son.

“Jokowi’s political influence is declining, because when you’re outside the government, that power will gradually fade,” Cecep said.

Still, he warned that Prabowo’s “political legitimacy” could be affected if invoking the right of inquiry led to Gibran’s impeachment.

“Gibran isn’t just a separately elected vice-president, he’s part of an elite compromise. Will Prabowo also be held politically accountable for Gibran’s nomination?” Cecep said.

Gibran’s dismissal could also lead the public to question “the legitimacy of the government elected in the 2024 presidential election”, he said.

Made suggested that the proposal for a parliamentary inquiry into Gibran’s diploma was a tool for political posturing within the ruling coalition, and direct impeachment remained “unlikely” to avoid “infighting” over his replacement.

“Currently, the parties in Prabowo’s coalition are manoeuvring, throwing the ball to each other and doing political bargaining to gauge what advantages they can maximally gain [from the case],” Made said.

“We are the biggest victims of all of this. This political game doesn’t solve anything. It doesn’t help us get out of the crisis, it actually makes it worse.”

item.title: [SCMP] Will the US midterm ‘blue tsunami’ erode China’s faith in Xi and Trump’s relationship?
item.description:
China may start looking for ways to make its deals with the United States less dependent on the personal relationship between presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump after the midterm elections left the US leader in a weaker position to deliver results, analysts have said.

Some observers believe Beijing will start paying closer attention to what the White House can achieve without support in Congress, while others say it may seek closer engagement with the Democrats given their ability to “poison” relations between the two countries.

Tuesday’s elections left the Democrats set to take control of both the House and Senate in January after the “blue tsunami” flipped former Republican strongholds.
item.content:encoded:
China may start looking for ways to make its deals with the United States less dependent on the personal relationship between presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump after the midterm elections left the US leader in a weaker position to deliver results, analysts have said.

Some observers believe Beijing will start paying closer attention to what the White House can achieve without support in Congress, while others say it may seek closer engagement with the Democrats given their ability to “poison” relations between the two countries.

Tuesday’s elections left the Democrats set to take control of both the House and Senate in January after the “blue tsunami” flipped former Republican strongholds.

Although Beijing has repeated its long-standing position that the midterms were strictly a domestic affair and said it would continue pushing for closer cooperation with Washington, the results are likely to severely weaken Trump’s hand.

[Democrats] could create various obstacles, poison the atmosphere of US-China relations, and sour the mood for these encounters

Xin Qiang, Fudan University

The Democrats’ majorities give them the power to block legislation, control federal spending and launch investigations into the Trump administration for the final two years of his term.

But the shift could test the efforts to stabilise ties that have seen Trump and Xi meet twice this year, with further meetings expected at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen next week and the Group of 20 meeting in Miami in December.

Xin Qiang, a professor and deputy director of the Centre for American Studies at Fudan University, said the Democrats could “make things difficult” ahead of these meetings.

“They could create various obstacles, poison the atmosphere of US-China relations, and sour the mood for these encounters,” he said.

Xin also said they could put pressure on Trump over Taiwan, which Beijing considers a red line in ties with Washington.

He said he expected Congress to press Trump to resume arms sales to Taiwan, which have been put on hold, and to push bills strengthening US military support for the self-ruled island.

“With the Democratic Party in control, Congress will almost certainly initiate more pro-Taiwan actions in these areas,” he said. “Given the constraints imposed by Congress, it is likely to become even more difficult for Trump to elevate US-China relations.”

Beijing views Taiwan as part of China and has never renounced the use of force to reunite it with the mainland.
