The US, in common with most countries, does not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington opposes any attempt to take the island by force and is committed by law to supplying it with weapons.

Zhao Minghao, another professor at Fudan University, said several newly elected Democratic lawmakers were staunch supporters of Taiwan who had called for stronger deterrence against Beijing over the island.

“Their entry into Congress is expected to elevate the focus on the Taiwan issue, likely leading to demands for the Trump administration to accelerate new arms sales to Taiwan and bolster US-Taiwan military and security ties,” he said.

Zhao said a Democrat-controlled Congress was also “set to accelerate measures – including new legislation – aimed at tightening export controls on advanced AI chips and semiconductor manufacturing equipment destined for China, as well as restricting investments in China’s chip sector”.

The Republican losses could also shape how Trump approaches his meetings with Xi. Trump has partly blamed the losses on the war in Iran, telling reporters that rising fuel prices driven by the conflict were the main reason, although he remained defiant about his decision to order the strikes.

Vice-President J.D. Vance has also attributed the Republican Party’s crushing defeats to the decision to attack Iran.

“The reason we lost is the war,” he wrote in a lengthy post on social media on Wednesday. “The president himself said so last night.”

Sun Chenghao, a fellow at Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy, said voter frustration over the high cost of living could push Trump to seek trade gains with Beijing when he met Xi, or give him grounds to lower tariffs and stabilise supply chains.

“With the cost of living having become a major point of pressure within the United States, Trump is likely to place greater emphasis on outcomes that can be easily showcased to voters, such as those involving agricultural products, market access and tariff arrangements,” he said.

Even with heavy Republican losses, Trump had not lost all his leverage with Beijing, Sun said, citing US advantages in markets, finance and technology.

“The erosion of Trump’s political capital primarily weakens his ability to convince the other side to trust his long-term commitments. He may place a stronger emphasis on reciprocal returns, raise his asking price or even employ tough rhetoric to deflect domestic criticism,” he said.

But once Democrats take control of Congress in January, they could scrutinise deals the White House has made with China and limit Trump’s ability to ease export curbs in exchange for commercial agreements.

“Therefore, China-US relations may see continued economic and trade engagement alongside deepening technology and security friction,” Sun said.

“The challenge ahead is turning the leaders’ consensus into policies that can be implemented on a sustained basis.”

[Trump is] not in a particularly favourable position to manage relations with Beijing

Zhao Minghao, Fudan University

According to Fudan University’s Zhao, Trump is “not in a particularly favourable position to manage relations with Beijing” following the midterms.

“For its part, Beijing places great importance on maintaining strategic stability; however, defining the new parameters of the China-US relationship with Trump presents certain challenges.

“Factors such as the decline in Trump’s personal political authority and the checks and balances imposed by the US Congress will only add further complexity to the bilateral relationship,” Zhao said.

When asked about the elections, foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning repeated Beijing’s line that it was a domestic matter.

She added: “China stands ready to continue working with the US to uphold and deliver on the important common understandings reached by the two heads of state, enhance communication, properly manage differences, expand cooperation, and build a constructive relationship of strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness and reciprocity.”

Zhao also said: “I believe Beijing will also place greater emphasis on strengthening communication with the Democratic Party.”

Sun agreed that Beijing needed “to continue strengthening communication with both parties in Congress, as well as with local authorities and the business community”, adding that such contacts had helped distinguish lasting, substantive disagreements from rhetoric driven by elections or partisan politics.

But Sun said Beijing was likely to pay closer attention to Trump’s ability to deliver on his commitments.

“In the remainder of his term, Trump can still influence diplomacy, sanctions, export licences and military deployments. A decline in his political appeal will not eliminate these practical powers,” he said.

He added that the two sides should look to “refine the implementation” of the agreements they have already reached and clarify which items the US executive branch could deliver on its own and which required congressional funding or changes to the law.

“Furthermore … the relevant authorities, implementation steps and specific timelines should be clearly defined – thereby reducing the reliance on the personal relationship between leaders for the agreement’s execution,” he said.

Zhou Bo, a senior fellow at the Centre for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University, was more optimistic in his outlook, suggesting that while the midterm election results had “sent shock waves across the US”, the impact they would have on US-China relations was far less severe.

Major-power relationships such as China-US relations were not as fragile as people thought and possessed “inherent resilience”, the retired senior colonel in the People’s Liberation Army said.

“Most importantly, China today is not what it used to be; its national strength is on an entirely different level,” he added, arguing that Beijing could now deal with Washington from a position of strength.

Beijing, he said, could substantially step up the scope and severity of its countermeasures if Washington took actions Beijing considered unfair.

“At its core it simply means being evenly matched – a relationship where the two sides stand on roughly equal footing and possess comparable power,” Zhou added.

He suggested that the impact a Democrat-controlled Congress would have on Taiwan and future US arms sales to the island was also limited.

As China’s strength grows, Beijing possesses far more leverage and countermeasures to constrain Washington

Zhou Bo, CISS

“It is not that the US doesn’t want to sell, but that doing so will become increasingly difficult. The reason is straightforward: as China’s strength grows, Beijing possesses far more leverage and countermeasures to constrain Washington,” he said.

He also said that even if the Democrats tried to push Trump on arms sales, “I think it’ll be difficult for him this year because his schedule of high-level meetings is so packed”.

Zhou added that Trump needed stable US-China relations as part of his legacy, and while his negotiating position with Beijing might be slightly weakened by the midterm election losses, they would not fundamentally alter ties between the two countries.

Beijing, too, would adopt a wait-and-see approach, he said, adding that he expected no fundamental recalibration of its US policy.

Additional reporting by Cici Cao and Fan Chen

item.title: [SCMP] Is EU’s Southeast Asia push facing a funding crunch as China widens lead?
item.description:
An EU funding crunch is threatening to stifle the bloc’s ambitions to expand its influence in Southeast Asia, as Brussels grapples with a budget deadlock that could slow infrastructure investments across the fast-growing region.

The funding squeeze could hinder the green transition and regional connectivity goals of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, even as Brussels seeks greater strategic autonomy amid competition with Beijing’s economic clout.

Analysts expect the European Union to prioritise domestic spending pressures over overseas commitments, arguing Europe can still leverage higher-quality, sustainable investments rather than attempting to match China’s financial muscle.
item.content:encoded:
An EU funding crunch is threatening to stifle the bloc’s ambitions to expand its influence in Southeast Asia, as Brussels grapples with a budget deadlock that could slow infrastructure investments across the fast-growing region.

The funding squeeze could hinder the green transition and regional connectivity goals of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, even as Brussels seeks greater strategic autonomy amid competition with Beijing’s economic clout.

Analysts expect the European Union to prioritise domestic spending pressures over overseas commitments, arguing Europe can still leverage higher-quality, sustainable investments rather than attempting to match China’s financial muscle.

Launched in 2022, the EU-Asean Global Gateway strategy aims to bolster regional infrastructure backed by €10 billion (US$11.2 billion) in public funding through 2027 via its primary external financing tool, the Global Europe instrument.

“With over 680 million people, a huge middle class and a very dynamic economy in terms of manufacturing, services and tech, Asean is a massive market for the EU,” said Rahul Mishra, an associate professor at India’s Jawaharlal Nehru University. “For the EU, it’s a partner with which it shares a range of interests, aspirations and concerns.”

However, the programme’s future is clouded by an impasse over the EU’s 2028-2034 Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF). In July last year, the European Commission proposed an overall budget of nearly €2 trillion (US$2.25 trillion) – including €200 billion for Global Europe, up from €79.5 billion currently.

The plan met swift resistance from the “frugal” bloc – Germany, Austria, Denmark, the Netherlands, Finland and Sweden – which demanded cuts of several hundred billion euros before granting the required unanimous approval.

“The multiannual financial framework was growing in size every year, and this year it cracked through the psychological barrier of €2 trillion for the first time in the original proposal,” said Roland Vogt, an associate professor of global and area studies at the University of Hong Kong. “That is something very unpalatable to a lot of the member states who are net contributors.”

Brussels argues the expanded budget is needed to juggle defence, competitiveness, migration and climate priorities alongside traditional agricultural and regional cohesion subsidies.

Cuts to Global Europe loom

To break the stalemate, the current Irish presidency of the Council of the EU proposed a compromise trimming Global Europe funding to €148.9 billion – a roughly 25 per cent cut from the original proposal.

The compromise drew fierce pushback from the European Parliament, which must also approve the budget.

“Global Europe is the EU’s foreign and development policy superpower. Amid worsening global crises, Europe must step up its engagement with the world,” said Robert Biedron, co-rapporteur for the parliament’s development committee. “If we fail now, we will have to deal with the much more expensive consequences later.”

Analysts doubt lawmakers can hold the line.

“I don’t think the European Parliament can win, because the pressure from the countries which pay for the EU budget is so strong,” said Iain Begg, a professorial research fellow at London School of Economics’ European Institute. “The likelihood of Global Europe being successfully increased again by the European Parliament, I would regard as a very low probability.”

A spokesperson for the European Commission said it was committed to working constructively with other EU institutions and member states to secure an agreement on the MFF.

“The question is not what needs to be done, but how to finance and deliver on these priorities. In this context, we need a budget that matches Europe’s ambitions,” the spokesperson said. “The commission’s proposal is now in the hands of the co-legislators. The commission stands ready to support this work.”

The budget impasse comes as Brussels balances strained ties with Washington and Beijing against mounting domestic liabilities. Debt across five member states exceeds 100 per cent of their gross domestic product, with the International Monetary Fund warning that European public debt could double over the next 15 years without budgetary discipline.

“What is quite clear is that domestic issues prevail for now. Cohesion and agricultural funds are politically very difficult to touch as well,” said Konrad Szatters, a Brussels-based China analyst at the Association for International Affairs. “So, if something needs to be cut from the MFF, it might be the external action, because it’s just not the highest priority for national governments amid the ongoing financial squeeze.”

Wider funding gap for Asean

For Asean, this means less direct funding for Southeast Asia’s green transition and connectivity projects – the core of Brussels’ regional agenda.

“Asean is already grappling with a massive infrastructure financing gap, and reduced concessional funding would only make it harder to raise the capital that’s needed,” Mishra said. “There’s a real risk of an uneven green transition, with more financially robust countries able to carry on and less well-off ones potentially left behind.”

He warned that cross-border integration could stall, weakening momentum towards a cohesive regional economy. According to the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development, Southeast Asia needs US$210 billion annually through 2030 to close its infrastructure and sustainability investment gap.

“Green transition and sustainable connectivity continue to be global priorities for the EU, which is good news for Asean,” said Andrew Sherriff, associate director of institutional relations and partnerships at European “think-and-do” tank ECDPM. “However, Europe wants to align future spending in these areas not just with Asean priorities, but also more explicitly with its own interests and the European private sector through mutually beneficial partnerships.”

Failure to finalise the 2028–2034 MFF before next year could also stall new initiatives, despite European Council President Antonio Costa urging a deal before year’s end.

“Current initiatives agreed to be funded prior to 2027 would not be affected,” Sherriff said, noting emergency rules allow rolling over existing budgets. “However, without clarity on the budget for 2028–2034, launching new initiatives – including those related to the Global Europe instrument and the associated EU-Asean Global Gateway initiative – would be difficult unless the latter are funded directly by EU member states.”

This Week in Asia has contacted the Asean Secretariat for comment.

Head-to-head with China

Spending limits also blunt Europe’s ability to counter Beijing, which the Lowy Institute ranks as Southeast Asia’s most influential partner, financing 31 per cent of regional infrastructure projects in 2024.

“The bureaucracy is too big, and the capital available is too little. That’s one of the reasons why Europe has been losing out to China, because China can come in and basically say: ‘We’re bringing projects, including the financing,’” Vogt said.

Szatters said the EU must lean into project quality rather than trying to match Beijing’s spending power.

“The EU is not a state. Its budget heavily relies on member states’ contributions,” Szatters said. “Any substantial increase in funding for such initiatives requires agreement among the 27 member states, and ultimately somebody has to pay for it.”

“What we can do is outperform China in the sustainability and quality of investments for a long-term gain.”

item.title: [SCMP] Joshua Cooper Ramo on whether the US can handle the stress test of China’s rise
item.description:
Joshua Cooper Ramo is chairman and CEO of Sornay, an investment and advisory firm. Previously he was CEO of Kissinger Associates. Ramo is the author of the new book Darwin’s Lock: America, China and the Shared Future of Nations. His 2004 analysis of “the Beijing consensus” contrasted the Western and Chinese economic development models. He is the author of two New York Times best-selling books and now lives in Shanghai with his family.

For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

You moved from competitive aerobatic flying and becoming one of the youngest senior and foreign editors at Time to living in Beijing in the early 2000s, and later into high-level strategic advisory work in China and at Kissinger Associates. Looking back, what prompted that shift? How has that experience shaped your understanding of what it means to “see clearly” at a time when competing narratives increasingly define global affairs?
item.content:encoded:
Joshua Cooper Ramo is chairman and CEO of Sornay, an investment and advisory firm. Previously he was CEO of Kissinger Associates. Ramo is the author of the new book Darwin’s Lock: America, China and the Shared Future of Nations. His 2004 analysis of “the Beijing consensus” contrasted the Western and Chinese economic development models. He is the author of two New York Times best-selling books and now lives in Shanghai with his family.

For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

You moved from competitive aerobatic flying and becoming one of the youngest senior and foreign editors at Time to living in Beijing in the early 2000s, and later into high-level strategic advisory work in China and at Kissinger Associates. Looking back, what prompted that shift? How has that experience shaped your understanding of what it means to “see clearly” at a time when competing narratives increasingly define global affairs?

I loved my career as a journalist – the war zones, the meetings with heads of state, the power of writing for millions of readers. But the “hands off” nature of the work did not fit me in the end. I was reporting on a world that was changing with incredible, accelerating speed. I did not want to be on the sidelines. I wanted to do something. And my personality craved depth. I had a desire to satisfy a curiosity about how giant historic forces felt when they moved. I wanted to know what was likely to break and what was likely to be built. I had seen this engine of creative destruction at work while covering Silicon Valley as a journalist. I knew that pressure was coming for the world at large.

As foreign editor of Time I had visited China and I had a sense of a potential gathering force there. I wanted to be close to it. And I was interested in the deep question of war and peace, of how tragedy in international relations could be avoided. I wondered: Could I make a difference in US-China relations? So, I decided to devote myself to this problem for a few years.

When I moved to China in 2002, my friends largely thought I was nuts. I walked away from a good career and a comfortable life to spend eight hours a day studying Chinese, living in the smog of developing Beijing and trying to navigate a culture I did not understand in the least.

I did not have a lot of prospects or resources. To supplement the few hours of Chinese class I could afford every day, my “night school” was riding around Beijing by taxi at night talking with the drivers as we went from one Starbucks to another. (Little did I know I would join the board of directors of Starbucks a few years later.) I loved the experience from the first day.

Before I moved from New York to Beijing, a friend gave me some advice: “It’s important to be bilingual, but it is more important to be bicultural.” Even now, after 25 years in China, I still find this is a great spur to action.

Chinese culture taught me very quickly to see differently. And then doing business in China is also a merciless education. Commercial life in China is an instant hit of the sweaty, struggling intensity of a mercilessly competitive and innovative economy. The profound work ethic of the Chinese people is breathtaking, as is the innovation and the speed. To feel these struggles and triumphs up close, alongside friends, is a great education.

After I’d been in China a few years, Henry Kissinger – who had known a great uncle of mine – hired me to run his China business. Henry then asked me to become vice-chairman and co-CEO of his whole firm, which of course I accepted.

I think it’s safe to say no Westerner in all of Chinese history had the sort of access and exposure to the gears of Chinese power that Kissinger had. It was an amazing education. Not only did the two of us spend hours with top Chinese figures; it was also that Henry wanted to understand what he was seeing and hearing, so those intense meetings were paired with days of discussion and debate. It was an honour to be a part of his China life, and to learn from a master how one could be both passionately patriotic about America and also open-minded and curious about China.

My nearly 20 years with Henry also deepened my feeling of responsibility. Was it inevitable that the US and China would be enemies? In his book On China, Henry ended by explaining that my idea of “coevolution” was the only way forward. My latest book, Darwin’s Lock, takes that idea of coevolution and spells it out in detail. I explain that the choice between the US and China isn’t who wins or loses, but something even more severe: between coevolution and coextinction.

In 2004 you coined the “Beijing Consensus” as an alternative to the Washington Consensus. In your new book, Darwin’s Lock, you argue that the US and China are locked in a relationship of “coevolution”, with the stark choice being “coevolution or coextinction”. How has your thinking evolved over the past two decades, and why do you see coevolution, rather than competition or decoupling, as the most useful framework for understanding the future of US–China relations?

When I wrote the Beijing Consensus in 2004, it was a deeply heterodox idea. “There’s only one way to develop an economy” was the general view of economists. Certainly, my own education had been firmly informed by this “Washington Consensus” confidence. What I saw in China made me question that certainty. The weight of Chinese culture and ideas was something I could really feel, from the first moment I stepped off the plane in Beijing.

The country had thousands of years of political theory and history that wouldn’t be shrugged off by new ideas. Life ran as much based on relationships as it did rules. The link between the state and market was completely different than in the West. So, I started to ask if different paths to different kinds of modernity might be possible and even necessary.

As I travelled [in] China, saw where money was made and lost, it became sharply obvious that a different logic was at work. Not one that rejected the ideas of Western economics, but that demanded a different approach.

I developed the idea of coevolution out of some work I was doing on complexity theory for my 2008 book The Age of the Unthinkable. At that time, I came to see that Darwin’s logic was perhaps the most powerful in all of science: that a simple test – are you fit or not – decides survival. And that pressure either kills something or forces it to evolve. Then I found the idea not just of evolution but of coevolution: that species can work together to become more fit over time.

Well, it was super clear to me that our world was entering a period of really revolutionary change, really an “age of the unthinkable” as I called it. This process would force a fitness test on everything. It would stress-test our politics, our economics, our security and even maybe the Enlightenment values that had organised Western society for hundreds of years.

Many people like to see the world of global affairs as an “I live and you die” sort of battle on every front. But science has shown us that is not the case. If life were only merciless competition, we’d all still be living in caves and banging each other on the head. Much human progress has come from mutually beneficial cooperation. It’s why cities work or nations thrive. The demand to be fit in a really stressful time is so extreme that species will do whatever it takes to survive. So the question is, how might we achieve this for the US and China?

China’s rise has reshaped global power structures in ways few predicted two decades ago, yet Western media and policy circles often struggle to tell nuanced stories about China, oscillating between hype and fear. Based on your experience, what are the biggest blind spots in how China’s rise is understood and covered in the West? How can journalists, policymakers and business leaders tell more accurate, multidimensional stories about China’s trajectory?

Westerners need to make a real effort to see China for what it really is, with no prejudgment, and this takes effort and modesty. Kissinger used to say: “If your mental model about something is wrong, every decision you make will be wrong.” It’s a good point. So much of the problem for Westerners is just an inability to accept Asia as it is: filled with smart, ambitious, driven figures with a rich cultural, scientific and spiritual tradition that is no better or worse than the West, just different. That is the right framework.

I recall people in Washington confidently telling me in 2023 that China was a decade away from developing large language models. Wrong framework, wrong conclusion.

One common error is to zoom in on a single aspect of Chinese life – the political structure, the real estate market, questions about the younger generation – and to tell a whole story of China from a few data points. China is so complex you can tell any story you want about it if you pick and choose your facts. The Western “experts” running around yelling about how Leninist China is cannot explain the biotech revolution or the Shenzhen nightclub scene or the emerging philosophical debate about consciousness of AI using a Daoist framework.

Doak Barnett or John King Fairbank or Ezra Vogel approached China as foreign scholars. Their writing holds up even decades later. They teach that humility is maybe the most important part of curiosity. And that understanding China is not just an intellectual game.

You have to feel China. You cannot know it from a book. I fear too many well-intentioned “experts” on China do not always have that feeling.

It’s probably also of some use to try to give up the inclination to use Western terms to label Chinese situations. That rush to label Chinese using Western political terms has always made me feel a bit uncomfortable.

There is a limit to how far Western ideas can take you in the Chinese context. It’s like trying to describe a basketball game using football terminology. I guess it’s as if Chinese analysts were warning that Trump is a “Hanfeizist”. If this is done in the spirit of opening a discussion about comparative political evolution, that is maybe of some use. But if it’s done to flatten debate and judgment? To distort something complex by simplifying it? Well, it’s not really intellectually honest or wise. For American policymakers it’s dangerous.

The mood in both Washington and Beijing has darkened considerably in recent years. Some argue that the world is entering a new Cold War. Do you agree with that characterisation? Are we entering a fundamentally new era in US-China relations, or is this another phase in a longer cycle of adjustment?

It’s popular to say we’ve entered a new Cold War. But what we face is, as I argue in the book, much more dangerous. The Cold War pitted two ideologically divergent nations against each other in an era of careful nuclear balance. There was a great discrepancy between the abilities of each nation. Our age is much more complex. And more perilous as a result.

China is not the USSR in any sense – not politically, technologically, culturally or historically. The weapons systems of our age are far more dangerous – faster, harder to control, more widespread. And we’re also living in a world that has been globalising for 40 years now, so that has left behind a network of connections that has its own evolutionary logic.

It means danger can spread super quickly. You are what you are connected to, and in our age we are all connected to each other, like it or not. I think one leap we need to make is to stop calling our age the “post-Cold War” era. No one called the Enlightenment the “post-Dark Ages”. We’ve entered a new period. I have called it the “Age of Network Power”, but no matter what you want to call it, the new logic of power is that we are all defined by what we are connected to – and that web around us is, fuelled by data and AI and zero-latency connectivity – changing at unprecedented speed.

I think we’ve entered a new phase of US-China ties. Both nations have the ability to substantially hurt the other. That is new, and it introduces a new phase of deterrence, but also of danger. We are very early in the power phase transition this is causing, in moving from one stable equilibrium to another.

It’s unclear what that next balance point will look like – and we know from science that it is the transitions between equilibria that are the moments of greatest uncertainty, risk and possibility. My point in Darwin’s Lock is that we can move to a new equilibrium of what biologists call “reciprocal helpfulness” in which each nation can become more fit and together influence our changing world.

Think of whatever particular fear might have been haunting you lately – an AI disaster, a biological risk or an economic crisis – in each case imagine a world where the US and China are working together, constantly, to manage these and other risks while also finding productive interconnection. There is no inherent reason this is not possible; it’s just a matter of finding a safe path to get there.

I think arms racing and accidents, racism and misunderstanding, these will all be a part of US-China relations for years to come. Our problem then is how to design a realistic, safe strategy to coevolve, and that is what the book tries to outline.

Many in Washington now view interdependence with China as a strategic vulnerability rather than a source of stability. Has the original case for engagement failed? Why should policymakers embrace a framework of coevolution when both countries increasingly define the relationship in terms of security, technological rivalry and strategic competition? Where does healthy interdependence become dangerous dependency?

Today the US and China have what biologists call “obligate mutualism” – each depends critically on the other. You can try to pretend that this is not the case, that somehow you could just wall off the two nations and each is strong enough to exist in isolation, but that would demand possibly catastrophic adjustments.

China depends on the US for markets, for compute, for education, for financial market discipline and for a list of other elements essential to development. And the US depends on China not only for critical minerals or pharmaceuticals or masses of imported goods, but also for talent (look at who staff most of the essential US AI research labs and companies). It’s not like this interdependence was architected by anyone; it was a result of evolutionary pressures in the global economy.

The idea of some Americans that it is possible to ‘strangle’ Chinese AI development is misguided

Joshua Cooper Ramo

China and the US both have benefited from this. And one of the lessons of nature is that when you try to unwind a system of obligate mutualism, you usually kill the participants.

But it’s not only that internal dynamic. It’s also the fact that our world is rocking with dangerous crises. The US and China are like two guys wrestling in a house that is on fire. They are fighting the wrong enemy. This lets us see that “interdependence” is not a weakness; it’s the most effective response to new evolutionary pressure.

The fundamental question of evolution is this: can you solve problems faster than they threaten to kill you? This is as true for cells in your body as it was for Greek city-states confronted with Persian attacks in ancient Western history. It’s our question too. And the US and China can best be regarded as problem-solving machines. They are engineered to address the dangers and opportunities that their citizens each face.

The result of 40 years of globalisation is that the US and China each have distinct skills that the other cannot replicate any time soon. Interdependence is important not only as a stabilising force, but because it means each nation is bringing the best ideas and skills to problems of global stability that threaten both countries.

What is the biggest misconception Americans have about China today? And what is the biggest misconception Chinese people have about the United States?

Americans have no sense of how hard-working, creative and energetic the Chinese people are, of how much they are willing to sacrifice for prosperity and stability. And they assume China wants to “beat” America and be number one in the world. I’m not sure that is correct.

Chinese people often misjudge America by only looking at the headlines. What makes America honestly amazing is the power of self-organisation. No nation on earth is as good as the US at bringing diverse groups of people – I mean not only nationally diverse, but also men and women – into productive alignment. There’s a lot that is worrisome about the US situation now, but the ability of America to fuse a sense of personal freedom with a feeling for group ambition is a wonder.

If Washington and Beijing are destined to compete, where do you still see meaningful scope for cooperation? Is there one area where cooperation is not just desirable, but unavoidable?

I think you have to reframe this. It’s a mistake to think of competition and cooperation as binary choices. Our world is full of examples of places where both occur at the same time. It’s no accident that the place where this kind of “coopertition” is most common is Silicon Valley, where firms are extremely comfortable competing and cooperating at the same time. What’s really going on here is information exchange, an understanding that knowing and doing more makes each company more fit for what is ahead. The same is true for the US and China.

It is clear the US and China have a shared interest in limiting nuclear proliferation, in stopping the spread of dangerous weapons, in global financial stability and environmental progress – and a long list of similar issues. But the key is changing how we think about our work in these areas. If the overall relationship is seen in zero-sum terms, then any cooperation becomes impossible. The right choice is to accept the shared destiny of America and China and to then use that fused “coopertition” to develop an approach to the dangers and opportunities of our age.

Taiwan remains widely regarded as the most dangerous flashpoint in the relationship. How do you assess the risks over the next decade, and what concerns you most?

First, we should remember that it’s rarely the most obvious flashpoints that lead to war. Crises can spin out of control no matter where they start. Today there are too many potential hotspots for the US and China and not enough effort to manage them.

Chinese history should reassure us that some safe path can be found. Sometimes in international relations there are issues where you want to speed up the situation, while in others you want to slow it down. It’s important to know the difference.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly becoming a new arena of strategic competition. You have said that you “cannot understand the intensity of innovation in China unless you’re there”. What are Western policymakers and executives still getting wrong about China’s AI ecosystem, and what is the biggest blind spot in America’s current AI and China strategy?

What we’re seeing in China today is what I think we can safely call a “full stack fork” in the AI ecosystem. I mean that the whole Chinese AI system – from the way large language models (LLMs) are designed to how chips are used to how systems are deployed, and even in areas like the philosophy of AI-human relations or safety – all of this is shifting into an approach that suits China’s needs and abilities.

Chinese companies have proved themselves to be excellent fast-followers and even fine-tuners in LLM development. To be sure, Westerners completely missed this for the most part. It baffles many serious US AI figures. But I think the split between the two ecosystems is more fundamental and more important. And that is what is really invisible to most Americans.

Another aspect is that success for a nation in the AI future may be less about the strength of the models or the technology, but rather about the ability of a society to absorb the shock of these systems. Chinese society has many “shock absorbers” that may be of use.

The idea of some Americans that it is possible to “strangle” Chinese AI development is misguided. It also misses the fact that Chinese AI systems are now taking paths that US systems will not take. We can see this in areas like the way Chinese are approaching energy efficiency or safety, for example. And in terms of architecture, Chinese sensor-based AI systems and world models may have some real advantages over US ones.

Even the philosophical questions about AI consciousness or human-machine ties take on different aspects when you examine them with, say, a Daoist lens.

Americans like to see AI as a race with China. But it has few characteristics of a race: it’s hard to say what the rules are. There is no clear finish line. It’s not obvious what it means to win.

A coevolutionary framework would encourage interdependence of the AI systems in the US and China, but regard this more as two nations each building gardens in the same ecosystem. Each is different; each designed for national conditions that are distinctive.

But sharing the same larger context and possibly even finding ways to share information can help each side become fitter. This is about cultivation, and careful cultivation, not racing.

Your earlier books, The Age of the Unthinkable and The Seventh Sense, argued that leaders fail because they do not understand complexity, networks and the way connection itself transforms the objects it links. Are today’s leaders any better at grasping those forces, or are we still repeating the same mistakes in new forms?

I wish I could say I see complex thinking at work in politics today, but it’s pretty rare. We have to find a way to get leaders to think in biological terms, to understand the ability of systems to evolve and change – and to accept that we live in a complex world, not a complicated one.

When we say “complicated” we mean like a jet engine, something made of lots of parts but fundamentally predictable. A “complex” system is more like a forest – also filled with lots of pieces, but interacting in ways that are hard sometimes to predict or manage.

When you accept that the world is biological in nature, it means you need to pay a lot of attention to the places where resilience could break down. But it also means you really need to find ways to encourage and trust in the self-organisation of the system.

If you could advise President Trump and President Xi on one concrete step each to reduce the risk of conflict, what would those be?

The first leap is accepting a coevolutionary framework. Rather than trying to replace the “obligate mutualism” that ties the US and China today, the right question is “What can each nation do to help both become fit for the world ahead?”

Once you get out of an “I live/you die” view, there is a long list of practical things that can be done.

The two should agree to help stop global nuclear weapons proliferation. They should work to establish treaties for space and cyber and AI weapons systems. They should reinvigorate global institutions such as the WTO or the UN. And they should also – and we have an effort trying to start this – use AI tools to help manage the relationship to avoid crises.

But the single most important concrete step is to accept the shared fate of the US and China, and then institutionalise that in deep working groups on the many problems of our age. This should be a historic, important time for diplomacy.

Looking ahead to 2030, paint us two contrasting scenarios: one in which coevolution works, and one in which it fails. What are the key turning points that determine which path the relationship takes?

Imagine in 2030 a world in which the US and China have jointly agreed to work on the major problems of our world – AI safety, global warming, economic stability, nuclear proliferation or the dozens of wars around the planet now.

Consider the possibility of the best minds from each nation asking “how can we solve this problem together” and taking the attitude of being on the same side of the table on these issues of global destiny. At the same time, competition between the countries in science or commerce or finance is intense, but grounded in rules that make for really fair competition.

The path to coextinction is one in which there is no cooperation on these issues. The planet continues to bake, species are destroyed, arms racing tips into conflict, nations struggle against economic uncertainty and face wild domestic political pressures, and racism and nationalism begin to define how each nation sees the other.

The key turning point? I don’t think there’s one. That old line about health, that “the best time to take care of your health was 20 years ago, the next best time is now” applies here. Now is the best time to reframe relations and build a safe system so coevolution can begin. Every passing day means lost opportunity.

item.title: [SCMP] ArchipelaGoGo! The Inter-Island Festival is back to celebrate Hong Kong’s more laid-back lifestyles
item.description:
What do the curators and organisers of the 2026 Inter-Island Festival have in common? All three of them – Yip Kai-chun, Chan Chun-kit and Gloria Furness – traded life in urban Hong Kong for one of the city’s outlying islands for similar reasons: to be close to nature, experience a sense of community and enjoy a quiet lifestyle.

However, they got more than they bargained for: connection. Peng Chau specifically “has a lot of people from the creative industries who move out [of the city] and start over”, says Furness, the newer resident out of the three. It’s how the compact land-mass, measuring less than one sq km, became ground zero for the Inter-Island Festival, a month-long event celebrating the coastal societies on Hong Kong’s outlying islands through exhibitions, workshops, installations and talks.

Founded in 2019, the Inter-Island Festival takes inspiration from the inter-island ferry (“cross-water ferry”) connections between the outlying islands of Cheung Chau and Peng Chau and Lantau’s Chi Ma Wan and Mui Wo. Its first iteration, in 2021, came to fruition through the efforts of more than 50 collaborators, who put together 40-plus tours, workshops, exhibitions, performances and screenings, attracting more than 10,000 visitors to experience island culture.
item.content:encoded:
What do the curators and organisers of the 2026 Inter-Island Festival have in common? All three of them – Yip Kai-chun, Chan Chun-kit and Gloria Furness – traded life in urban Hong Kong for one of the city’s outlying islands for similar reasons: to be close to nature, experience a sense of community and enjoy a quiet lifestyle.

However, they got more than they bargained for: connection. Peng Chau specifically “has a lot of people from the creative industries who move out [of the city] and start over”, says Furness, the newer resident out of the three. It’s how the compact land-mass, measuring less than one sq km, became ground zero for the Inter-Island Festival, a month-long event celebrating the coastal societies on Hong Kong’s outlying islands through exhibitions, workshops, installations and talks.

Founded in 2019, the Inter-Island Festival takes inspiration from the inter-island ferry (“cross-water ferry”) connections between the outlying islands of Cheung Chau and Peng Chau and Lantau’s Chi Ma Wan and Mui Wo. Its first iteration, in 2021, came to fruition through the efforts of more than 50 collaborators, who put together 40-plus tours, workshops, exhibitions, performances and screenings, attracting more than 10,000 visitors to experience island culture.

After a three-year hiatus, the Inter-Island Festival finally makes its return for a third edition, taking place on Cheung Chau, Lantau and Peng Chau across five consecutive weekends, from November 1 to 29. Yip and Chan are among the founding members, while Furness joins the team for the first time after previous involvement as a volunteer coordinator.

When asked how the trio got together, they point to the very connection already present among the creative communities of the outlying islands. “I feel like everybody knows everybody,” says Yip, an independent artist and curator who has organised other events on the island. It was Chan, a co-founder of social enterprise and research lab Islanders and a long-time resident of Peng Chau, who introduced Yip to life on the island, leading the latter to eventually make the move from Sham Shui Po.

Furness became acquainted with Chan and Yip through various arts and cultural gatherings, and they invited her to join the Inter-Island Festival team this year to “deepen their collaboration” and leverage her experience in events planning and curation, gained from working with the biennial Hong Kong International Photo Festival exhibition and Koon Man Space, a photography-resource centre in Tsuen Wan.

“We all have similar backgrounds and networks,” says Furness. “We moved at various times [to Peng Chau] from the same circle, which is also part of our lore now.”

Yip conceived the idea for the Inter-Island Festival after moving to Peng Chau in 2017 and learning of the ferry network, little known to non-residents. “We mostly think of Victoria Harbour when riding the ferry [in Hong Kong], but the inter-island ferry is different. You see unfamiliar mountains and waters; that’s very special,” he says.

It sparked something in him, encouraging him to explore more of the city’s outlying islands.

Moreover, learning of the Lantau Tomorrow Vision project, a government land-reclamation initiative formally proposed in 2018, with the goal of building artificial islands off Lantau near Kau Yi Chau and Hei Ling Chau, further ignited his fervour, as the anticipated marine-habitat destruction and carbon emissions were expected to cause irreparable harm and “irreversibly change” the treasured environment of the islands. “Maybe a festival [about the islands] will create a bond between each of the ports that will be affected by the construction” and demonstrate their need to be preserved, Yip decided.

Dr Michael Rivera, a biological anthropologist at the University of Hong Kong who grew up in Mui Wo, shares that recent urban developments and events that “highlight traditional island culture” have also accelerated the desire for preservation. Largely, Hong Kong’s outlying islands are “marketed as tourist destinations”, he says. “But, at the same time, that [creates] an urgency, where people on those islands or who care about those islands feel that they need to share and conserve the narratives, livelihood and memories that are in these places.”

Conceived as a response, the Inter-Island Festival becomes a physical anchor to the stories of the islands’ inhabitants – such as the kaito captain, surnamed Wong, and his team, who bring Peng Chau residents across the water, and a fish-farm owner, Mo Lo, who commutes from Mui Wo to his farm in Chi Ma Wan – in living form. Between the islands, the connections are felt through daily life: a Peng Chau resident hikes in Chi Ma Wan, goes to the beach in Cheung Chau and dines in the cooked-food market in Mui Wo. Yip, Chan and Furness, together with local curators, exhibitors and artists, preach the gospel of their islands as a self-sustaining network of people and culture rather than being dependent on the city.

But it wasn’t smooth sailing upon launch, despite the evident passion driving the project. Yip admits that “the first edition was a pain”. Originally scheduled for 2020, the Inter-Island Festival was postponed three times due to Covid-19 social-distancing measures. In the weeks leading up to the event, there was concern that “attracting more visitors to the islands could overwhelm the community and inconvenience the residents” during the pandemic. After multiple delays, they decided to host it anyway, over three days on the last weekend of March 2021, focusing on the art, tradition, nature and environments of the four locations. Yip even organised an open house showcasing his life as an islander and his artworks.

A reprise followed in November 2023, with an expanded agenda taking place across four weekends. As part of the programme, visitors could listen to the sounds of the islands’ non-human neighbours – a running river, the chirping of birds and a buffalo bathing – and examine an installation designed as a home for bees. Peng Chau resident Jiming Lu, who serves as a local curator and coordinator for the upcoming edition, held two guided tours, one of Peng Chau cinema and the other of the island.

It took longer than expected for the curator-organisers to come back with the next instalment. “We really needed to take a break after the last edition, because it was quite overwhelming. It’s a lot of work,” says Chan.

Instead, they used the time to reflect on how to improve the event. One change that Yip, Chan and Furness are making this year is to “centralise” the festival on a different island each weekend, rather than host programmes simultaneously across all four, as it was done in the past, to help reduce the inter-island travel strain on visitors during their day trips.

Another challenge is timetabling. Entirely volunteer-run, the Inter-Island Festival is “really a bottom-up initiative, so we have to organise it according to everyone’s schedule”, says Furness. Plus, the islands are going through post-pandemic changes. “People are developing new creative spaces”, which take time to be incorporated into the event. In a way, the economic and structural development of the islands – such as the opening of new shops and businesses, adding another layer of self-reliance for the islanders who choose to live outside urban Hong Kong – and the festival have a “symbiotic relationship”. Even as a co-founder, Chan still encounters something new each time he visits the other islands to meet people who can represent the communities and business owners. “I’m still discovering more about these islands, including Peng Chau, through the festival.”

Next month, the Inter-Island Festival will include local co-curators and coordinators who reside in or are deeply familiar with Cheung Chau, Chi Ma Wan and Mui Wo, as the core team members all live on Peng Chau.

“We [want to] give more curatorial power to the local [collaborators] and allow our neighbours to be more involved within the umbrella of the festival,” says Yip. Compared with other public revitalisation projects, the Inter-Island Festival focuses on uplifting residents. “We want them to realise how precious island life is” and not take it for granted, he adds.

Centred on the theme “ArchipelaGoGo!”, this year’s edition will explore what living together as a cluster of islands looks like in 2026 through the lens of inter-island mythologies and the tidal beings that live on, around and under the ocean. Feature Projects, which pair researchers with creative practitioners over a six-month period to develop works around a specific theme, will include a literature scholar from Lamma Island working with a dancer, a woodworker partnering with a bamboo artist and a marine paleobiologist teaming up with two ceramic artists.

Moreover, the festival team selected 20 Micro Projects and 20 self-initiated Satellite Projects from the open call. Some of these include a hands-on workshop using oyster shells as a palette to create textured artwork in Peng Chau; a photography exhibition on the Cheung Chau Bun Festival; a community walk of Mui Wo to map out the neighbourhood through smell, touch and sound; and a tour across the mudflats in Pui O, which are home to snails, mangroves and fiddler crabs. Local businesses will also organise their own activities and discounts during the Inter-Island Festival.

Recruiting on-the-ground expertise is essential to fully represent the diversity of these islands. The four communities at the heart of the Inter-Island Festival each have their own distinct culture and rich tradition, though they share deep historical roots tied to maritime trade, fishing and, eventually, integration through the inter-island ferry network.

Peng Chau’s past can be traced back to the Neolithic period; a substantial fishing community called the island home, drawn by its sheltered bays and freshwater sources. In the 1960s, Peng Chau became a manufacturing powerhouse, with more than 30 types of factories, including the Great China Match Factory, once Southeast Asia’s largest producer of matches.

Mui Wo’s history has been recorded as far back as the Southern Song dynasty (1127-1279), when fleeing imperial court officials sought refuge from the invading Mongols in the area in 1277. Mui Wo’s silver mine, used to extract galena, operated until the end of the 19th century. In the 50s, the community blossomed as a farming hub, focusing on rice and vegetables.

Chi Ma Wan, a bay on southeastern Lantau, was a melting pot for Hong Kong’s early settlers, including the Hakka, Hoklo, Punti and Tanka. Farming and fishing dominated the peninsula, and its Shap Long Reservoir was once the main water source for Cheung Chau, Peng Chau and Hei Ling Chau. Later, camps housing Vietnamese refugees were built there.

Cheung Chau flourished as a fishing and trading port during the early Ming dynasty (1368-1644). Given its propensity for attracting mariners, it’s little wonder early-19th century pirate Cheung Po-tsai chose to hide his loot in one of the caves there – or so the legend goes. Nowadays, it’s the annual Cheung Chau Bun Festival, celebrating Pak Tai, the Taoist water deity and protector of fishermen and seafarers, that sees travellers scrambling to the island.

“We have always been a maritime society, reliant on coastal resources and seafood to survive. About a century ago, the population really expanded when more and more waves of boatpeople moved to these islands,” says Rivera. With the inception of the inter-island ferry route, closer ties between the islands were established, allowing them to have a connected, archipelagic relationship, rather than exist as isolated places.

But just as the islands have evolved into the coastal societies they are today, there has also been a shift in the way people see them, particularly during and after the Covid-19 pandemic.

In 2021, homes on Hong Kong’s outlying islands saw an almost 30 per cent increase in transactions, according to Midland Realty. While reports from the Census and Statistics Department do not detail urban-to-island migration trends, demographic data from last year reveals that the Islands district, which includes Cheung Chau, Mui Wo and Peng Chau, grew to about 196,000 residents. (Chi Ma Wan, while also part of the Islands district and once populated with villages and settlements, is largely uninhabited these days. Some descendants visit regularly but don’t “live” there year-round any more.)

“Part of what makes the [outlying] islands attractive is the cheaper rents,” says Rivera. “You can also expect a stronger network with your neighbours and a stronger sense of place.” He adds that, on the islands, “your entire space is a third space”, in that “your house is also part of the third space – there’s no barrier between them any more”.

In September 2025, the Hong Kong government shelved the Lantau Tomorrow Vision blueprint until further notice, but the mission of the Inter-Island Festival continues.

For Yip, Chan and Furness, living on Peng Chau is an exploration of how individuals can grow together, away from gentrification or “city mentality”, mirroring the connection, community, culture and creativity they hope to preserve with the Inter-Island Festival.

Furness believes that one can only fully understand the “islander” way of life through lived experiences. What might seem unusual to urbanites is second nature to them. By simply looking out the window, “I can tell the time based on which boat is coming in”, she says. For Yip, he can guess the typhoon signal by observing how the trees move in the wind.

Chan hopes that the Inter-Island Festival can grow to become like the Hungry Ghost Festival, where “people get together regardless of their backgrounds”. Different generations nurture their own traditions while still growing organically, much like the stories and lives on the islands. When you live the “island life” long enough, says Chan, “you start changing to its ways”.

The 2026 Inter-Island Festival runs until November 29. Tickets for individual events in the programme are sold separately here

item.title: [SCMP] Malaysia’s Najib to remain in prison as legal questions linger despite fine payment
item.description:
Malaysia’s disgraced former prime minister Najib Razak moved closer to house arrest after Umno on Friday paid a 50 million ringgit (US$12.3 million) fine required under the terms of his royal pardon.

The clemency granted by King Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar in September allows Najib to serve the remainder of his sentence under house arrest until August 2028, after more than four years behind bars for corruption linked to the 1MDB sovereign wealth fund.

Despite the payment, Najib has not been transferred home yet. The Attorney General’s Chambers, in a statement issued later on Friday, said Najib should remain in prison until legal questions over his royal pardon and its implications for his separate 1MDB sentence were resolved.
item.content:encoded:
Malaysia’s disgraced former prime minister Najib Razak moved closer to house arrest after Umno on Friday paid a 50 million ringgit (US$12.3 million) fine required under the terms of his royal pardon.

The clemency granted by King Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar in September allows Najib to serve the remainder of his sentence under house arrest until August 2028, after more than four years behind bars for corruption linked to the 1MDB sovereign wealth fund.

Despite the payment, Najib has not been transferred home yet. The Attorney General’s Chambers, in a statement issued later on Friday, said Najib should remain in prison until legal questions over his royal pardon and its implications for his separate 1MDB sentence were resolved.

His exit from prison may renew scrutiny of Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s governing alliances, analysts said, after Transport Minister Anthony Loke from the Democratic Action Party (DAP) pledged to resign once Najib begins his house arrest.

Loke reiterated on Friday that his resignation would take effect immediately upon Najib’s arrival home, but said Home Minister Saifuddin Nasution Ismail had told him the former prime minister had not yet been transferred to house arrest.

“I received confirmation from Saifuddin that Najib was taken to a dental clinic for a dental examination scheduled for today,” Loke told reporters, addressing reports that Najib had left Kajang Prison. “That means he has not yet been sent home.”

He added: “If he steps into his house tonight, it takes effect tonight. If tomorrow, then tomorrow.”

Umno secretary general Asyraf Wajdi Dusuki said the Najib Razak Solidarity Fund, launched on September 18, had raised sufficient money and the party had completed the payment process at the Kuala Lumpur High Court on Friday morning.

“The amount collected through the Najib Razak Solidarity Fund, which was launched on September 18 to help former prime minister Najib Razak, has reached its target and is sufficient,” he said in a statement. “Umno completed all payment procedures at the Kuala Lumpur High Court this morning.”

However, the statement did not disclose the total amount raised or identify major donors.

“Umno hereby officially closes the special Najib Razak Solidarity Fund account established to receive public donations and there is no further need for crowdfunding for this purpose,” Asyraf said.

Najib’s lawyer, Muhammad Farhan, told reporters that the court-issued house arrest order was delivered to Kajang Prison. Farhan and Najib’s special officer Ahmad Lutfi Azhar were also spotted entering the court’s criminal registry office in the afternoon.

Local media reported that police tightened security around Najib’s residence in Kuala Lumpur’s upmarket Langgak Duta neighbourhood. His lawyer previously identified the home as the designated location in the house arrest documents.

Anwar said he differed with Umno over its payment of Najib’s fine.

“My personal view is that I disagree because, although we have a sense of friendship with Najib, that should not give the public the impression that corruption involving billions of ringgit can be tolerated in this way,” he told reporters after Friday prayers.

“Umno’s decision is its right and we respect the legal process as well as the decision made by the king.”

Home truth

Amir Fareed Rahim, director of strategy at political consultancy KRA Group, told This Week in Asia that Najib’s house arrest would embolden Umno, energise the party’s members and strengthen its confidence in reclaiming conservative Malay votes.

“A revitalised Umno may believe it can regain lost ground on its own rather than rely on an electoral partnership with PAS,” he said.

Umno’s Barisan Nasional coalition and Pan-Malaysian Islamic Party have agreed to cooperate in the November 14 Melaka state election, including joint campaigning and a shared manifesto, despite Umno remaining part of Anwar’s federal government.

Amir cautioned that younger and undecided voters could instead be reminded of the corruption scandals surrounding Umno, adding that Najib’s opponents could punish Anwar’s Pakatan Harapan coalition if they blamed it for the concession.

That discontent could undermine turnout among PH supporters, although a rallying of the coalition base was also possible, he said.

Ahmad Mohsein Azman, a senior analyst at consultancy BowerGroupAsia, said the immediate political test would be whether Loke followed through on his resignation pledge and how Anwar managed the repercussions.

Loke, who leads DAP, resigned from cabinet in September. He said it would take effect once Najib returned home after Anwar asked him to continue serving temporarily.

Loke submitted his resignation letter in September, but Anwar asked him to continue serving until the fine was paid and Najib was allowed home, the transport minister told Friday’s press conference.

“My position has not changed,” he said. “I have informed the secretary general and ministry officials that as soon as Najib arrives home, my resignation takes effect immediately.”

He said he chaired a ministry meeting after Friday’s cabinet session to settle administrative matters and ensure a smooth handover, adding that his decision reflected the party’s position.

DAP respected the king’s constitutional authority over pardons but believed granting Najib house arrest risked sending “an inappropriate message to future generations”, Loke said.

According to Mohsein, questions will be raised about how viable a coalition PH will be in the next general election.

“The best way for Anwar to regain the trust of his supporters is to move on from this issue and revitalise his broader commitment to reform; something that should be manifested even before the next general election.”

Najib, 73, began serving his sentence in August 2022 after Malaysia’s highest court upheld his conviction over the misappropriation of 42 million ringgit from SRC International, a former subsidiary of 1MDB.

His original 12-year prison term was halved in 2024 and his fine reduced from 210 million ringgit to 50 million ringgit before King Sultan Ibrahim granted the conditional house arrest pardon on September 18.

Najib, who governed Malaysia from 2009–18, has consistently denied wrongdoing over the scandal, in which more than US$1 billion allegedly flowed into accounts linked to him.

According to US investigators, more than US$4.5 billion was siphoned from 1MDB between 2009 and 2015 through an international embezzlement and money laundering scheme, financing luxury properties, a superyacht and other extravagant purchases.

The house arrest arrangement covers his SRC sentence but Najib also faces a separate 15-year prison term following his conviction in the main 1MDB case last December, scheduled to begin after the SRC term ends on August 23, 2028. The High Court last month rejected his application to stay the execution of his sentence pending appeal.

item.title: [SCMP] China’s scrap dealers are scrambling for waste. So why is the recycling sector booming?
item.description:
Shanghai scrap collector Li Jie has a problem, one which would appear unusual to most: trash is getting too valuable.

“Ordinary recyclables like cardboard and plastic are now hard to come by,” he said. “Their prices have risen so much that there are so many collectors, including many companies.”

The wave of new players has made it harder to find those materials, and others such as copper and aluminium. But even at small volumes, he said, the business remains profitable and he has no desire to leave.
item.content:encoded:
Shanghai scrap collector Li Jie has a problem, one which would appear unusual to most: trash is getting too valuable.

“Ordinary recyclables like cardboard and plastic are now hard to come by,” he said. “Their prices have risen so much that there are so many collectors, including many companies.”

The wave of new players has made it harder to find those materials, and others such as copper and aluminium. But even at small volumes, he said, the business remains profitable and he has no desire to leave.

In the first nine months of this year, revenue in mainland China’s waste recycling sector was up 1.8 per cent year on year, according to the National Bureau of Statistics, but profits jumped 63 per cent.

Analysts attributed this trend in large part to the prolonged conflict in the Middle East – now in its ninth month – which was still disrupting shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, a waterway that used to carry around one-fifth of the world’s oil supplies. The joint US-Israel war on Iran had driven up energy prices and pushed primary material costs higher, they said, and scrap prices had risen with them.

China’s emissions-reduction commitments were also boosting the resource-recycling industry, and government trade-in programmes designed to encourage consumption were making the recycling system increasingly important, they added.

Between early January and this week, the scrap ternary battery price index rose over 8 per cent on an annual average basis, according to data from bulk commodity consultancy Sublime China Information, with scrap yellow cardboard prices up nearly 11 per cent and recycled polythene prices over 27 per cent higher.

Scrap copper and aluminium prices have also been relatively high in China this year, with scrap copper up over 7 per cent this week compared with the start of the year, and scrap aluminium now slightly higher than January after pulling back from peaks recorded in April and June.

Sublime China analyst Cong Peihao said the rise in copper and scrap copper prices was linked to the situation in the Gulf.

The closure of the Strait of Hormuz following the outbreak of war had tightened sulphur supplies and, combined with China’s ban on sulphuric acid exports, raised concerns about the rigid demand for sulphuric acid in parts of Africa and Chile for use in wet-process copper production, he said.

People generally just keep reusing household items as long as they still work, so there isn’t as much recyclable waste to collect as you might imagine

Li Jie, Shanghai scrap collector

“Market worries about potential disruptions to electrolytic copper supply created an expectation gap that drove both electrolytic copper and scrap copper prices higher,” Cong said.

In recent months, geopolitical fluctuations in the Middle East and the rise in copper prices had reduced the likelihood of interruptions to smelter production, he said, easing concerns about supply disruptions.

Sublime China analyst Sui Jie said the Middle East conflict had also been a key driver of rising recycled polythene plastic prices.

From late February, the conflict had disrupted global petrochemical supply chains, sending domestic virgin resin prices into a sustained uptrend, he said.

“The widening gap between virgin and recycled material prices significantly boosted downstream manufacturers’ willingness to buy recycled resin, providing direct support for the recycled plastics market,” Sui said.

At the same time, limited upstream scrap feedstock supplies had kept the market in a “tight supply, high prices” pattern, offering solid cost support for recycled polythene prices, he added.

The surge in waste prices has coincided with increased emphasis from Beijing on the importance of national resource security and green industrial transformation.

Its “dual-carbon” policy – which aims to see carbon emissions peak by 2030 and carbon neutrality achieved by 2060 – “has re-priced the value of scrap commodities”, said Xu Xiaoting, director of public affairs at Aifenlei, a Beijing-based company specialising in waste sorting and recycling.

“In addition, the trade-in policies of the past few years have, in the short term, created some extra supply-side volume for the scrap recycling industry,” she said.

China’s trade-in policy – backed by about 250 billion yuan (US$37.48 billion) in central government funding this year – subsidises consumers who replace old cars, home appliances and digital devices with new energy-efficient or smart products.

China’s top economic planning agency, the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC), called the increasing amount of recyclable waste a growing “urban mine” in an article posted on its website in August.

“Against the backdrop of intensifying geopolitical rivalry and rising resource protectionism, strengthening domestic resource security has become a practical imperative for safeguarding industrial and supply chain security,” it said, urging the tapping of discarded mobile phones, computers, vehicles that had reached the end of their lives and old household appliances for additional resources.

Last year, China recycled over 230 million waste electrical and electronic products, dismantled 10.46 million vehicles and reused 400,000 tonnes (441,000 short tons) of batteries, according to a report from the China National Resources Recycling Association in April charting growth in the sector.

Overall, it recycled 417 million tonnes (460 million short tons) of renewable resources last year, up 4.1 per cent year on year and marking a third consecutive year of growth, the association said.

However, Li, the Shanghai scrap collector, said growth would be higher if consumers were more willing to spend.

“Overall consumption has remained weak this year,” he said. “People generally just keep reusing household items as long as they still work, so there isn’t as much recyclable waste to collect as you might imagine.”

With people remaining concerned about the state of the economy and their future incomes, government figures show the trade-in programme has been losing momentum.

Home-appliance replacements in the first nine months were down about 20 per cent year on year, and overall sales of goods under the programme in the first half of the year fell to 1.1 trillion yuan, from 1.6 trillion yuan in the same period for 2025.

Individuals and businesses had swarmed into the recycling sector amid the recent price increases, Aifenlei’s Xu said, but most were small players.

“Most of the newcomers are operating without licences, occupying public spaces, piling things up wherever they like and polluting the environment,” she said. “There’s really no difference between them and the waste recycling stations of more than 20 years ago.”

As a result, Xu said she viewed the short-term boom as a bad thing because it created urban management challenges, disrupted market order and posed safety hazards.

But, she added, the influx of people joining the sector was good for the industry in the long run.

“The fact that capital and labour are both willing to come in means the industry has value and prospects,” Xu said. “Also, I think it can force the industry to become more standardised – with more people and intensifying competition, the government will have no choice but to regulate it.”

Zhang Miao, the founder of Shanghai Ecocycle, a think tank focused on the circular economy, said that a manufacturing giant like China had huge demand for raw materials, and recycling waste materials was an important supplement to its supply chain.

“In the meantime, because China’s manufacturing sector is extremely comprehensive, the recycling industry that supports it is equally comprehensive,” she said. “As a result, China is very strong in terms of both the completeness of the industrial chain and its technological level.”

But she called on the industry to improve sorting at the source to produce better quality recycled materials.

“If you don’t sort at the source, say by picking bottles out of mixed or kitchen waste, the recycled bottles will be full of contaminants,” she said.

The Institute of Public and Environmental Affairs, a Beijing-based NGO, said in a report released in January that while leading cities such as Suzhou and Shanghai had built “world-class sorting systems”, voluntary waste sorting was not yet common in most Chinese cities.

A city waste-sorting index compiled by the institute gave Suzhou, in eastern China’s Jiangsu province, a score of 96 out of 100 last year and neighbouring Shanghai a score of 84. But the average score of the 104 cities it assessed was just 18.04.

item.title: [SCMP] China narrows the path to elite official training scheme for citizens graduating overseas
item.description:
China is further narrowing access to a key government recruitment programme for overseas-educated graduates, limiting their pathways into the country’s civil service and party-state system.

More than a dozen provincial-level regions, including Beijing and Shanghai, opened applications for the 2027 xuandiaosheng recruitment rounds in September and October.

Xuandiaosheng, or the “selected graduates” system, is designed to select and train university graduates to become elite cadres and officials within the party and government. Recruits must spend several years working at the grass-roots level in townships and sub-districts before moving into leading government and party roles.
item.content:encoded:
China is further narrowing access to a key government recruitment programme for overseas-educated graduates, limiting their pathways into the country’s civil service and party-state system.

More than a dozen provincial-level regions, including Beijing and Shanghai, opened applications for the 2027 xuandiaosheng recruitment rounds in September and October.

Xuandiaosheng, or the “selected graduates” system, is designed to select and train university graduates to become elite cadres and officials within the party and government. Recruits must spend several years working at the grass-roots level in townships and sub-districts before moving into leading government and party roles.

None of the local government notices released so far has offered an application channel for overseas-educated graduates, continuing a trend that was evident last year.

An Australian-educated arts graduate who called herself James said she had considered the xuandiaosheng programme among her main career options as she looked for work this year.

“Job hunting is already so difficult. I really valued the opportunity to apply for the xuandiaosheng programme but now I have no chance at all,” she said.

Part of her decision to pursue a master’s degree overseas was driven by what she perceived as welcoming signs from the programme around 2023. At least 10 provincial-level regions, including Beijing and Guangdong, explicitly listed selected top-ranked overseas universities as eligible in their xuandiaosheng recruitment notices for the 2023 and 2024 graduating cohorts.

Similar frustrations have surfaced on RedNote, a Chinese social media platform also known as Xiaohongshu. “I can’t believe it. I went to graduate school just to qualify for the programme,” one comment read.

The programme dates back to 1965, when China’s leaders saw rural assignments for university graduates as a way to train “successors to the revolution”, according to state media outlet Xinhua’s Liaowang magazine.

President Xi Jinping has backed the programme since at least 2008, when he was still vice-president. He has called for its improvement and urged officials to select outstanding university graduates to train for grass-roots positions.

In 2018, the Communist Party’s Organisation Department issued new guidelines to strengthen and improve the xuandiaosheng programme, calling for more targeted recruitment, as well as stricter training and management of recruits.

The party describes the programme as a sourcing project for “building a high-calibre, professional cadre”, according to its official website.

Entry requirements are stricter than for regular civil service recruitment and vary by region, as the central government and local governments run their own xuandiaosheng recruitment programmes.

But they generally require applicants to be party members and outstanding student leaders, and favour local universities or well-known institutions with high global rankings.

For students whose undergraduate degrees did not meet eligibility requirements, earning a further degree from an overseas university on the approved list used to offer a route into the programme. That door seems to have closed.

“From 2024 and 2025 onwards, the programme shifted to recruiting exclusively from mainland Chinese universities, effectively shutting out overseas graduates,” said Jasper Jiang, an adviser who helps overseas students prepare for civil service and public institution recruitment and posts preparation advice on RedNote.

The shift became apparent in late 2024, when provincial-level governments began releasing their 2025 xuandiaosheng recruitment notices.

[Restrictions] potentially increase the relative attractiveness of domestic education for students interested in government careers

He Qiwei, University of Edinburgh

Of those that had listed overseas universities in their 2023 and 2024 recruitment notices, only Shanghai and Henan continued to accept overseas graduates.

By this year, none did, with some provinces, including Heilongjiang in the northeast, explicitly stating in their recruitment notices that graduates from overseas universities were excluded.
