Cleo, who gave only her first name, said she had once been eager to join the government, only to find the key route into government service had already closed to her when she graduated in 2025.

“Overseas-educated graduates are not eligible for the xuandiaosheng programme, leaving me with little choice but to sit the broader national and provincial civil service exams,” said the Hong Kong-educated postgraduate, who ultimately failed to enter the civil service.

Jiang said it had become more difficult for overseas-educated graduates to enter the civil service, partly due to “growing competition from returning graduates for fewer positions” now that the xuandiaosheng programme was off the table.

China has cut its national civil service recruitment for two consecutive years, with positions falling more than 10 per cent – from about 39,700 for the 2025 intake to 35,700 for 2027 – according to Xinhua.

Victor Shih, a professor at the University of California San Diego’s School of Global Policy and Strategy, said national security concerns could be among the reasons behind the restrictions.

“Senior leaders may suspect those who have lived overseas of being sympathetic to foreign perspectives, or worse, of engaging in espionage on behalf of foreign countries,” Shih said.

He said such concerns could affect “both recruitment into the government and promotions”, although there had been exceptions.

Chinese state security authorities identified overseas students among citizens considered vulnerable to recruitment by foreign espionage agencies, according to a post published by Xinhua on its social media account last year.

“The overseas student community has long been a target of foreign espionage and intelligence agencies,” the Ministry of State Security said in a post on its social media account in July 2025. The ministry also identified overseas-based personnel and people with access to classified information as recruitment targets for foreign agencies.

Ja Ian Chong, an associate professor of political science at the National University of Singapore, said competition among major powers could be one reason for the heightened emphasis on national security.

“Competition with the United States and its allies, as well as friction with places such as Europe and Australia, means it may be easier to suspect the sensibilities or even loyalties of people with significant external contact,” Chong said.

He Qiwei, an assistant professor at the University of Edinburgh’s economics school, said “eligibility for the xuandiaosheng programme is itself a valuable opportunity”, as it determined who could compete for a place in the government’s elite talent pipeline.

“The recent restrictions in certain provinces may have implications beyond the immediate recruitment process,” He said.

“They change which groups of graduates have access to this career pathway and could potentially increase the relative attractiveness of domestic education for students interested in government careers.”

While studying abroad was once seen as a route to better jobs and higher pay, the value of an overseas degree appears to have declined in China’s increasingly competitive job market in recent years.

A 2006-07 survey found that returnees from Japan, Canada and Hong Kong earned about twice as much as their locally educated counterparts, according to David Zweig in a 2018 article for the University of Hong Kong’s Centre for Higher Education Research.

By 2015, the premium had narrowed. Returnees with postgraduate degrees earned about 20 per cent more than their domestic counterparts, while overseas bachelor’s degrees offered no significant earnings advantage, according to a 2021 study by Du Zaichao, Sun Yuting, Zhao Guochang and Zweig and published in The China Quarterly.

A 2025 résumé experiment published in China Economic Quarterly, conducted by He Haoran, An Lulu and Lin Jiayue, also found that applicants educated overseas were 16.2 per cent less likely to receive interview feedback than comparable applicants educated in China.

item.title: [SCMP] EU’s Southeast Asia push hits funding crunch as China widens lead
item.description:
An EU funding crunch is threatening to stifle the bloc’s ambitions to expand its influence in Southeast Asia, as Brussels grapples with a budget deadlock that could slow infrastructure investments across the fast-growing region.

The funding squeeze could hinder the green transition and regional connectivity goals of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, even as Brussels seeks greater strategic autonomy amid competition with Beijing’s economic clout.

Analysts expect the European Union to prioritise domestic spending pressures over overseas commitments, arguing Europe can still leverage higher-quality, sustainable investments rather than attempting to match China’s financial muscle.
item.content:encoded:
An EU funding crunch is threatening to stifle the bloc’s ambitions to expand its influence in Southeast Asia, as Brussels grapples with a budget deadlock that could slow infrastructure investments across the fast-growing region.

The funding squeeze could hinder the green transition and regional connectivity goals of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, even as Brussels seeks greater strategic autonomy amid competition with Beijing’s economic clout.

Analysts expect the European Union to prioritise domestic spending pressures over overseas commitments, arguing Europe can still leverage higher-quality, sustainable investments rather than attempting to match China’s financial muscle.

Launched in 2022, the EU-Asean Global Gateway strategy aims to bolster regional infrastructure backed by 10 billion euros (US$11.2 billion) in public funding through 2027 via its primary external financing tool, the Global Europe instrument.

“With over 680 million people, a huge middle class and a very dynamic economy in terms of manufacturing, services and tech, Asean is a massive market for the EU,” said Rahul Mishra, an associate professor at India’s Jawaharlal Nehru University. “For the EU, it’s a partner with which it shares a range of interests, aspirations and concerns.”

However, the programme’s future is clouded by an impasse over the EU’s 2028-2034 Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF). In July last year, the European Commission proposed an overall budget of nearly 2 trillion euros (US$2.25 trillion) – including 200 billion euros for Global Europe, up from 79.5 billion euros currently.

The plan met swift resistance from the “frugal” bloc – Germany, Austria, Denmark, the Netherlands, Finland and Sweden – which demanded cuts of several hundred billion euros before granting the required unanimous approval.

“The multiannual financial framework was growing in size every year, and this year it cracked through the psychological barrier of 2 trillion euros for the first time in the original proposal,” said Roland Vogt, an associate professor of global and area studies at the University of Hong Kong. “That is something very unpalatable to a lot of the member states who are net contributors.”

Brussels argues the expanded budget is needed to juggle defence, competitiveness, migration and climate priorities alongside traditional agricultural and regional cohesion subsidies.

Cuts to Global Europe loom

To break the stalemate, the current Irish presidency of the Council of the EU proposed a compromise trimming Global Europe funding to 148.9 billion euros – a roughly 25 per cent cut from the original proposal.

The compromise drew fierce pushback from the European Parliament, which must also approve the budget.

“Global Europe is the EU’s foreign and development policy superpower. Amid worsening global crises, Europe must step up its engagement with the world,” said Robert Biedron, co-rapporteur for the parliament’s development committee. “If we fail now, we will have to deal with the much more expensive consequences later.”

Analysts doubt lawmakers can hold the line.

“I don’t think the European Parliament can win, because the pressure from the countries which pay for the EU budget is so strong,” said Iain Begg, a professorial research fellow at London School of Economics’ European Institute. “The likelihood of Global Europe being successfully increased again by the European Parliament, I would regard as a very low probability.”

This Week in Asia has reached out to the European Commission for comment.

The budget impasse comes as Brussels balances strained ties with Washington and Beijing against mounting domestic liabilities. Debt across five member states exceeds 100 per cent of their gross domestic product, with the International Monetary Fund warning that European public debt could double over the next 15 years without budgetary discipline.

“What is quite clear is that domestic issues prevail for now. Cohesion and agricultural funds are politically very difficult to touch as well,” said Konrad Szatters, a Brussels-based China analyst at the Association for International Affairs. “So, if something needs to be cut from the MFF, it might be the external action, because it’s just not the highest priority for national governments amid the ongoing financial squeeze.”

Wider funding gap for Asean

For Asean, this means less direct funding for Southeast Asia’s green transition and connectivity projects – the core of Brussels’ regional agenda.

“Asean is already grappling with a massive infrastructure financing gap, and reduced concessional funding would only make it harder to raise the capital that’s needed,” Mishra said. “There’s a real risk of an uneven green transition, with more financially robust countries able to carry on and less well-off ones potentially left behind.”

He warned that cross-border integration could stall, weakening momentum towards a cohesive regional economy. According to the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development, Southeast Asia needs US$210 billion annually through 2030 to close its infrastructure and sustainability investment gap.

“Green transition and sustainable connectivity continue to be global priorities for the EU, which is good news for Asean,” said Andrew Sherriff, associate director of institutional relations and partnerships at European “think-and-do” tank ECDPM. “However, Europe wants to align future spending in these areas not just with Asean priorities, but also more explicitly with its own interests and the European private sector through mutually beneficial partnerships.”

Failure to finalise the 2028–2034 MFF before next year could also stall new initiatives, despite European Council President Antonio Costa urging a deal before year’s end.

“Current initiatives agreed to be funded prior to 2027 would not be impacted,” Sherriff said, noting emergency rules allow rolling over existing budgets. “However, without clarity on the budget for 2028–2034, launching new initiatives – including those related to the Global Europe instrument and the associated EU-Asean Global Gateway initiative – would be difficult unless the latter are funded directly by EU member states.”

This Week in Asia has contacted the Asean Secretariat for comment.

Head-to-head with China

Spending limits also blunt Europe’s ability to counter Beijing, which the Lowy Institute ranks as Southeast Asia’s most influential partner, financing 31 per cent of regional infrastructure projects in 2024.

“The bureaucracy is too big, and the capital available is too little. That’s one of the reasons why Europe has been losing out to China, because China can come in and basically say: ‘We’re bringing projects, including the financing,’” Vogt said.

Szatters said the EU must lean into project quality rather than trying to match Beijing’s spending power.

“The EU is not a state. Its budget heavily relies on member states’ contributions,” Szatters said. “Any substantial increase in funding for such initiatives requires agreement among the 27 member states, and ultimately somebody has to pay for it.”

“What we can do is outperform China in the sustainability and quality of investments for a long-term gain.”

item.title: [SCMP] EU-China truce under strain as both sides brace for potential trade war
item.description:
Weeks after the European Union and China struck a deal aimed at averting a looming trade war, the two sides remain at loggerheads over what is wrong with their relationship, how to fix it and who is to blame.

At an event in Brussels this week, threats were exchanged and differences rose to the surface. With the ink barely dry on their fragile trade peace, it was clear that both were still preparing for a trade war.

“If the EU insists on adopting restrictive and discriminatory measures against China, China will have to take countermeasures to firmly safeguard its interests,” Beijing’s ambassador to the EU, Cai Run, warned on Thursday.
item.content:encoded:
Weeks after the European Union and China struck a deal aimed at averting a looming trade war, the two sides remain at loggerheads over what is wrong with their relationship, how to fix it and who is to blame.

At an event in Brussels this week, threats were exchanged and differences rose to the surface. With the ink barely dry on their fragile trade peace, it was clear that both were still preparing for a trade war.

“If the EU insists on adopting restrictive and discriminatory measures against China, China will have to take countermeasures to firmly safeguard its interests,” Beijing’s ambassador to the EU, Cai Run, warned on Thursday.

Speaking at the same event – which was sponsored by China’s mission to the EU – Stefano Grassi, a senior official who helps coordinate the European Commission’s China policy, returned criticism of his own.

“Where we are now with China … [is] a unidirectional, unsustainable structural imbalance, and this can be corrected in a managed diplomatic way or, unfortunately, [it] will lead to a big turmoil and a lot of protectionism, a lot of closure of markets that will hurt both buyers and sellers,” Grassi said.

A day earlier, EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic outlined plans to unveil a package of tools on December 9 that would be, in part, aimed at helping businesses “in case of a possible tit-for-tat retaliatory situation”.

He said the EU sought to ensure “we could react much, much faster, even by limiting exports into the EU, especially from countries which are treating us unfairly”.

A widely circulated WeChat post from prominent Chinese trade expert Cui Fan this week said Beijing could launch anti-discrimination and industrial and supply-chain security investigations, export controls and reciprocal import restrictions if the EU made good on promises to develop a “kill switch” to shut off the market to Chinese firms.

“China is closely monitoring and studying the EU’s policy developments and has prepared a range of targeted countermeasures,” Cui wrote.

Work will continue in the hope of adding to the deal in which China will accept an EU quota of 350,000 per year on its hybrid car exports without retaliating.

The EU’s top trade enforcement official, Denis Redonnet, led a group of medical device manufacturers on a “matchmaking” trip to Shanghai on Thursday. The EU has restricted China’s market access in the sector due to a lack of reciprocation.

“China and the EU have stressed that the second meeting was a new starting point rather than an endpoint. The negotiations and consultations ahead remain demanding,” envoy Cai said on Thursday.

This jarred, however, with what a delegation of European Parliament trade lawmakers took away from a trip to China last week.

“We see this as a first step to rebalance the trade imbalances, and here I think China pushed back a bit … that is an important message for us. They, as I read them, didn’t see this as a first step of many,” said centre-right member Jorgen Warborn, who was among those to meet Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao for two hours.

Socialist member Kathleen van Brempt, who was also on the trip, said Wang had indicated that “the deal on the hybrid cars is not to be seen as a model to proceed”.

“They want to start negotiations on a full-fledged investment or free trade agreement, but that is a trap,” she told the parliament’s trade committee on Wednesday.

“We’re open to that, but they are negotiations on a huge deal that will take years … our industries are under siege now.”

While some MEPs praised the positivity of talks, van Brempt suggested there were some clashes.

“It was crystal clear they do not accept our narrative. They don’t have to, but they do not accept our figures on overcapacity, on overproduction. They mocked a little bit when we used the figures,” the Belgian politician said, adding that Beijing had a long list of EU laws about which they complained.

Addressing that committee later in the day, Sefcovic hit out at China’s trade surplus over the EU, saying “we’ve been making it crystal clear that our deficit with China is not sustainable”.

“Because of its growth and pace and dynamics, it went well beyond trade optics, and therefore it becomes political.”

At Thursday’s China-backed event, commission official Grassi said the bloc’s fears over China’s role in global imbalances could be attributed to latent trauma from the euro-zone crisis, which he said was caused by Europe’s internal imbalances.

Grassi said the lesson learned was that “when you are in a situation of macroeconomic imbalances in a highly integrated economy … the risks are for all the participants in the system”. He added that imbalances “lead to traumatic adjustment”.

Several Chinese speakers, however, rejected the diagnosis and downplayed the deficit talk, suggesting that despite the surprise trade deal, they were far from a mutual diagnosis of their relationship problems.

“I think energy prices, high tariffs from Washington to Brussels, or every capital city in Europe, that’s a major reason. So the trade deficit with China is just consequences. It’s not a reason. It’s not the cause,” Cui Hongjian, director of European Union studies at Beijing Foreign Studies University, told the event.

During a Q&A session, a Chinese diplomat said that for hundreds of years China had had a trade surplus over Europe “but this didn’t prevent Europe from becoming a global leader in terms of economic development, social progress, technical innovation and classical music”.

The rhetorical dissonance stretched beyond trade and into technology.

During a panel discussion on technology, several Chinese speakers said the sides should establish a dialogue on AI issues, but Gunnar Wiegand, a former top EU diplomat on Asia, said such a format existed in the EU-China digital dialogue, which Beijing cancelled “just two weeks before it was supposed to happen in June”.

Sun Chenghao, head of the US-Europe programme at the Centre for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University, told the event that when proposing China-EU cooperation on AI, a European friend had said it was impossible because of concern “China would transfer data to Russia”. He said China had the same concerns “that Europeans will transfer our data to the US”.

Further technological tensions were telegraphed in Berlin this week, where German newspaper Handelsblatt said the government was preparing to classify 5G base stations as “security relevant”, a move that could lead to a de facto exclusion of Chinese companies Huawei Technologies and ZTE.

Despite the mutual suspicion, officials on both sides insist progress is possible without resolving every disagreement.

Joanna Szychowska, who manages EU trade policy on Asia, said October’s deal had transpired because the two sides had set aside competing interpretations of the relationship.

“We decided to focus on what really is a problem and how we want to tackle it,” Szychowska said.

item.title: [SCMP] Philippines’ project budget allocations spur accusations of pork barrel politics
item.description:
A road project with coordinates pointing to Nigeria. A government building apparently located in the Sahara Desert. Another road mapped to a sea near Brunei.

These are among the unlikely locations listed for infrastructure projects in the Philippines’ proposed 2027 national budget, according to independent watchdogs that have discovered the discrepancies, highlighting problems with government transparency and accountability.

Their scrutiny of Manila’s proposed 7.2 trillion pesos (US$114 billion) spending plan has raised questions about whether certain huge allocations could be used to buy political support ahead of elections.

A road project with coordinates pointing to Nigeria. A government building apparently located in the Sahara Desert. Another road mapped to a sea near Brunei.

These are among the unlikely locations listed for infrastructure projects in the Philippines’ proposed 2027 national budget, according to independent watchdogs that have discovered the discrepancies, highlighting problems with government transparency and accountability.

Their scrutiny of Manila’s proposed 7.2 trillion pesos (US$114 billion) spending plan has raised questions about whether certain huge allocations could be used to buy political support ahead of elections.

The controversy has put pressure on President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr’s administration to demonstrate its commitment to transparency.

On Tuesday, Undersecretary Claire Castro, chief of the Presidential Communications Office, called on the budget watchdogs to report to her office any “red flags” they had found in the proposed national budget.

“You are needed so that the president will hear [your concerns],” she said in a November 3 press briefing.

But Adolfo Jose “AJ” Montesa, a co-convenor of the People’s Budget Coalition, said in an interview on Wednesday that no one from the presidential palace had formally contacted his group about the government’s offer, with its members only finding out about it in the news.

This Week in Asia has reached out to Castro about her offer and has not received a reply by publication time.

Among the projects that the People’s Budget Coalition and its partner organisations, BetterGovPh, are questioning is a planned 30 million peso farm-to-market road in the southern Philippine province of Quezon. Its listed coordinates placed it in the Celebes Sea near Indonesia, said public policy expert Kenneth Abante.

The watchdogs had also previously flagged a 7-million-peso building project intended for the southern province of Misamis Oriental in the national budget. When they plotted its listed coordinates, they found the planned project appeared to be in the Sahara Desert.

The House of Representatives later corrected the error when it modified the president’s budget and passed it last month.

However, the critics noted that the House’s version retained another road project proposed by the president, this time on the central Philippine island of Negros, with GPS coordinates placing it in Nigeria.

While incorrect coordinates do not necessarily mean the projects themselves are fictitious, the watchdogs argue that such discrepancies highlight weaknesses in the scrutiny of proposed public spending.

Last month, the People’s Budget Coalition and BetterGovPh introduced what they described as the first-ever public tracker of lawmakers’ budget insertions, allowing users to examine changes made to the proposed national budget.

The groups, comprising mostly young volunteer professionals from the private sector, have grown increasingly alarmed by what they see as a lack of accountability and transparency in the budget preparation process.

Montesa accused House appropriations committee chair Mikaela Suansing of failing to deliver on promises of greater transparency, saying civil society groups had been given just three minutes each to present their concerns at a recent consultation that Suansing did not attend.

He also questioned the transparency of an October 1 budget subcommittee hearing, saying journalists were excluded from a four-hour closed-door session before the proceedings were live-streamed.

“I noticed it felt very rehearsed, very scripted,” he said, adding that his “personal reading was that the real meeting happened during the executive session”, which he described as “horse-trading”.

According to the watchdogs’ calculations, a House-approved bill for general appropriations contained an additional 190 billion pesos worth of infrastructure spending that they characterised as “pork” – discretionary allocations that critics say could be used by politicians to cultivate support among voters.

This Week in Asia has reached out to Suansing’s office for comment and has yet to receive a reply.

Several sources said Suansing was on “maternity leave”. She also appeared to have deactivated her official Facebook account and did not list an email address on the House website.

Montesa said the lack of public explanation for the amendments was the watchdogs’ main concern.

“We would have liked to see the rationale for making those decisions. For example, right now, we are flagging the 190 billion pesos worth of insertions in infrastructure. So we would have liked to see how they could have come to those decisions, including the infrastructure projects, which don’t have project documents.”

Zy-Za Nadine Suzara, an independent public budget analyst who previously worked at the Department of Budget and Management, said in a separate interview that the president had also submitted what she considered pork barrel allocations to Congress.

Among them were proposed “allocations to local government units” of 109.1 billion pesos, “local government support fund” at 58.8 billion pesos and “financial assistance to local government units” totalling 37.5 billion pesos.

At a budget hearing on October 22, the president’s sister, Senator Imee Marcos, questioned the additional “no rhyme or reason” allocations, calling them “a lot of aid”. She added: “This is too much politicking.”

The controversy has also prompted an outcry from 36 prominent business groups in the country, including the Makati Business Club, the Federation of Filipino-Chinese Chambers of Commerce & Industry and the Financial Executives Institute of the Philippines.

In a joint statement issued on October 29, they urged Congress to “remove every insertion that lacks technical basis”.

The groups said they found it “deeply troubling” that the additional allocations were reportedly funded in part by cutting 130 billion pesos from foreign-assisted projects, 9.5 billion pesos from calamity funds, 1.76 billion pesos from the EDSA Busway and 4.9 billion pesos from health programmes.

“Cutting them delays the high-impact projects that lower logistics costs and attract investments. Raiding calamity funds in a country that is exposed to disasters is indefensible,” they said.

The groups urged lawmakers to restore the funds that had been removed unless Congress could justify each reduction. They reminded Congress that “a budget free of politically driven insertions” would boost investor confidence and ensure that “every peso builds the infrastructure, schools and health services the nation truly needs”.

Montesa expressed concern about poor budgetary decisions affecting the poor, saying that if they had to show up at the doors of senators and congressmen to get the help they needed, such as for hospitalisation, then “it’s bad. It’s pork.”

item.title: [SCMP] US and Brazil deliver double blow to the populist right. Will Europe feel the impact?
item.description:
In the space of roughly 10 days, the two largest democracies in the Americas delivered setbacks to the populist right.

In Brazil, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva staged a narrow but remarkable comeback, defeating Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, in a run-off election after trailing in the first round.

This week, American voters handed control of both chambers of the US Congress to Democrats in a sharp rebuke of candidates riding on US President Donald Trump’s “Make America Great Again” movement.
item.content:encoded:
In the space of roughly 10 days, the two largest democracies in the Americas delivered setbacks to the populist right.

In Brazil, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva staged a narrow but remarkable comeback, defeating Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, in a run-off election after trailing in the first round.

This week, American voters handed control of both chambers of the US Congress to Democrats in a sharp rebuke of candidates riding on US President Donald Trump’s “Make America Great Again” movement.

Together the results challenge the seemingly unstoppable global rightward shift that has defined much of the past decade. They may also reflect a broader anti-incumbency mood in which voters are punishing leaders for failing to deliver on prices, jobs and basic services.

The US “blue wave” continued a string of losses for the right, following the rejection of Bolsonaro in Brazil and the defeats of former Serbian president Aleksandar Vucic and former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orban, said John Feffer, director of Foreign Policy in Focus at the Institute for Policy Studies, a think tank in Washington.

Feffer added that voters in today’s “quicksilver environment of social media” responded positively to candidates who “promise sweeping change”.

“And thus, the political pendulum swings from left to right and back again.”

However, he argued that the far-right movement was not “just another conventional option on the political menu”.

The movement “offers something radically different because it threatens to undermine the very democratic norms by which it has achieved power”, Feffer said.

Europe: the next testing ground

All eyes now turn to Spain, where incumbent Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has framed the outcome of the US midterm elections as a sign that the global right-wing wave is running out of steam.

“Yesterday, American society voted against policies that only impoverish. Against hatred. Against sexism. Against climate change denial and against the privileges of the elites,” he said on social media on Tuesday.

Sanchez, who is fighting for his own political survival in a snap general election scheduled for late November, added: “It happened in Brazil. It just happened in the US. And it will happen soon in Spain.”

But while populist candidates have hit stumbling blocks in the Americas, the right-wing wave in Europe remains remarkably resilient and continues to expand its institutional footprint, with France and Germany sitting right at the centre of the storm.

In France, Marine Le Pen’s National Rally has moved from the political fringes to become a major force, wielding growing influence over minority governments despite repeated efforts to keep the party out of power.

In Germany, the Alternative for Germany (AfD) has made historic electoral gains, particularly in the east, challenging the post-war political consensus.

Trump: a liability for the right

While Trump has cheered on Europe’s right-wing figures, hosting Orban at Mar-a-Lago and fostering ties between American conservative groups and European populists, the European movements do not rely on Washington to survive.

In fact, far-right politicians in Europe have been distancing themselves from Trump following the Republican rout and his growing unpopularity across the continent, despite previously drawing parallels to his Maga movement.

“Trump had promised his voters not to pursue an interventionist foreign policy … This broken promise has now come back to haunt the Republicans,” AfD co-leader Alice Weidel told German media, referring to the Iran war.

According to Francesco Strazzari, professor of international relations at the Scuola Superiore Sant’Anna in Pisa, Italy, “the story of the US midterms goes beyond the Democratic victory”.

“For Europe’s far-right nationalists, alignment with Trump no longer means riding a growing political wave. They have to recalculate,” he wrote on social media on Tuesday.

Trump has tried to position himself as a leader of the global right-wing movement. He celebrated Javier Milei’s 2023 victory in Argentina, maintained close ties with the Bolsonaros in Brazil and backed Nayib Bukele in El Salvador.

But ties have been souring for some time. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, once seen as a close ideological ally, has openly criticised Trump over trade, Ukraine and his foreign policy.

In April last year, Mark Carney of Canada’s Liberal Party defeated Pierre Poilievre, the Conservative Party leader backed by Trump, to become prime minister, dealing another setback to the American president’s efforts to build political influence beyond the US.

This year, Trump aggressively endorsed Bolsonaro in Brazil, even calling the result “rigged” and a “terrible look”, without evidence.

Oliver Stuenkel, a senior fellow affiliated with the Democracy, Conflict and Governance Programme at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, said the rightward shift in Latin America “is more fragile than it seems and may not last as long as expected”.

He pointed to Bolsonaro’s defeat in Brazil, along with signs of political instability and weak approval ratings for right-wing leaders elsewhere in the region, as evidence of that fragility.

Bolivia’s centre-right president, Rodrigo Paz, who took office in November last year after nearly 20 years of socialist rule, has faced repeated protests over subsidy cuts and living costs.

Right-wing Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast rose to power in March. His approval rating has plunged from nearly 60 per cent at the start of his term to 27 per cent. The drop has been driven by a weak economy and, more recently, controversy over the early release of convicted sex offenders.

The Brexit cautionary tale

The roots of the modern right-wing populist wave can be traced back to 2016. As Britain voted to leave the European Union, Trump was preparing to rewrite American conservatism. Both events marked a turning point in a political shift driven by ultranationalism, anti-globalisation and a rejection of the post-war liberal order.

But the promises of that moment have faced their own tests. Britain continues to grapple with the economic consequences of Brexit. The US, too, has faced economic and political challenges under Trump. In both countries, the promise of national renewal has collided with the realities of governing.

John Van Reenen, Ronald Coase School professor at the London School of Economics, described it as a “populist doom loop” in an October paper published by the Centre for Economic Policy Research.

He wrote that sluggish gains in living standards fuelled support for populist parties offering simple solutions, such as ending immigration.

“Populists demand bad economic policies and usually get some of these indirectly through pressurising centrist parties. This leads to even weaker growth, more voter unrest and further undermines the ‘establishment’, giving more support to the populists.”

What comes next

Feffer argued that the central challenge for the left and centre was to build “a new, robust internationalism” that delivered tangible benefits to ordinary people while protecting the planet for future generations.

Until then, far-right movements would continue to attract support through their anti-globalisation agenda, even if they lost individual elections, he said.

“They don’t want to be subject to the pendulum swings of democratic politics. They want to rip out the pendulum so that they can remain in power indefinitely,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] How Singapore confronts AI fears of ‘broken’ career ladder, no pause button
item.description:
Singapore is seeking to flip the script by turning its land and manpower constraints into reasons to embrace AI instead of fearing it, even as the technology carries the spectre of job losses and cyberthreats in the wrong hands, a senior official has said.

Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo argued that pragmatism would give her resource-scarce country an edge without becoming overly reliant on any single power or AI provider.

At the Family Business Summit in Hong Kong on Wednesday, co-organised by the South China Morning Post and Blue Pool Capital, Teo also warned that AI was advancing faster than societies could adapt, potentially leaving younger workers facing a “broken rung” on the career ladder, while businesses shifted spending on wages to AI technology.
item.content:encoded:
Singapore is seeking to flip the script by turning its land and manpower constraints into reasons to embrace AI instead of fearing it, even as the technology carries the spectre of job losses and cyberthreats in the wrong hands, a senior official has said.

Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo argued that pragmatism would give her resource-scarce country an edge without becoming overly reliant on any single power or AI provider.

At the Family Business Summit in Hong Kong on Wednesday, co-organised by the South China Morning Post and Blue Pool Capital, Teo also warned that AI was advancing faster than societies could adapt, potentially leaving younger workers facing a “broken rung” on the career ladder, while businesses shifted spending on wages to AI technology.

“AI hasn’t given us much time to pause and reflect more deeply,” Teo said. “I think our biggest challenge today is that the timeline is very compressed, whereas human society previously had much more time to adapt to the impact of technological change.”

Teo was candid about the looming concerns facing her country, often touted as the regional leader in artificial intelligence.

“If organisations transition into an environment where more of their expenditure goes towards tokens and less towards wages, we have to ask what happens to the revenue model of the state,” she said at a fireside chat attended by some 100 business executives, investors, academics and celebrities.

“What will sustain the way governments deliver public services? So that’s another layer to think about. It’s a very heavy topic for dinner, I’m afraid.”

Singapore’s scarce resources also seem to signal an inevitable limit to its growth, as neighbouring Malaysia excavates land to build data centres. Last month, the state’s monetary authority projected a slowdown in the pace of AI-driven economic growth in its review.

But Teo remains upbeat. “Rather than ask, ‘Is there a limit to how much we can do with AI, given the land and manpower constraints?’, I think we should flip the question around: ‘Wouldn’t we be even more constrained if we didn’t learn to master this technology?

“That was our perspective. The question then becomes: how do we make the most of the resources available to us? That was the approach we took.”

Earlier this year, Teo announced that the state would invest over S$1 billion (US$780 million) over five years into research to strengthen AI capabilities and global competitiveness, including talent development.

On Wednesday, she outlined five imperatives that guide Singapore’s AI policy: infrastructure, workforce and enterprise capabilities, governance, regulations, and international cooperation.

AI sovereignty was a topic among global policymakers, and would be achieved by very few countries if the criteria were building and owning an entire AI stack, Teo said.

“Many countries also have different fiscal priorities. In Singapore’s case, we have an ageing population. From that perspective, I think defining AI sovereignty in terms of ownership is unrealistic,” she said.

“If you define AI sovereignty as being able to use the technology on your own terms, by developing your own capabilities and plugging in to different innovation ecosystems, you stand a better chance and that’s the way we look at it.”

But the city state, often hailed as a neutral ground, is increasingly caught between an intensifying superpower AI rivalry. Singapore was among seven signatories when Pax Silica – a US-led initiative that aims to help partners strengthen supply chains for minerals essential to AI – launched last December.

It has since received and is assessing an invitation to join the Shanghai-based World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation (Waico), which was formed in July.

Receiving such invitations was “almost like managing an investment portfolio”, said Teo, who noted that Singapore’s participation in such blocs took place at different phases of its development and served different objectives.

“When we receive an invitation to join an initiative such as Waico, we look at it seriously and consider the obligations and commitments involved,” she said. “Waico is a serious organisation with an established structure, so we’re assessing how it fits into our priorities.”

Teo said Singapore engaged in bilateral relations with China through a digital policy dialogue, with both states meeting regularly to discuss issues such as AI safety, governance and adoption.

The minister was also asked if Singapore would be granted access to Mythos – Anthropic’s recent and advanced model which can autonomously identify software vulnerabilities – if the state requested it.

US giant Anthropic, creator of the AI model Claude, picked Singapore for its first office in Southeast Asia which opened last month. A stone’s throw away is Microsoft’s research lab, which was launched last year to study deployment and chase breakthroughs in frontier AI.

In an initiative called Project Glasswing, Anthropic gave a trusted group of governments and companies such as Nvidia and Cisco access so they could start scanning their cybersecurity systems for vulnerabilities and patching them.

“It is helpful to be on Glasswing but do you need to be on it to improve your cybersecurity? The answer is not necessarily,” said Teo, noting that many of Mythos’ capabilities were already available in open models.

The minister said while “it is good to have access” to the most sophisticated technology, “it would be a mistake to think that that’s the only way you can strengthen your own capabilities and cyber defences”.

No Chinese firms were invited to use the model given Anthropic’s labelling of China as an “adversarial nation”, and the company has excluded Hong Kong from its list of supported locations, alongside mainland China and Macau.

Singapore is in constant conversation with China, which has made many open-weight models – an approach Teo says the city state strongly supports.

“We believe it strengthens the environment for AI adoption, but also because we believe it is the only path to ensure that most of humanity can benefit from this technology,” she said.

With AI now dominating most of her portfolio’s job scope, Teo similarly uses the technology in her day-to-day life.

She revealed that she vibe-coded her personal AI agent, which scans the globe for news articles and delivers a summary – curated based on her interest – to her via WhatsApp every morning.

“It reads about 16,000 articles every single day – that’s a lot more than I can manage.”

item.title: [SCMP] China’s new PLA theatre chiefs identified as anti-corruption drive clears ranks
item.description:
Beijing has hinted at the new leadership line-up in its military theatre commands, with fresh faces emerging during last week’s party conclave in the seating area reserved for key commanders, filling vacancies left by China’s anti-corruption drive.

The fifth plenum of the Communist Party’s 20th Central Committee, which concluded last Thursday, focused on party discipline and political loyalty, confirming the expulsion of 33 full and alternate Central Committee members, including 16 senior military officers.

The expulsions were the latest consequences of an unprecedented anti-corruption storm that has swept through the People’s Liberation Army (PLA), triggering far-reaching personnel changes across its senior ranks.
item.content:encoded:
Beijing has hinted at the new leadership line-up in its military theatre commands, with fresh faces emerging during last week’s party conclave in the seating area reserved for key commanders, filling vacancies left by China’s anti-corruption drive.

The fifth plenum of the Communist Party’s 20th Central Committee, which concluded last Thursday, focused on party discipline and political loyalty, confirming the expulsion of 33 full and alternate Central Committee members, including 16 senior military officers.

The expulsions were the latest consequences of an unprecedented anti-corruption storm that has swept through the People’s Liberation Army (PLA), triggering far-reaching personnel changes across its senior ranks.

Among the latest generals expelled from the party were three former theatre command leaders responsible for directing military operations in their respective strategic regions: Liu Qingsong, former political commissar of the Eastern Theatre Command; Huang Ming, former commander of the Northern Theatre Command; and Wang Haijiang, former commander of the Western Theatre Command.

Their downfall means the PLA’s anti-corruption campaign has officially engulfed almost all of the commanders and political commissars who have led the military’s five theatre commands since 2025.

The commands are core to the PLA’s war readiness and responsible for deploying, training and directing military forces in their respective strategic regions, with a particular emphasis on joint operations.

For much of the past year, it was not known who was leading the five commands, but the emergence of nine generals from the theatre commands, together with the insignia identifying their respective units, offers fresh clues about who is in charge of them.

Their seating positions at the plenum are consistent with the protocol reserved for top roles in their specific military units, with places in the session despite not being full or alternate members of the Central Committee.

It is not clear, however, if they are serving in an acting capacity, as such appointments are not made public.

Most previously served as deputies to their predecessors.

There have been several precedents of theatre commanders being elevated to the Central Military Commission (CMC), the PLA’s highest command body. This generally took place when they were being promoted to higher positions.

Lieutenant General Zhang Jichun is likely to be the acting political commissar in the Eastern Theatre Command. His last publicly disclosed position was deputy political commissar of the command.

A veteran of the PLA Rocket Force, Zhang spent much of his career in political work within the service. Earlier in his career, he headed the political work department of the Rocket Force’s Base 55 – a position previously held by CMC vice-chairman Zhang Shengmin.

General Yang Zhibin, commander of the Eastern Theatre Command, whose appointment was announced last year, was also present. Together, Yang and Zhang Jichun are responsible for the East China Sea and Pacific strategic directions, including the Taiwan Strait.

Two consecutive former commanders of the theatre before Yang – He Weidong and Lin Xiangyang – were both expelled from the Communist Party at last year’s plenum.

For the Southern Theatre Command, which oversees southward operations, including in the South China Sea, Vice-Admiral Wang Xianfeng has emerged as the likely commander.

Wang Xianfeng’s last known position was deputy commander of the Southern Theatre Command. He previously served as president of the Dalian Naval Academy, widely regarded as the cradle of the Chinese navy.

No obvious candidate is seen as his current political commissar in the footage.

Former Southern Theatre commander Wu Yanan and political commissar Wang Wenquan were both absent from last year’s plenum and the latest plenum.

Lieutenant General Liang Ping has emerged as the likely political commissar of the Central Theatre Command. Liang’s prior known posting was as deputy political commissar of the command, which is headquartered in Beijing and is responsible for defending the capital and providing operational support to other theatre commands.

He previously headed the political work bureau of the CMC’s discipline inspection commission at a time when Zhang Shengmin was overseeing the military’s anti-corruption campaign.

General Han Shengyan, who was also present, was earlier confirmed as the theatre’s commander.

Han’s predecessor, Wang Qiang, disappeared from the public eye before last year’s Victory Day parade on September 3. His political commissar, Xu Deqing, has been out of sight since the plenum last autumn.

In the Western Theatre Command, which focuses on security along the China-India border and in the strategic regions of Xinjiang and Tibet, Lieutenant General Wen Junfei has emerged as the likely acting commander. Wen’s last publicly disclosed position was deputy commander of the Western Theatre Command.

He previously served in the Central Theatre Command in 2022 alongside two officers who now hold the rank of full general – Han Shengyan and Wang Gang.

His political commissar appears to be Lieutenant General Zhang Shaoying, whose previously known post was deputy political commissar of the Western Theatre Command.

General Wang Haijiang, formerly of the Western Theatre Command, was expelled from the party at the latest plenum, while its former political commissar, Li Fengbiao, was stripped of his seat in the national legislature in June.

Lieutenant General Peng Jingtang has emerged as the likely acting commander of the Northern Theatre Command, which is headquartered in Shenyang and responsible for the Korean peninsula, the Yellow Sea and the Sea of Japan, or East Sea, including regular joint exercises with Russian forces in the region.

Peng previously commanded the PLA’s Hong Kong garrison, and his last publicly disclosed position was deputy commander of the Northern Theatre Command.

His political commissar is Vice-Admiral Li Dongyou, whose last publicly disclosed position was deputy political commissar of the command.

Li Dongyou previously served as political commissar of the Liaoning, China’s first aircraft carrier, which is home-ported in Qingdao, within the Northern Theatre Command’s area.

Footage also showed that Vice-Admiral Zhang Like – who was promoted to head the National Defence Mobilisation Department no later than last October – was absent from this plenary session, as well as from a major event last month to commemorate the 90th anniversary of the Long March.

The generals filling these vacancies do not hold seats on the Communist Party’s Central Committee but are expected to be named to the committee following next year’s party congress.

Since 2023, some 30 generals have come under investigation, while a further nine have vanished from the public eye. All previously held senior positions within the PLA.

item.title: [SCMP] India vows to dig its way out of China machinery curbs
item.description:
India’s ambitious plans to construct high-speed railways, metro networks and strategic roads through the Himalayas could be hampered by China’s proposed restrictions on tunnel-boring machines, exposing a dependence on foreign technology that New Delhi may find difficult to overcome.

Experts say while the curbs are unlikely to halt construction, they could slow major projects and have intensified calls for India to develop its own advanced tunnelling equipment.

The restrictions also threaten to complicate a cautious thaw in relations between the Asian neighbours, raising questions about how far their economic ties can recover amid persistent strategic tensions.
item.content:encoded:
India’s ambitious plans to construct high-speed railways, metro networks and strategic roads through the Himalayas could be hampered by China’s proposed restrictions on tunnel-boring machines, exposing a dependence on foreign technology that New Delhi may find difficult to overcome.

Experts say while the curbs are unlikely to halt construction, they could slow major projects and have intensified calls for India to develop its own advanced tunnelling equipment.

The restrictions also threaten to complicate a cautious thaw in relations between the Asian neighbours, raising questions about how far their economic ties can recover amid persistent strategic tensions.

India’s Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal said on Tuesday that Delhi would not bow to pressure or make concessions to secure critical technology from China, but would instead develop its own manufacturing capabilities if supplies were restricted.

“If they don’t give us tunnel-boring machines, we will develop it in India. India is not someone who will give in,” Goyal said.

But he sought to strike a conciliatory note, saying Delhi did not want to damage its relationship with Beijing.

“Our ties with China are good and will improve in the absence of new obstacles,” he said.

Beijing’s export controls, announced on October 19 and due to take effect on November 18, would require licences for shipments of certain tunnel-boring machines and components to countries with which China has disputes, while exports elsewhere would face registration requirements.

China said the measures were intended to protect national security, citing the equipment’s potential military and civilian uses. It did not identify which countries would face the stricter licensing requirements.

Nevertheless, the restrictions have raised concerns in India, which has a long-standing border dispute with China, amid reports of renewed stand-offs between troops along their disputed Himalayan frontier.

The two countries have spent the past year trying to repair relations strained by a deadly clash between their troops in the Galwan Valley in 2020, with direct flights resuming last year after a five-year hiatus.

In September, Chinese President Xi Jinping visited India for the first time in seven years, holding a bilateral meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the sidelines of the Brics summit.

The tunnel-boring machine restrictions are not the first Chinese export controls to raise concerns in India.

Goyal said Delhi was also trying to reduce its dependence on China for rare earth minerals, following curbs imposed by Beijing last year that hurt India’s technology and automotive industries.

“When they stopped rare earths, we did not go begging to them,” the minister said, adding that some start-ups were now producing motors without rare earth minerals.

Experts said China’s latest curbs were unlikely to disrupt tunnel construction outright, as India also relied heavily on conventional excavation methods such as blasting and other equipment. However, they warned that the restrictions could slow the pace of development.

India has embarked on a massive multilayered expansion of its railway network, including a bullet train project through a Mumbai-Ahmedabad corridor and construction of roads, tunnels and bridges across Himalayan mountain ranges where it shares a border with China.

Tunnel-boring machines are particularly important for complex projects, including tunnels beneath densely populated areas where conventional excavation methods may be less suitable.

“We’ve been importing these machines for every metro and rail tunnel, and very few people asked why we weren’t making them here. China’s move has forced that question [upon India],” said Vijayaram Suryamurthy, executive director of Port City Nidhi Ltd, a multi-domain financial services firm in Tamil Nadu.

He said India could easily develop the steel shell of a boring machine, but other parts such as the cutter head, hydraulics and the control systems would require more sophisticated engineering skills.

“If the government gives manufacturers some certainty on orders, and we tie up with European, Japanese or Korean partners, this can work. Start with servicing and spares, build the skills, and the bigger pieces will follow,” Suryamurthy said.

However, developing the manufacturing capabilities would take time, he noted.

“I think anyone who says India can stop importing TBMs [tunnel-boring machines] next year is being too optimistic. For the next couple of years we’ll still need imports. The change is that we can’t keep relying on one source,” Suryamurthy said.

“China’s new controls are a risk we have to plan around, and that’s really what this is about.”

China dominates the global market for tunnel-boring machines and India is among its main customers. India imported machines worth US$486 million in 2025-26 and half of them came from China, according to India’s Business Standard newspaper.

The Indian government has been working towards a US$1.2 billion incentive programme before China’s curbs to boost the domestic manufacturing of tunnel-boring machines, lifts for high-rise buildings and firefighting equipment.

India has aggressively sought to boost its manufacturing sector since the Covid-19 pandemic through incentive programmes for a range of industries spanning electronics to automobiles, driven by global supply chain disruptions.

Domestic opportunity

Biswajit Dhar, an independent development economist, noted that China’s curbs implied that Indian companies would need to seek explicit permission for machine imports, and re-routing through third countries would not be possible.

With China’s latest export restrictions extending to artificial intelligence, biopharma and photovoltaic technologies for solar energy, Dhar said that could have an even greater impact on India’s ambitions for solar energy expansion.

India aims to achieve net-zero emissions by 2070 and slash its fossil fuel imports amid soaring oil and gas prices.

“We have been talking about reviving our manufacturing sector. We hope the government gets more serious now and puts its best foot forward,” he said.

Since March, India has selectively relaxed restrictions on Chinese investments in electronic components, capital goods and solar cells.

The easing of restrictions had raised hopes that it could boost local manufacturing and reduce imports for inputs such as pharmaceutical intermediates, but Dhar warned that China’s curbs could now weigh on India’s manufacturing of cutting-edge biomedicines.

“India has to prioritise manufacturing for critical areas such as energy and pharmaceuticals. Chances can’t be taken,” he said.

Srinivaasan Balakrishnan, analyst with Delhi-based think tank Indic Researchers Forum, said the hurdles should be seen as an opportunity to create a multi-trillion rupee infrastructure pipeline by backing the domestic industry.

“Handled with focused incentives and technology partnerships, this can turn a supply chain vulnerability into a lasting manufacturing strength,” he said.

He suggested adopting a hybrid path of rising domestic content combined with selective imports and technology transfer as a realistic route for the next few years.

item.title: [SCMP] Beijing doubles down on Type 071 amphibious warships, signalling a Taiwan focus
item.description:
Beijing is accelerating production of its Type 071 amphibious transport docks by expanding construction to a second shipyard, potentially strengthening its ability to move troops and military equipment across the Taiwan Strait in a conflict.

The expansion comes amid long-standing United States assessments that Beijing lacks enough landing ships and logistical support for a large-scale assault on Taiwan, suggesting the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) may be moving to address a significant shortcoming in its ability to conduct such an operation.

Recent assessments indicate that six new Type 071 vessels are at various stages of construction or fit-out at two shipyards – four at Hudong-Zhonghua’s Changxing Island facility in Shanghai and two at CSSC Offshore & Marine Engineering Group’s Longxue shipyard in Guangzhou.
item.content:encoded:
Beijing is accelerating production of its Type 071 amphibious transport docks by expanding construction to a second shipyard, potentially strengthening its ability to move troops and military equipment across the Taiwan Strait in a conflict.

The expansion comes amid long-standing United States assessments that Beijing lacks enough landing ships and logistical support for a large-scale assault on Taiwan, suggesting the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) may be moving to address a significant shortcoming in its ability to conduct such an operation.

Recent assessments indicate that six new Type 071 vessels are at various stages of construction or fit-out at two shipyards – four at Hudong-Zhonghua’s Changxing Island facility in Shanghai and two at CSSC Offshore & Marine Engineering Group’s Longxue shipyard in Guangzhou.

According to Janes Fighting Ships, two of the vessels in Shanghai were launched in August and October but have yet to enter service, while the other two remain under construction.

Naval News reported on Friday that one Type 071 was launched in Shanghai in August, with two more under construction there and another two in Guangzhou, confirming simultaneous production at two yards for a class previously built exclusively in Shanghai. The report, however, did not account for another Type 071 launched in Shanghai last month.

Designed to carry troops, armoured vehicles, helicopters and hovercraft, the Type 071 is a key component of China’s amphibious fleet.

According to the International Institute for Strategic Studies’ “Military Balance 2026” report, the Chinese navy operates eight Type 071s and four larger Type 075 helicopter assault ships. While it is not clear when the six new hulls will be commissioned – or whether all are destined for the PLA Navy – adding them to the existing fleet would increase its Type 071 force by 75 per cent to 14 vessels.

Jim Fanell, a retired US Navy captain and former intelligence director of the US Pacific Fleet, viewed the simultaneous construction as evidence of Beijing’s determination to ramp up its amphibious capabilities.

Using two naval shipyards to construct this class of amphibious warship simultaneously indicated how urgently Beijing was pursuing the capability to attack Taiwan, he said.

Fanell estimated that the six additional vessels could carry 3,600 to 4,800 marines and 24 hovercraft, based on a capacity of 600 to 800 personnel and four craft per ship.

He envisaged the larger fleet operating alongside the PLA Navy’s Type 075 helicopter assault ships and the catapult-equipped Type 076 Sichuan, which is undergoing trials, in formations similar to US Navy expeditionary strike groups.

Based on the number of amphibious assault ships and transport docks in service or under construction, Fanell said the PLA “could likely field at least five [such groups] by 2030”.

Under the structure he described, each group would include an amphibious assault ship, two Type 071 transport docks, a Type 055 cruiser and up to two destroyers or frigates. His projection assumes the Sichuan enters operational service, although Beijing has not announced plans to form such strike groups.

Lyle Goldstein, a specialist in Chinese naval warfare at Brown University in the US, said he was “a little bit surprised” by the renewed construction after several years without new Type 071s.

He suggested the restart could reflect confidence in the established design, a shift in shipbuilding priorities or an urgency to develop a credible option for an assault on Taiwan. The additional vessels could also improve the PLA Navy’s ability to conduct operations in the East and South China seas.

In a conflict, Goldstein envisaged the additional Type 071s operating alongside Type 075 and Type 076 assault ships, helicopters and drones to deploy elite troops during the initial stages of an amphibious operation.

He suggested that those forces could seize positions near key ports, bridges or other critical locations – potentially in northern and eastern Taiwan – before larger numbers of troops and supplies arrived aboard slower civilian vessels.

With 14 Type 071s, the PLA could divide its forces across three to five target areas, he said, potentially using diversionary attacks and targeting less heavily defended areas to improve the chances of establishing a foothold, even if some landings failed.

Such operations would nevertheless carry substantial risks. Goldstein acknowledged that the ships would be heavily targeted by Taiwanese forces and potentially by countries intervening on Taiwan’s behalf, making surprise, speed and coordination essential.

The Pentagon’s December 2025 report on Beijing’s military capabilities identified significant amphibious assault limitations, concluding that the PLA Navy almost certainly lacked the conventional air and maritime lift capacity for a large-scale attack on Taiwan, and noting no significant expansion of its tank landing ships and medium-sized landing craft.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

Fanell argued that organising additional amphibious warships into expeditionary strike groups could help address long-standing doubts about the PLA Navy’s ability to transport sufficient forces across the strait.

To further offset any capacity shortfall, the Pentagon report noted, the PLA Navy had continued to train with commercial roll-on/roll-off ferries, signalling an effort to integrate dual-use civilian vessels into its amphibious operations.

Goldstein went a step further, disputing the premise that Beijing faced major lift and logistics constraints at all. With mainland China’s extensive port infrastructure and decades of groundwork, he argued, the PLA could draw on hundreds or even thousands of civilian vessels to pour reinforcements and supplies across the strait.

“I’m not convinced of any major shortcomings in China’s amphibious lift and logistics,” he said.

Yet for Goldstein, the significance of the additional warships was not limited to their potential use in a conflict. A larger amphibious fleet could also strengthen Beijing’s ability to pressure Taiwan without launching an assault.

He said he still believed Beijing sought to “win without fighting”, suggesting the additional warships could be “part of an effort to step up its capabilities for intimidation”.

item.title: [SCMP] Big Apple vs Pearl of the Orient? How higher taxes in New York may open door for Hong Kong
item.description:
On November 4 last year, Zohran Mamdani won the New York mayoral election on a promise to make the city more affordable, with expanded social programmes funded in part by raising taxes on the city’s wealthiest residents and most profitable corporations.

Nearly a year since his upset victory, he has secured one major piece of that agenda: a surcharge on high-end second homes. He also continues to push for higher corporate and income taxes.

The proposals have intensified criticism of Mamdani, a self-described democratic socialist, with opponents arguing that his approach to taxing the wealthy amounts to “socialism in action”.
item.content:encoded:
On November 4 last year, Zohran Mamdani won the New York mayoral election on a promise to make the city more affordable, with expanded social programmes funded in part by raising taxes on the city’s wealthiest residents and most profitable corporations.

Nearly a year since his upset victory, he has secured one major piece of that agenda: a surcharge on high-end second homes. He also continues to push for higher corporate and income taxes.

The proposals have intensified criticism of Mamdani, a self-described democratic socialist, with opponents arguing that his approach to taxing the wealthy amounts to “socialism in action”.

Speaking at the Milken Institute Global Conference in May, Citadel founder Ken Griffin warned that Mamdani was sending a clear message that New York “does not welcome success”, raising the prospect of moving parts of his firm’s operations out of the city.

Halfway across the globe, Hong Kong is charting an entirely different course. The Asian financial hub is rolling out fresh tax breaks and other red-carpet incentives to lure high-net-worth individuals (HNWIs), aiming to solidify its position as a premier global wealth management centre.

This year’s Global Financial Leaders’ Investment Summit, kicking off on Monday and bringing dozens of Wall Street and European heavyweights to Hong Kong, gives the city a high-profile platform to make its case.

Analysts and overseas scholars said New York’s tax push gave Hong Kong “a timely opening” to lure wealthy families reassessing where to base themselves, along with the capital they control.

Hong Kong could become “an attractive destination” for wealthy families considering a move away from the US, they added, although it remained uncertain how much tax policy alone influences relocation decisions.

Wall Street voices opposition

Since taking office in January, Mamdani has pushed state and city lawmakers to consider an array of proposals targeting the wealthy. His most significant win so far is the “pied-a-terre” levy on second homes, which took effect on July 1.

The annual levy applies to non-primary residences worth US$5 million or more, with graduated rates ranging from 0.8 to 1.3 per cent of a property’s value. Separate rates apply to condominiums and co-ops valued at US$1 million or more until July 2028.

Mamdani thrust the policy into the spotlight when he filmed a video outside the US$238 million Manhattan penthouse of Griffin, citing the property as an example of high-end second homes targeted by the levy.

Griffin later described the video as “creepy and weird”, saying Mamdani’s actions brought back the “trauma” of his time in Chicago, where he clashed with local leaders over crime and public policy before relocating Citadel’s global corporate headquarters to Miami in 2022. He added that Citadel would expand job creation in Miami rather than Manhattan as a result.

Beyond real estate, the mayor has proposed increasing the city’s income tax rate by 2 percentage points for residents earning more than US$1 million annually, which would lift the top rate to roughly 5.9 per cent from 3.9 per cent. He has also called on New York state to raise its top corporate tax rate to 11.5 per cent from 7.25 per cent.

While state governor Kathy Hochul rejected both tax increases this year, Mamdani’s allies are preparing another push in 2027, with Gustavo Gordillo, co-chair of New York’s Democratic Socialists of America chapter, maintaining that “we have lots of work left to do”.

Other Wall Street figures have also voiced opposition. After meeting Mamdani in May, JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon said higher taxes on the rich risked undermining the city’s position as a business hub.

Dimon said New York must compete with cities including Shanghai, Hong Kong, Singapore and Nashville, warning that people “vote with their feet”.

You do not have to pass a tax to move people. You just have to convince them it’s coming, or could come

Larry Ikard, Yuvarra

New York already collects more tax per resident than any other US state. State and local governments took in more than US$12,000 per resident in the 2024 financial year, 71 per cent above the national average, according to the Citizens Budget Commission, a New York fiscal watchdog.

New York City residents also face the country’s highest combined top income tax rate, at about 14.8 per cent, compared with 13.3 per cent in second-placed California.

Combined with high living costs and uneven public services, those fiscal burdens threatened New York’s ability to attract and retain high-income residents, the watchdog warned.

The wealth migration debate

While New York city officials described the proposed tax measures as “a fair way” to address inequality and raise revenue for essential services, some financial industry executives and analysts warned the moves could push affluent residents to lower-tax jurisdictions, taking capital with them.

Larry Ikard, CEO of Yuvarra, an independent lender serving HNWIs, said New York’s evolving tax landscape was prompting wealthy residents to rethink where they live “to a huge extent”.

“You do not have to pass a tax to move people. You just have to convince them it’s coming, or could come,” he said, adding that wealthy families treated calls to “tax the rich” as a signal to start planning ahead.

Kevin Chen Kaifeng, chief economist at Horizon Financial and a member of the Economic Club of Miami, said an exodus was already under way, with senior bankers and lawyers increasingly relocating to Florida.

Large financial firms such as JPMorgan Chase were no longer expanding headcount in New York, he said.

The bank’s New York City workforce has fallen to about 24,000 from 30,000 a decade ago, while its Texas headcount has increased to 32,000 from 26,000, Dimon said in his April shareholder letter.

Goldman Sachs was also moving hundreds of employees out of New York, asking staff to relocate to Dallas or Salt Lake City, international media reported in March last year.

Emanuele Colonnelli, a professor of finance and entrepreneurship at the University of Chicago Booth School of Business, said higher tax rates might not trigger immediate relocations, but they inevitably influence “long-term decisions” around retirement, business sales and the timing of moves after children finish school.

Long-term data points to a decline in New York’s share of high earners. The proportion of US households reporting annual income of more than US$1 million that lived in New York was 9 per cent in 2023, down from 12.7 per cent in 2010 – the steepest decline among US states, according to the Citizens Budget Commission.

The latest Internal Revenue Service data, covering tax returns filed in 2022 and 2023, showed New York lost a net US$9.9 billion in adjusted gross income to other states. Florida gained a net US$20.6 billion.

Florida has no state income tax or estate tax and offers a lower cost of living than New York. The number of tax filers there reporting annual income above US$1 million nearly quadrupled between 2010 and 2023, according to the commission.

Ikard said destinations in Latin America and Europe, including Panama, Costa Rica and Portugal, have also steadily attracted American retirees by offering a high quality of life, relatively low living costs and healthcare systems increasingly geared towards US expatriates.

What can Hong Kong offer?

Hong Kong is stepping up efforts to attract global wealth, pitching its low-tax regime, international connectivity and emerging financial sectors to affluent families.

Salaries tax is capped at a standard rate of 15 per cent on the first HK$5 million (US$637,000) of net income and 16 per cent above that level, while corporate profits are taxed at a headline rate of 16.5 per cent. The city largely taxes only locally sourced income and levies no capital gains, dividend or estate taxes.

In June, the government introduced a bill to widen tax concessions for privately offered funds and family-owned investment vehicles. The proposal would also extend the zero-tax treatment of qualifying carried interest from private equity to hedge funds and other investment strategies.

Colonnelli said Hong Kong “combines relatively low local taxes with the financial sophistication and international connections of a major business centre”. Families, he added, “do not necessarily have to choose between a tax-friendly location and being at the centre of business activities”.

The city ranked third globally in the latest Global Financial Centres Index, behind only New York and London, and placed ahead of London in business environment, human capital and financial sector development.

Boston Consulting Group reported in May that Hong Kong had narrowly overtaken Switzerland as the world’s largest cross-border wealth management hub, overseeing US$2.9 trillion in assets.

Hong Kong was also the preferred retirement destination among wealthy expatriates, chosen by 67 per cent of HNWIs polled in a survey by British wealth management and financial advisory firm St James’s Place covering 450 affluent residents in the city.

The city government is building on that foundation. Its first five-year plan places wealth management ambitions in the opening chapter as part of its “four centres and one hub” strategy, alongside efforts to expand the offshore yuan business and commodities trading.

Access to mainland China added to the appeal, analysts said.

Initial public offerings in Hong Kong raised more than HK$388 billion in the first three quarters of the year, more than double the amount recorded a year earlier, KPMG said. The consultancy attributed the growth to A+H listings, where mainland China-listed firms secure a Hong Kong listing, and specialist technology companies.

Hong Kong’s proximity and connections to mainland China and other Asian markets “can make it easier to build business relationships and pursue investment opportunities there”, Colonnelli said.

The city is also positioning itself as a digital assets hub. It has licensed cryptocurrency exchanges since 2023 and granted its first two stablecoin issuer licences in April.

The government has issued digital green bonds three times since 2023, while regulators have approved tokenised investment products. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority plans to test tokenising HK$1.3 trillion of Exchange Fund Bills by year-end.

Regulatory clarity is one of the city’s biggest draws, according to Sascha Goetz, CEO of RootstockCollective, which supports the bitcoin-linked Rootstock blockchain.

“In the US, it’s a lot of back and forth,” he said, citing the US Senate’s failure in September to advance a crypto market-structure bill. “For a family office planning 10 years ahead, that uncertainty is a real cost.”

What might hold wealthy families back?

Despite Hong Kong’s efforts to attract global wealth, analysts said tax rates were only part of the equation. Wealthy families must also consider the durability of tax policies, the predictability of regulations and whether a city could meet their needs beyond business.

A key structural constraint for American nationals is the limited relief available under US tax law.

American citizens and green-card holders are generally taxed on their worldwide income regardless of where they live. Relocating to Hong Kong could reduce their exposure to New York state and city taxes, which together carry a top marginal rate of about 14.8 per cent, but it would not eliminate federal income tax rates of up to 37 per cent.

New York also retains advantages as a global financial centre. Nasdaq was ranked first among worldwide exchanges by initial public offering funds raised in the first nine months of 2026, ahead of Hong Kong, driven by the listings of SpaceX and SK Hynix, KPMG said.

It also topped the Global Financial Centres Index, ranking five points ahead of Hong Kong.

Hong Kong is 12 to 13 hours ahead of New York, making it not a practical choice for most executives

Kevin Chen Kaifeng, Horizon Financial

Beyond tax and market access, “long-term legal and regulatory predictability, and the evolution of US-China relations” remained a key consideration for global capital, Colonnelli said.

Since the national security law took effect in 2020, followed by local security legislation in 2024, debate over Hong Kong’s autonomy has intensified. The government has said the laws restored stability and rejected criticism from Washington and other Western nations.
