A February survey by the American Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong found that 94 per cent of respondents were confident in the city’s rule of law – up from 83 per cent a year earlier – although 59 per cent cited geopolitical tensions as a primary operating hurdle.

Beijing’s tighter oversight of wealth held abroad is another consideration for families with business interests on both sides of the Pacific. China’s tax authority urged residents in January to declare overseas income earned from 2022 to 2024, and began taxing offshore trusts at 20 per cent in July.

Broader trade dynamics also cloud the horizon. A September summit in Washington between President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump produced a two-month extension of the trade truce through January 10, leaving deeper structural disputes unresolved.

“The concern is not just what is permitted today, but whether that will remain possible over the next decade,” Colonnelli said.

“A known tax bill can be planned for, but uncertainty about the rules governing a family’s wealth is harder to manage.”

For many families, however, practical lifestyle considerations outweigh macroeconomic ones. “The biggest considerations are probably very human ones: schools, housing costs, time zones and distance from family,” Ikard said.

Hong Kong remained the world’s least affordable housing market for a 16th year, according to international public policy research organisation Demographia, while 71 per cent of American Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong members cited living costs as the top obstacle to hiring foreign talent.

Time zone differences present another challenge. Hong Kong is 12 to 13 hours ahead of New York, making it “not a practical choice for most executives”, Chen said.

“Hong Kong’s appeal to Americans has to go beyond the tax bill,” Ikard said.

item.title: [SCMP] Scary deals? What makes Hong Kong shun death-linked homes while France embraces the risk
item.description:
Even as Hong Kong remains the world’s least affordable housing market, many buyers still shun heavily discounted homes linked to an “unnatural death”, such as murder or suicide, according to property agents.

Prices for such properties could fall by as much as 50 per cent, while rents were typically about 20 per cent below market rates, they added.

The aversion stands in stark contrast to parts of Europe, particularly in France, where buyers are often willing to purchase homes under a “vente en viager” arrangement that can see properties sold at discounts of up to 80 per cent below market value.
item.content:encoded:
Even as Hong Kong remains the world’s least affordable housing market, many buyers still shun heavily discounted homes linked to an “unnatural death”, such as murder or suicide, according to property agents.

Prices for such properties could fall by as much as 50 per cent, while rents were typically about 20 per cent below market rates, they added.

The aversion stands in stark contrast to parts of Europe, particularly in France, where buyers are often willing to purchase homes under a “vente en viager” arrangement that can see properties sold at discounts of up to 80 per cent below market value.

Under the system, an elderly homeowner agrees to sell a property in exchange for an upfront payment and a monthly annuity that continues for the rest of their life.

The arrangement allows sellers to supplement their retirement income while remaining in their homes. For buyers, the main attraction is the steep discount, even if they may have to wait for years before taking possession.

In effect, buyers are betting on how long sellers will live before they can claim the property.

“In Hong Kong, there is no official definition or registry for ‘haunted houses,’ or xiong zhai in Chinese,” said Ivy Wong, managing director of Centaline Mortgage.

“The term generally refers to properties associated with unnatural deaths, such as murders, suicides or fatal accidents, which are distinctly separated from natural deaths such as passing away from old age.”

The “haunted houses”, particularly those linked to sensational murder cases, could receive a zero valuation or be deemed ineligible for valuation, making it difficult to secure a mortgage, according to Eric Tso Tak-ming, chief vice-president at mReferral Mortgage Brokerage Services.

“Because the difficulty of reselling these properties in the future is exceptionally high, valuation firms significantly reduce their valuations,” Tso said. “Consequently, it is very difficult for banks to approve the buyer’s desired loan amount, and they often lower the loan-to-value ratio.”

Recently, a low-floor flat with a private podium in Metro Town in Tseung Kwan O was sold for HK$4.5 million (US$574,000), significantly below the more than HK$7 million valuation for a comparable home on a similar floor in another tower of the same project.

The reason, according to one agent, was that a person had fallen from a higher floor and landed on the flat’s private podium, stigmatising it as a “haunted house”.

Murders, especially those involving multiple victims, grisly details or extensive media coverage, tend to have the most severe impact on home assessments and could result in outright mortgage rejections

Ivy Wong, Centaline Mortgage

In some cases, online mortgage valuation platforms operated by banks do not generate valuations for homes associated with such incidents.

There were also cases where the “negative impact even spilled over, causing online valuations for the entire floor to become unavailable”, Centaline Mortgage’s Wong said.

Banks and surveying firms relied heavily on internal databases and media reports of tragic incidents to conduct case-by-case assessments, she added.

Banks, however, do not all take the same approach. “While some adopt a highly conservative approach and outright reject mortgage applications for stigmatised properties, the majority rely on individual assessments to determine approval and set conditions,” Wong said.

Assessments depend on factors including the nature and severity of the incident. Murders, especially those involving multiple victims, grisly details or extensive media coverage, tended to have “the most severe impact” and could result in “outright mortgage rejections”, she said.

Suicides involving charcoal burning, jumping or hanging, as well as fatal accidents such as falls or gas explosions were generally viewed as less severe, and more open-minded banks could still consider mortgage applications for such properties, Wong added.

Valuations for homes linked to high-profile murder cases would typically fall by 50 per cent or more, while those associated with suicides or fatal accidents could decline by at least 30 per cent, she said.

However, if an incident occurred decades ago and the property had changed hands or been leased multiple times since, some banks could “view the negative impact as diluted, resulting in a more favourable assessment”, Wong said.

France and several other European countries, including Belgium, Switzerland, Spain, Italy and Germany, take a markedly different view of death in relation to property transactions under the “vente en viager” arrangement.

“What sets France apart is how common private, person-to-person ‘viager’ sales are, with a well-developed legal framework around them,” said Alex Balkin, head of Savills French Riviera.

The arrangement offered advantages to both sellers and buyers, Balkin added.

For sellers, the benefits included additional retirement income while remaining in their homes, annuity payments indexed to inflation and part of the income receiving a “favourable tax treatment”, he said.

Sellers were also well-protected, as contracts typically contained clauses allowing them to reclaim the property and retain payments already received if buyers stopped paying.

For buyers, the property’s price was discounted to reflect occupancy and the seller’s life expectancy, while payments were spread over time, removing the need for a traditional bank mortgage, according to Balkin.

Some Hong Kong-based buyers had inquired about purchasing French property through a “vente en viager” arrangement, said Sebastien Salin, a Hong Kong-based French entrepreneur and the founder of Acheterpourlouer, a real estate advisory firm that helps expatriates and foreigners to buy properties in France remotely.

“There’s a number of clients who have shown an interest, but it’s a limited percentage,” Salin said.

Depending on the seller’s age, discounts could reach as much as 80 per cent of market value, he added.

“This arrangement is getting more popular because a lot of people are getting older and don’t have much income, but they have a nice flat,” Salin said. “So they want to get some extra funds to make sure they have enough income during the remaining years of their life.”

There is, however, a famous example of a transaction that went badly wrong for the buyer.

In 1965, Jeanne Calment sold her home in Arles, France, at age 90 under a “vente en viager” arrangement to Andre-Francois Raffray, a 47-year-old lawyer.

Raffray paid Calment 2,500 French francs a month for 30 years before dying in 1995. His widow continued the payments until Calment died in 1997 at the age of 122. By then the family had paid more than twice the home’s value, according to Savills. France replaced the franc with the euro in 1999, when 2,500 francs equalled around US$405.

“It’s a little bit like gambling,” Salin said.

In Hong Kong, the aversion to properties linked to unfortunate circumstances stemmed from “the prevailing cultural beliefs and superstitions that are deeply ingrained in local Chinese society,” according to a spokesman from Centaline Property Agency.

There were, however, prospective buyers or tenants willing to consider these properties, he said.

“Individuals who do not subscribe to local superstitions, such as Catholic buyers, expatriates and atheists, are much more open to living in these homes,” he said.

“This is particularly driven by budget constraints or a desire to save money, as the significant rental discounts of around 20 per cent below standard market rates make these properties a highly cost-effective option.”

Even so, the long-term value of these properties generally does not fully recover or keep pace with the broader property market.

“While general market growth may result in a slight increase in value, these properties almost invariably continue to trade at a significant discount relative to comparable, unaffected properties in the same neighbourhood,” the spokesman said.

item.title: [SCMP] Southeast Asia battles Big Tech to protect children online
item.description:
Indonesia officially barred under-16s from using “high-risk” social media earlier this year. But that hasn’t stopped the son of one Jakarta-based writer from using it.

Aged 14, he already had accounts on Instagram and TikTok – among the platforms Jakarta said children would be banned from using – as well as popular video game Minecraft and gaming platform Roblox. To register, he simply lied about his age.

“He can access everything,” Inne Abidin said of her son. “His friends use everything too.”
item.content:encoded:
Indonesia officially barred under-16s from using “high-risk” social media earlier this year. But that hasn’t stopped the son of one Jakarta-based writer from using it.

Aged 14, he already had accounts on Instagram and TikTok – among the platforms Jakarta said children would be banned from using – as well as popular video game Minecraft and gaming platform Roblox. To register, he simply lied about his age.

“He can access everything,” Inne Abidin said of her son. “His friends use everything too.”

Since March, Indonesia has had some of Southeast Asia’s strictest rules governing children’s social media use.

Yet like elsewhere in the region, such restrictions are only as effective as the systems Big Tech platforms put in place to identify underage users – and keep them out.

From Malaysia to Vietnam, the Philippines and Singapore, governments that once merely urged platforms to protect children are now imposing rules designed to force social media companies to take responsibility.

Patchy compliance

Indonesia’s child protection regulations have already had an effect on how social media companies operate.

In April, Meta Platforms raised the minimum age for a Facebook, Instagram or Threads account from 13 to 16 in Indonesia, with YouTube following suit later that month. Both said they would begin a phased deactivation of accounts belonging to underage users.

TikTok, which was the first platform to comply with the new rules, raised its minimum platform age to 16 on March 28. By October, it had deactivated 9 million underage accounts, Indonesia’s digital affairs minister announced on Wednesday.

And online gaming platform Roblox now scans Indonesian users’ faces to estimate their age, restricts some communication features for children and has added age-based account limitations.

Yet youngsters seemingly still find ways to skirt the rules. To combat this, Indonesia’s government has given tech companies until the end of the year to complete comprehensive self-assessments detailing how their algorithms, age-verification and ad-targeting systems protect children.

If the platforms fail to comply, the Communications and Digital Affairs Ministry has finalised a sanctions mechanism that – once codified into law – would allow Indonesia to levy fines of up to 6 per cent of tech firms’ global revenue. Applied to Meta’s reported revenue for 2025, that would amount to roughly US$12 billion.

Such a fine would not be without precedent. In August, Meta agreed to pay a coalition of US states up to US$18 billion to settle lawsuits alleging Facebook and Instagram were deliberately designed to make children addicted and caused them harm.

The settlement also forced sweeping changes to how teens experience the platforms, including daily usage limits, overnight usage blocks and strengthened age-verification controls.

Meta has reportedly migrated some 22.5 million Indonesian platform users across to these “teen accounts”, but for the country’s government this does not go far enough.

“While we see this as progress, we still do not consider Instagram and Facebook teen accounts to be low-risk,” Communication and Digital Affairs Minister Meutya Hafid told reporters in Jakarta on Wednesday. “They remain categorised as high-risk.”

Child protection is hard to oppose publicly, so resisting it carries a high reputational cost

Unggul Sagena, digital rights advocate

For Southeast Asia, the unavoidable question now being asked is whether governments can turn the threat of penalties into real change.

“In my view, the level of cooperation comes down to a few factors: how valuable the market is, how credible the government’s enforcement is, whether the rule threatens the platform’s global business model, how closely it aligns with obligations they already meet elsewhere and whether it carries legitimacy,” said Unggul Sagena, head of internet access at the Southeast Asia Freedom of Expression Network, an Indonesian digital rights organisation that advocates for internet freedom and user safety.

As the region’s largest economy, the sheer size of Indonesia’s consumer market – as well as its risk-based approach to online child protection – lent its arguments and regulations weight that smaller countries lacked, Unggul said.

“Global platforms are complying,” he said. “Even if not yet fully.”

Part of the reason for the changes is the legal machinery Indonesia already has in place, including a regulation passed in 2020 that obliges platforms to act on government takedown orders within tight deadlines, as short as four hours in urgent cases.

“The government has also taken the issue directly to headquarters,” Unggul said, noting that the communications minister met representatives from Meta’s global public policy and safety leadership team in New York last month to push for faster deactivation of underage accounts.

“Child protection is hard to oppose publicly, so resisting it carries a high reputational cost,” he added.

Still, Indonesia’s proposed fine framework has yet to be legally codified and many question marks remain over how it will ultimately be implemented.

Unresolved issues include how to collect fines from companies with no local assets, how to accurately verify global revenue “and what due process exists when the same ministry writes the rules, judges compliance and imposes the sanction”, Unggul said.

Blocking sites, meanwhile, “hurts Indonesian users more than the companies”, he said. “And the government can order [content] removals, but it still has little visibility into how the platforms are actually designed.”

The threat of high fines could push platforms to invest more in safety-by-design and high-privacy defaults for children, said Indriyatno Banyumurti, executive director of ICT Watch, an Indonesian civil society organisation focused on digital literacy.

But he warned that legal clarity and consistent enforcement were key, stressing that child safety “should not depend solely on voluntary corporate commitments”.

Indriyatno said much would depend on how violations were defined, how compliance was monitored, how evidence was assessed and whether sanctions could be applied fairly and consistently.

Regional rules

Indonesia’s social media ban may have been Southeast Asia’s first, but it is far from alone in trying to make Big Tech take responsibility for children’s safety online.

In Malaysia, rules in force since June now bar under-16s from opening or maintaining social media accounts and require platforms to verify users’ ages. Companies that fail to comply face fines of up to 10 million ringgit (US$2.5 million), with further penalties for ignoring regulatory directives.

Vietnam is considering a draft decree that would limit under-16s to a view-only mode of social media, preventing them from posting content, commenting, sharing or reacting to other posts. Accounts would have to be registered using a parent or guardian’s details under the proposed rules, with platforms compelled to block age-inappropriate material and place caps on children’s online gaming time.

The Philippines’ approach has been more piecemeal. It already legally forces internet providers to block child sexual abuse material or face heavy penalties and has used regulatory pressure to squeeze direct concessions from platforms. Lawmakers are also considering introducing age limits and other measures.

In August, Meta and Roblox agreed to strengthen age checks, parental controls and content takedowns following talks with Philippine authorities over child safety and online radicalisation. A spate of school shootings this year also spurred officials in Manila to order Reddit and Discord to appoint local representatives to coordinate on online threats. Discord was briefly blocked before agreeing to cooperate.

Singapore requires social media giants to shield users, including children, from harmful material under its Online Safety (Miscellaneous Amendments) Act that came into effect in 2023, with non-compliance carrying a financial penalty of up to S$1 million (US$781,500).

App stores have been legally required to verify the ages of users who want to download age-restricted material in the city state since April this year. And an Online Safety Commission, launched in June under legislation passed last year, has the power to order the immediate removal of harmful content and restrict offending accounts.

While these efforts have helped effect some change, analysts say the results have been uneven.

“Platforms do respond, but market size is a factor they consider,” said regional tech policy adviser Paco Pangalangan, a technology and human rights fellow at the Harvard Kennedy School in the US. “A large market might get more attention, while a smaller one might get a slower, more minimal version. Whether there’s a law matters too.”

By his count, most of the big social media companies do not even have in-country representatives in five of Asean’s 11 member states.

“So there’s often no real channel for regulators or civil society to raise problems,” Pangalangan said.

Strength in numbers

Individual governments, especially those that represent sizeable markets with credible enforcement mechanisms, may be able to force social media platforms to comply with their rules.

But global technology companies can also opt to deal with countries one by one, which analysts and advocates say makes it harder for smaller markets to exert sustained pressure. One solution could be to present a more united front.

“A regional coalition can push Big Tech to create child-friendly ecosystems in ways no single country can,” Unggul said. “Individually, each Asean country is a market platforms can afford to deprioritise. Together, the region is not.”

Pangalangan said that, taken as a whole, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations could leverage the region’s more than 400 million social media users to strengthen its hand in negotiations..

“Collectively, we have a market that platforms can’t afford to simply deprioritise,” he said.

“If we can agree on common standards, including requirements around how platforms are designed, there’s less room for platforms to play one country off against another or just wait things out.”

Allan Cabanlong, Asean regional director for cybersecurity and cloud services provider CyberCX’s regional cyber advisers programme and a former assistant secretary at the Philippines’ Department of Information and Communications Technology, agreed that collective action could hand regional governments greater bargaining power.

“A broom with one strand cannot sweep,” he said. “We have hundreds of millions of users in Asean. If the Philippines were to stand alone, it would not be listened to.”

As this year’s Asean chair, the Philippines could push the protection of children online higher up the regional agenda, Cabanlong said, while the bloc could also work to strengthen its existing mechanisms for digital regulation.

Asean would not be starting from scratch. Its declaration on the protection of children from online exploitation and abuse, adopted in 2019, and associated regional plans of action already recognise online harm to children as a cross-bogrder issue.

Other frameworks on personal data protection – and a declaration on safe and responsible social media use, adopted last October – widen that scope to include online radicalisation and AI-related risks.

But few observers expect a single, regional law on children’s social media use to be the end result.

“Asean does not necessarily have to start by creating one identical social media law for all member states,” said Ysrael Diloy, executive director of Stairway Foundation, a non-profit children’s rights organisation in the Philippines.

“Given differences in national legal systems, regulatory structures and capacities, that may not be the most realistic starting point.”

Indriyatno agreed that a more realistic approach would be for Asean to agree on common expectations for factors such as risk assessments, minimum standards of platform accountability, privacy defaults for children and cooperation on cross-border cases.

“Regulators could also develop more compatible requirements for platform transparency and information sharing,” he said.

Alejandro Reyes, chief strategic officer of non-profit organisation AI Safety Asia, said national regulators would also need to share information and cooperate more closely.

“If Singapore identifies a serious failure in a platform’s child-safety systems, its counterparts in Malaysia, the Philippines and elsewhere should have access to those findings,” he said.

“Joint investigations, shared technical expertise and coordinated enforcement would make it harder for companies to exploit differences between national regulatory regimes.”

Such a baseline would not demand identical laws, but it would provide common ground in dealing with companies that straddle borders.

It would also carry risks. “The concern here is that child protection is part of a much broader framework of government control over online content and expression,” Reyes said, urging caution given the differences in countries’ legal systems, political priorities and enforcement capacity.

Other issues, according to Unggul, include the fact that Asean members currently compete for technology investment, have very different track records when it comes to free expression and make decisions as a bloc by consensus.

“Collective leverage only works if it is credible and rights-based, and that is where civil society across the region must make sure the coalition strengthens accountability rather than state control over content,” he said.

“Child safety must not become cover for censorship. Bargaining power comes not only from penalties but from legitimacy.”

Limits of laws

Governments can restrict access, require age verification and impose penalties on platforms, but they cannot regulate the behaviour of children and families, online child safety experts say.

Fandy Zulmi, programme manager at the Centre for Child Study and Protection in Indonesia, pointed to recent Communications Ministry data showing that three out of five Indonesian children had falsified their age to access restricted platforms.

Without stronger digital literacy, parental involvement and robust reporting mechanisms, Indonesia’s social media ban for children might simply move the risks “somewhere else”, he said.

“It is still too early to conclude that the policy has effectively deterred children from going online,” Fandy said.

Indonesia’s implementation challenge begins with the fact that there are between 60 million and 80 million children in the country whose circumstances differ enormously, according to Diena Haryana, founder of the Sejiwa Foundation, a Jakarta-based child welfare organisation.

“Where they live, what education their parents have, what digital parenting awareness the parents have, whether the parents themselves have digital skills – all of that varies massively, especially between somewhere like Jakarta and rural areas,” she said.

Some parents used social media platforms to keep children occupied while they worked, Diena said, while others were more aware of the risks involved with giving their children unfettered access.

“We all need to work much harder to make sure children understand what the regulation is, why it exists and how implementation should actually work,” she said.

But ultimately, it is the platforms themselves that bear the brunt of the responsibility for child safety, according to Pangalangan.

“They already know where many of the harms are,” he said. “They don’t need a law to fix things they control in their own products.”

item.title: [SCMP] North Korea digs in for US stand-off as Democratic midterm wins dim summit hopes
item.description:
North Korea is bracing for a prolonged confrontation with the United States, analysts say, after sweeping Democratic gains in the US midterm elections diminished the likelihood of renewed diplomacy between Kim Jong-un and President Donald Trump.

As Americans cast their ballots on Tuesday, Pyongyang test-fired a new surface-to-air missile system and carried out a strike drill with long-range strategic cruise missiles early on Wednesday, Korean time – its fourth weapons test in a week.

The launches came hours after Kim Yo-jong, the sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, blasted Washington on Tuesday for linking Pyongyang to a US$6.3 billion cryptocurrency theft from Binance, calling the FBI’s findings a “grave political provocation”.
item.content:encoded:
North Korea is bracing for a prolonged confrontation with the United States, analysts say, after sweeping Democratic gains in the US midterm elections diminished the likelihood of renewed diplomacy between Kim Jong-un and President Donald Trump.

As Americans cast their ballots on Tuesday, Pyongyang test-fired a new surface-to-air missile system and carried out a strike drill with long-range strategic cruise missiles early on Wednesday, Korean time – its fourth weapons test in a week.

The launches came hours after Kim Yo-jong, the sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, blasted Washington on Tuesday for linking Pyongyang to a US$6.3 billion cryptocurrency theft from Binance, calling the FBI’s findings a “grave political provocation”.

She warned that Pyongyang had matters to “reconsider” in response to US hostility, but stopped short of threatening retaliation, leaving the door open to dialogue.

On Wednesday, she said: “The choice for peace includes dialogue, of course, but this is not surely equated with national interests for us.”

Oh Gyeong-seob, a senior researcher at the Korea Institute for National Unification, said the Democrats’ victory was unwelcome news for Pyongyang, which endured strict sanctions under the previous Biden administration.

The Biden administration insisted that dialogue could not take place without a commitment to denuclearisation, and demanded that any summit be preceded by working-level talks to resolve differences – a stark contrast to the top-down diplomacy favoured by Trump, Oh said.

“The North is deeply wary of the [Binance] heist sparking further US and international sanctions, and this concern adds to the reasons for Pyongyang to seek dialogue. Kim Yo-jong’s statement reflects this concern,” Oh said.

However, Oh added there was little chance that the Trump administration and Pyongyang could reach a compromise acceptable to a Democrat-led Congress.

“Pyongyang knows this fact, and it is bracing itself for prolonged confrontation as well,” he said.

Leif-Eric Easley, a professor of international studies at Ewha Womans University, said that while the midterm results dealt Trump a major blow, he was unlikely to moderate his style or policy positions.

“Instead, domestic constraints could encourage him to pursue dramatic and controversial diplomatic initiatives,” Easley said, adding that Trump might seek deals with Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin or Kim Jong-un, while stepping up pressure on allies to shoulder defence costs and offer economic concessions.

A Democratic-controlled Congress, however, would likely investigate Trump’s decisions, scrutinise agreements and resist sanctions relief for Russia or North Korea, he said.

“So Washington might see more assertive presidential diplomacy but less certainty about implementation,” Easley said.

South Korea supported renewed Trump-Kim diplomacy, but a summit that shelved denuclearisation would weaken deterrence and spark policy friction among Washington, Seoul and Tokyo, he added.

“North Korea’s numerous weapons tests, record crypto heists, aggressive rhetoric against Seoul and sanctions-violating cooperation with Moscow seriously complicate engagement,” Easley said.

Lim Eul-chul, a professor at Kyungnam University’s Institute for Far Eastern Studies, said the election results had dampened expectations for the top-down, transactional diplomacy preferred by Kim.

With Democrats taking control of Congress, any effort by Trump to alter political dynamics through a North Korea-US summit would face stiff resistance from congressional control over spending, investigative powers and sanctions legislation, Lim said.

“From Pyongyang’s perspective, even an agreement reached with Trump could be at risk of collapsing at any time. North Korea would therefore seek to avoid a repeat of the 2019 Hanoi summit’s failure,” he said, referring to the collapse of talks after the two sides failed to agree on sanctions relief in exchange for nuclear dismantlement.

North Korea had a deep-seated conviction that “the essence of the US hostile policy towards North Korea will never change”, Lim said. Given this distrust, Pyongyang saw little incentive to engage in dialogue with Washington, risking the uncertain implementation of an agreement for limited tangible benefits, he added.

“North Korea is likely to further consolidate a survival structure capable of neutralising US sanctions pressure through comprehensive military and economic cooperation with China and Russia,” Lim said.

Such ties would allow Pyongyang to pursue its defence and economic development plans with less concern for Washington’s reaction while preparing for “a prolonged strategic confrontation”, he added.

“The current political situation is likely to reinforce North Korea’s conviction that developing its independent nuclear capabilities, regardless of changes in the US administration or the ruling party, was the correct and strategically superior choice.”

“The development, test-firing and training of new weapons systems are expected to become increasingly routine and regularised,” Lim said.

Against this backdrop, North Korea’s Wednesday tests paired technical verification of a new air-defence missile system with simulated target strikes by long-range strategic cruise missiles.

Lim said the simultaneous deployment of defensive and offensive systems in a single day was intended to show improved electronic warfare capabilities and technologies for evading low- and high-altitude air-defence networks.

Yang Moo-jin, a professor at the University of North Korean Studies, said it was rare for North Korea to launch defensive surface-to-air missiles together with offensive cruise missiles.

“The near-simultaneous timing of the missile launches and Kim Yo-jong’s statement is also unusual, suggesting that the actions were planned in advance to coincide with the US midterm elections,” Yang said, adding that the launches were intended to draw attention to North Korea and underscore its strategic significance.

The tests also served as a retaliatory show of force against Freedom Flag, a two-week joint South Korea-US air drill that will last until Friday, Yang said.

By pairing weapons demonstrations with Kim Yo-jong’s statement, Pyongyang was signalling that its words were backed by action and that it would match any perceived US hostility with corresponding measures, he said.

“Pyongyang is conveying that dialogue and confrontation, peace and military exercises and improving relations and disrespect for its sovereignty cannot coexist,” Yang said.

“However, North Korea is also signalling that dialogue, peace and improved relations remain possible if the Trump administration respects the North Korean regime and abandons what Pyongyang regards as hostile policies towards the country, including joint US-South Korean military exercises.”

item.title: [SCMP] Will New Zealand’s election reshape its ‘softly-softly’ approach to Trump?
item.description:
Cost of living issues are expected to dominate this weekend’s election in New Zealand, but the outcome could also determine whether Wellington maintains its cautious approach to US President Donald Trump or pursues a more independent foreign policy, analysts have said.

With the major parties locked in a close contest ahead of Saturday’s vote, the next government’s approach to Washington, as well as its defence priorities, could hinge on the smaller parties needed to form a coalition.

Robert Patman, a professor of international relations at New Zealand’s University of Otago, said a key issue at stake was whether Wellington would continue its so far unsuccessful “softly-softly” approach to the second Trump administration.
item.content:encoded:
Cost of living issues are expected to dominate this weekend’s election in New Zealand, but the outcome could also determine whether Wellington maintains its cautious approach to US President Donald Trump or pursues a more independent foreign policy, analysts have said.

With the major parties locked in a close contest ahead of Saturday’s vote, the next government’s approach to Washington, as well as its defence priorities, could hinge on the smaller parties needed to form a coalition.

Robert Patman, a professor of international relations at New Zealand’s University of Otago, said a key issue at stake was whether Wellington would continue its so far unsuccessful “softly-softly” approach to the second Trump administration.

“Or whether it pragmatically recognises that the Trump administration is unlike previous administrations and opts for closer relations with a new constellation of middle and small powers,” Patman said, citing similar moves by Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney.

New Zealanders will head to the polls amid mounting concerns over living costs, unemployment and healthcare, with both major parties promising to address the country’s economic difficulties.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon’s centre-right National Party came to power in 2023 on a promise to “build the economy” and has governed in coalition with the ACT and New Zealand First (NZ First) parties.

National has emphasised economic management, restoring a budget surplus and expanding the country’s retirement savings scheme.

The main opposition, the centre-left Labour party led by former prime minister Chris Hipkins, has focused on reducing living costs, improving healthcare and transport, and investing in housing, jobs and public services.

A 1News Verian poll published on Tuesday placed National at 30 per cent and Labour at 29 per cent, pointing to a closely fought election in which smaller parties could play a decisive role.

Under New Zealand’s mixed-member proportional electoral system, parties generally need at least 5 per cent of the party vote or an electorate seat to enter parliament, making coalition negotiations crucial to determining who governs.

Patman said a significant shift in Wellington’s approach to Washington was unlikely if the current National-led coalition were re-elected, given what he described as the broadly pro-Trump orientation of NZ First and ACT.

However, if a Labour-led coalition involving the Greens and the Opportunity Party came to power, Wellington could adopt a much more measured approach and “realign foreign policy to sit more consistently with New Zealand values and interests”, Patman said.

New Zealand has largely maintained a careful, muted diplomatic posture towards major US foreign policy and security shifts under Trump, according to analysts.

When Washington rolled back reciprocal tariffs on New Zealand exports, Wellington maintained a non-confrontational response and prioritised behind-the-scenes diplomacy.

Patman pointed to Canada as a possible model for how Wellington could navigate an increasingly unpredictable international environment.

In a landmark address at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, Carney argued that the traditional post-war, US-led international rules-based order had collapsed and been replaced by great-power bullying and the weaponisation of trade.

To shield Canada from what he calls a “geopolitical rupture”, Carney has shifted foreign policy to prioritise closer relations with middle and small powers.

Apart from pursuing an unprecedented “associate membership” framework with the European Union, Ottawa has spearheaded the Partners for Multilateralism initiative alongside Brazil, the EU, Kenya, India and Australia.

David Capie, a professor of international relations at Victoria University of Wellington, said the election had mainly focused on affordability issues, with the economy struggling and people feeling the impact of higher energy prices.

With both main parties polling poorly, whoever emerged the winner on Saturday night would need coalition partners to form a government, Capie noted.

“The wild card is the emergence of a new centrist party – Opportunity – which has said it could work with either National or Labour,” Capie said. “If it gets above the 5 per cent threshold and into parliament, it could well hold the balance of power.”

Capie warned that the polls, currently too close to call, might not produce clear results on Saturday night. “Negotiations to form a government could potentially take weeks.”

Opportunity, led by Qiulae Wong, is campaigning independently and positioning itself to hold the balance of power as a potential “kingmaker”.

Richard Shaw, professor of politics at Massey University’s College of Humanities and Social Sciences, said if the present government was returned to power, National would still be the largest party but was likely to have fewer seats at the cabinet table.

“This means that the anti-immigration policies of NZ First, and the anti-Maori policies of both the ACT and NZ First parties will have greater salience than was previously the case,” Shaw said.

NZ First advocates strict reforms designed to reduce non-essential immigration and prioritise New Zealand citizens. ACT and NZ First have also sought to dismantle race-based policies and ethnic prioritisation in addressing structural inequities, leading indigenous advocacy groups to slam their agendas as “anti-Maori”.

Last month, NZ First released a new policy titled “Defence, Security and Protection of the Realm”, which calls for a six-year reform plan to rebuild the New Zealand Defence Force.

Apart from proposing a massive funding surge aimed at expanding military capabilities to match a more demanding strategic environment, the policy also suggested rapidly growing the country’s military forces to over 20,000 personnel.

Shaw said if the right-wing bloc formed the next government, NZ First could have more seats in parliament and therefore more leverage.

“Winston Peters will almost certainly retain responsibility for foreign affairs,” Shaw said, referring to the NZ First leader and New Zealand’s foreign minister.

Still, it was difficult to see potential coalition partners lining up to reverse some of the commitments already made, Shaw said.

These include scrapping the current frigate procurement programme, which involves spending an estimated NZ$6 billion (US$3.4 billion) to NZ$8 billion upfront, while redirecting funds towards uncrewed air, surface and undersea drones, and a second amphibious warship.

Patman said even if the present coalition were re-elected, it was doubtful whether defence expenditure would increase beyond the current 2 per cent.

National and Labour were also unlikely to accept NZ First’s defence posture, which de-emphasised maritime security, Patman added.

If the current coalition retains power, Capie expects the Defence Capability Plan – a 15-year strategic blueprint unveiled in April 2025 to rebuild and modernise the defence force – to move forward.

Apart from upgrading strike capabilities, missile systems, naval and aerial fleets, the NZ$12 billion plan over the first four years will also further invest in uncrewed and drone surveillance vehicles as well as space technology.

“If there were a change of government, defence would be one area where you will see renewed debate,” Capie said. “There are a lot of different interests at play for New Zealand, including meeting our commitment as a treaty ally to Australia.”

item.title: [SCMP] Data centre dissent: why American voters aren’t buying Trump’s China AI pitch
item.description:
Strong voter backlash in the US midterm elections against AI infrastructure projects, including data centres, indicates that framing the domestic buildout as key to competing with China failed to convince Americans and underscores the need to address local concerns, according to analysts.

“The argument that we need to build more data centres to win in AI against China no longer seems to have the kind of resonance it did before, if it ever did, frankly,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution’s John L. Thornton China Centre.

Lizzi Lee, a fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute, echoed that assessment, saying: “The lesson is that invoking China as a justification for tech and industrial investment is becoming less effective.”
item.content:encoded:
Strong voter backlash in the US midterm elections against AI infrastructure projects, including data centres, indicates that framing the domestic buildout as key to competing with China failed to convince Americans and underscores the need to address local concerns, according to analysts.

“The argument that we need to build more data centres to win in AI against China no longer seems to have the kind of resonance it did before, if it ever did, frankly,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution’s John L. Thornton China Centre.

Lizzi Lee, a fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute, echoed that assessment, saying: “The lesson is that invoking China as a justification for tech and industrial investment is becoming less effective.”

The Trump administration and the Republican Party cited rivalry with China to barrel through AI infrastructure across the country, but voters chose to prioritise local concerns about soaring power bills, water use and quality of life above Washington’s technological competition with Beijing.

Democrats, having won control of the House and Senate, are promising to step in with new guardrails and map out a fresh path forward on AI development.

Experts, however, say achieving a consensus will still be difficult given US President Donald Trump’s opposing priorities and a persistent lack of bipartisan agreement.

Tuesday’s elections saw Democrats who campaigned against unchecked AI and data centre expansion score major victories, winning Senate races in Texas and Ohio and gubernatorial races in Texas, Georgia and Ohio.

In addition, voters in dozens of townships across the country approved measures to ban or restrict the construction of new data centres.

“Competition with China on AI simply did not factor into the races as far as the electorate was concerned,” said Sourabh Gupta, resident senior fellow at the Institute for China-America Studies.

The Trump administration framed AI infrastructure expansion as vital to keeping pace with China and preserving US leadership, while downplaying local communities’ concerns, along with calls to slow the development of frontier models amid safety risks.

“We are leading China in AI, we’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins,” Trump said in September.

In the short term, Paul Triolo, a partner at the DGA-Albright Stonebridge Group, thinks it is unlikely that fears about the US-China AI race will override local concerns about data centres, such as electricity prices and water supplies.

“Right now the idea of a race around AI is not that appealing when job losses, AI safety and AI data centres form a solid negative trifecta around the issue, putting China competition well down the list for most voters,” he added.

On AI safety, Trump has favoured voluntary industry oversight over government regulation. He met leading AI executives at the White House in September and backed a voluntary pact requiring companies to monitor and audit their own systems, describing the agreement as “morally binding”.

“I can imagine Trump continuing to be reluctant to rein in AI progress in the US and for him to continue to want to frame it as America being number one and beating China in AI,” Chan said.

However, the argument that the US must outpace China in AI carries less weight for residents living near data centres, who are more concerned about the projects’ direct impact on their communities.

Lindsay Shaw and Jessica Medeiros know first-hand the toll of America’s data centre boom. They live in Loudoun County, northern Virginia, which has the most data centres per capita in the world.

Across the street from their homes in Sterling, a massive facility runs day and night, subjecting them to gas turbines, diesel fumes and relentless industrial noise.

“Living next to a data centre, I’ve learned that progress looks a lot different on a PowerPoint slide than it does from your backyard,” Medeiros said. “I think voters are sending a message that growth matters, but so does listening to the people who live with the impacts.”

Shaw agrees the vote signals a broader appetite for accountability rather than an anti-technology or anti-AI stance.

“Whether the argument is to win the AI race against China or just to house and protect our data – we need them. All of us use AI and the internet in our daily lives,” she said. “Whatever reason is used, though, does not justify the impact on communities.”

Medeiros shared that view, arguing that communities shouldn’t suffer to advance a broader political agenda, whether tied to AI, China or economic growth.

“I just don’t believe that Trump’s push to win the AI race with China should be at the citizens’ expense,” she said. “I think he’s using competition with China to move faster and build bigger, while expecting us to just accept the consequences.”

While Medeiros hopes the election results will force officials across the country to weigh community impact before building new data centres, Shaw remains sceptical.

“I’ll feel more hopeful when I see leaders actually standing up for the people and plan and build these in industrial areas and not among communities,” she said.

“I hope Americans in other areas are more successful in working with big tech, but with enough money, I’m not sure any leader would stand up for their communities”

Fresh off winning the midterms, Democrats are promising to do just that.

Ted Lieu, who comfortably won re-election from California’s 36th Congressional District and is the co-chair of the Democratic Commission on AI in Congress, said on Wednesday that his party plans to step in with new guardrails around data centre construction and broader AI regulation.

“Two things will change next term,” Lieu said. “We will hold public hearings on AI. We will pass legislation, reasonable guardrails, on AI.”

The House Democratic Commission on AI is an internal party panel created to build policy expertise, engage tech stakeholders and shape legislative guardrails and oversight for artificial intelligence.

Democrats could push for legislation related to data centres, but they would need Republican support to pass anything, said Triolo.

“Even more important than the AI infrastructure buildout will be discussion in the new Congress on regulating how models are developed and released and what the government oversight role should be,” he added.

As AI safety issues have dominated the debate on government oversight over the past few months, calls for congressional action have already emerged.

Triolo said safety oversight is likely to take more bandwidth in the new Congress than attempts to legislate national restrictions on data centres, which have remained a largely local issue.

“If Chinese firms appear to be keeping pace or even surpassing US AI firms in some areas, there will be more calls for both an easy hand on regulation and more support for data centre buildouts in a Democrat-led Congress,” added Triolo, who specialises in China and technology policy.

item.title: [SCMP] 5 takeaways from US midterms as Democrats sweep Congress and Trump faces Iran reckoning
item.description:
A Democratic victory that reached from Texas to Kansas changed the terms of Donald Trump’s final two years in office.

When the new US Congress convenes in January, Democrats will control both chambers. They can block his legislation, challenge spending on the war in Iran and scrutinise the deals he strikes with Beijing.

The day after his party lost control of Congress, Trump invited reporters to the construction site of his new White House ballroom to watch workers raise the final steel beam.
item.content:encoded:
A Democratic victory that reached from Texas to Kansas changed the terms of Donald Trump’s final two years in office.

When the new US Congress convenes in January, Democrats will control both chambers. They can block his legislation, challenge spending on the war in Iran and scrutinise the deals he strikes with Beijing.

The day after his party lost control of Congress, Trump invited reporters to the construction site of his new White House ballroom to watch workers raise the final steel beam.

Asked about the prospect of impeachment, he dismissed the idea, then turned back to the reason he had brought them there. “Watch the beam go up,” he said.

The visit also gave Trump a chance to respond to his vice-president, J.D. Vance, who had blamed the Iran war for the defeat.

Many voters who backed Trump in 2024 had turned out again on Tuesday and voted for Democrats, Vance said.

Trump put the emphasis on higher fuel prices and stood by his decision to go to war. “If I had it to do again, I’d have to do it again,” he said.

Here are five takeaways from the US midterms.

1. The Democratic wave reached deep into Trump country

In Texas, James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton to become the first Democrat to win a US Senate race in the state since 1988. In South Carolina, doctor Annie Andrews defeated Republican Senator Darline Graham. Trump had carried both states by double digits just two years earlier and had backed both losing candidates.

Kansas delivered the longest break with the past. Adam Hamilton defeated Republican Senator Roger Marshall, ending a Senate winning streak that dated to 1932. In Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown won the seat Vance had vacated to become vice-president.

The final size of the majority was still taking shape on Wednesday.

At noon Eastern time, the Associated Press had yet to call the Senate races in Alaska and Mississippi. Democrats had already secured control without either seat.

2. Vance blamed the war. Trump blamed the price of fuel

Republicans had spent much of the campaign watching whether the people who backed Trump in 2024 would turn out again. Vance said the party had drawn too much comfort from seeing those voters show up. Many came back, he said, and cast their ballots for Democrats.

“The reason we lost is the war,” Vance wrote on X. He cited an unnamed pollster who had asked former Trump voters what it would take to win them back.

Ending the conflict topped the list, Vance said, followed by tackling the cost of living. An NBC News exit poll found that 62 per cent of voters thought the US had made the wrong decision in taking military action against Iran.

Speaking from the ballroom site, Trump offered a narrower explanation. He said the war had hurt Republicans by driving up petrol prices, but defended his decision to take military action.

He also maintained that Republicans would have won had his name been on the ballot. “We weren’t able to transfer the love to candidates,” he said of the crowds at his rallies.

3. Schumer put household costs first and pointed to Congress’ leverage over Iran

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer described his party’s first assignment in terms of choices families faced at home: buying petrol to get to work or groceries to feed their children, paying for healthcare or keeping the heat on.

Lowering those costs, he said, was the first thing Democrats had to do to earn the trust of voters who had given them another chance.

On Iran, Schumer was emphatic about the goal and less specific about the means. “This war must end. It must end,” he said.

Asked whether Democrats would use defence funding as leverage, he pointed to congressional “power of the purse” and said some Republicans already supported ending the conflict. He stopped short of proposing a funding cut.

Schumer also pledged to tackle government corruption. His warning on investigations came with a condition: if Trump defied the law or the will of the American people, Democrats would investigate and take him to court. “The days of Trump’s supplicant Senate are over,” he said.

4. House Republicans need a new leader

As recently as October, House Speaker Mike Johnson expected to keep leading Republicans even if Democrats took the chamber. “I intend to stay and lead,” he told CBS News.

On Wednesday, the Louisiana Republican, who won re-election to his own seat, told staff he would not seek the minority leader’s job.

House Majority Leader Steve Scalise of Louisiana and Judiciary Committee chairman Jim Jordan of Ohio looked like the strongest candidates to replace him. The two had sought the speakership in 2023, when neither could assemble enough support and Johnson emerged as the compromise choice.

This time, only Republican members will vote, in a leadership election scheduled for November 10.

Asked at the White House whether he would take sides, Trump offered a short answer: “We’ll stay out of it.”

5. Trump can still negotiate with Xi, but he may have less to offer

Beijing called the election a US “domestic affair”, and Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said China wanted to build on the understandings Trump and President Xi Jinping had reached. Trump will still be able to negotiate directly with Xi, but Democratic control of Congress could narrow what he can offer Beijing in return for concessions.

One example is a waiver from US technology export restrictions. Feng Chucheng, founder of Beijing-based consultancy Hutong Research, told the South China Morning Post that a Republican Congress might have granted such a waiver, giving Trump something to offer Xi at the negotiating table. Democrats would be less inclined to grant one, Feng said.

Technology is also an area where lawmakers could press Beijing harder. Fudan University professor Zhao Minghao expects a Democratic Congress to take a tougher stance on artificial intelligence, export controls and Taiwan, even as Washington’s broader strategy towards China holds steady.

California congressman Ted Lieu said on Wednesday that House Democrats would use their new majority to hold public hearings on the AI industry and advance legislation to regulate it.

Lieu, a co-chair of the House Democratic Commission on AI and the Innovation Economy, accused the Trump administration and House Republicans of making a “conscious decision to let the AI industry run wild”.

He called that a mistake both as policy and as politics, citing growing public opposition to the rapid expansion of data centres.

item.title: [SCMP] South Korea wants a cyber tsar, but can it beat complacency?
item.description:
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung’s push for a centralised cybersecurity agency after his passport details were leaked could face widespread inertia despite what he considers a national security priority.

Tech experts warn that creating a new organisation alone will do little to address the deeper problem of complacency, with businesses and government agencies viewing tighter cybersecurity as an unnecessary expense until a serious breach occurs.

Lee’s proposal comes amid growing scrutiny of South Korea’s cybersecurity vulnerabilities, notably after passport details and other personal information of 168 people, including the president, his wife and senior security officials, were reported to be accessible online for nearly five months.
item.content:encoded:
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung’s push for a centralised cybersecurity agency after his passport details were leaked could face widespread inertia despite what he considers a national security priority.

Tech experts warn that creating a new organisation alone will do little to address the deeper problem of complacency, with businesses and government agencies viewing tighter cybersecurity as an unnecessary expense until a serious breach occurs.

Lee’s proposal comes amid growing scrutiny of South Korea’s cybersecurity vulnerabilities, notably after passport details and other personal information of 168 people, including the president, his wife and senior security officials, were reported to be accessible online for nearly five months.

The leak, involving a passenger list from Lee’s June trip to Europe, prompted an emergency investigation and plans to reissue affected passports. However, authorities later said the incident resulted from an accidental disclosure rather than hacking.

Lee on Tuesday proposed to his officials to “actively consider” appointing a “powerful and effective cybersecurity tsar organisation” to coordinate fragmented government functions overseeing online security.

Park Dong-chul, a professor specialising in security issues at Chung-Ang University, said: “Many companies in this country still regard cybersecurity as little more than a costly nuisance until they suffer a serious security breach. Many of them still resort to reactive, piecemeal measures to contain the damage after an incident occurs.”

At the cabinet meeting on Tuesday, Lee cited a growing wave of cyberattacks at home and abroad when he called for a comprehensive nationwide response system, capable of detecting early signs of attacks and implementing preventive measures.

“With advances in AI, hacking techniques are becoming increasingly sophisticated, advanced and commonplace, exposing clear limitations in existing security systems centred on inspections and responses after incidents occur,” he said.

Park said South Korea should address low public awareness of the importance of cybersecurity if it were to establish the new organisation.

“I wonder whether such a new layer of oversight would be effective as long as the widespread perception persists that investing in cybersecurity is like throwing money out of the window,” he added.

Professor Lim Jong-in of Korea University’s Graduate School of Information Security said a powerful state body was needed to coordinate government and business responses at short notice, given that cybersecurity responsibilities were fragmented across agencies.

Cybersecurity responsibilities are divided among several agencies, with the National Intelligence Service (NIS) overseeing security at critical public infrastructure, the science ministry handling much of the private sector and the Financial Services Commission overseeing financial-sector security.

“In the face of mounting attacks driven by AI agents, there is no time for government agencies to sit down together to discuss responses as in the past,” Lim said. “A 24/7 channel is required to ensure a quick response.”

Lim said cooperation from the private sector would be essential to operating such an organisation smoothly, citing Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, losing US$6 billion to hacking within 20 minutes.

Binance said on Tuesday that hackers had used fake job interviews and an internal artificial intelligence tool in the heist.

The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has attributed the theft to North Korea, identifying a hacking group it calls TraderTraitor, a name previously linked to other cryptocurrency thefts.

On Tuesday, Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, flatly dismissed the FBI’s findings, calling them a “grave political provocation” against Pyongyang.

With its extensive intelligence capabilities, the NIS is expected to play a leading role in the proposed oversight organisation.

Lim dismissed concerns over the concentration of intelligence powers in the agency’s hands. “Unlike under past authoritarian governments, transparency and public oversight prevent government agencies from surveilling the people,” he said.

Youm Heung-youl, professor emeritus of information security at Soonchunhyang University, told the Korea Times that it remained unclear if the government planned to establish the new organisation through legislation or create a governmentwide committee.

If the government opted for a committee, Youm suggested that Lee be its chairman to accord it sufficient authority under South Korea’s presidential system.

“I personally think it would be better for the president to chair it, even if it is a committee under the president,” he said.

“What matters most is that it has real authority. It shouldn’t be a committee that exists only in name.”

Hwang Suk-jin, a professor at Dongguk University’s Graduate School of Information Security, agreed that the current ministry-by-ministry approach had limitations in dealing with AI-powered attacks and simultaneous security breaches.

“When financial companies assess their own security using regulators’ checklists, actual vulnerabilities can be missed, or the checks can become a formality,” Hwang said.

He called for regular “penetration tests” and on-site inspections to identify vulnerabilities and verify that companies had addressed them, rather than relying solely on self-assessments.

The government has recently stepped up security inspections in response to emerging cyber threats.

On Tuesday, the NIS said that it had been conducting joint cybersecurity inspections across the public sector since May, in cooperation with other government agencies to address growing cyber threats. It has urgently requested more than 2,100 central government agencies and local governments to conduct their own security inspections using a checklist.

The agency plans to complete inspections of internet-facing systems at major public-sector information and communications infrastructure facilities by mid-November.

Its move comes as the country’s financial watchdog, the Financial Services Commission, said last month that cybersecurity incidents involving 100,000 customer records had been confirmed at 16 financial firms, including commercial banks, savings banks and credit finance companies.

Financial regulators have announced plans to tighten identity checks and access controls, improve information sharing and increase corporate executives’ responsibility for cybersecurity.

Last month, Seoul raised the country’s cyber crisis warning level by one notch to “caution”, the second-lowest level in its four-tier system, amid global efforts to address two critical security flaws in PHP, or Hypertext Preprocessor, a widely used programming language.

The government also plans to inspect around 170 major private-sector IT infrastructure facilities to identify security weaknesses.

item.title: [SCMP] Republicans face prospect of ‘civil war’ as Trump’s air of invincibility starts to fade
item.description:
In the weeks leading up to the midterm elections, US President Donald Trump displayed unwavering confidence in his star power, urging supporters to close their eyes and “pretend I’m on the ballot”.

But Tuesday night’s disastrous results for the Republicans – the first time in 20 years both houses of Congress have changed hands at the same time – have punctured the aura of invincibility that once shielded Trump and allowed him to keep potential critics in line with the threat that opposing him could end their careers.

According to analysts tracking the post-election fallout, the Republican Party is increasingly at risk of a power struggle between Trump’s supporters and more traditional establishment figures.
item.content:encoded:
In the weeks leading up to the midterm elections, US President Donald Trump displayed unwavering confidence in his star power, urging supporters to close their eyes and “pretend I’m on the ballot”.

But Tuesday night’s disastrous results for the Republicans – the first time in 20 years both houses of Congress have changed hands at the same time – have punctured the aura of invincibility that once shielded Trump and allowed him to keep potential critics in line with the threat that opposing him could end their careers.

According to analysts tracking the post-election fallout, the Republican Party is increasingly at risk of a power struggle between Trump’s supporters and more traditional establishment figures.

Feng Chucheng, founding partner of the consultancy Hutong Research, said the results showed Trump had become “growingly detached” from grass-roots voters squeezed by rising living costs, inflation, tariffs and the Iran war.

“It’s very likely there will be an internal civil war within the Republican Party, leading to the 2028 presidential race to determine whether or not the Republicans want to find an alternative to Donald Trump,” he said.

“Who are they going to endorse in 2028 for the Republican candidacy? Are they going to endorse [Vice-President] J.D. Vance, who is seen as a protege of Trump, who is seen as a Maga successor of Trump? Or are they going to go back to people more orthodox like [Secretary of State] Marco Rubio, for example?” Feng asked, pointing to Rubio’s bipartisan confirmation as a sign of his broader appeal.

Feng argued the perceived risks of challenging Trump had weakened, adding: “Because you saw a lot of people aligning with Donald Trump, you saw Donald Trump on the campaign trails in the final weeks of the midterm elections, campaigning for this, endorsing these Republican candidates, and they all lost.

“They will have to first figure out, why did we lose all these critical toss-up elections? … They have to figure out who to blame. And right now, it looks like it’s Trump and the Iranian wars that they’re going to blame for their losses in these battlefield states.”

Wei Zongyou, a professor at Fudan University’s Centre for American Studies in Shanghai, described the results as a “blue tsunami”, predicting that “the GOP [Republicans] will look for a scapegoat after this”.

He said the losses could embolden establishment Republicans and dissenters to challenge Trump’s authority, adding: “They will use this opportunity to build up their strength and wait for the right moment.”

The discontent, however, extends beyond the Republican establishment. Wei pointed to growing dissatisfaction within Trump’s own Make America Great Again movement, including among far-right conservatives and China hawks, over some of his decisions.

“His influence within the Republican Party will certainly decline,” he said, adding that more Republicans may begin to see Trump not as an electoral asset but as a “political liability”.

Denis Simon, from the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, a think tank in Washington, agreed that the results seemed to have “considerably” weakened Trump’s control of the party.

He added the midterms “have created a potentially important opening” for the Republicans the president had marginalised and those who “believe the party has become too dependent on Trump’s narcissistic personal leadership”.

Trump has systematically sidelined both traditional conservatives such as ex-Congresswoman Liz Cheney and national-security hawks like former national security adviser John Bolton, ex-secretary of state Mike Pompeo and former ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley, treating them as political liabilities.

Simon added that a Republican revolt against “Trump’s political style and methods is not necessarily a revolt against Trump’s policy agenda”.

He said: “Now Republican politicians face a different question: is the cost of remaining associated with Trump greater than the cost of disagreeing with him?”

He outlined three possible forms of rebellion, saying Republicans could try to distance themselves from the president; lawmakers may try to oppose him on issues such as China, tariffs, Iran and congressional oversight; or leading figures could challenge his control over candidate selection in the run-up to the next round of elections.

Diao Daming, a professor at Renmin University in Beijing, argued that even if Republicans thought the defeat was down to Trump’s poor performance in office, “would they necessarily win without him? I think that is equally uncertain”.

Austin Strange, an associate professor of international relations at the University of Hong Kong, said some Republicans had been vocal about their “displeasure with certain policies or gestures that Trump has recently made regarding China”.

“The midterm results – and the widespread perception that Trump’s recent policies were electoral liabilities rather than assets – certainly won’t make such individuals less likely to publicly voice their views,” he said.

Strange also said many members of Congress were China hawks, adding: “There has been a clear, bipartisan trend towards depicting US-China relations on fundamentally competitive terms.”

But he argued the main foreign policy focus was likely to be elsewhere, saying: “So while the need to more effectively manage relations with China remains an important agenda acknowledged by many … it will probably continue to take a back seat for now.”

Feng said he doubted that the China hawks would quickly regain real power within the party.

“These people, they are strategists. They are foreign-policy makers. They don’t have as much of an influence as someone coming from a Republican stronghold,” he said.

“John Bolton can say whatever he wants on TV shows with regard to Trump. Pompeo can say whatever he wants on TV shows with regard to Trump, but he will not really influence the electoral outcomes in that regard.”

He added that Trump now had less room for manoeuvre on China.

Once Democrats take control of Congress in January, they will be even less willing to let him use congressional China bills as bargaining chips in negotiations with Beijing. “That’s a net gain for Beijing,” he said.

Strange also said Republican lawmakers were likely to focus on their domestic priorities and would be unlikely to accommodate the president’s requests for flexibility on China legislation.

Sourabh Gupta of the Institute for China-America Studies framed the night as a defeat for neoconservatives and “defence-first” Republicans, with the balance inside the party shifting towards figures such as Vance or the former TV host Tucker Carson who are wary about nation-building and fighting wars abroad.

He was blunt about the prospects for the figures Trump had marginalised, arguing that “their brand of foreign policy is dead in the current Republican Party. Trump was the one who killed it before he got swept into his own misadventure.”

Feng and other analysts also argued there was still life in the Maga movement.

“I would say it’s not about whether or not Maga can continue to ride on Trump after he finishes his term,” he said. “It’s more about whether or not the people that ride on Maga will continue to claim that they are still Maga when Trump is gone.”

Ali Wyne, an analyst from the International Crisis Group, said: “Obituaries for the movement would be premature.

“President Trump would not have won twice, and more decisively in 2024 than in 2016, had it not had deep roots in the American body politic. The midterm results demonstrate, however, that his grip on his core base is diminishing.

“It is difficult to imagine, moreover, that any Republican successor could come close to exerting a comparable grip or dominating the media environment as thoroughly.”

Meanwhile, Simon from the Quincy Institute argued: “Too soon to say dead. Can say mortally wounded.”

item.title: [SCMP] How Hong Kong’s yuan push is becoming a challenge to the US dollar
item.description:
In September, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu unveiled the city’s first five-year plan along with his policy address, highlighting Hong Kong’s strategic role in promoting the greater use of the yuan outside mainland China as a key priority.

In the first of a four-part series on the internationalisation of the yuan, Lam Ka-sing and Denise Tsang examine Hong Kong’s efforts as an international financial centre to reform its market infrastructure, including building a larger offshore renminbi ecosystem.

As Chinese President Xi Jinping and his American counterpart, Donald Trump, met in Washington for a historic summit last month, Hong Kong was preparing for a longer-term move: reducing reliance on the US dollar and boosting the yuan’s global use.
item.content:encoded:
In September, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu unveiled the city’s first five-year plan along with his policy address, highlighting Hong Kong’s strategic role in promoting the greater use of the yuan outside mainland China as a key priority.

In the first of a four-part series on the internationalisation of the yuan, Lam Ka-sing and Denise Tsang examine Hong Kong’s efforts as an international financial centre to reform its market infrastructure, including building a larger offshore renminbi ecosystem.

As Chinese President Xi Jinping and his American counterpart, Donald Trump, met in Washington for a historic summit last month, Hong Kong was preparing for a longer-term move: reducing reliance on the US dollar and boosting the yuan’s global use.

While the two leaders got down to business, a mainland China-based asset management firm rolled out a suite of new renminbi products in the city to considerable fanfare. China Asset Management (Hong Kong), the city’s largest provider of listed offshore renminbi products, presented the broad range of exchange-traded funds to bankers, journalists and investors.

The company, already known for launching the world’s first offshore tokenised yuan money market fund, is not merely pursuing retail investors. It is also at the front line of a coordinated institutional push to build financial protection around Chinese capital against Western market volatility.

The firm’s CEO, Gan Tian, pointed to the recent Middle East crisis as a major “stress test” that demonstrated the Chinese currency’s resilience, noting that the renminbi remained firm even as the US dollar surged and Asian peers like the Japanese yen fell sharply.

“On the path to yuan internationalisation, in this stress test in the first half, the People’s Bank of China has already sent a clear message to the smartest investors in the world,” Gan said.

“If de-dollarisation is a medium- to long-term trend, once you pull your money out of the US dollar, where exactly should you put it? The renminbi is the unparalleled choice.”

Driven by intensifying US-China rivalry and the strategic need to mobilise mainland capital safely abroad despite capital controls, Hong Kong is rapidly transforming its market infrastructure – building a larger offshore renminbi ecosystem, developing independent gold clearing and testing alternative payment channels.

Once primarily a bridge for Western capital entering the mainland, Hong Kong is now positioning itself to support China’s financial resilience, analysts say. The aim, they add, is to establish the city as a launch pad for financial products and payment channels that rely less on traditional Western networks.

Earlier this year, Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po expressed confidence that Hong Kong, currently behind New York and London in the global ranking of international financial centres, would climb to at least second place within 10 to 15 years.

In a recent interview with the South China Morning Post, Chan explained the city’s efforts on yuan internationalisation and their relevance to Hong Kong’s status as an international financial centre.

Chan singled out Hong Kong’s unique role as a firewall for China’s financial security, with yuan-related products and services tested in the city.

“From China’s standpoint, to build a strong country, we need to have a strong currency. But this needs time,” Chan said.

“To strengthen the global utilisation and influence of renminbi, it is the user-case scenario, a substantive business-user case.”

‘Tremendous room for growth’

Chan said he expected global use of the yuan to rise amid geopolitical tensions.

He noted that China accounted for 14 to 15 per cent of global imports and exports combined, but only about 4 per cent of trade was invoiced in yuan last year. The ratio had grown a lot compared with a year earlier, he said.

Foreign investors have shown a strong appetite for trading in mainland stocks through cross-border schemes such as Northbound Stock Connect.
