“There is tremendous room for future growth, particularly given the geopolitical context. Most countries are trying to use their own currency in terms of trading,” Chan said.

Hong Kong is the world’s biggest offshore renminbi market, with about 1.3 trillion yuan of deposits as at the end of July, according to the Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau.

A high-profile move to tap international capital took place in August when China’s Ministry of Finance sold 15 billion yuan worth of sovereign bonds in Hong Kong to a strong response from institutional investors.

The sale took place just days after the city launched a long-awaited tool designed to help global investors hedge against risks in the mainland bond market.

Ho Lok-sang, adjunct professor of economics at Lingnan University, said the renminbi remained very much underutilised and did not reflect China’s economic strength, leaving huge potential for wider use.

“What we are after in the long run is that we want to build a more inclusive kind of system,” Ho said.

“At present, the current system, which is very much predominated by the US dollar, is not really an inclusive system, and especially as it has been weaponised.”

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent advocated in early September for Washington to use its financial power as a foreign policy tool to advance the interests of American allies, including ‌in financial and political situations abroad.

Meanwhile, the US Treasury Department has warned under its “Operation Economic Outcast” that entities facilitating money laundering or sanctions evasion on behalf of Iran risk being cut off from the US financial system, citing several Hong Kong-based companies that did business with Iran.

“China has been thinking strategically against the possibility that the US might impose different kinds of sanctions, and China is really extremely alert … strategically very, very smart,” Ho said.

Testing ground

Hard data shows the shift away from US dollar-centric systems is well under way in Hong Kong’s capital markets.

Beijing is using Hong Kong to test a China-led multilateral central bank digital currency platform, mBridge, as a potential alternative to the traditional US dollar-dominated payments system. The effort has gained momentum in recent years amid heightened tensions between the world’s two largest economies and growing concerns over the reliability of the US dollar as it becomes politicised.

The project faced a setback late last month after a key participant – the Saudi Central Bank – confirmed its departure after completing what it described as “a limited proof-of-concept” trial in May last year.

Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury Christopher Hui Ching-yu told the SCMP in an interview earlier this month that the Saudi departure would “not really” affect the wider experiment.

“Fundamentally, what we try to do is, through Hong Kong, at the same time through these measures, to engage different players across the industry in such a way that they can work on some live cases or new cases to test out this technology,” Hui said.

“So technology as it is, people still see the benefit. At the same time, what Hong Kong should do is continue contributing our expertise and also our relevance here.”

Beyond payments infrastructure, Hong Kong is also seeking to make the yuan more attractive for corporate financing.

Multinational firms need to borrow large sums of cash to run their global operations. Historically, many borrowed yen because Japan had the lowest interest rates.

But recently, the script has flipped. Japan’s 10-year sovereign bond yield rose above 3 per cent in early September, while China’s dropped below 1.7 per cent, Gan of ChinaAMC (HK) said.

Global companies were now flocking to Hong Kong to borrow yuan by issuing dim sum bonds – offshore renminbi-denominated bonds – because they offered cheaper funding, Gan said.

He noted that this rush for cheap borrowing had caused the dim sum bond market to explode to 1 trillion yuan, making it significantly larger than Hong Kong’s traditional stock IPO market.

When massive Chinese companies, such as appliance maker Midea, made profits overseas, they faced a huge problem: exchange rates were swinging wildly, Gan said.

Midea suffered a foreign exchange loss of almost 6 billion yuan in six months because the value of the currencies it was holding dropped. Normally, companies buy financial “insurance” with hedging to protect against these US dollar swings, but that insurance can cost 2.5 per cent of the hedged amount every year.

To reduce losses from volatile exchange rates, Chinese companies were simply refusing to convert their cash. Instead, they were parking their overseas profits directly into offshore yuan funds in Hong Kong, Gan said.

Liquidity boost

Chan, the finance chief, has pledged a multipronged strategy to boost yuan liquidity through an array of products. In addition to Chinese treasury bonds, he has pointed to opportunities in stock trading.

He said authorities would consider expanding the number of listed companies whose shares investors could trade using offshore yuan. At present, there are 23 such companies with renminbi business counters.

Chan said another strategy was to allow China-based investors to use renminbi to trade in Hong Kong-listed shares through the Southbound Stock Connect scheme.

“If we can achieve that, the liquidity will be quickly increased,” he said. “In summary, we want to have more product offerings.”

For Hong Kong’s manufacturers and traders, the stakes extend beyond financial markets.

Anthony Lam Sai-ho, chairman of the Federation of Hong Kong Industries, said that pricing commodities in renminbi would link finance more directly with physical supply chains, giving manufacturers a “natural hedge” against exchange rate volatility.

“If we can trade commodities in renminbi … it provides manufacturers and stakeholders with an additional method to hedge and predict procurement costs, reducing currency fluctuation,” Lam said.

He added that while markets were accustomed to US dollar pricing, importing raw materials such as rice or base metals directly in local currencies or renminbi would reduce the risk of being caught between shifting exchange rates.

“It is less about avoiding the US dollar out of fear, and more about giving the market an additional option to balance trade,” Lam added.

Commodity trading had so far started with gold but could extend to other metals, energy, grains, soft commodities and even livestock, Lam said.

Alternative clearing networks, meanwhile, are expanding their reach. China’s Cross-border Interbank Payment System (CIPS) processed 180 trillion yuan in cross-border payments in 2025, up 373.6 times the 2015 level, according to its website.

CIPS said it provided secure, efficient, convenient and low-cost cross-border renminbi payment and settlement services for global users, offering an additional channel beyond the US-dominated financial system.

That existing US dollar-based system relies heavily on Swift, the Belgium-based Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication, which connects more than 12,500 institutions across more than 220 countries and territories and enables global trade.

Dollar payments are also settled through the Clearing House Interbank Payments System (Chips), a private-sector, high-value clearing and settlement system that helps financial institutions move domestic and cross-border wire payments, according to its website.

Under Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu’s policy address in September, the government has established the Hong Kong Precious Metals Central Clearing Company and will implement targeted measures to boost the trading and settlement of gold futures contracts using the offshore renminbi.

Kenny Shui Chi-wai, vice-president of think tank Our Hong Kong Foundation, said market participants would have another option if access to dollar-based channels were restricted.

“A gold clearing system allows gold transactions via a local central ledger without relying on the Swift messaging network or the Chips payment system, thereby providing an alternative store of value,” Shui said.

“Unlike fiat currencies, gold is a physical commodity that inherently holds value, making it a trusted safe asset not directly tied to any jurisdiction.”

Gan of ChinaAMC (HK) said that having huge physical gold reserves in Hong Kong provided foreigners using offshore renminbi in the city with a “Plan B” if they wanted to convert or transfer those funds.

“They do not need to convert their assets into US dollars, British pounds or Japanese yen to move them globally; they can directly exchange them for physical gold in Hong Kong and have it delivered anywhere in the world,” he said.

“Therefore, gold, acting as a ‘Plan B’ and the most important collateral asset of the future, will support the development of the offshore renminbi in Hong Kong.”

The peg question

The Hong Kong Securities and Futures Professionals Association warned that an overnight shift away from the US dollar was unrealistic.

“If de-dollarisation is overemphasised, international investors might interpret it as a signal of declining openness,” said the association’s chairman, Mofiz Chan.

Chan said Hong Kong had to strike a delicate balance between securing multiple sources of capital and maintaining its international free-market reputation with compliance, transparency and neutral standing.

To make this “financial armour” truly functional, the association called for specific technological and regulatory upgrades.

Gregory Yu, head of markets at Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing, told the SCMP that the exchange was focused on building a more comprehensive offshore renminbi ecosystem spanning equities, fixed income, currencies and commodities, and it was actively exploring opportunities to expand the range of yuan-denominated products.

“Initiatives including the continued expansion of the LME’s warehouse network in Hong Kong strengthen the market infrastructure that supports trading, storage and delivery activities across the region,” Yu said, referring to the London Metal Exchange.

Yu added that the bourse continued to explore opportunities to enhance market efficiency through innovation, including in digital assets and tokenisation.

“Together with ongoing market infrastructure enhancements, these efforts strengthen Hong Kong’s role as the world’s leading offshore renminbi hub and reinforce its position as an international financial centre connecting China and the world,” Yu said.

But any push to reduce reliance on the US dollar runs up against a basic constraint: the Hong Kong dollar remains pegged to it.

Ho Lok-sang argued that linking exclusively to the US dollar exposed Hong Kong to extreme economic swings, recalling the 1985 “super dollar” phase, when the city lost its export competitiveness.

“It’s much, much, much better if we can peg a basket of currencies … and now devise a way to seamlessly adopt the system without any shock at all,” Ho said.

“We can continue with the linked exchange rate system, but we just link with the basket,” he added, referring to a GDP-weighted basket that would include the renminbi, euro, yen, British pound and the US, Australian and Canadian dollars.

Chan, the finance chief, along with city leader John Lee Ka-chiu have said repeatedly the government has no intention of changing the 43-year-old peg, which has been underpinning the city’s economy.

At the end of the day, the key buzzwords are hedging and strategic planning, analysts say.

And the official regulatory response has been to rapidly deepen the multi-asset ecosystem and expand mutual market access to facilitate this capital transition.

“For Hong Kong, this means strengthening its role as a resilient international financial centre while supporting the financing of Chinese technology companies and renminbi internationalisation,” Shui of the think tank said.

item.title: [SCMP] Five takeaways from US midterms as Democrats sweep Congress and Trump faces Iran reckoning
item.description:
A Democratic victory that reached from Texas to Kansas changed the terms of Donald Trump’s final two years in office.

When the new US Congress convenes in January, Democrats will control both chambers. They can block his legislation, challenge spending on the war in Iran and scrutinise the deals he strikes with Beijing.

The day after his party lost control of Congress, Trump invited reporters to the construction site of his new White House ballroom to watch workers raise the final steel beam.
item.content:encoded:
A Democratic victory that reached from Texas to Kansas changed the terms of Donald Trump’s final two years in office.

When the new US Congress convenes in January, Democrats will control both chambers. They can block his legislation, challenge spending on the war in Iran and scrutinise the deals he strikes with Beijing.

The day after his party lost control of Congress, Trump invited reporters to the construction site of his new White House ballroom to watch workers raise the final steel beam.

Asked about the prospect of impeachment, he dismissed the idea, then turned back to the reason he had brought them there. “Watch the beam go up,” he said.

The visit also gave Trump a chance to respond to his vice-president, J.D. Vance, who had blamed the Iran war for the defeat.

Many voters who backed Trump in 2024 had turned out again on Tuesday and voted for Democrats, Vance said.

Trump put the emphasis on higher fuel prices and stood by his decision to go to war. “If I had it to do again, I’d have to do it again,” he said.

Here are five takeaways from the US midterms.

1. The Democratic wave reached deep into Trump country

In Texas, James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton to become the first Democrat to win a US Senate race in the state since 1988. In South Carolina, doctor Annie Andrews defeated Republican Senator Darline Graham. Trump had carried both states by double digits just two years earlier and had backed both losing candidates.

Kansas delivered the longest break with the past. Adam Hamilton defeated Republican Senator Roger Marshall, ending a Senate winning streak that dated to 1932. In Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown won the seat Vance had vacated to become vice-president.

The final size of the majority was still taking shape on Wednesday.

At noon Eastern time, the Associated Press had yet to call the Senate races in Alaska and Mississippi. Democrats had already secured control without either seat.

2. Vance blamed the war. Trump blamed the price of fuel

Republicans had spent much of the campaign watching whether the people who backed Trump in 2024 would turn out again. Vance said the party had drawn too much comfort from seeing those voters show up. Many came back, he said, and cast their ballots for Democrats.

“The reason we lost is the war,” Vance wrote on X. He cited an unnamed pollster who had asked former Trump voters what it would take to win them back.

Ending the conflict topped the list, Vance said, followed by tackling the cost of living. An NBC News exit poll found that 62 per cent of voters thought the US had made the wrong decision in taking military action against Iran.

Speaking from the ballroom site, Trump offered a narrower explanation. He said the war had hurt Republicans by driving up petrol prices, but defended his decision to take military action.

He also maintained that Republicans would have won had his name been on the ballot. “We weren’t able to transfer the love to candidates,” he said of the crowds at his rallies.

3. Schumer put household costs first and pointed to Congress’s leverage over Iran

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer described his party’s first assignment in terms of choices families faced at home: buying petrol to get to work or groceries to feed their children, paying for healthcare or keeping the heat on.

Lowering those costs, he said, was the first thing Democrats had to do to earn the trust of voters who had given them another chance.

On Iran, Schumer was emphatic about the goal and less specific about the means. “This war must end. It must end,” he said.

Asked whether Democrats would use defence funding as leverage, he pointed to Congress’s “power of the purse” and said some Republicans already supported ending the conflict. He stopped short of proposing a funding cut.

Schumer also pledged to tackle government corruption. His warning on investigations came with a condition: if Trump defied the law or the will of the American people, Democrats would investigate and take him to court. “The days of Trump’s supplicant Senate are over,” he said.

4. House Republicans need a new leader

As recently as October, House Speaker Mike Johnson expected to keep leading Republicans even if Democrats took the chamber. “I intend to stay and lead,” he told CBS News.

On Wednesday, the Louisiana Republican, who won re-election to his own seat, told staff he would not seek the minority leader’s job.

House Majority Leader Steve Scalise of Louisiana and Judiciary Committee chairman Jim Jordan of Ohio looked like the strongest candidates to replace him. The two had sought the speakership in 2023, when neither could assemble enough support and Johnson emerged as the compromise choice.

This time, only Republican members will vote, in a leadership election scheduled for November 10.

Asked at the White House whether he would take sides, Trump offered a short answer: “We’ll stay out of it.”

5. Trump can still negotiate with Xi, but he may have less to offer

Beijing called the election a US “domestic affair”, and Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said China wanted to build on the understandings Trump and President Xi Jinping had reached. Trump will still be able to negotiate directly with Xi, but Democratic control of Congress could narrow what he can offer Beijing in return for concessions.

One example is a waiver from US technology export restrictions. Feng Chucheng, founder of Beijing-based consultancy Hutong Research, told the South China Morning Post that a Republican Congress might have granted such a waiver, giving Trump something to offer Xi at the negotiating table. Democrats would be less inclined to grant one, Feng said.

Technology is also an area where lawmakers could press Beijing harder. Fudan University professor Zhao Minghao expects a Democratic Congress to take a tougher stance on artificial intelligence, export controls and Taiwan, even as Washington’s broader strategy towards China holds steady.

California congressman Ted Lieu said on Wednesday that House Democrats would use their new majority to hold public hearings on the AI industry and advance legislation to regulate it.

Lieu, a co-chair of the House Democratic Commission on AI and the Innovation Economy, accused the Trump administration and House Republicans of making a “conscious decision to let the AI industry run wild”.

He called that a mistake both as policy and as politics, citing growing public opposition to the rapid expansion of data centres.

item.title: [SCMP] Armour vs altitude: India’s light tank dilemma along China border
item.description:
India’s new high-altitude combat tank was designed to go where its heavier armoured fighting vehicles cannot: the thin mountain air, narrow roads and small bridges along its disputed border with China.

In its base configuration, the Zorawar weighs some 25 tonnes – light enough to be flown all the way to the Line of Actual Control – but a push to make it strong enough to withstand high-calibre autocannon fire could add an extra seven tonnes to that loadout.

Reports of renewed stand-offs between Indian and Chinese troops at the border, including one carried by The Hindu newspaper on October 23, have injected fresh urgency into the debate surrounding how much the tank should weigh.
item.content:encoded:
India’s new high-altitude combat tank was designed to go where its heavier armoured fighting vehicles cannot: the thin mountain air, narrow roads and small bridges along its disputed border with China.

In its base configuration, the Zorawar weighs some 25 tonnes – light enough to be flown all the way to the Line of Actual Control – but a push to make it strong enough to withstand high-calibre autocannon fire could add an extra seven tonnes to that loadout.

Reports of renewed stand-offs between Indian and Chinese troops at the border, including one carried by The Hindu newspaper on October 23, have injected fresh urgency into the debate surrounding how much the tank should weigh.

First phase of developmental field firing trails of Indian Light Tank successfully conducted. The field trials have successfully met the intended objectives in desert terrain. During trials the tank demonstrated required accuracy on the intended targets. @DefenceMinIndia https://t.co/cm9qr4uHsJ

— DRDO (@DRDO_India) September 13, 2024

During previous confrontations, India airlifted its older, Russian-origin T-72s and T-90s, which weigh between 45 and 50 tonnes each, to the border territory of Ladakh, where they have faced off against China’s lighter Type 15, weighing 33–36 tonnes.

But question marks hang over the performance of these heavier main battle tanks in the sub-zero conditions and low-oxygen environment of the high Himalayas, as the Observer Research Foundation, an Indian think tank, noted in a 2021 report.

China’s Type 15, by contrast, is easier to run and maintain at altitude and has been in service since the end of 2018.

The Zorawar was developed by India’s state-run Defence Research and Development Organisation and the private engineering group Larsen & Toubro over a two-year period, from its formal approval in March 2022 to the first public unveiling of a prototype in 2024.

It comes equipped with a 105mm rifled gun in a Belgian-designed Cockerill turret – the rotating upper section of the tank – that is hardened against small arms fire and artillery shrapnel, but not the armour-piercing shells designed to punch through metal that are fired by Chinese autocannons.

India’s army is reportedly pushing for the tank’s armour to be upgraded to Nato’s highest standards of ballistic protection, known as STANAG Level 6, able to withstand 25mm and 30mm armour-piercing rounds.

Doing so would not only add weight, but also force redesigns and prolong the tank’s development cycle. As a result, army chief General Upendra Dwivedi told Indian media earlier this year that he expected the Zorawar to enter service in 2028–29, overshooting the original 2027 target.

‘The urgency is real’

Ashok Bhim Shivane, a retired lieutenant general who previously led the Indian Army’s mechanised forces and commanded a strike corps – one of its major offensive formations – delivered a blunt assessment of why such a delay was a problem.

“The urgency is real,” he told This Week in Asia. “A light tank for areas where the medium-category T-90/T-72 cannot reach or operate is a critical requirement as of the day before yesterday.”

Heavier armour needs a stronger engine. At altitudes above 4,500 metres (15,000 feet), where the Zorawar would have to operate, thinner air could result in a 20 per cent drop in engine power, Shivane said – unless the tank’s current 764-horsepower engine was upgraded to a 1,000-horsepower one.

“There is also a design question. The Belgian turret cannot take the heavier armour,” said Shivane, who helped build the case for a home-grown light tank and has been closely involved with its development.

The additional armour could add up to seven tonnes to the tank’s weight, he said, arguing that to rectify some of these issues, India should further localise its design, which he described as currently between 40–45 per cent indigenous by value.

India plans to field an initial 59 Zorawars and 354 in total. Shivane said he wanted to see the first batch inducted by 2028 “with a documented baseline, instrumented trials and funded upgrade lots”, meaning a thoroughly tested, finalised design with funding already secured for upgrades.

He proposed a “spiral approach” to production that gradually added capability in stages, with stopgap measures to plug any vulnerabilities that should arise.

“A tank that does not exist cannot be trained on. A user trial under real conditions teaches what no laboratory can,” he said.

Sanjay Iyer, a retired Indian Army brigadier, agreed that fielding the first batch of Zorawar tanks that had already been through trials would be preferable to waiting for a heavier version that so far existed mostly on paper.

“I do understand where the army is coming from. No commander wants to send crews up to the LAC in a vehicle they don’t fully trust,” he said, referring to the disputed India-China border by the abbreviated form of its official name. “Still, these tanks won’t be arriving in an empty theatre.”

An armoured brigade of T-72s and T-90s, typically ranging from 135 to 150 tanks, was already in Ladakh “and the Zorawar brings what those tanks can’t easily give you”, Iyer said.

“It can be flown in, it can use the smaller bridges and narrow roads, and it can get up to heights where a 45-tonne tank struggles,” he said. “Used alongside the heavier tanks on the flatter ground, even 59 of them would give the brigade a good deal more flexibility.”

China’s decade lead

The Zorawar is part of a broader overhaul of India’s armoured forces, which includes upgrading the T-72 and T-90 fleet using Soviet-era and Russian engineering drawings, alongside developing indigenous systems.

India has the world’s fifth-largest tank fleet with an estimated 3,900 main battle tanks, while China has the largest with more than 5,800 units, according to data compiled by US-based military tracking site Global Firepower.

Iyer said China was nearly a decade ahead of India in light tanks, noting that its Type 15, launched eight years ago, had a 1,000-horsepower engine and came equipped with a 105mm gun.

“On paper the baseline Zorawar is lighter,” he said, describing the power-to-weight ratio as “broadly similar” and the guns as “comparable”.

But other factors must also be taken into account, including road, rail and air links, and the industrial capacity to build tanks at scale, Iyer said.

India’s tank fleet was older and behind on protection technology, he said, but not hopelessly so – further noting that the army had moved more T-90s and T-72s into Ladakh in a bid to narrow the gap.

Neither the Zorawar nor the Type 15 had yet seen combat, Iyer said. “The advantage India has in acclimatised troops and high-altitude experience is real and should not be underrated,” he added.
